title: Footprints in the Sand
objective: This workshop gives children an opportunity to reflect on their life and create a sand painting that represents their journey.
materials:
• Colored sand (can be purchased at Discount School Supply)

  • White glue (Elmer's glue)

  • Glue sticks

  • Heavy black construction paper

  • Colored construction paper

  • Colored pencils

  • Toothpicks
setup:
Sample supplies and table setup
 

You are welcome to provide any and as many of the decorative material as you like.

If you see the need, you can cover the tables with newspaper or tablecloths to protect them against glue, sand, etc.

You may want to print a copy of the Native American Sand Painting background handout to share with the participants, if you see fit.

Depending on the sand manufacturer packaging, you may feel the need to transfer each color sand into smaller plastic containers.

You have the option to punch small footprints, using the footprint hole puncher, out of different color construction paper; plenty for each child.

It may be helpful to create a small sample in advance to show the children what the finished art piece can look like. If you choose to do so, we suggest creating a basic sample and using only the material you're providing, so that children aren't overwhelmed by any "artistic" challenges.

You have complete freedom to alter or adapt any portion or element of this workshop to cater to your specific group's needs.
creation:
Sample sand painting

You can now invite those who wish to create to begin doing so. You may wish to remind them that there is no right or wrong way to create. They are free to draw anything, and use any colors that they like. This is their story and their window of time.

It doesn't matter what it looks like. What's important is that they are taking this time to honor their life journey and creating something that is expressive and meaningful to them.

Some children may need help with certain creation elements, so feel free to offer assistance where you see the need.
closing:
You can give children a chance to share their sand painting and the story it tells, anything they discovered or experienced during creation, or anything else they may wish to share. This can be a very powerful art project and children can come away with a stronger sense of their personal journey, and a look at how far they've traveled.

If no one feels comfortable sharing, that's perfectly okay. You can reinforce that when we take time to explore our own personal story, we can learn so much from them.
description: Gives participants an opportunity to learn new ways of telling their story. Through using the technique of sand painting, inspired by a Native American tradition, participants will use symbols to tell a story they would like to share.
optional_materials:
• Footprint hole puncher

  • Newspaper tablecloths

  • Native American Sand Painting background handout

  • Paper plates (1 per table to collect unused and loose sand)
introduction:
If you see fit, you can share the Native American Sand Painting background handout with the children. You can read it to them, or print a copy for each child to read on their own. It's entirely up to you.
 

"Today, you will have an opportunity to think about your life journey, places you've been, things you've experienced, and create a painting that tells the story of your life, however you wish to tell it."

"Everyone's experiences are different. Some things that happen to us can be happy, exciting or fun and sometimes things that happen can be sad or difficult. What we are going to do is tell a story in a simple way using symbols and words. Your story can be anything you want it to be. You can decide where your story starts and where you want it to go."

"This project has been inspired by the Native American art form known as sand painting. In the Native American tradition, sand paintings were created to tell stories. Today, you'll get a chance to use sand painting to tell the story of your journey."

"Before we begin, I want you to know that this is your window of time. This means that this can be a safe space to notice your thoughts, feelings, and needs. Since this space is your window of time, everything you say or do is voluntary. During this time, there is no right or wrong way to participate or create. I'm going to share some basic instructions, but you get to choose how you want to participate. You can follow along completely, or you may want to do something different, it's completely up to you. During your window of time, you have complete freedom to choose. However you choose to spend this time will be perfectly okay. I am here to support you in any way that I can, so please feel free to ask for what you need."
demonstration:
Sketching symbols from their story
 
 
  Outlining symbols with glue
 
 
  Sprinkling sand
 
 
  Adding footprints
 
 
  Mapping out the journey
 
 
  Finished sample

You can introduce the art supplies and share the following creation steps with the children. If you've made a sample in advance, this may be a good time to share it for reference.

You may also consider demonstrating some of the creation steps, as you see the need. Specifically, steps 2-4 below (adding colored sand).


Step 1:
"You can begin by taking two pieces of black construction paper and using a glue stick, glue them together, one on top of the other. This makes the paper stronger and can prevent the paper from wilting when applying the amount of glue that this workshop requires."


Step 2:
"Next, you can take a light colored pencil and begin to sketch out your life journey, by drawing anything that has been a part of that journey. For example, if a playground is part of your journey, and that's a place you like going to, you can draw a swing-set or a teeter-totter. Or, maybe the beach is somewhere you love going to, so you can draw an ocean anywhere you like on the paper. You can think about where you would like your story to begin; it could be at a park, the forest, a playground, your home, or anywhere that you like. You can then think about where you want to go next. Maybe it's sunny out, or maybe it's cold and raining, maybe there's snow on the ground. You can add to your story by drawing however many symbols that are part of your life journey. There is no right or wrong way. Anything you choose to draw that represents the important things in your life will be perfect."


Step 3:
"Next, you get to paint your drawing using colored sand. To do this, you can first gently squeeze white glue to outline or fill in each element of your drawing (basically use the drawing as an outline for the glue). You can then choose any color sand that you like for each item, and sprinkle the sand on top of the glue. So for trees, you can sprinkle green sand on the leaves. It's probably best to squeeze glue then add your choice of color sand to one item at a time, to prevent the glue from drying up."

"You can even mix some sand of one color with some of sand of another color to come up with a new color. Feel free to have fun and get as creative as you like with the sand."

"Once you've painted your drawing with sand, you can lift the paper to dump any loose sand into the paper plate. If there are any gaps showing white glue, you can fill it by simply adding more sand."


Step 4:
"Once you're done with the sand painting, you can use the footprint shapes (if available) and glue them anywhere on the paper to show the path you have walked. You can use any color and as many different colors of footprint shapes that you like."

If you're not providing footprint shapes, you can invite the children to either draw them, or draw a road, or river, or anything else that could symbolize a path/timeline.
opening_circle:
You can give children a chance to journal about their life journey. You are welcome to use our suggested prompts below, or your own.

  • "My journey begins with ___________ ."

  • "I would like my journey to lead to __________ ."

title: Shrinky Dink Blessing Charms - Holidays with HeART Series
objective: This workshop aims to give children an opportunity to connect and bond with loved ones and celebrate the holidays through the creation of special Shrinky Dink bracelet charms, which they can use to show loved ones that they care and perhaps even begin new family traditions.
materials:
• Shrinky Dink cutouts 

  • Permanent markers

  • Color pencils

  • Scissors

  • Ribbon or yarn

  • Toaster oven

  • Hole punch
setup: Depending on the age group, you have the option to cut out the various shapes from the template in advance, or simply print enough templates and give the children an opportunity to cut it out themselves. It's entirely up to you.
creation:
You can guide them step by step and create along with them or guide them however you see fit. It's entirely up to you.

Step 1:
If you have already cut out the template shapes, you can invite the children to start coloring them. If not, you can simply invite them to select or design their own templates, cut them out, then start coloring. It's entirely up to you.

"For those of you who wish to participate, you can begin by selecting from any template/shape that you like. You are also welcome to create you own designs. You can draw symbols, or even write words, or both. I'd like to encourage you to think about any words, symbols, or colors that you connect with as you reflect on your blessing and get as creative as you like. You have complete freedom to use any of the materials to design your Shrinky Dink." 

Step 2: 
"Now that you've finished coloring, you may cut out your shape with scissors." 

Step 3: 
"If you would like to add ribbon or wire to your Shrinky Dink to wear as a bracelet or hang on a wall, you can punch a hole in the plastic prior to baking (once Shrinky Dinks are baked, you cannot alter them)."

Step 4:
"Now your blessing Shrinky Dink is ready to bake. For those of you who want to shrink your charms, you can place the pieces onto a cut out piece of brown paper bag or cookie sheet, with the shiny side facing up. This will help prevent the plastic from folding onto itself."

Step 5:
To bake, you can simply place the Shrinky Dinks (on the brown paper bag or cookie sheet) in the oven at 300°F for 1-3 minutes. Please be mindful that a toaster over can get very hot even on the outer surface. Also, it's important to make sure the Shrinky Dink charms are not touching while in the oven as they may stick together. You can continue to bake until the pieces have flattened.

Step 7:
You may safely remove the charms from oven and allow them some time to cool (generally 1 to 2 minutes).

Step 8 (optional):
For those who punched a hole in their blessing Shrinky Dink, they may now use ribbon or yarn and loop it through the hole. If you have provided beads, you may invite the children to add them onto the ribbon at this time.
closing: For the closing, you may give the children an opportunity to share their amazing blessing charms and anything they learned, felt or experienced in the process of creating, or anything else they wish to share. Of course, this is purely optional and if no one feels comfortable sharing, it's perfectly okay.

You could open with a circle of blessing-sharing and then make Shrinky Dink charms, or possibly, by inviting the children to write down things they are grateful for as an opening warm-up exercise. Again, you have complete freedom to adapt or alter any part of this workshop to cater to your group's needs. 

"Before we begin, I want you to know that this workshop is a window of time for you. This means that this is a safe space to notice your thoughts, feelings, and needs. Since this space is your window of time, everything you say or do is voluntary. I’ll offer a suggested workshop idea, share about the materials we have available, and invite you to create, but there’s no wrong way to do this. It doesn't matter what it looks like. What matters is taking this time to truly honor your thoughts and feelings, however they come out. If you can’t think of anything or draw a blank on what to create or write, feel free to just observe. However you choose to spend this time will be perfectly okay. This is your time. title: Journey Keepers
objective: This workshop aims to provide a creative opportunity for participants to explore what footprints they want to leave in the world and how all of their journeys combined can create a brighter future.
materials:
• Shrinky Dink plastic (Ruff-N-Ready type)

  • Colored pencils

  • Individual pencil sharpeners

  • Small paper plates for shavings

  • Permanent markers

  • Scissors

  • Hole punchers

  • Craft wire

  • Wire cutters/pliers

  • Assorted beads

  • Assorted findings (fishhook earrings, key chains, jump rings)

  • Assorted ribbon

  • Toaster oven

  • CD player

  • CD's of relaxing music

  • Paper to journal on

  • Foot templates

    • Template 1

    • Template 2

    • Template 3

    • Template 4
setup:
A table set with footprint templates and other materials  

You may consider printing enough photocopies of the various foot templates for all the participants. You can save significant time if you pre-cut the Shrinky Dinks into 3 1/2" x 4" squares to fit the size of our templates.

You may wish to try this project in advance to have some samples to share, and also to get a feel for how the Shrinky Dinks cook. It’s can be very exciting to watch.

Depending on the oven type you will be using to bake the Shrinky Dinks, you may consider preheating the oven to 300° so that once participants have finished designing their Journey Keepers, you can immediately place them in there to bake.
warm_up:
"For those of you who wish to participate, I'd like to invite you to think about what imprint you would want to make on the world, and take a moment to journal your thoughts. I'd like to encourage you to think about what footprints you want to leave in your life and in the lives of those around you. What steps do you want to take in your life to create a hopeful future?"

"I would also like to invite you to think of one commitment that you'd like make to yourself, based on those questions. It could be a promise to yourself such as 'I will trust myself and be gentle with myself,' 'I will be kind to others,' 'I will live a peaceful life,' or 'I will try to make the world a better place with the choices I make,' or anything else you would like to do more of or have more of in your future. Please remember, there is no right or wrong way to do this. Anything you think of is perfect."
creation:
Baked and decorated Shriny Dink Journey Keepers

"Once you have thought about what commitment you want to make to yourself, you can begin to create your foot. You can write this commitment on your foot as a reminder of the footprints you want to leave in the world. Or you can draw symbols, or just use colors to express yourself. However you wish to design your feet will be perfect."

"For those of you who wish to participate, you can start by choosing one of the foot templates in front of you. You have complete freedom to choose whatever template you like. You are also welcome to create your own template, if you wish."


Step 1:
"You can now trace the foot on the rough side of the Shrinky Dink. You may choose any of the colors on the table. Remember, there is no right or wrong way to create. It doesn't matter what it looks like. What matters is you take this moment to honor your thoughts, feelings and desires for your future."

Step 2:
"Next, you can color and create the design that will fill in your foot. Pencils can only be used on the rough side of the Shrinky Dink, and Sharpies will work on either side."

Step 3:
"Once you are finished designing and coloring, you can decide whether you would like to add wire and beads to your foot. If you wish to do so, you can now use a hole punch to place holes where you want the wire to run through. Once the Shrinky Dinks are cooked, they cannot be altered."

Step 4:
"You may now cut out your foot with scissors. If you need help, please feel free to ask for it."

Step 5:
Now the feet are ready for baking. As a facilitator, you can decide if you wish to give participants the opportunity to place their Shrinky Dink feet in the oven, or assist them with this step.

To bake, you can place the Shrinky Dink, shiny side up, on a flat metal tray and place inside the toaster oven and bake at 300° until Shrinky Dink has completely flattened (usually about one minute). You can invite the participants to watch the amazing transformation.

Step 6:
Once baked, you can remove the Shrinky Dinks and allow them to cool (usually another minute or two).

Step 7:
Now, you can invite those who wish to decorate their Journey Keepers with wire and beads to do so.
closing:
For the closing, you may give the participants an opportunity to share their amazing Journey Keepers, what commitment they made to themselves, and anything they learned, felt or experienced in the process of creating, or anything else they wish to share. Of course, this is purely optional and if no one feels comfortable sharing, it's perfectly okay.

You may wish to thank the participants for their courage to honor themselves.
 

       
Sample feet   Feet with ribbon and beads

You can follow along completely, or you may want to do something different, it's completely up to you. During your window of time, you have complete freedom to choose. I am here to support you in any way that I can, so please feel free to ask for what you need."

Step 2:
"Next, you can color and create the design that will fill in your foot. Pencils can only be used on the rough side of the Shrinky Dink, and Sharpies will work on either side."

Step 3:
"Once you are finished designing and coloring, you can decide whether you would like to add wire and beads to your foot. If you wish to do so, you can now use a hole punch to place holes where you want the wire to run through. Once the Shrinky Dinks are cooked, they cannot be altered."

Step 4:
"You may now cut out your foot with scissors. If you need help, please feel free to ask for it."

Step 5:
Now the feet are ready for baking. As a facilitator, you can decide if you wish to give children the opportunity to place their Shrinky Dink feet in the oven, or assist them with this step. Please be mindful that a toaster oven can get very hot even on the outside surface.

To bake, you can place the Shrinky Dink, shiny side up, on a flat metal tray and place inside the toaster oven and bake at 300° until Shrinky Dink has completely flattened (usually about one minute). You can invite the children to watch the amazing transformation.

Step 6:
Once baked, you can remove the Shrinky Dinks and allow them to cool (usually another minute or two).

Step 7:
Now, you can invite those who wish to decorate their Journey Keepers with wire and beads to do so.
closing:
For the closing, you may give children an opportunity to share their amazing Journey Keepers, what promise they made to themselves, and anything they learned, felt or experienced in the process of creating, or anything else they wish to share. Of course, this is purely optional and if no one feels comfortable sharing, it's perfectly okay.

You may wish to thank the children for their courage to honor themselves.
 

       
Sample feet   Feet with ribbon and beads
description: To provide a creative opportunity to explore what footprints you want to leave in the world and how all of our journeys combined can create a non-violent future.
introduction:
"Today, you will have an opportunity to create your own special journey keeper. How you choose to live your life can make a difference in the world, and the path you choose to walk can leave its imprint. You will have an opportunity to make one promise to yourself about your life, the steps you want to take in your life, and the footprints you want to leave."

"Before we begin, I want you to know that this is your window of time. It's a time for you to focus on your thoughts, needs and feelings. During this time, there is no right or wrong way to participate or create. I'm going to share some basic instructions, but you get to choose how you want to participate. You can follow along completely, or you may want to do something different, it's completely up to you. During your window of time, you have complete freedom to choose. I am here to support you in any way that I can, so please feel free to ask for what you need."

title: The Monster in Me / Monstro Dentro De Mi
full_name: Joanne Webb, Melissa Falco-Williams, and AWBW Staff
objective: To provide participants with the opportunity to explore difficult emotions in a safe and fun way, and give voice to the feelings that may be hidden inside, by creating artwork that represents the “monster” within.
materials:
• CrayPas (or oil pastels)

  • Thick white paper (twice as much as the number of participants)

  • Watercolor sets

  • Watercolor brushes

  • Cups for water (2 per participant; one for cleaning brush and one for wetting it)

  • Newspaper / disposable table covers (to cover the table)

  • Paper towels (for drying brushes)

  • Feeling Target Warm-Up plates

    • (You can click on the above link and use the templates and instructions provided in the Set-Up section to create the "feelings plates" used in this workshop. These should be created in advance)
setup:
Sample space set-up
 

You may wish to cover your workstations with newspaper, or disposable table covers to avoid getting wet paint on them.

We suggest setting up all the material so that participants have easy access to them.

Each participant should ideally have 2 water cups in front of them; one for cleaning the brush and the other to dip into and wet the brush before dipping it in the color of their choice.

Depending on the space you're working with, you may wish to set up the Feelings Target warm-up plates in advance. You can do the warm-up inside or outside. It's entirely up to you.
warm_up:
“Before we begin our workshop, I'd like to invite you to join me in a game where we will each have a chance to share about our feelings. When we talk about our feelings, whether they are ones we like or ones that are difficult for us, it gives us the freedom to be ourselves and notice what's alive for us.”

"We each have many different feelings, and even sometimes we feel all of these emotions simultaneously. In one day, we can feel joyful, upset, angry, and proud. Remember that while many of these feelings may seem uncomfortable, strange, challenging, or frustrating, it is important to acknowledge each and every one of them. Of course, this is optional, so if you prefer to observe, or use this time to do something else entirely, that's perfectly okay."

To start this warm-up, you can lay out the "feelings plates" (see set-up section for details) on the floor and invite those who wish to participate to stand a few feet away from the plates and toss a penny/sandbag towards them. If the penny/sandbag lands on a face, the participant can share a story about the last time (or any time) they felt that particular feeling. For example, if the penny lands on the “happy” face, the participant can share about the last time (or anytime) they felt happy. If the penny/sandbag lands between two feelings, the participant can talk about either one of the feelings (moving the penny/sandbag on top of the feeling the participant wishes to talking about). The other participants can practice listening as each person shares.

If any of the participants don't feel comfortable sharing, that's perfectly okay. They can simply observe.

You can also incorporate more embodied art into the warm-up by giving participants the option to make a statue of the feeling instead of sharing verbally. For example, you might say: "Another option is that instead of speaking, you can show us an image (statue) of that emotion. For example, here's what I look like when I'm nervous (create a statue with your body, perhaps by hiding your face behind your hands and crouching down)."

You might also give the participants an opportunity to practice making images together by saying, "Let's do a demo. Everyone show what you look like when you're feeling excited in 3-2-1-freeze."

If it’s feasible, you can also do this warm up outside.

 

Alternative Warm-up:

Here is another warm-up exercise option you can do.

"I'd like to invite you to join me in a warm-up that aims to help the each of us relax our bodies, get in touch with our feelings and the way we express ourselves, and prepare and inspire us for when we sit down to create."

"Those of you who wish to participate, let's begin by standing up and forming a circle."

"We can start by reaching our right arm up as far as it will extend. Now, reach your left arm up as far as it will extend, then put them down."

"Now, try to stretch your face into a big yawn and breathe out a sigh and then let go."

"Now, try to squish your face as tight as a prune and then let go."

"Now, begin chewing as if there were a huge piece of gum in your mouth. Try chewing on the right side of the mouth and then moving it to the left side of the mouth."

"Reach both arms up and then bring them down in a hanging position by bending from the waist."

"Stand back up, vertebrae by vertebrae until you are standing up straight."

"Now... All together:

  • "Everybody make a sound that expresses silliness."

  • "Make a sound that expresses anger."

  • "Make a sound that expresses fear."

  • "Make a sound that expresses sadness."

  • "Make a sound that expresses relief."


(For an extended version of this warm up see "variations.")
creation:
"For those of you who wish to participate, I now invite you to begin creating the monster within. As you create, remember that this is a safe place for you. You don't have to know who your monster is or what they look like when you begin, they will appear and take their own shape as you create. You are free to use any of the material provided. If you have any questions, please feel free to ask me."
 

  Monster in Me examples
closing:
A monster taking shape
 
 
  A close-up of another Monster in Me

For the closing, you can give participants an opportunity to share their monster, if they wish. You can invite the participants share in pairs or as a group; whichever way you feel would be best for your particular group. If the participants share in pairs, you can invite have them decide who will share first and who will practice listening, sharing one at a time for about 3 minutes each. You can let them know when to switch, or leave it up to them.

You can encourage participants to share with questions like:

“What does your monster feel like? What is it thinking?”

You can invite the participants to think about and/or share what their monster needs in order to feel better.

"Does it need to be loved? Does it need to be understood? Sometimes monsters have important things to say if you listen to what they need in order to feel better."

You can thank the participants for sharing and for being brave by exposing their monsters within.

Alternate Closing:

If you are doing this as an anger management workshop, you also have the option to close by brainstorming a "Safety Plan" with the participants to help them process their anger. Some helpful tips to share with them include:

  • Talk to a friend you can trust

  • Count to ten

  • Take out art supplies and draw a picture of your anger

  • Journal about your anger

  • Take deep breaths

  • Listen to music

  • Walk away

  • Dance or exercise


Again, please feel free to alter or adapt any element or portion of this workshop to cater to your specific group's needs.
description: Using a simple technique with oil pastels and watercolors, each person will have the opportunity to reflect on their own personal experiences with domestic violence, explore difficult emotions in a safe and fun way, and give voice to the feelings that may be hidden inside by creating artwork that represents the “monster” within.
notes:
If using this workshop to help the participants release or process anger, we suggest beginning by having a discussion on "What is Anger?" Please click here to see the entire Processing Anger Workshop Series.

If you'd like to include journaling in this workshop, here is a journaling handout that you can distribute to the participants.
tips:
We recommend that you start anger workshops with a discussion; don't be afraid to talk to the participants about their anger. Anger is nothing to be ashamed of, it is important to look at and talk about it to try to understand it.

Some anger prompts that we like are:

  • What is Anger? What does it look like and what does it sound like?

  • What was the trigger to your anger?

  • What did you think about it?

  • How did it make you feel?

  • How did you act?

  • What effect did it have on you and those around you?
objective_spanish:
Proveer oportunidades a participantes para reflexionar sobre sus experiencias personales con violencia domestica, explorar emociones difíciles de una manera segura y divertida, dando le una voz a los sentimientos que puedan estar escondidos adentro de uno mismo creando una pieza de arte que representa el “mostró” dentro.

Materiales:
Craypas
Papel blanco grueso (doble el número de participantes)
Acuarelas
Brochas
Vasos de agua- 1 por participante
Espejos de mano

Tiempo:
Calentamiento: 15 minutos
Introducción y Demostración: 10 minutos
Creación: 50 minutos
Circulo de clausura: 15 minutos
Tiempo total: 1 hora y 30 minutos

Calentamiento:
Vamos a empezar el taller de hoy día con un calentamiento que nos ayudara a relajar nuestros cuerpos, conectar con nuestros sentimientos y la manera que nos expresamos, preparar y inspirar nos para cuando nos siéntenos a crear.  Vamos a comenzar con crear un círculo.

Empezamos con extender nuestro brazo derecho hacia arriba, hasta donde alcancen.

Ahora su brazo izquierdo hacia arriba, hasta donde alcancen.

Estiren su cara en un bostezo grande y espiren profundamente.

Ahora aprieten su cara fuerte como una pasa y luego suelten lo.

Empiecen a masticar, en visionen que tienen una goma de mascar grande dentro de su boca- mastica de el lado derecho de tu boca, luego muevo lo a el lado izquierdo.

Extiende los dos brazos hacia arriba y luego baja los dejando los caer, doblando en la cintura.
Párense, vertebre por vertebre hasta que su espaldas estén rectas.

Ahora… Todos juntos!

Todos hagan un sonido expresa algo tonto…

Hagan un sonido que expresa enojo.

Hagan un sonido que expresa miedo.

Hagan un sonido que expresa tristeza.

Hagan un sonido que expresa descanso.

Ahora vamos a sentarnos y empezar.

Introducción y Demostración técnica:
Hay una parte de nosotros que no demostramos a los demás, a no ser que siéntanos ciertas emociones, por ejemplo cuando nos sentimos tristes y ponemos una cara feliz, es como tener una persona adentro que no queremos exponer.  Hoy estamos creando un dibujo que expone esa persona que llevamos dentro, el nombre del taller es Mostró dentro de mi.

Vamos a empezar con conocer los materiales que utilizaremos para crear nuestros Monstros.  Voy ha empezar con una demostración creando mi mostró, luego empezaran a crear su propio mostró.  Recuerden sus monstruos no serán igual, porque demostramos nuestras emociones y experiencias de diferente maneras.  Todos sentimos, enojo, tristeza, felicidad, y miedo… pero se manifiesta de diferente manera con deferente gente.

(Caminen mientras dan la demostración, ayuda mantener la atención de la gente)

El primer material es como una crayola, se llama pastel.  Mi mostró tendrá una cara y voy a utilizar el pastel para crear la forma de la cara.  Voy a dibujar una forma … (dibuja la forma).  Pueden usar toda la pagina para crear su mostró.  Pueden utilizar toda la página para dibujar el cuerpo, o su cara, o pueden incluir un ambiente.  Hay muchas maneras en que sus monstros pueden tomar forma.

Ahora voy a utilizar acuarelas… Primero voy a mojar la brocha y escogeré mi color.  (Demuestra como los pasteles mantienen el color dentro de la forma.  Agrega otra forma con el pastel y demuestra como limpiar la brocha y como resiste el color cuando agregas la acuarela sobre el pastel.)

Que ven en la mesa que no se haiga explicado?

Espejos.  Levanten el espejo y mírense.  Noten como cambia su cara cuando hacen diferentes expresiones, cuando sonríes, miren sus dientes y cuando arrugas las cejas.

Ahora quiero que miren en el espejo, quiero que miren dentro de ustedes y vean si pueden ver el mostró adentro.  Como se siente tu  mostró?  Como se ve?  Tu mostró se ve feliz, triste, enojado, asustado?

No tienen que contestar estas preguntas con palabras, vamos a exponer estos monstros en el papel dejen que se expresen solos.  Cuando estén listos, bajen su espejo y empiecen a crear.

Creación:
Recuerden mientras que trabajan, este es un lugar seguro para ustedes.  No tienen que saber quien es su mostró ni como se ve cuando comiencen , se aparecerán y tomaran su propia forma mientras que van creando.

Circulo de Clausura:
Da le una oportunidad a cada mujer para compartir su mostró.  Pueden compartir en parejas o como grupo (dependiendo de lo que sea mejor para el grupo).  Cuando comparten en parejas una persona compartirá primero mientras que la otra practica a escuchar, compartiendo una por una 3 minutos cada una.  Avisa cuando es tiempo de cambiar.

Puedes animar a las mujeres que compartan con preguntas como:  “Como se siente tu mostró?  Que esta pensando?”  Pregúntales a las mujeres que necesitan sus monstros, para sentirse mejor.  Necesita amor? Necesita que lo entiendan?  A veces monstros tienen cosas importantes que decir si escuchan lo que necesitan para sentirse mejor.

Da gracias a las mujeres por compartir y por ser valientes en exponer a sus monstros que llevan dentro.
optional_materials:
You can also facilitate this workshop using printable worksheets. If you are utilizing the worksheets in lieu of the regular workshop materials, be sure to send a digital copy or print them out for your participants if you are meeting in person.

  • The Monster in Me Worksheet

  • Spray bottle (filled with water; one per table will do; you can also use a broad house-painting brush instead)

 
The Monster in Me Worksheet
introduction:
"There is a side of us we don't show to other people unless we feel certain emotions. For example, when we feel sad, sometimes we try to put on a happy face, and it's like we have another person inside that we don't want to show. Today, you will have an opportunity to create a drawing that exposes that person inside in a safe and creative way."

"Before we begin, I want you to know that this is your window of time. This means that this can be a safe space to notice your thoughts, feelings, and needs. During this time, there is no right or wrong way to participate or create. I'm going to share some basic instructions, but you get to choose how you want to participate. You can follow along completely, or you may want to do something different, it's completely up to you. During your window of time, you have complete freedom to choose. I am here to support you in any way that I can, so please feel free to ask for what you need."
demonstration:
A Windows Program Facilitator creating
 
Another Windows Program facilitator
creating her monster

"I'd like to invite you to take a look at the materials available to create your monsters. I'm going to show you how to use them by starting to create my monster and then you'll have the opportunity to create your own. Now, remember that no two monsters will be the same because we show our emotions and experiences in different ways. Everyone feels angry, sad, happy, afraid, but those feelings can look very different on different people, and each of us can have our own unique way of expressing them."

"The first material is like a crayon and is called an oil pastel (or CrayPas). My monster is going to have a face and I'm going to use this oil pastel to create the shape of a face. I'm going to draw a shape... (draw any shape). You can use the whole page to create your monster, if you like. You can make the body fill up the whole page, or it's face, or it could be in an environment. There are lots of different ways that your monster can take its shape, and you have complete freedom to draw it however it feels right to you."

You can use a spray bottle now to wet the paper. You'll see the CrayPas (or oil pastel) resisting the water. Wetting the page will allow the watercolors to be dropped and fill the spaces.

"Next, I'm going to use these watercolors... First, I'm going to get the brush really wet then I'll pick my color."

You can demonstrate how the watercolor can be used on the paper and how the oil pastels hold the color inside the shape.

You can add some other shape with an oil pastel, and show how to clean their brush in one water cup then dip into the other water cup to wet it.  You can show how the watercolor over the oil pastel resists the color.

title: My Time
objective: This workshop gives children an opportunity to envision how they wish to fill their days so they can have the life they want, through the creation of a special clock.
materials:
• Construction paper (white or light colored preferred)

  • Colored pencils

  • Pencil sharpeners

  • Markers
setup:
You can lay out the art supplies so that each participant can easily access them.

It may be helpful to create a sample in advance to show the children what the finished art piece can look like. If you choose to do so, we suggest creating a simple sample so that children aren't overwhelmed by any "artistic" challenges.

You have complete freedom to alter or adapt any portion or element of this workshop to cater to your specific group's needs.
warm_up:
You are welcome to use our suggested relaxation exercise or your own. We have found that guided relaxations are most effective when spoken in a soft, slow tone, pausing where it feels right.


"Before we start, I'd like to invite you to join me in a brief relaxation exercise. If you prefer, you can just observe. Observing is participating."

"For those of you who want to follow along, you can close your eyes if you feel safe, or you can keep them open. However you are most comfortable."

"Now try to imagine a very special clock. What makes it special is that it can look any way you want it to look. So take a deep breath and then gently let all the air out... As you concentrate on your breathing, realize this is a time for you."

Breathing in, you start to feel your body become more and more relaxed... Start to imagine your special clock... Notice its shape... Is it a tall clock like a grandfather clock? Maybe your clock is just a large round wall clock. Or maybe it looks like a wrist watch. Try to imagine the details of your clock... anything that comes to your mind will be perfect."

"Breathing in and out, notice your body becoming more deeply relaxed and the shape of your clock becoming more and more clear..."

"Now picture the face of the clock and picture all the numbers slowly flying away and notice that now this is your own clock and your own time. Begin to picture exactly what you want in your life on the face of your clock. Maybe there are words or certain colors or shapes that you picture."

When you are ready, you can gently open your eyes and begin to draw the clock you just pictured in your mind, or start the process and see where your creativity wants to go."
creation:
You can use the markers or colored pencils in front of you to draw your very own clock with things you want in your day that can help you create a life that feels good in your body, mind and heart. The most important thing to remember as you make your clock is that you get to choose how you spend your time, and, what your clock looks like."

"Remember, there is no right or wrong way to draw your clock and it doesn't matter what it looks like. What's important is that you are taking this time to honor the things you want in your life and create something that is meaningful to you."
 

       
Floating numbers   Filling the day with things that matter   Making time for all the important things
closing:
You can give children a chance to share their amazing clocks and how it felt to make up how they wish to spend their time, or anything else they may wish to share.

Of course, this is optional and if no one feels comfortable sharing, that's perfectly okay.
description: To create your very own clock that will show how we want to fill our days so we can have the life we want.
optional_materials:
You can also facilitate this workshop using printable worksheets. If you are utilizing the worksheets in lieu of the regular workshop materials, be sure to send a digital copy or print them out for your participants if you are meeting in person.

  • My Time Worksheet (English)

  • My Time Worksheet (Spanish)

   
My Time Worksheet (English)     My Time Worksheet (Spanish)
introduction:
"Today, you have an opportunity to make your own special clock that will have just the things you want to spend your time doing. There are all kinds of clocks; grandfather clocks, cuckoo clocks, wrist watch, clock radio. Can anyone think of any other type of clock?"

"On the face of your clock, you get to put all the things you want to do to fill up your day. You can use colors, draw images, shapes or symbols, or write words that represent the things you want to do during your day so yo can have the life that you want."

"Before we begin, I want you to know that this is your window of time. This means that this can be a safe space to notice your thoughts, feelings, and needs. Since this space is your window of time, everything you say or do is voluntary. During this time, there is no right or wrong way to participate or create. I'm going to share some basic instructions, but you get to choose how you want to participate. You can follow along completely, or you may want to do something different, it's completely up to you. During your window of time, you have complete freedom to choose. However you choose to spend this time will be perfectly okay. I am here to support you in any way that I can, so please feel free to ask for what you need."
opening_circle:
Mixed up numbers on the clock
 
 
  A clock with no numbers at all

You can invite the children to think about and share important things they spend their time doing everyday, such as sleeping, going to school, chores, homework etc.

Then, they can share some fun things they would like to do with their time, that they may not not get to do often, if ever. For instance, go to the beach, play sports, watch TV, eat ice cream, go to the movies etc.


"Remember some important things about planning your time. If you spend the whole day eating sweets, it may seem like fun but you'll most likely feel sick after or may have a hard time focusing. And if you spend the whole day only watching cartoons on TV, you won't get to learn things or get your body strong. It is important to plan things on your clock that will be fun and also the things that help you have the life you want when you grow up. Can you think of what some of those things might be?"

(You can give them examples such as music, sports, school, art, dancing, learning, playing, exercise, helping others, chores, fun time with friends and family, or any other examples relevant to your group).

"All these things can help fill your days and create something that we call balance. This balance can help us have the life we want."

title: Coat of Arms / Escudo de Armas
objective: This workshop gives children an opportunity to explore how they are strong, unique and special, and create a personal Coat of Arms with special symbols that represents them.
materials:
• Coat of Arms template (1 per participant)

  • Markers

  • Colored pencils

  • Pencil sharpeners

  • Crayons
setup:
You are welcome to provide any and as many of the suggested art supplies as you like. You are also welcome to add your own.

You can print a Coat of Arms template for each participant.

If possible, you can invite children to bring photos of themselves or family to add to their creations.

You may want to create a sample to show children what the finished art piece can look like. If you choose to do so, we suggest a simple sample and using only the material you're providing so that children aren't overwhelmed by any "artistic" challenges.

You can lay out the materials so they are easily accessible to all the children.

As a facilitator, you have complete freedom to alter or adapt any portion or element of this workshop to cater to your specific group's needs.
creation:
Drawing the Coat of Arms:

You can now invite those who wish to create to begin.

Children can use the Coat of Arms templates provided as a basis for their creation, or they may create one from their imagination. There's no right or wrong way to create the Coat of Arms.

Children are free to create however they like. Here is one suggested way you can share with them:

You can invite children to divide the Coat of Arms into 4 sections. Then use markers, crayons, or colored pencils to draw the following:

In the upper left box:
Pick and draw a thing, animal, shape, or color that represents their family (examples: flags, fish, lions or a combination of a few, etc.).

In the upper right box:
Draw a symbol of their favorite thing to do. An activity that makes them happy or that makes them feel special. For instance, they may like swimming, dancing, favorite family outing, a holiday or going to the beach, etc.

In the lower left box:
Draw people who they consider their family. For instance, this could include siblings, grandparents, cousins, etc. If they have a photo of their family they've brought, they can glue that here.

In the lower right box:
Draw what makes them feel safe. Draw people, places, or things that help them stay safe and feel strong. For example, a hug from their mom, dad, or guardian; going to school or their favorite stuffed animal, etc.


You can offer these suggestions and remind them that they are just suggestions and that they are free to decorate and design their Coat of Arms however way they choose. It doesn't matter what it looks like. What's important is that they are taking this time to honor their strength and creating something that is expressive and meaningful to them.

Once the Coat of Arms is finished, they can cut it out and add any additional decorations available (glitter glue, beads, feathers, buttons, stickers and yarn) to make it just as unique and special as they are.
 

Part 1: What represents my family
 		 Part 2: My favorite thing to do
 
Part 3: People in my family Part 4: What makes me feel safe
closing:
You can invite the children to share their new Coat of Arms with the group, if any wish to do so. Of course, this is optional and if no one feels comfortable sharing, that's perfectly okay.

You can thank the children for their strength and courage to be here today.
description: To provide each participant with an opportunity to create a Coat of Arms with special symbols that represent who they are. This allows the children to explore how they are unique and special and how that makes them strong.
notes: If you have limited materials, this workshop may be done with just pencil and paper, or paper and crayons. If you need to keep your materials very simple, that's great, too.
objective_spanish: Este taller les brinda a los niños la oportunidad de explorar cómo son fuertes, únicos y especiales, y crear un Escudo de armas personal con símbolos especiales que los representan.
materials_spanish:
• La plantilla de escudo de armas (1 por participante)
• Marcadores
• Lápices de colores
• Sacapuntas
• Crayones
setup_spanish:
Te invitamos a proporcionar cualquiera y tantos artículos de arte sugeridos como desee. También es bienvenido a añadir su propio.

Puede imprimir una plantilla de escudo de armas para cada participante. Si es posible, puede invitar a los niños a traer fotos de ellos mismos o familiares para agregar a sus creaciones.

Es posible que desee crear una muestra para mostrar a los niños cómo puede verse la pieza de arte terminada. Si decide hacerlo, le sugerimos una muestra simple y que utilice solo el material que está proporcionando para que los niños no se sientan abrumados por ningún desafío "artístico".

Puede colocar los materiales para que sean fácilmente accesibles para todos los niños.

Como facilitador, tiene total libertad para alterar o adaptar cualquier parte o elemento de este taller para satisfacer las necesidades de este grupo específico.
creation_spanish:
Ahora puedes invitar a los niños que deseen crear para comenzar.

Los niños pueden usar las plantillas de Escudo de Armas que se proporcionan como base para su creación, o pueden crear una a partir de su imaginación.

No hay una manera correcta o incorrecta de crear el Escudo de Armas. Los niños son libres de crear lo que quieran.

Aquí hay una forma sugerida de compartir con ellos: Puedes invitar a los niños a dividir el Escudo de Armas en 4 secciones.

Luego usa marcadores, crayones o lápices de colores para dibujar lo siguiente: En el cuadro superior izquierdo:  Elijan y dibujen una cosa, animal, forma o color que represente a su familia (ejemplos: banderas, peces, leones o una combinación de algunos, etc.).

En el cuadro superior derecho: Dibujen un símbolo de una cosa favorita para hacer. Una actividad que los hace felices o que los hace sentir especiales.

Por ejemplo, les puede gustar nadar, bailar, salir en familia, ir de vacaciones o ir a la playa, etc. En la casilla inferior izquierda: Dibujen personas que consideran familia.

Por ejemplo, esto podría incluir hermanos, abuelos, primos, etc. Si tienen una foto de su familia que han traído, pueden pegarla aquí.

En el cuadro inferior derecho: Dibujen lo que los hace sentir seguros. Dibujen personas, lugares o cosas que los ayuden a mantenerse seguros y sentirse fuertes. Por ejemplo, un abrazo de su mamá, papá o tutor; ir a la escuela o su peluche favorito, etc.

Puede ofrecer estas sugerencias y recordarles que son solo sugerencias y que son libres de decorar y diseñar su Escudo de Armas de la forma que prefieran.

No importa lo que parece. Lo importante es que se toman este tiempo para honrar su fuerza y crear algo que sea expresivo y significativo para ellos. Una vez que el Escudo de Armas está terminado, pueden recortarlo y agregar cualquier decoración adicional disponible (pegamento brillante, cuentas, plumas, botones, pegatinas e hilados) para que sea tan único y especial como lo es.
closing_spanish:

introduction:
My Coat of Arms

"Before we begin, I want you to know that this is your window of time. This means that this can be a safe space to notice your thoughts, feelings, and needs. Since this space is your window of time, everything you say or do is voluntary. During this time, there is no right or wrong way to participate or create. I'm going to share some basic instructions, but you get to choose how you want to participate. You can follow along completely, or you may want to do something different, it's completely up to you. During your window of time, you have complete freedom to choose. However you choose to spend this time will be perfectly okay. I am here to support you in any way that I can, so please feel free to ask for what you need."

"Today, you have an opportunity to create a Coat of Arms to represent you."

"Coat of Arms were used many years ago. They were made to show what people stand for, what is important to them, where they were from, and who they were. Today you are invited to make your own Coat of Arms to tell others about you and why you are strong."

title: My Wishing Well
objective: This workshop gives children an opportunity to make resolutions for the new year by helping them decide what they would wish for in their lives (other than material things) and create a personal wishing well.
materials:
• Paper drinking cups (one for each participant)

  • Colored tissue paper (variety of colors)

  • Mod Podge (or a solution of 1/2 water 1/2 white glue in a cup)

  • Thick paint brushes (to use with Mod Podge)

  • Paper towels

  • Pipe cleaners

  • Scissors

  • Hole punch

  • Permanent markers

  • Small stones (you can purchase or collect your own from nature)

  • Paper

  • Pens
setup:
Gathering stones

You can purchase stones or collect some from nature in advance. It's up to you. If possible, you can even incorporate the stone collection into your workshop by inviting the kids to take a walk outside so that they can collect their own stones.

You may consider creating a sample wishing well in advance to show the children what it can look like. If you choose to do so, we suggest creating a simple sample using only the material you're providing, so that children aren't overwhelmed by any "artistic" challenges.

You also have the option to create your own stones using Sculpeys (see Tips section for more details). This is entirely up to you.

As a facilitator, you have complete freedom to alter or adapt any portion or element of this workshop to cater to your specific needs.
warm_up:
"Before we start this project, I'd like to encourage you to let go of any disappointments you may have had last year, and write down any things we wish hadn't happened."

Depending on the age group and their specific needs, you can suggest some examples of disappointments that you may have had or things that you wish hadn't happened. You have flexibility to adapt or alter to cater to your group.
creation:
Decorating the rocks

Step 1:
To begin, you can invite each child to select any 3 stones and write one wish on each of the stones (they can select more than 3 if you wish to provide them with more stones). They can use any of the material and design their stones however way they like. They can draw symbols or shapes instead of write words, if they prefer.


Step 2:
Next, they can set the stones aside while they create the wishing well.


Step 3:
Each child gets a cup and they can decorate it anyway they choose, using the tissue paper and Mod Podge, and any of the material provided. They can cut or rip shapes and pieces of the tissue paper and use the Mod Podge to stick the pieces all the way around the cup. They can add glitter, ribbons, foam stickers, pom poms and any other embellishments available.

You may wish to remind them that there is no right or wrong way to create. It doesn't matter what it looks like. What's important is that they're taking this time to honor their wishes and creating something that is meaningful to them.
 

    
  Wishing Wells

Step 4:
You can punch two holes across from each other near the top of the cup and attach the pipe cleaners for the handle. You can loop the pipe cleaner around the hole to get it to stand up.


Step 5:
Finally, you can place blue crumpled up tissue inside the cup, to look like water, and place the stones inside. Of course, you are free to use any color paper.
closing:
Inside view of a Wishing Well    

For the closing, you may give the children an opportunity to share their Wishing Wells and the 3 wishes they made for themselves, anything they learned, felt or experienced in the process of creating, or anything else they wish to share. Of course, this is purely optional and if no one feels comfortable sharing, it's perfectly okay.
description: To help children make resolutions for the new year by deciding what they would wish for in their lives (other than material things) and creating a personal wishing well.
tips:
The older children might have fun creating their own rocks for this project. Sculpey works well for this. If you choose to incorporate this into your workshop, you might want to demonstrate how to make swirly Sculpey rocks first. Here are the instructions:

Material:

  • Super Sculpey (or polymer clay)

  • Toaster oven

 

Sculpey Creation:

Step 1: (Creating the Stones)
You can choose at least two colors. You may wish to remind the participants that they have complete freedom to choose any and as many colors as they like. It doesn't matter what it looks like. A pinch of each color is enough to make the stones.

Step 2:
You can take each color and roll it into a "snake."

Step 3:
Next, you can wrap each "snake" around each other like a candy-cane and twist together.

Step 4:
You can now roll the snake into a ball.

Step 5:
Now you may roll the ball out into a larger "snake" until the colors are blended just the way you want them.

Step 6:
Finally, you can roll the "snake" into a ball, then flatten the ball into to the shape of stone you like. If you want, you can repeat steps 4 and 5 to create a more marbled effect.

Step 7: (Baking)
To bake, you can use a thick piece of paper or brown paper grocery bag to line the toaster oven tray. You may also use a foil lined cookie sheet.

Please be mindful that even the outer surface of the toaster oven can get very hot!

You can bake the Sculpey at 275°F for 15 minutes (for each ¼ inch of clay thickness).

Please allow about 10 minutes for the stones to cool before handling them.

introduction:
"Today, we'll have a chance to start making plans for the New Year. Sometimes, you hear grown-ups making something called 'a new year's resolution.' A resolution is a decision that you make to change something or make it better in your life. For example, my resolution is to exercise more to keep me healthy (or whatever else you wish to share). Your resolution could be to get better grades, or spend more time with friends, or anything else you wish."

"All resolutions start with having a wish to do something. You can make many of your wishes come true by working hard and never giving up. Today, you'll get a chance to think about those wishes and make your very own Wishing Well. Remember, the wishes you get to make today are not for things you want from other people, these are wishes you want for yourself."

"Before we begin, I want you to know that this workshop is a window of time for you. This means that this can be a safe space to notice your thoughts, feelings, and needs. Since this space is your window of time, everything you say or do is voluntary. I’ll offer a suggested workshop idea, share about the materials we have available, and invite you to create, but there’s no right or wrong way to do this. It doesn't matter what it looks like. What matters is taking this time to truly honor your thoughts and feelings, however they come out. If you can’t think of anything or draw a blank on what to create or write, feel free to just observe. However you choose to spend this time will be perfectly okay. This is your time. Please ask for what you need, and know that I’m here in support of you."
opening_circle:
You can open by inviting the children to think about what they would wish for. You may encourage them to think about something other than things that can be bought, like toys or candy. You might want to suggest some things like: wishing for more time to play, or learning how to swim, or someone to teach them to play an instrument. You may want to help the younger children to write down their wishes. The older children can write them down themselves.

Feel free to offer assistance where you see the need.

title: Shrinky Dink Blessing Charms - Holidays with HeART Series
objective: This workshop aims to give participants an opportunity to connect and bond with loved ones and celebrate the holidays through the creation of special Shrinky Dink bracelet charms, which they can use to show loved ones that they care and perhaps even begin new family traditions.
materials:
• Shrinky Dink cutouts 

  • Permanent markers

  • Color pencils

  • Scissors

  • Ribbon or yarn

  • Toaster oven

  • Hole punch
setup: You have the option to cut out the various shapes from the template in advance, or simply print enough templates and give the participants an opportunity to cut it out themselves. It's entirely up to you.
creation:
You can guide them step by step and create along with them or guide them however you see fit. It's entirely up to you.

Step 1:
If you have already cut out the template shapes, you can invite the participants to start coloring them. If not, you can simply invite them to select or design their own templates, cut them out, then start coloring. It's entirely up to you.

"For those of you who wish to participate, you can begin by selecting from any template/shape that you like. You are also welcome to create you own designs. You can draw symbols, or even write words, or both. I'd like to encourage you to think about any words, symbols, or colors that you connect with as you reflect on your blessing and get as creative as you like. You have complete freedom to use any of the materials to design your Shrinky Dink." 

Step 2: 
"Now that you've finished coloring, you may cut out your shape with scissors." 

Step 3: 
"If you would like to add ribbon or wire to your Shrinky Dink to wear as a bracelet or hang on a wall, you can punch a hole in the plastic prior to baking (once Shrinky Dinks are baked, you cannot alter them)."

Step 4:
"Now your blessing Shrinky Dink is ready to bake. For those of you who want to shrink your charms, you can place the pieces onto a cut out piece of brown paper bag or cookie sheet, with the shiny side facing up. This will help prevent the plastic from folding onto itself."

Step 5:
To bake, you can simply place the Shrinky Dinks (on the brown paper bag or cookie sheet) in the oven at 300°F for 1-3 minutes. Please be mindful that a toaster over can get very hot even on the outer surface. Also, it's important to make sure the Shrinky Dink charms are not touching while in the oven as they may stick together. You can continue to bake until the pieces have flattened.

Step 7:
You may safely remove the charms from oven and allow them some time to cool (generally 1 to 2 minutes).

Step 8 (optional):
For those who punched a hole in their blessing Shrinky Dink, they may now use ribbon or yarn and loop it through the hole. If you have provided beads, you may invite the participants to add them onto the ribbon at this time.
closing: For the closing, you may give the participants an opportunity to share their amazing blessing charms and anything they learned, felt or experienced in the process of creating, or anything else they wish to share. Of course, this is purely optional and if no one feels comfortable sharing, it's perfectly okay.

title: My Relationship Boundaries… Revealed!
objective:
Key Topic: Teen Dating Violence: Intervention and Prevention

This Workshop Falls Under the Theme of Teen Dating Violence Since 2010, we have been developing this program to serve the teens in our community and in our programs. This curriculum is offered to and is useful for BOTH women's and children's leaders as most agencies work with this population in some capacity. A HUGE thank you to Giovanna Martinez of WomenShelter of Long Beach for enhancing our Teen Dating Violence curriculum.

   
   

Objective
To introduce participants to the concept of boundaries and having healthy levels of independence in their intimate relationships.

   
 
       Optional printable worksheet
   

Materials
Relationship Boundaries handout
Scratch Art Boards (can be purchased at discountschoolsupply.com)
Toothpicks, pencils, or any object that can be used to scratch off the black layer off the art board
Pens
Scratch paper
Tablecloth or newspaper (to cover the table as the Scratch Art Boards can be very messy)

You can also facilitate this workshop using this printable worksheet. If you are utilizing the worksheet in lieu of the regular workshop materials, be sure to send the sheet or print copies out for your participants beforehand depending on the setting.

Preparation
Please be aware that the black scraps that come off the art board when you scratch through are very messy and stain easily. You may want to lay out newspaper on top of the table the participants will use when they create. Make sure to print out enough handouts for each participant.

 
A participant's boundaries revealed  

Timeframe:
Introduction: 10 min
Opening Circle: 20 min
Creation: 20 min
Closing: 20 min
Total: 1 hr 10 min

Introduction
Today we are going to focus on boundaries and having healthy levels of independence in your intimate relationships. Ask the group, "does anyone know what a boundary is?" After hearing the group's thoughts, if necessary, give an example such as a fence. A boundary is an invisible fence that protects us. There are various types of boundaries. The most obvious type of boundary is a physical boundary. To demonstrate this concept ask one of the group members to join you at the front of the room and stand facing you, approximately ten feet away. Tell them that you're going to start walking towards them and it is their job to stop you when you get to the point where they would feel uncomfortable if you got any closer. Once they stop you, tell the group that exercise just revealed the volunteers physical boundary. Then speak to the group about the importance of identifying and honoring not only your physical, but also your emotional boundaries in your relationships. While emotional boundaries may be less obvious than physical boundaries, it's necessary to be aware of them.  It's up to each and every one of us to decide what is and what isn't okay in an intimate (dating) relationship and to make sure our partner is aware of and respects those boundaries.

Warm Up
Give each person a piece of scratch paper and a pen. Ask the group to use circles to represent two people in a relationship. Have them position two circles on a piece of paper to show what a healthy relationship looks like, and then position two more circles to show what an unhealthy relationship looks like. In each example, are the circles far away from each other, close together, overlapping or touching? If the participants have difficulty doing this on their own, you can make it a group activity and have them instruct you as you draw the circles in front of the group. Then pass the Relationship Boundaries handout to the participants. Read through and generate a discussion about the information on the handout, and their ideas about healthy and unhealthy relationship boundaries. Be sure to talk about the importance of maintaining a healthy level of independence within a relationship. In fact one "red flag" of an abusive relationship is being completely immersed in your partner's life and detaching from your friends, hobbies, and the activities that are not connected to your significant other.

 
Revealing boundaries  

Creation Process
Pass out the Scratch Art Boards and a scratch tool. Keeping in mind everything we have just discussed, I want you to think about what boundaries you want to create in your intimate/dating relationships. What do you want to share with your partner? What do you want to keep just for yourself? Now using your Scratch Art Board reveal your relationship boundaries. Scratch words, shapes, symbols or even pictures onto your Scratch Art Board to represent what you will and will not allow in your relationship to maintain healthy boundaries.   

Share examples such as:
-Write the name of a friend or family member to remind you not to lose touch with people who are close to you (other than your partner).
-Draw a mouth to remind you to be open, and honest, and that you have a voice and the right to speak up for yourself.
-Draw two shapes that are the same size to symbolize how you and your partner are equal and have mutual respect for one another.

Keep in mind that what you create doesn't have to make sense to anyone but you. Try not to censor yourself when you create; your project should serve as a reminder of what you want in your intimate/dating relationships. If you are open and honest with yourself about what you want and don't want in your relationship, you will be able to talk to your partner about it and work together to make it happen!  

 

Closing
Ask each participant to share anything they want about their creation, and what knowledge they will take with them from today. You may also ask participants what steps they will take to implement these boundaries in their current or future relationships, or where they will display or keep their project and why. Thank the participants for jumping into this complex, yet very important topic of boundaries, and encourage them to keep their project as a reminder to make sure they feel safe, comfortable and happy in their relationships.

 

Note About Introducing Embodied Art
Consider sharing with your participants the benefits of moving their bodies in playful and safe ways. Understanding what’s meaningful about movement and body awareness can help participants feel at ease expanding their comfort zones. For more about embodied art workshops and how to introduce them in your groups, see Introduction to Embodied Art Workshops.
