title: Community Story Tree
objective:
Objective:
Using the tree as a symbol of life, participants will have the opportunity to express their stories and share their hopes and visions for a violence-free future. Through images of roots, bark, branches, leaves, fruits, and s ky, participants will join together to create a special tree embodying their community commitment against domestic violence.

     
   AWBW Community Story Tree  

Materials:
Note on materials: Feel free to use some or all of the suggested materials. This workshop works well with simple materials or mixed-media.

 

Square Canvas tiles (one per participant) (see dickblick.com for inexpensive pre-stretched canvas of various sizes) We used tiles that are 12 inches X 12 inches.
AWBW Community Story Tree Grid (colored version, black and white)
Acrylic paints
Paintbrushes (various sizes)
Sponge Brushes
Puffy paints
Cray-pas
Embroidery thread
Yarn
Tissue paper
Fabric
Glitter
Sponges
Markers/Sharpies		   Rafia
Artificial flowers
Sticks
Dried Leaves
Stamps
Glue / Tacky glue
Collaging materials
Mod Podge
Paper plates (to be used as paint palettes)
Water cups
Wall putty - 4 pieces per tile (optional)
Level for hanging (optional)









 

 

 

 

 

 

 

Other Options for Story Tree grid:
Footprint Tree Grid (Color version included)
Footprint Heart-Tree Grid (Color version included)
Leaf Tree Grid (Color version included)
Crescent House Community Story Tree Grid 

 

     
   AWBW Community Story Tree Grid  
     
   AWBW Community Story Tree
Color Version		  

Set-Up/Prep:
Whether you use the AWBW Community Story Tree Grid (72 squares) or you create your own tree on the Blank Grid provided you will need to either use a transparency and projector or a capable artist to sketch out the design directly onto the canvas tiles.

If you choose to create your own tree, start by creating a sketch on the blank grid provided or onto a similar grid that fits the proportions of the space and size of tiles you will be using.

Be sure to have a color version of the overall tree available, so participants will have a rough guide for the color scheme of their tile.

Note: It's helpful if you mark the back of each canvas tile with a number that corresponds with the position of the tile on the grid, such as A1, A2. That way the participants can refer to the chart to see where their tile is located on the overall tree. Also, it's helpful that you put an arrow on the back of each tile pointing to the top, to ensure that participants are creating with the correct side up.

Warm-up:
Ask the participants to stand up, take a deep breath and stretch their "tree limbs" way up to the sky as they reach higher and higher. Have them spread all their fingers as far as they can and take another deep breath in and breathe out as they shake their "leaves" and flutter in the breeze (repeat as necessary). In addition, or alternately, have participants walk around the room (or standing in one place) as they to sway and stretch their "branches" and "roots" while continuing to breathe.

Introduction:
Your voice is important in helping to create a future free from domestic violence. Using  images of roots, bark, branches, leaves, and fruit I welcome you to express your own experiences, hopes, dreams, and commitment toward ending domestic violence in our communities. You may choose to delve into your past to share your personal stories of pain and triumph. Or you may reflect on the wishes, hopes, and dreams you have for the future. Each artist will use this creative opportunity to explore the issue of domestic violence in any way that is most meaningful for you.

Creation:
Start the process by explaining to the group that each person will be creating one tile from the overall design. Explain that once they have selected their tile, they will need to note the section number on the back of their canvas and refer to the "color" chart to see where their tile is located on the overall tree.

 

 

Introduce the project by saying something like,"We are all part of ending domestic violence. What words, shapes, symbols, or images represent or tell your story? How does your story speak out about domestic violence? What story would your root, bark, or leaves tell? How do you hope to affect the future? What story or wisdom does your heart want to share?"

 

"Feel free to be creative as you express yourself. For example, is your bark made up of loving hands? Is your sky filled with faces taking deep, soothing breaths? Do your words reveal the new directions you are taking in your life or your hopes for a better future? Maybe there are creatures in your branches. Maybe there is someone peeking out of a hole in your bark! Maybe your leaf is splitting open to show a road into your hopes and dreams. How does your story speak out against domestic violence? Feel free to play...and let your voice be heard!"

       
       Community Story Tree tiles      

Welcome participants to be creative with the materials. "Feel free to paint, collage, draw, or use mixed media. It will be powerful to see a tree created with many diverse art styles. Don't be afraid to layer colors/materials. Puffy paints are a great way to add dimension. You can smudge cray-pas with your fingers to make a blended effect. You can use Mod Podge as a glue or to create a glossy finish for your piece."

Welcome artists to include words in their art. Let them know, "it would be okay if a piece of the tree could be entirely covered with words or it could include just a few. It's fine to hide the words, make them tiny, almost invisible, or large and bold. Please think of a title for your piece and include the words somewhere on your square. You can also add quotes, inspirational words, or personal reflections...whatever expresses the story you want to tell."

Remind them along the way to "use the colored sketch as a 'rough' guide for their color scheme. Doing this will help to give the overall tree a sense of cohesiveness. But please feel free to play. The 'fruits' were left white like a blank canvas. If you have fruit in your square, invent your own way to represent what you want to say. Be sure you cover all parts of the tile with color so no parts of the canvas are left white."

Another important reminder will be to "try to stay 'within' the lines provided, so that each piece will fit with the surrounding pieces like a puzzle."

As participants complete their individual tiles, have them assemble them into the tree. We recommend using a level to evenly hang the tiles and Wall Putty, if available, to secure the tree tiles in place. Hang the tree for all to see and to represent a community statement.

Note: This can be simply a group bonding project or you may welcome the entire community, shelter staff, board members, friends, and family members to join survivors and express their stories and share their hopes and visions for a future free from domestic violence.

When completed, this project lends itself to become a powerful and beautiful exhibit. To view the AWBW's Community Story Tree, click here. To view Community Story Trees Across the Country, click here. The Community Story Tree will be made of up of a series 'tiles' each telling its own unique story about the journey toward creating a violence-free future (see design at left). Together, the tiles will create a mosaic of commitment to ending violence.

Closing:
As the workshop comes to an end, even if the participants aren't all finished with their work, it is very important to have a closing circle of sharing. After such a deep creative process, it is particularly valuable to take time for each participant to sit back and look at his or her work from a distance, to share what he or she sees in it. Ask participants to acknowledge the different feelings and thoughts that were present throughout the creative process.

Invite the participants to take a step back and admire the tree as a whole. Ask them to acknowledge their stand in the community against domestic violence, for sharing their journey, and the impact and commitment they have made together.

Through images of roots, bark, branches, leaves, fruits, and sky, participants will join together to create a special tree embodying their community commitment against domestic violence.
tips:
Note About Introducing Embodied Art
Consider sharing with the youth the benefits of moving their bodies in playful and safe ways. By sharing this information with them, you empower them to feel a sense of ownership over their bodies and their expression. For more about embodied art workshops and how to introduce them in your groups, see Introduction to Embodied Art Workshops.

Note About Exhibiting Community Story Trees
Collaborating agencies such as Pacific Clinics - Bonita Family Center in Los Angeles have created their own Community Story Tree to remain as a permanent installation to show their community's commitment to end domestic violence.

Color Version		  

Set-Up/Prep:
Whether you use the AWBW Community Story Tree Grid (72 squares) or you create your own tree on the Blank Grid provided you will need to either use a transparency and projector or a capable artist to sketch out the design directly onto the canvas tiles.

If you choose to create your own tree, start by creating a sketch on the blank grid provided or onto a similar grid that fits the proportions of the space and size of tiles you will be using.

Be sure to have a color version of the overall tree available, so participants will have a rough guide for the color scheme of their tile.

Note: It's helpful if you mark the back of each canvas tile with a number that corresponds with the position of the tile on the grid, such as A1, A2. That way the participants can refer to the chart to see where their tile is located on the overall tree. Also, it's helpful that you put an arrow on the back of each tile pointing to the top, to ensure that participants are creating with the correct side up.

Warm-up:
Ask the participants to stand up, take a deep breath and stretch their "tree limbs" way up to the sky as they reach higher and higher. Have them spread all their fingers as far as they can and take another deep breath in and breathe out as they shake their "leaves" and flutter in the breeze (repeat as necessary). In addition, or alternately, have participants walk around the room (or standing in one place) as they to sway and stretch their "branches" and "roots" while continuing to breathe.

Introduction:
Your voice is important in helping to create a future free from domestic violence. Using  images of roots, bark, branches, leaves, and fruit I welcome you to express your own experiences, hopes, dreams, and commitment toward ending domestic violence in our communities. You may choose to delve into your past to share your personal stories of pain and triumph. Or you may reflect on the wishes, hopes, and dreams you have for the future. Each artist will use this creative opportunity to explore the issue of domestic violence in any way that is most meaningful for you.

Creation:
Start the process by explaining to the group that each person will be creating one tile from the overall design. Explain that once they have selected their tile, they will need to note the section number on the back of their canvas and refer to the "color" chart to see where their tile is located on the overall tree.

Introduce the project by saying something like,"We are all part of ending domestic violence. What words, shapes, symbols, or images represent or tell your story? How does your story speak out about domestic violence? What story would your root, bark, or leaves tell? How do you hope to affect the future? What story or wisdom does your heart want to share?"

"Feel free to be creative as you express yourself. For example, is your bark made up of loving hands? Is your sky filled with faces taking deep, soothing breaths? Do your words reveal the new directions you are taking in your life or your hopes for a better future? Maybe there are creatures in your branches. Maybe there is someone peeking out of a hole in your bark! Maybe your leaf is splitting open to show a road into your hopes and dreams. How does your story speak out against domestic violence? Feel free to play...and let your voice be heard!"

       
       Community Story Tree tiles      

Welcome participants to be creative with the materials. "Feel free to paint, collage, draw, or use mixed media. It will be powerful to see a tree created with many diverse art styles. Don't be afraid to layer colors/materials. Puffy paints are a great way to add dimension. You can smudge cray-pas with your fingers to make a blended effect. You can use Mod Podge as a glue or to create a glossy finish for your piece."

Welcome artists to include words in their art. Let them know, "it would be okay if a piece of the tree could be entirely covered with words or it could include just a few. It's fine to hide the words, make them tiny, almost invisible, or large and bold. Please think of a title for your piece and include the words somewhere on your square. You can also add quotes, inspirational words, or personal reflections...whatever expresses the story you want to tell."

Remind them along the way to "use the colored sketch as a 'rough' guide for their color scheme. Doing this will help to give the overall tree a sense of cohesiveness. But please feel free to play. The 'fruits' were left white like a blank canvas. If you have fruit in your square, invent your own way to represent what you want to say. Be sure you cover all parts of the tile with color so no parts of the canvas are left white."

Another important reminder will be to "try to stay 'within' the lines provided, so that each piece will fit with the surrounding pieces like a puzzle."

As participants complete their individual tiles, have them assemble them into the tree. We recommend using a level to evenly hang the tiles and Wall Putty, if available, to secure the tree tiles in place. Hang the tree for all to see and to represent a community statement.

Note: This can be simply a group bonding project or you may welcome the entire community, shelter staff, board members, friends, and family members to join survivors and express their stories and share their hopes and visions for a future free from domestic violence.

When completed, this project lends itself to become a powerful and beautiful exhibit. To view the AWBW's Community Story Tree, click here. To view Community Story Trees Across the Country, click here. The Community Story Tree will be made of up of a series 'tiles' each telling its own unique story about the journey toward creating a violence-free future (see design at left). Together, the tiles will create a mosaic of commitment to ending violence.

Closing:
As the workshop comes to an end, even if the participants aren't all finished with their work, it is very important to have a closing circle of sharing. After such a deep creative process, it is particularly valuable to take time for each participant to sit back and look at his or her work from a distance, to share what he or she sees in it. Ask participants to acknowledge the different feelings and thoughts that were present throughout the creative process.

Invite the participants to take a step back and admire the tree as a whole. Ask them to acknowledge their stand in the community against domestic violence, for sharing their journey, and the impact and commitment they have made together.
description: Using the tree as a symbol of life, participants will have the opportunity to express their stories and share their hopes and visions for a violence-free future. Through images of roots, bark, branches, leaves, fruits, and sky, participants will join together to create a special tree embodying their community commitment against domestic violence.
tips:
Note About Introducing Embodied Art
Consider sharing with your participants the benefits of moving their bodies in playful and safe ways. Understanding what’s meaningful about movement and body awareness can help participants feel at ease expanding their comfort zones. For more about embodied art workshops and how to introduce them in your groups, see Introduction to Embodied Art Workshops.

Note About Exhibiting Community Story Trees
Collaborating agencies such as Pacific Clinics - Bonita Family Center in Los Angeles have created their own Community Story Tree to remain as a permanent installation to show their community's commitment to end domestic violence.

title: The Reasons We Smile / Las Razones que nos hacen Sonreír
objective: This workshop aims to encourage participants to remember that even though life can bring them challenges, there are always reasons for them to smile.
materials:
• Sheets of white paper

  • Markers

  • Crayons

  • Colored Pencils
setup: If you wish to prepare your materials beforehand, we recommend that you set out a stack of white paper, a box of crayons, colored pencils, and markers on each table.
warm_up: "First I'd like to invite you to join me in a brief relaxation exercise. For those of you who wish to participate, if you feel comfortable and safe, you can start by closing your eyes. If you prefer to keep them open that's perfectly okay too. The idea is that you feel comfortable and safe. Now I'd like to encourage you to think about a typical day in your life. Rather than focusing your thoughts on everyday worries like the ones just mentioned, try to clear your mind place your focus on simple joys... maybe a friend told you something nice or gave you a surprise treat... maybe you remember when you saw a beautiful butterfly land on a flower right next to you... maybe you got a good grade on a test and you feel proud. Try to think of all the little things that happen throughout the day that are worthy of the biggest smile you can give. Feel free to take a few more minutes to imagine all of those wonderful moments... big and small... that you experience, even in one day, that make you smile. And when you feel ready, please open your eyes."
creation:
"I would now like to now invite you to take a piece of paper and draw a smile. Feel free to make the mouth with teeth as large as you want. You can draw the smile however way you like. If you like, you can color the background too, or leave it blank. It's entirely up to you." 

Next, I'd like to invite you to fill each tooth with words, shapes, symbols, or thoughts that bring you a smile. Remember, there is no wrong way to do this. Anything that makes you smile, big or small will be perfect. It could be your pet, it could be a book, it could be a person, a song, a thought, a dream, a goal, anything you that makes you smile, write or draw it in each tooth. You can have as few and as many things you like."

 

     
   The Reasons We Smile creation     The Reasons We Smile creation
closing:
For the closing, you may give the participants an opportunity to share their amazing smile creations and anything they learned, felt or experienced in the process of creating, or anything else they wish to share. Of course, this is purely optional and if no one feels comfortable sharing, it's perfectly okay.

You can invite the participants to show their smiles to the group.

You may also wish to consider thanking the participants for sharing (if they did) and being bold, creative and thoughtful in thinking about the reason they smile.

"Remember that you are the only one who can see, feel, and appreciate the reasons you have for smiling. Those reasons are all unique, special, and wonderful. It is perfectly normal to  feel like frowning sometimes. I'd like to encourage you to try to shake it off and remember that there are things in your life all around you that can make you smile."
description: Helps to remind the participants that even though life can bring us challenges, there are always reasons for us to smile.
objective_spanish: Este taller tiene como objetivo animar a las y los participantes a recordar que a pesar que la vida puede traerles desafíos, siempre hay razones para sonreír.
materials_spanish:
• Hojas de papel blanco.
• Marcadores
• Crayones
• Lápices de colores
timeframe_spanish:
Introducción: 5 min
Calentamiento: 5 min
Creación: 35 min
Cierre: 10 min
Total: 1:00 hora
setup_spanish: Si desea preparar los materiales de antemano, le recomendamos colocar una pila de papel blanco, una caja de crayones, lápices de colores y marcadores en cada mesa.
warm_up_spanish:
"Primero, me gustaría invitarles a unirse conmigo en un breve ejercicio de relajación. Para aquellas o aquellos de ustedes que desean participar, si sienten comodidad y seguridad, pueden comenzar cerrando los ojos. Si prefieren mantenerlos abiertos, eso es perfectamente bien también. La idea es que se sientan cómodas y cómodo y seguras y seguros. Ahora me gustaría animarles a pensar en un día típico en su vida.

En lugar de centrar su atención en preocupaciones cotidianas como las que acabo de mencionar, traten de despejar su mente y enfocarse en alegrías simples... tal vez una amistad les dijo algo bonito o les dio un regalo sorpresa ... quizás recuerden cuando vieron una hermosa mariposa en una flor justo junto a ustedes... tal vez recibieron una muy buena calificación en un examen y sintieron mucho orgullo. Intenten pensar en todas las pequeñas cosas que suceden a lo largo del día que son dignas de la sonrisa más grande que pueden tener.

Siéntanse libres de tomarse unos minutos más para imaginar todos esos momentos maravillosos.... grandes y pequeños... que experimenten, incluso en un día, que les haga sonreír. Y cuando se sientan listas o listos, por favor abran los ojos ".
creation_spanish:
"Ahora me gustaría invitarles a tomar un pedazo de papel y dibujar una sonrisa. Siéntanse libres de hacer que la boca con los dientes sea tan grande como quieran. Pueden dibujar la sonrisa como deseen. Si lo desea, pueden colorear el fondo también, o dejarlo en blanco. Todo depende de cada quien".

A continuación, me gustaría invitarles a llenar cada diente con palabras, formas, símbolos o pensamientos que les hagan sonreír. Recuerden, no hay una manera incorrecta de hacer esto. Cualquier cosa que les haga sonreír, grande o pequeña, será perfecta.

Podría ser su mascota, podría ser un libro, podría ser una persona, una canción, un pensamiento, un sueño, una meta, cualquier cosa que les haga sonreír, escríbanlo o dibújenlo en cada diente. Pueden tener cuántas cosas deseen."
closing_spanish:
Para el cierre, puede darles a las y los participantes la oportunidad de compartir sus increíbles creaciones de sonrisas y todo lo que aprendieron, sintieron o experimentaron en el proceso de creación, o cualquier otra cosa que deseen compartir. Por supuesto, esto es puramente opcional y si nadie se siente cómoda o cómodo compartiendo, está perfectamente bien.

Puede invitar a las y los participantes a mostrar sus sonrisas al grupo. También puede considerar agradecer a las y los participantes por compartir (si es que lo hicieron) y por ser audaces, creativas, creativos,  reflexivas y reflexivos al pensar sobre la razón que les hace sonreír.

"Recuerden que ustedes son las y los únicos que pueden ver, sentir y apreciar las razones que tienen para sonreír. Esas razones son únicas, especiales y maravillosas. Es perfectamente normal sentir ganas de fruncir el ceño a veces. Me gustaría animarles trata de sacudirse y recuerden que hay cosas en su vida y a su alrededor que pueden hacerte sonreír ".
optional_materials:
Optional printable worksheet

You can also facilitate this workshop using a printable worksheet. If you are utilizing the worksheet in lieu of the regular workshop materials, be sure to send the sheet or print copies out for your participants beforehand depending on the setting.

  • The Reasons We Smile: English | Spanish
introduction:
"Sometimes we have an easier time saying what we are unhappy about than talking about the things that make us happy. For example, 'I don't want to go to work today,' or 'I don't like getting up early in the morning' or 'I hate sitting in traffic,' or everyday statements like 'I'm hungry, tired, bored, hot or cold.' All these things can negatively impact our day without us even realizing it."  

"Every day it seems so easy to notice the reasons that make us frown that we often forget that we have plenty of things to smile for. Today, you have an opportunity to take time to appreciate the things, big and small that make us smile."

"Before we begin, I want you to know that this workshop is a window of time for you. This means that this is a safe space to notice your thoughts, feelings, and needs. Since this space is your window of time, everything you say or do is voluntary. I’ll offer a suggested workshop idea, share about the materials we have available, and invite you to create, but there’s no wrong way to do this. It doesn't matter what it looks like. What matters is taking this time to truly honor your thoughts and feelings, however they come out. If you can’t think of anything or draw a blank on what to create or write, feel free to just observe. However you choose to spend this time will be perfectly okay. This is your time. Please ask for what you need, and know that I’m here in support of you."
introduction_spanish:
"A veces nos resulta más fácil decir de qué no estamos contentas o contentos en vez de hablar de las cosas que nos hacen felices. Por ejemplo, 'No quiero ir a trabajar hoy' o 'No me gusta levantarme temprano en la mañana' u 'odio estar en el tráfico' o declaraciones cotidianas como 'tengo hambre, estoy cansada/cansado, aburrida/aburrido, tengo frío o tengo calor '. Todas estas cosas pueden tener un impacto negativo en nuestro día sin que nos demos cuenta." 

"Todos los días parece tan fácil notar las razones que nos hacen fruncir el ceño que a menudo olvidamos que tenemos muchas cosas por las que sonreír. Hoy, tienen la oportunidad de tomarse el tiempo de apreciar las cosas, grandes y pequeñas, que les hacen sonreír.”

"Antes de comenzar, quiero que sepan que esta es su ventana de tiempo. Esto significa que este puede ser un espacio seguro para que noten sus pensamientos, sentimientos y necesidades. Dado que este espacio es su ventana de tiempo, todo lo que digan o hagan es voluntario. Durante este tiempo, no hay una forma correcta o incorrecta de participar o crear. Voy a compartir algunas instrucciones básicas, pero pueden elegir cómo quieran participar. Pueden seguirlas al pie de la letra o quizás prefieran hacer algo diferente, depende completamente de cada quien. Durante su ventana de tiempo, tienen total libertad para elegir. Cual sea su elección de pasar este tiempo, estará perfectamente bien. Estoy aquí para ayudarles de cualquier manera que pueda, así que por favor no duden en pedirme lo que necesiten.”

title: I CAN WE CAN
objective:
Objective:
Using their own hand as a canvas, each participant in this workshop will take a creative window of time to notice the possibility and power that lies within them, and then make a pledge to claim one I CAN to end violence in their lives. By participating in the workshop, participants will join a movement and a community that supports their vision and those of others taking steps to end violence in our communities.

 

 

AWBW wants to support Leaders throughout the country to take an additional step of using the I CAN WE CAN workshop to engage their community. Using art to move your community towards change is a powerful and inviting Community Engagement strategy. We encourage you to include members of the broader community in this project (volunteers, board, staff, personal friends), as it truly takes all of us to create change. Documenting the art created by survivors and non-survivors you share this project with via photography is an essential step in using art to engage your community through this project. The details of the Community Engagement aspects of this project are outlined throughout this workshop in italics.

 

Pre-workshop Planning:
The first step in leading this workshop is to take a moment to consider when, where, how, and with whom you will gather to create.

You will also need to decide in advance if you have the capacity to offer this workshop as a Community Engagement opportunity. Through documenting the workshop and uploading your artwork to the AWBW I CAN WE CAN website, you can share your agency's online gallery through social media or as a link.

Leaders not able to take this additional step are still encouraged to use this workshop with survivors, staff, and in their communities. This project offers a creative window of time to notice what we all can do to end violence and welcome them to join by adding their name to our anonymous online pledge.

 

 

 

 

To help you prepare to facilitate this workshop please consider the following:
Prepare yourself: Be sure to try out the project yourself, in advance, from beginning to end. This is very important and will give you an idea of what your participants will be experiencing during the workshop and how you want to organize your supply layout and timeline.

Make arrangements to offer your group ample time for check-ins, creation, processing, and a closing circle (and photography). You may even consider creating an outline of how you will manage your workshop time and share it with the group to help them pace their creation process.

To get an idea of what the I CAN WE CAN workshop is like, watch this short video of an AWBW community workshop: click here. 

Prepare your supplies: You might be surprised by the materials and how they feel as you use your hand as a canvas. Becoming familiar with the supplies and the creation process yourself will make it much easier to support those you are leading and also identify any supplies you would like to include or omit. The list below is simply a suggested list of supplies; we welcome you to be bold, get creative and add any supplies you like such as Henna or cosmetic make-up. Anything goes!

Prepare your group: Some people may have preconceived notions about art. You may want to begin by asking your group, “Who is scared of art? Who has not done art since grade school?” After they reply, it is a wonderful opportunity to assuage any apprehension by assuring the participants that there is no wrong way to do this project. "During Windows time we have the opportunity to focus on enjoying the process and allowing your authentic expression to come out."

Final Note to facilitator: When guiding an empowerment art group of any size, creating a safe and calming environment is of utmost importance. To help you “set the stage” for your I CAN WE CAN group, we have included a welcome that promotes empowerment using AWBW’s philosophy of creating a window of safety, freedom, creativity, and respect. You will also want to add your intention for this workshop and what your role will be in the group. Explain in advance if you plan to participate or be in the room as a compassionate observer to support and document their I CAN WE CAN pledge.

If necessary, remember to establish guidelines with input from group members. Guidelines should include mutual respect for one another, acceptance of all feelings and expressions, and an agreement of confidentiality.

 

 

 

Timeframe:
1-2 hour(s) to facilitate the I CAN WE CAN workshop only.
2-3 hours to facilitate workshop and document it for the community engagement project and online exhibit. Add an additional hour to make this workshop part of AWBW's Community Engagement Project and have a personalized gallery created of your groups artwork on AWBW's I CAN WE CAN website.

Additional Set-Up/Prep Instructions for Community Engagement:
Set aside 2 hours of uninterrupted space and time to lead this workshop with a group. The 2-hour time frame is recommended to provide enough time for check-ins, creation, processing, a closing circle, and photography.

You may want to designate a wall space or use a poster board or other blank wall or material to use as the background for the photos to be taken in front of. This is especially important because when working indoors, space is limited. Lighting should also be taken into consideration to ensure the photos are of high quality and representative of the participants' creations. We also encourage you to first practice using the camera that you will use during the workshop so that you are comfortable photographing the creations.

To expedite the photograph taking process, it is helpful to have the Art/Media Releases available for the participants to complete at the beginning of the workshop. Ask the participants to bring their Art/Media Release with their name written legibly on it when you take their photographs. This is very important since it will allow you to match the artwork to necessary releases, prior to uploading them to the I CAN WE CAN gallery.

Additional supplies:
Camera
Art/Media Release for each participant
Art/Media Release for each participant - Spanish

 

 

 

Materials:
Face paint, makeup, washable markers - anything washable to write on skin
Eyeliner pencils
White-out pens
Paint brushes and/or sponges to apply face paint
Pens
Copy paper for journaling and sketching
Non-bleeding tissue paper and permanent markers (you can write on the paper and then apply it to your hand using water!)
Scissors
Spray bottle for water
Water
Baby wipes or make-up remover and cotton balls
Music
See I CAN WE CAN gallery for more supply ideas!
Pledge Sheet Sign-in

 

 

I CAN WE CAN Workshop Steps:
Step 1: Welcome
"This is 'a window of time' to practice respecting your thoughts, feelings, needs, and vision. This workshop is designed to enable us to re-focus our energy from the things we think we cannot do, to what each of us is capable of doing to end violence in our lives and in those around us! Be gentle with yourself and honor all that has come before this moment. Embrace and notice that today you are safe and free to choose I CAN.

"As you notice your power and the possibility that lies within you, know that whether what comes to you seems 'too small' to be important or seems 'too big' to be possible, please try to trust that your ideas are just right. When you truly honor your heart, you can create a change that ripples out from you to those around you and to the community at large, as part of a global change. Your I CAN, no matter how small or big is part of changing the world. If you need to take a break or opt out of any aspect of the project, please do so. If you need some support, let me know, as part of my role here today is to be here for each of you."

 

 

Step 2: Check-in:
Take a moment to check-in with the group by asking each person to share their name and a word or a sentence about how they are feeling in this moment. "Are you feeling nervous, excited, afraid, or happy? Please know that today is about you and you are safe and encouraged to do, say, and feel whatever is your unique expression.

"Who would like to start the opening circle sharing your name and how you feel about being here today?"

The check-in is important since it brings everyone's voice into the room and allows for connection and trust.

 

 

 


Step 3: Warm-up:
"Many of us have heard all of all our lives that we can’t have or be who or do what we really want, whether it was someone in our family, friends, society, our community, or even our own thoughts. Maybe one of the things you have been told is that 'it is not possible to live free from violence' or that 'it is selfish to get what you want or you feel you deserve.'

"We are going to take a moment to release those doubts and 'I Can't' thoughts and notice the power we already have inside. Pick a partner to share for one minute about something that you thought could not do, or were told you could not do, but you did and it made you stronger as a result. It can be anything you would like to share. We will take turns sharing for the full minute so that each person can share one at a time. I will help you take turns by timing a minute and letting you know when it is time to switch speakers."

After everyone has shared: Validate the group by thanking them for taking the time to notice that they have the power to do what they want.

 

Step 4: Introduction to the Creation Process:
"The I CAN WE CAN project is about the difference we can ALL make in ending all forms of abuse by taking a moment, a creative 'window of time,' to notice our own personal vision and commitment to end violence using our own hands.

"Today each of us will make a personal commitment or pledge for ending violence in our own lives. Please remember that there is no wrong way to participate in this project and every aspect of this workshop is voluntary. Please honor your feelings, thoughts, and ideas about how you want to create your expression for ending violence."

Step 5: Releasing "I Can’ts" (Optional step):

 

 

 

 

 

In preparing to move the threshold of what we can do to help end violence, it can be quite powerful to take some time looking closely at any "I Can'ts" we carry. Be aware that acknowledging what we feel we can’t do can bring up intense feelings in participants. This is a step that is done with the intention of unburdening participants from perceived limitations and negative thoughts.

If you choose to do this exercise, be sure to allow 5 to 10 minutes for participants to free-write or journal without stopping and editing, about any "I Can'ts" they can think of. Next, ask them to share what came up for them with a partner or with the group (allow for at least 5 min. per participant). Lastly, you can provide some way to encourage the participants to let go of their "I Can’ts," whether it is by literally destroying them or creating a ceremony to unburden themselves of their "I Cant's."

Step 6: I CAN Reading (Optional step)
Reading an inspirational poem or even a quotation can be a powerful and a quick way to prepare your group. Below, we have included a reading by Marianne Williamson that one of our Leaders has found to be useful in facilitating this workshop. After doing a reading, you might try a brief relaxation to help participants get centered before beginning the creation process. Feel free to share another poem, story, or quote that you find inspiring and pertinent to this project.

"Before we begin creating, I want to share a reading called Our Deepest Fear by Marianne Williamson to help encourage us to think boldly and envision what I CAN we want to embrace today.”

“Our deepest fear is not that we are inadequate. Our deepest fear is that we are powerful beyond measure. It is our light, not our darkness that most frightens us. We ask ourselves, 'Who am I to be brilliant, gorgeous, talented, fabulous?'' Actually, who are you not to be? You are a child of God. Your playing small does not serve the world. There is nothing enlightened about shrinking so that other people won't feel insecure around you. We are all meant to shine, as children do. We were born to make manifest the glory of God that is within us. It's not just in some of us; it's in everyone. And as we let our own light shine, we unconsciously give other people permission to do the same. As we are liberated from our own fear, our presence automatically liberates others.”

 

 

Step 7: Brief Relaxation
"Now, if you feel comfortable enough to do so, please close your eyes or just sit quietly. Take a minute to breathe and think about or imagine your vision for your I CAN. Try to picture it in your mind, however it comes to you, as an image, a place, or a list of things you truly want. Notice how it feels in your body to make this pledge to yourself and share it with the world. Do you feel joy, power, peace? Take as long as you need but remember that your I CAN might be something simple and personal or it can be your greatest vision. Keeping your vision and the poem in mind, be bold when creating your I CAN hand! "

 

Step 8: I CAN Creation:
"Now, think about being part of a circle of people around the globe committed to ending violence. If each of us notices a new step we want to claim and act on, we can move the world. What I CAN do you want to claim today? Again, no idea is too small or too large. Just notice what resonates in your heart as most meaningful for you. When you are ready, begin to create your I CAN hand using your hand as your canvas. Place your I CAN message on it however you like. Your I CAN expression can be painted on, glued on or placed on paper and held in the palm of your hand. Anything goes! We will create art that represents the I CAN each of our hearts is telling us to reach for and we will using our own hand as a canvas for that expression. "

 

Step 9:  Documenting I CAN Pledge Hands:
You may want to have a camera ready and encourage the participants to have you take their picture once they are done creating. This can streamline the photography process since people will finish creating at different times.

"Taking a photo of your I CAN hand is part of the creative process so be as creative as you like with it. Your I CAN hand could be against whatever background you wish, a color of paper, your face, blades of grass, or torn/shredded I Can'ts--whatever most powerfully expresses your I CAN!"

Step 10:  Closing Sharing:
You may want to end by giving each participant an opportunity to share anything they want with the group about their experience with the workshop. After each person is done creating you can say, “Now I would like to give everyone an opportunity to share something about their experience here today. We will go around the room and each take turns sharing anything you want about your I CAN pledge, what you created, and your overall experience with the workshop.”

Step 11:  Participant Evaluations and Workshop Closing
Pass out participant evaluations and thank all participants for taking a window of time to notice their strength and what they CAN do to end abuse! Share with them that by creating their I CAN pledge they are joining other survivors and non-survivors coming together to end abuse. If possible, provide the participants the pledge sheet sign-in to add their names (or pseudonyms) and join the I CAN WE CAN movement. After the workshop, you will need to go the I CAN WE CAN website to add the names from the pledge sign-in by clicking "Join Us."

 

 

Step 12: Submit I CAN WE CAN Pledge Hands for Customized Online Exhibit
Let the group know that you will be adding their voices to the I CAN WE CAN project by uploading a photo of their creation to the I CAN WE CAN website. Or, when appropriate, you could ask the participants to upload their photo themselves and sign the I CAN WE CAN pledge online. To keep your groups' pledge hands together, be sure to enter them using your program name. If possible share the online gallery with participants and let them know that their artwork and pledge will help inspire others to do what they can to end abuse in their own lives and their communities. Finally, be sure to share your online gallery or own pledge hand with your community using the tools provided in the I CAN WE CAN website.

 

 

 

 

Tips

Supply tips for participants:

• Feel free to plan and gather all materials you will need create you hand before you start working,   since using only one hand will make it more difficult to work.

• Washable markers on tissue paper may run and stain when wet, so be sure to cover your work surface and clothing. The colored tissue paper may also run and stain your hands. Tissue squares will run.

• When you wet the paper, the washable markers will run, so use only permanent markers with the tissue paper.

  • Even washable markers may not wash off right away, so you may have your I CAN with you all day (depending on the number of times you wash your hands).

  • Be mindful of the amount of face paint you are taking; a little goes a long way and you can always come back for more.

  • Be gentle when writing on tissue paper with permanent markers and/or white out pens since they may rip the paper.

  • Sharpies and other permanent markers will stain your hand for several days.

  • Use scratch paper if you wish to sketch your design prior to creating
description: Using their own hand as a canvas, each participant in this workshop will take a creative window of time to notice the possibility and power that lies within them, and then make a pledge to claim one I CAN to end violence in their lives. By participating in the workshop participants will be joining a movement and a community that supports their vision and those of others taking steps to end violence in our communities.
notes:
Workshop Variations
Shrinky Dinks
Materials:
Shrinky Dink material (Ruff-N-Ready)
Adult hand template
Child hand template
Permanent markers
Colored pencils and sharpeners
Scissors
Hole puncher
Toaster oven
Beads (optional)
1/8 inch ribbon, yarn, embriodery thread, or craft wire

Creation:
"Now that you have identified an I CAN, it is time to create a Shrinky Dink to serve as a tangible reminder of your I CAN. Place your I CAN message on the shrinky paper however you like. Your I CAN expression can be words, swirls, colors, shapes. Anything goes! You are all incredibly powerful individuals and I invite you to be bold, let go of judgment, and allow your creative juices to flow!" 

Step One:
When creating the Shrinky Dinks, invite the participants to use the templates provided or create their own designs. Remind them to color on the rough side of the Shrinky Dink if using colored pencils; they can use permanent markers on both sides.

Step Two:
When the participants are finished coloring, they may use scissors to cut their Shrinky Dink into a shape. Then they will use the hole punch to create a hole in the Shrinky Dink. Remind them to be sure not to punch the hole too close to the edge of the Shrinky Dink paper.

Step Three:
Once the group members are done coloring, cutting, and punching a hole into their Shrinky Dink, they are ready for baking. Place the Shrinky Dink on a flat metal tray and place inside the toaster oven. We have found it is best to place a piece of a paper bag on the metal tray inside the oven with a corner turned up to make it easier to handle. Bake at 300 degrees until Shrinky Dink has completely flattened (this will take about one minute). Watch the amazing transformation! Remove the Shrinky Dink and allow it to cool.

Step Four:
Now the Shrinky Dink is ready for decorating with ribbon and beads. Thread ribbon through the hole and add beads. If you do not have access to ribbon you can just have the participants string the Shrinky Dinks from embroidery thread, yarn or wire. 

Clay Hands
Materials:
Super Sculpey Polymer Clay (have multiple colors available)
Toaster Oven
Hand shaped cookie cutter
Small coffee straws or skewers
1/8" ribbon, yarn, embroidery thread or craft wire
Beads (optional)
Permanent markers (metallic colors look great on dark colored clay)
White-out pens

Pre-workshop prep:
Prepare several Sculpey balls, enough for each person, in various colors. It is a great idea to demonstrate how to make swirly or marbled shapes out of Sculpey.

Creation:
Step One:
To blend the clay, choose at least three colors. Use no more than a pinch of each color. When choosing your clay, you may want to choose colors that feel powerful to you - any colors that come to mind when you think, "I CAN."

Step Two:
Roll each color into a "snake."

Step Three:
Wrap each "snake" around each other like a candy-cane and twist together.
Tip: Use at least three different colors of clay when blending them together. It also looks great when the colors complement each other.

Step Four:
Keep twisting the "snakes" until the colors are blended just the way you want them.
Tip: Be careful not to over-blend the colors as they can start to look muddy.

Step Five:
Roll the "snakes" into a ball. If you want, repeat steps 4 and 5 several times to create a more marbled effect.

Step Six:
Using a pen or a marker roll the ball flat to be about 1/4 inch thick. Use a hand-shaped cookie cutter to cut the clay into the shape of a hand. Use a coffee straw, skewer or pencil to make a hole at the top so you can hang the hand after it bakes.
Tips:
1) Before using the cookie cutter, pIck up and flip the clay periodically so it doesn't stick to the paper/surface you are working on.  
2) It's important to make sure that the clay is at least 1/4 of an inch thick; if they clay is any thinner the hand will easily break.
3) If the clay is sticking to the cookie cutter. it is helpful to put the clay (after the balls have been flattened) in the refrigerator and then use the cookie cutter after the clay is cold.
4) When making the hole in the hand, make sure it is not too close to the edge (to prevent the hand from breaking).

Step Seven:
Using a foil lined tray, place the clay hand in the oven. Bake the Sculpey at 275 degrees for 15 minutes (for each ¼ inch of clay thickness). Always allow the clay to cool completely before handling it.

Step Eight:
"Now that you have identified an I CAN, it is time to create on your I CAN clay hand to serve as a tangible reminder of your I CAN. Place your I CAN message on the clay hand using the permanent markers and/or white out pens however you like. Your I CAN expression can be words, swirls, colors, shapes. Anything goes! You are all incredibly powerful individuals and I invite you to be bold, let go of judgment, and allow your creative juices to flow!"
Tip: If the clay hands are dark in color, metallic permanent markers work great to make sure the color stands out.

Step Nine:
Encourage the participants to use ribbon, yarn, embroidery thread or wire to hang their I CAN hand and use beads to decorate.
Tip: If you offer beads, keep in mind that it will add significant time to the creation process.

Paper Collage
Materials:
Paper in assorted styles, textures, patterns and colors (rice, metallic, novelty, card stock, etc.)
Glue sticks
Permanent markers (metallic colors look great on dark paper)
White out pens
Scissors

Technical Demonstration:
Share about the different types of paper and writing utensils that are available. Demonstrate how the permanent markers and white out pens draw beautifully on every type of paper. You may want to show your participants the different effects you can get by layering the paper. You can also show them how adding a background image can add hidden meaning and also make a collage "pop!"

Another option is to encourage participants to select materials and glue them down without asking yourself 'why' you are choosing these particular materials. Work 'from your instincts' and cut, glue, scribble, and draw out anything that feels right at the moment.

Another wonderful collage technique is to not use scissors. Tearing the paper adds more texture!

Creation:
"Now that you have identified an I CAN, it is time to collage a paper hand to serve as a tangible reminder of your I CAN. Using the collage materials and glue, create your I CAN however you like. Your I CAN expression can be words, swirls, colors, shapes. Anything goes! You are all incredibly powerful individuals and I invite you to be bold, let go of judgment, and allow your creative juices to flow!"


Pre-cut Paper Hands
Materials:
Paper in assorted colors (card stock is preferred)
Adult hand template
Child hand template
Small hand template with fingers together (works great to create a bookmark)
Pencil
Scissors
Permanent markers (metallic colors look great)
White-out pens

Pre-workshop prep:
Use a template or trace your hand (with a pencil) on a piece of heavyweight paper (card stock is ideal). Then use scissors to cut out the hand. Please note that if you are cutting multiple hands, this can be time consuming and may leave your hands feeling sore. If possible, recruit volunteers to help trace and cut the hands.

Creation:
"Now that you have identified an I CAN, it is time to create your very own paper I CAN hand.  Your creation will serve as a tangible reminder of the I CAN you have chosen to embrace today. Place your I CAN on the paper however you like. Your I CAN expression can be words, swirls, colors, shapes. Anything goes! You are all incredibly powerful individuals and I invite you to be bold, let go of judgment, and allow your creative juices to flow!"  


Paper Hand Mandala
Materials:
Poster board or large piece of foam core
Glue dots
Easel, stand, or table to display the mandala

Pre-workshop Prep:
Make sure you have an easel, stand, or table to place the poster board or foam core on so that the mandala is highly visible to the participants. If possible, having the board or foam core in an upright position encourages participation since it allows people to see the beautiful creation unfold. Before the workshop begins, you may want to prepare a hand and attach it to the middle of the board. This will ensure the mandala is centered. Having pre-cut paper hands in multiple colors helps create a colorful and eye-catching mandala.

Creation:
After each person is done creating their I CAN hand, ask them if they'd like to have their photo taken in front of the mandala. We've found that people, especially youth, love having their photo taken. Because many people have camera phones, you can offer to take the picture with their phone so they leave with a tangible reminder of their creation.

Next, ask if they'd like to take their hand home or if they want to add it to the mandala. If they choose to add it to the mandala, attach a glue dot to the base of the palm or wrist of the hand (on the back of the paper they created on). This helps ensure that everyone attaches their hand in a uniform way, and also creates a visually pleasing and cohesive mandala.

Note: If you have enough supplies, you can encourage participants to make one for your board and one to take home.

 

Henna

Henna Background and History:
Henna tattoos are a kind of temporary body art involving the application of a natural dye paste which leaves behind a reddish-brown color. It is traditionally applied to women's hands and feet for religious ceremony, weddings and other celebrations.

Materials:
Ready-made henna paste - before you purchase, check the expiration date and ensure there are no additives or preservatives and no para-phenylenediamine (PPD)
Plastic bowl and spoon
Lemon juice
Sugar
Plastic wrap
Triangular piece of cellophane or mylar, or squeeze bottle
Toothpick or straight pen
Cotton balls
Butter knife or other blunt object
Toilet paper
Plastic wrap
Tape

Pre-workshop prep:
We strongly recommend watching a video about how to make and apply henna. YouTube has many examples, this is our favorite. You will also want to apply a very small drop of the henna on each of your participants skin to test if they are allergic. The participant will feel a cooling sensation upon application. Please note this is a very important step as henna can permanently scar skin if the person has an allergy to it. Also make sure to avoid "black henna" ink containing para-phenylenediamine (PPD), a coal-tar product that is approved for use in hair dye but is known to cause skin reactions in some people. Avoid using any henna pastes that contain preservatives or additives. Traditional reddish-brown henna is not part of the warning. Please note that henna will stain any fabric it touches so make sure to use tablecloths and aprons.

Creation: (either follow the steps below or watch this video)

Step 1:
Check the date on the ready-made henna paste, the fresher the paste, the darker the henna will appear. Once purchased, it should be kept in your refrigerator for further freshness.

Step 2:
Put Henna paste in a plastic bowl, cover tightly with plastic wrap, and let it sit in a warm place for 30 minutes to several hours. You will know it is ready when it turns from green to dark brown or puddles of liquid have formed on top.

Step 3:
If you do not have a squeeze bottle, roll a piece of cellophane or mylar into a cone shape.  Tape the seem, fill the cone about half way with henna paste, fold the top down and tape it shut. Cut off tip of cone right before you begin applying. If you have a squeeze bottle, fill the bottle with henna paste.

Step 4:
Using a cone or squeeze bottle, apply henna paste to clean, dry skin.

Step 5:
"Now that you have identified an I CAN, it is time to create an I CAN on your hand to serve as a tangible reminder of the I CAN you choose to embrace today. Using the henna paste create your I CAN however you like. Your I CAN expression can be words, swirls, colors, shapes. Anything goes! You are all incredibly powerful individuals and I invite you to be bold, let go of judgment, and allow your creative juices to flow!" Use a toothpick or pin to fix any mistakes and clear the applicator.

Step 6:
When henna paste is dry, use a cotton ball to dab a glaze of equal parts lemon juice and sugar. This can help to preserve the tattoo, allowing it to remain on the skin for as long as 3 weeks. According to HennaTattoos.com, it is important to avoid exposing the tattoo to direct sunlight while the paste is still on. To ensure that your tattoo lasts as long as possible, avoid wetting it for at least one hour after it has been applied. When you are in the shower or in the bathtub, try to gently clean the area with water and mild soap instead of using an exfoliating wash or loofah sponge which could wear away at the dye, causing your tattoo to fade. If possible, let the henna dry for up to twelve hours. If you leave it on over night, cover the henna with first toilet paper and then plastic wrap.

Step 7:
After the henna has set and dried, flake it off using a plastic spoon or blunt object. You can even rub your hands together to allow for the pieces to flake off. Avoid washing with soap for 24 hours to allow the henna stain to last longer. You can squeeze a lemon on top to allow for further vibrancy and wash it off after 20 minutes.

title: Personal Needs Flower
objective: This workshop aims to give children an opportunity to identify and explore their personal needs by creating a flower that represents each of their needs.
materials:
• Colored construction paper

  • CrayPas (crayons, or oil pastels)

  • Glue sticks

  • Pens

  • Colored pencils

  • Markers

  • Envelops
setup:
Sample table set up

You can lay out all the supplies where they are easily accessible.

You may wish to prepare a sample in advance so that your demonstration can go quickly and leave plenty of time for creating. If you wish to do so, we suggest creating a simple sample so that participants aren't overwhelmed by any "artistic" challenges.

As a facilitator, you have complete freedom to alter or adapt any portion or element of this workshop to cater to your specific group's needs.
warm_up:
"Before we create our Personal Needs Flower, I'd like to invite you to join me in a relaxation exercise to help us begin to listen to our needs. If you prefer, you can simply observe. Observing is participating."
 
"For those of you who want to participate, if you feel comfortable closing your eyes, please do so and get comfortable in your seat. If you prefer, you can keep your eyes open. However you are most comfortable. Wiggle about until you feel cozy and comfortable. Check in and notice your body from the top of your head, moving slowly through to the tips of your toes. As you move your attention down your body, I’m going to be asking you some questions. Let the questions in and allow the answers to come up in whatever way feels comfortable. For some of you, it might mean hearing an answer in your mind. For others, it could be that you see the answers as pictures in your mind. Any way the answers come up for you is fine."
 

  • "Can you notice what your needs are?"

  • "Do you have any physical needs?"

  • "Are you comfortable or do you need to wiggle a bit to get comfortable?"

  • "Are you too warm or cool? Do you need the temperature changed?"

  • "Are you breathing?"

  • "Do you need to slow down your breathing by taking a deep inhale and exhale?"

  • "Are you thirsty? Are you tired? Are you hungry?"

  • "Are you aware of any emotional needs you have right now?"

  • "Do you have a need for comfort? Security? Safety?"

  • "Do you need to have someone safe to talk to? Is there something you'd like to share with that person?"


"I encourage you to take time to notice any hidden needs that you have. Tune in to your belly, to your heart, to the senses in your body. Pay attention to pictures, colors and memories that may appear. Just relax and take your time as you ask yourself, 'What are my needs'?"

"With these thoughts and pictures in your mind, begin to think about your flower. How would you like to create it? Will it look like a flower or something else? What color comes to mind for the center? Can you picture a face that represents the peaceful, nurturing, supportive part of yourself that is here to help you and notice your needs? Whenever you are ready, you can open your eyes and begin to create your flower."
creation:
Personal Needs Flower creation

As the children create their flowers, you can remind them that there is no right or wrong way to create their flower. The only important thing is that they keep noticing and honoring their own needs. You can encourage them to keep asking the question, "What are my needs?"

You can also encourage the children to decide how they want to finish their flower. Do they want to glue it together? Do they want to create any extra petals to carry with them to add more needs as they are discovered? Or do they wish to keep the pedals separate and keep them in an envelop (if provided).
closing:
For the closing, you can give children who feel comfortable doing so an opportunity to share about their Personal Needs Flower, and any discoveries they made as they took time to notice their needs. Of course, this is optional, and if no one feels comfortable sharing, that's perfectly okay.

You can remind the children: "This process does not end today. You can reflect back on it anytime, however it best serves you. Noticing what you need to feel safe, happy and healthy in your life is one of the most important jobs you will ever have, and one job that no one else can do for you."
description: This workshop invites participants to identify and explore their personal needs by creating a flower that represents each of their needs.
tips:
Note About Conflicting Needs:
Sometimes a person might notice that their different needs seem to be in conflict with each other. For example, the need to have more quiet alone time and the need to spend more playful, fun time with her children. This is okay.

The purpose of this workshop is to reveal the many needs, even conflicting ones that can be seen as part of our entire unique personality. By placing all the needs around a circle to create a flower, we see them all together.
optional_materials:
You can also facilitate this workshop using printable worksheets. If you are utilizing the worksheets in lieu of the regular workshop materials, be sure to send a digital copy or print them out for your participants if you are meeting in person.

  • Personal Needs Flower (English)

  • Personal Needs Flower (Spanish)

   
Personal Needs Flower     Personal Needs Flower
(English)     (Spanish)
introduction:
"Many of us are good at taking care of other people. Maybe you like to help your younger brothers and sisters with things they can't do for themselves, like brushing their teeth or showing them how to ride a bike. Maybe you've made a friend laugh when they were feeling sad or upset. At school, you might pass out papers or sharpen some pencils to help your teacher. Whatever it may be, we all have helped take care of someone. By doing this, you have taken care of their needs. Just like other people, we also have needs of our own. Today, you will have a chance to notice your personal needs and create something that can remind you that taking care of them is very important."

"Before we begin, I'd like to talk about what a need is. What do you think a need is? Needs are things that we should pay attention to and take care of in order for us to be healthy, safe, and happy."

"Let's start with the needs that are much easier to recognize; our physical needs. Our body has a great way of letting us know what it needs. For example, when we're hungry our bodies might make a grumbling sound, letting us know that it's time to eat. When we run around a lot, we may sweat and get really thirsty. When we have a cold, our bodies can cough and sneeze, telling us that it might need medicine. These are some ways that our bodies talk to us about our physical needs. These kinds of needs are pretty hard to ignore because they are so important and ignoring them can be serious. What would happen if we never ate, drank, or took care of our colds? Taking care of our physical needs keeps us healthy. What are some other physical needs that we have?"

"Some needs are a little harder to notice. These kinds of needs deal with our feelings and they can be easier to ignore. Our emotional needs are very important because they focus on feeling safe, comfortable, and loved. When we were younger, our parents or caregivers took care of a lot of this for us. They made us feel safe, comfortable, and loved by wrapping us in blankets, soothing us when we cried, and making sure we felt loved by either showing it and/or saying it. As we grow older, we slowly begin to learn how to do this on our own. Let's quietly think to ourselves about the ways we help ourselves feel safe, comfortable, and loved. It can be that you always listen to the rules you're given from your parents/caregivers, teachers, and other responsible adults. You may have a really good group of friends that you feel comfortable around to share anything with. And maybe you like the feeling of a great big hug."

"Now that you've learned more about your needs, you'll get a chance to create something that will remind you of how important they are."

"Before we begin, I want you to know that this is your window of time. It's a time for you to focus on your thoughts, needs and feelings. During this time, there is no right or wrong way to participate or create. You can follow along, or you may want to do something different, it's completely up to you. During your window of time, you have complete freedom to choose. I am here to support you in any way that I can, so please feel free to ask for what you need."
demonstration:
Torn flower center - adding a face to represent the peaceful, nurturing side of you
 
Drawing on petals
 
Keep your peals in a pile like a special deck of cards to carry with you in a special envelope

"In a moment, you'll have a chance to create a Personal Needs Flower. Even though it's called a flower, it can look like anything you want it to."

Step 1: Creating the Center
"The first step is to create the center of your flower. With the colored paper, you can tear a circle as small or as large as you would like. Tearing, instead of cutting, can be fun. You can create this center to represent you. You might want to draw a face that represents the peaceful, nurturing, supportive part of yourself that is here to help you. Whatever you choose is up to you."

Step 2: Creating the Petals
"The next step is to create the petals, each one representing one of your needs. To make each petal, you can choose a piece of colored paper, it could be same, or a different color for each, and tear it into whatever shape or size you want. The best part of this activity, is that you get to choose what your flower looks like. It could look like a rose, a tulip, a daisy, it could even look like a tree."

Step 3: Completing Your Flower
"The final step is deciding how you want to finish your flower. You could use a glue stick to attach your petals together, and glue them onto a larger piece of construction paper. Or, you could collect them in a pile that can travel with you. If you are going to keep your petals loose, you might want to decorate an envelope later on to keep them in (if you haven't provided envelops for them)."

"You can finish your flower in any way that helps remind you of the needs you noticed today. You could even make some extra petals without anything on them yet so you can add more needs as you discover them."

“Any questions? Remember, it means something very special to take this kind of time. This is your special time to be curious and playful and listen to your needs."

title: Heart Stories / Historias del Corazón
objective: This workshop provides participants an opportunity to listen to their hearts, value the stories within them, and be affirmed that others want to hear them, through the creation of a Heart Story art piece.
materials:
• Art supplies and materials for Heart Stories

    Cray-Pas

  • Thick white paper 5 1/2” X 7” (cover stock)

  • Brushes

  • Water cups/paper towels

  • Watercolors, tempera paints, or puffy paints

    • Note: Watercolors work best for having the Cray-Pas show through. Foam paint also works well with Cray-Pas resist.

  • Acrylic paints or puffy paints have the most bright and cool colors (but they stain clothes)

  • Tempera paints are good because they are washable (but they are thicker and tend to crack and get dull when they dry)
setup: You may wish to set up the materials so they are easy to access for all participants.
warm_up:
You may give participants an opportunity for an open discussion about their hearts by inviting them to answer "Heart Talk" questions, if they are comfortable doing so. Again, this is optional for you and them, depending on the needs and expectations of your group. If you choose to incorporate this warm-up into your workshop, you can ask them all or some of the following questions, or come up with questions and prompts of your own which may better suit your participants' needs.

We recommend writing some or all of the questions in a place that the group can read them. You can invite the participants to choose to answer three of the questions that they feel comfortable sharing.

Possible Heart Talk Questions:

  • What is something your heart is proud of?

  • Would you care to share something that makes your heart happy?

  • If your heart was a color today, what color would it be and why?

  • What makes your heart laugh?

  • If your heart could do something it has never done before, what would it do?

  • What makes your heart feel safe?

  • What makes your heart feel scared?

  • What makes your heart strong?

  • What makes your heart beat faster?

  • What makes your heart happy?

  • How do you look when your heart is sad?

  • How do you look when your heart is happy?

  • What does your heart need?

"Thank you all for sharing so bravely and openly. I truly was able to see and feel the beauty and love inside of all of your hearts and you."

"Now that you have thought deeply about what your hearts look like, feel like, and need, I'd like to invite you to create Heart Stories to share the different feelings you have in your heart. Maybe you would like to create your heart story based on what your heart would say if it could talk. Perhaps your heart wants to tell and express what color it would be inside and out. Or your heart could even share how it feels, what it looks like, etc. or any other way you would like to express your heart. There is no wrong answer. It's whatever you want it to be."
creation:
"This is your time to use as you wish. For those of you who wish to participate, I'd like to now invite you to create your heart story. This heart can look exactly like the heart inside your chest, it can be represented by the symbol of a heart, or it can look like something completely different. Feel free to follow your impulses and create whatever feels right to you using any of the materials you like. There is no wrong way to express yourself. And your creation does not need to include a heart shape. It can be whatever you want it to be."

"Now that you've created your amazing Heart Stories, I'd like to invite you to write any story that your hearts wants to tell. If you choose to, you can write down the story on your creation, on the back of the creation, or in your journal. You can write a word, random words, a sentence, poem, draw shapes and symbols, or not write anything at all. You have complete freedom to choose how you wish to do this. If you want, you can even turn your heart story into a beautiful card to share with others or to keep for yourself. How you create your "Heart Story" is up to you. You are the expert of your own heart."
closing:
You have the option to invite participants to end with a message to their hearts. You may invite them to share a way they want to take good care of their heart or give their heart love, or something else their heart needs. Sharing is completely optional.

"Thank you for creating and deeply sharing about your hearts and yourselves. Your hearts is beautiful and unique in its own way and each heart has an important story that needs to be heard. Whether you want to share this story with others is up to you.

Most importantly, I'd like you to remember that this heart is your own and it is capable of feeling, sharing, and giving many different emotions. You all have so much love to give and show and this creation can be a beautiful and tangible reminder of that.
description: This workshop supports participants in sharing their hearts and the stories they have to tell. This art creation provides an opportunity to listen to their hearts, value the stories within them, and be affirmed that others want to hear them, too.
objective_spanish: Este taller les brinda a las y los participantes la oportunidad de escuchar sus corazones, valorar las historias dentro de él y darse cuenta que otras personas desean escucharles, a través de la creación de una pieza de arte de una historia del corazón.
materials_spanish:
• Cray-Pas
• Papel grueso color blanco de 5 1/2 "X 7" 
• Pinceles
• Vasos de agua / toallas de papel
• Acuarelas, pinturas al témpera o pinturas de relieve
Nota: Las acuarelas funcionan mejor para que mostrarse a través de los Cray-Pas. La pintura de espuma también funciona bien con Cray-Pas.
• Las pinturas acrílicas o las pinturas de relieve tienen los colores más brillantes y frescos (pero manchan la ropa)
• Las pinturas témpera son buenas porque son lavables (pero son más gruesas y tienden a agrietarse y perder brillo cuando se secan)

Introducción: 5 min

setup_spanish: Es posible que desee preparar los materiales para que todo el grupo tenga acceso fácil a ellos.
warm_up_spanish:
Puede darles a las y los participantes la oportunidad de tener una discusión abierta sobre sus corazones invitándoles a responder las preguntas de "Charla del corazón", si se sienten cómodas o cómodos de hacerlo. Nuevamente, esto es opcional para usted y sus participantes, dependiendo de las necesidades y expectativas del grupo. Si elige incorporar este calentamiento en su taller, puede hacerles todas o algunas de las siguientes preguntas, o formular sus propias preguntas y sugerencias que puedan satisfacer mejor las necesidades de su grupo.

Recomendamos escribir algunas o todas las preguntas en un lugar donde el grupo pueda leerlas. Puede invitar a las y los participantes a elegir responder tres de las preguntas con las que se sientan más cómodas o cómodos.

Posibles preguntas para la “Charla del Corazón”:

o    ¿De qué es algo de lo que tu corazón se siente orgulloso?
o    ¿Te importaría compartir algo que haga feliz a tu corazón?
o    Si tu corazón fuera un color hoy, ¿de qué color sería y por qué?
o    ¿Qué hace reír a tu corazón?
o    Si tu corazón pudiera hacer algo que nunca ha hecho antes, ¿qué haría?
o    ¿Qué hace que tu corazón se sienta seguro?
o    ¿Qué hace que tu corazón se sienta asustado?
o    ¿Qué hace que tu corazón sea fuerte?
o    ¿Qué hace que tu corazón lata más rápido?
o    ¿Qué hace feliz a tu corazón?
o    ¿Cómo te ves cuando tu corazón está triste?
o    ¿Cómo te ves cuando tu corazón está feliz?
o    ¿Qué necesita tu corazón?

"Gracias a todas y todos por compartir tan valiente y abiertamente. Realmente se puede ver y sentir la belleza y el amor dentro de todos sus corazones y dentro de ustedes".

"Ahora que han pensado profundamente en cómo se ven, sienten y qué necesitan sus corazones, me gustaría invitarles a crear su propia Historia del Corazón para compartir los diferentes sentimientos que tiene cada quién en sus corazones. Tal vez les gustaría crear su propia historia del corazón basada en lo que su corazón diría si pudiera hablar. Tal vez su corazón quisiera contar y expresar qué color sería por dentro y por fuera. O su corazón podría incluso compartir cómo se siente, cómo se ve, etc. o cualquier otra forma de cómo le gustaría expresarse su corazón. No hay una respuesta incorrecta. Es de la forma que ustedes decidan que sea."
creation_spanish:
"Este es su momento y pueden usarlo como deseen. Para aquellas personas que desean participar, me gustaría invitarles a crear su historia de corazón. Este corazón puede verse exactamente como el corazón dentro de su pecho, puede ser representado por el símbolo de un corazón, o puede parecer algo completamente diferente. Siéntanse libres de seguir sus impulsos y crear lo que les parezca más adecuado utilizando cualquiera de los materiales que gusten. No hay una manera incorrecta de expresarse. Y su creación no tiene que incluir una forma de corazón. Puede ser lo que quieran que sea."

"Ahora que han creado sus increíbles Historias del corazón, me gustaría invitarles a escribir cualquier historia que sus corazones quisieran contar. Si lo desean, pueden escribir la historia de su corazón, en la parte posterior de la creación, o en su diario. Pueden escribir una palabra, palabras al azar, una oración, un poema, dibujar formas y símbolos, o no escribir nada. Tienen total libertad para elegir cómo desean participar. Si desean, incluso pueden convertir su historia del corazón en una hermosa tarjeta para compartir con alguien más o guardarla para ustedes. La forma en la que creen su "Historia del corazón" depende completamente de ustedes. Ustedes son las expertas y expertos de su propio corazón."
closing_spanish:
Tiene la opción de invitar a las y los participantes a terminar con un mensaje para sus corazones. Puede invitarles a compartir la forma en que desean cuidar o darle amor a su corazón, o cualquier otra cosa que su corazón necesite. Si las personas desean compartir o no es completamente opcional.

"Gracias por crear y compartir sobre sus corazones y ustedes mismas y mismos. Sus corazones son hermosos y únicos a su manera y cada corazón tiene una historia importante que debe ser escuchada. Depende de cada quien, si desean compartir esta historia con el grupo.

Lo más importante que me gustaría que recuerden que este corazón es suyo y que es capaz de sentir, compartir y dar muchas emociones diferentes. Todas y todos ustedes tienen mucho amor para dar y mostrar y esta creación puede ser un hermoso y tangible recordatorio de eso.
