"Has anyone used Cray-Pas before? Cray-Pas are a mix of crayons and oil pastels."

If the participants are familiar with Cray-Pas, you may remind them that they are oil pastel and they really stand out when you press down hard on the paper. If the participants have not used Cray-Pas before, you can demonstrate how to use the materials by creating a sample together. This is entirely up to you.

"When you're creating, I'd like to encourage you think about what the shape of your heart is. What color or colors is it? How big is this heart or hearts? Is the heart colored in or open? Does the heart have a face? Are there are any symbols around it? Does a heart story actually have to feature a heart shape, or can it be anything you wish it to be? Feel free to get as creative as possible. Remember, there is no wrong way to do it." 

You can invite the participants to give their input and suggestions on how to create the group/sample Heart Story.

"Next, you have the opportunity to add paint on top of and around the Cray-Pas. You have complete freedom to choose any color and draw any shapes or lines that you like. You can color using circular motions, or cover all of the white space. It's completely up to you."

"In a moment, you'll have the opportunity to create your own Heart Story. Again, this is optional and if you choose to observe or do something else entirely, that is perfectly okay too. If you choose to create, I'd like to encourage you to think about the feeling that you would like your heart to portray. Would you like to represent sadness? Happiness? A confused or worried heart? A heart that is in love? Maybe even a heart that feels many different feelings at once? What color or colors would you like to use to represent this heart? If you like, you can press down hard on the Cray-Pas, so the color really stands out. If you prefer, you can continue to add as many colors as you feel your heart needs to properly represent what is inside it."

"When creating, if you use lots of water to dilute the paint, the Cray-Pas will show through the water colors. If you use thick paints with less water, the Cray-Pas image beneath it is harder to see. Anyway you like your Heart Story to look will be perfect."
demonstration_spanish:

Siéntanse libres de ser lo más creativo posible. Recuerden, no hay una forma incorrecta de hacerlo.”

Puede invitar a las y los participantes para que aporten sus sugerencias sobre cómo crear la historia del corazón grupal de muestra.

"A continuación, tendrán la oportunidad de agregar pintura sobre y alrededor del Cray-Pas. Tienen total libertad para elegir cualquier color y dibujar cualquier forma o línea que deseen. Puede colorear con movimientos circulares, o cubrir todos los espacios en blanco. Depende completamente de ustedes ".

"En un momento, tendrán la oportunidad de crear su propia historia del corazón. Nuevamente, esto es opcional y si eligen observar o hacer completamente otra cosa, eso también está perfectamente bien. Si eligen crear, me gustaría animarles a pensar en la sensación que les gustaría que su corazón retratara. ¿Les gustaría representar la tristeza? ¿Felicidad? ¿Un corazón confundido o preocupado? ¿Un corazón que está enamorado? title: Positive Piggies
objective: To invite participants to learn about positivity and the uplifting effects it has on themselves and others.
materials:
• Positive Piggies template (side A and B)

  • Pipe cleaners

  • Tape

  • Glue sticks

  • Pencils

  • Markers

  • Colored pencils

  • Crayons

  • Scissors

  • Beanbag for warm up
setup: You may print enough templates (side A and B) for your group. You may wish to cut small strips of paper out for children to write and draw positive messages and images on. Depending on the age group and/or your time constraints, you may wish to cut the pigs out in advance.
creation:
Color your pig.  
 
Cut your pig out.  
 
Make sure to cut the slit into the pig.  
 
Create the tail with a pipe cleaner.  
 
Glue the pig together with the tail in between each side.  
 
Write positive messages for yourself and others.  
   

You can begin by inviting the children who wish to participate to find a seat at the table. You have the option of doing a demo of the following steps or create along with them. It's entirely up to you.

Step 1: Coloring
Each pig consists of two sides (side A and side B). When coloring the pigs, can encourage the children to express their personalities because the pigs will be a representation of themselves. You can remind the children that they can choose any design, pattern, color that they choose and be as creative as they like to be. There is no wrong way to create.

Step 2: Cutting out the Pigs
You can cut each side of the pig out. Note that side A contains a coin slot to be cut out.

Step 3: Creating the Tail
Next, you can create a tail for the pig by either drawing one or using a pipe cleaner. For those who wish to use a pipe cleaner, you can demonstrate to them how to twist it around their finger to create a curly tail if you wish.

Step 4: Gluing Together
To finish, you can line up the two sides of the pig and use a glue stick around the outer perimeter to glue them together. For those who created a pipe cleaner tail, you can insert it between both templates and then glue the pieces down.

Keeping the glue only on the perimeter of the templates allows the finished art piece to act as a pocket, which is what we'd ideally want.

"Now I'd like to invite you to put something much more valuable than money inside these piggy banks. On these strips of paper, you have the opportunity to write positive, uplifting things for the other group members. Not only can you write positive things, you can even draw something that you think can bring a smile to their face."

You may wish to give a couple of examples of a positive message that would best suit your group's needs.

"When you're creating your positive messages and drawings, I'd like to encourage you to be generous and try to write something positive for everyone. Our goal is to write or draw three things for each person in the group. But if you choose to, you can only write it for one person, or if you don't feel comfortable writing anything, that is perfectly okay too. You can let the person know who the message or drawing is from or you can remain anonymous, it's completely up to you."

"Next, you can fold your strips of paper once or twice and walk over to that person's pig and slip it into their slot. You can keep it a secret if you want your friends to be surprised when they finally get our messages."

"Now, if you like, I'd like to encourage you to try to write or draw a couple of positive messages for yourself and slip them into your own slot. It's always nice to say good things about ourselves. By the time we're done with this workshop our pigs' bellies will be full of positive notes for you to read."
closing:
Finished piggy.
   

As a facilitator, you have complete freedom to close the workshop however you wish. One way would be to invite the children to take out one message and read it to themselves or the class, if they wish. Another option would be to give anyone who wishes, an opportunity to share anything they may have learned or anything they may have experienced while creating their art pieces.

"Taking a look around at all of these plump pigs, I'm so glad to see that you have lots of uplifting things to say about one another. If you like, you can take a moment to reach into the coin slots of your pigs and take out one message and read it. This is, of course, optional. You can save them and read them at your own time. If you do wish to read one of your messages now or later, I'd like to encourage you to think about what it says and really take it in and realize that you are an awesome person."

"As we finish up our workshop and take our pigs home, I'd like to encourage you to keep them in a safe place. When you're feeling down, or just need a little boost, you can head on over to that safe place and take a moment for yourself, take a strip of paper out and read it, and remind yourself of how special you are and will always be."
description: Participants are invited to explore positivity and the uplifting effects it can have on themselves and others.
optional_materials:
You can also facilitate this workshop using printable worksheets. If you are utilizing the worksheets in lieu of the regular workshop materials, be sure to send a digital copy or print them out for your participants if you are meeting in person.

  • Positive Piggies (Spanish)

   
Positive Piggies (English)     Positive Piggies (Spanish)
introduction:
What does it mean to be positive? In the dictionary, it says that positive is a good, affirmative, or constructive quality or attribute.

You can invite the children to think about and/or share what "being positive" means to them. You may wish to give examples of positive comments such as, "you are perfect just the way you are," "your smile makes people happy," or "you're a great listener." The idea is that children have an opportunity to express and define their own positive comments.

"Before we begin, I want you to know that this workshop is a window of time for you. This means that this is a safe space to notice your thoughts, feelings, and needs. Since this space is your window of time, everything you say or do is voluntary. I’ll offer a suggested workshop idea, share about the materials we have available, and invite you to create, but there’s no wrong way to do this. It doesn't matter what it looks like. What matters is taking this time to truly honor your thoughts and feelings, however they come out. If you can’t think of anything or draw a blank on what to create or write, feel free to just observe. However you choose to spend this time will be perfectly okay. This is your time. Please ask for what you need, and know that I’m here in support of you."
opening_circle:
"First, I'd like to invite those of you who wish to participate to create a positivity circle. A positivity circle is a circle of friends who share positive things about themselves and each other. I can start by tossing a beanbag to one of you. When you catch the beanbag, you can say your name, if you like, and then one positive thing about you or someone else in the circle. Remember, you can choose to just say 'pass' and toss the beanbag to someone who hasn't had a chance to speak yet, if you don't wish to participate. If you just want to observe, that is okay too. Whatever you choose do to will be perfect."

"As the beanbag is going around, I'd like to encourage you to take a look at the people in the circle and try to notice all of the great things about them. You can take a moment to think about all of the great things about yourself as well."

When the positivity circle is over, you have the option to invite the children to share how they felt about the things that were said about them. Feel free to keep a record of all the different feelings to reference during the closing circle, if you wish.

title: Sun Kisses, Moon Hugs
objective: Using the concepts and images in the picture book Sun Kisses, Moon Hugs, participants have an opportunity to identify, express, and work through their feelings about separation, anxiety, grief, and loss, through painting.
materials:
•  
      Sun Kisses, Moon Hugs book
       
     
      Optional printable worksheet

    Foam paint (BioColor; preferably 4 or 5 different colors)

  • Paint palettes (plates)

  • Brushes

  • Oil pastels (CrayPas)

  • Sun Kisses, Moon Hugs book (by Susan Bernardo and Courtney Fletcher)

You can also facilitate this workshop using this printable self-led worksheet. If you are utilizing this sheet in lieu of the regular workshop materials, be sure to send the sheet or print them out beforehand for your participants depending on the setting.
setup:
Table setup
 
  Foam paint

You can prepare the paint palettes by adding a small mound of foam paint (3-5 colors in total) onto a plate, keeping in mind that a little bit goes a long way. You can always replenish the colors later if needed.

You can lay out the supplies so that each participant has easy access to them.

It may be helpful to create a sample in advance to get a feel for the creation process. You can always modify the complexity of the creation process as you see fit.

You have complete freedom to alter or adapt any portion or element of this workshop to cater to your specific group's needs.
warm_up:
Depending on the wants, needs, and expectations of your group, you can ask the participants to follow along and read the story with you, invite them to close their eyes and simply listen to the story, if they feel comfortable doing so, or you may encourage them to gather around you and engage in the words and pictures in the book Sun Kisses, Moon Hugs together.

After reading the story, you can ask the participants to share if they saw something in the book, to which they felt connected. If time permitting, you can also invite them to share how or what in nature can help them feel connected to the people they love and miss.
creation:
Creation in process

"This is your window of time to practice respecting and connecting to your thoughts, feelings, visions, and anything else that comes up for you. There is no wrong way create; simply notice your needs and honor your expression. If this means just sitting and noticing what your heart is feeling or if you need to put your head down, or just observe, that is okay too."

"When you are ready, you can begin to create a drawing to represent you and the person or thing you miss. Just like in the book, you can connect the two figures using the feelings in your heart, ideas from your imagination, images from the book, something in nature like sunshine rays, a tree, rainbow, or something that you have to remind you of this special person or thing."
closing:
You can invite participants to volunteer and share their creations, anything they discovered, felt or experienced during the workshop, or anything else they may wish to share.

Afterwards:
"Thank you all for being here today. Remember that, if we look for it, there are always ways for us to connect to and share our embodiment of love with those we feel far away from. Your participation today, whether you chose to create or not, is a wonderful reminder of how close our loved ones and prized possessions can actually be."
description: Using the concepts and images in the picture book Sun Kisses, Moon Hugs, participants can identify, express, and work through their feelings about separation, anxiety, grief, and loss. Participants can develop positive coping strategies to maintain their sense of connection and well-being even when loves ones are not physically present. Using creativity in a gentle, encouraging, and supportive environment can help to build resilience.
optional_materials:
• Baby wipes

  • Sponges
introduction:
"Has anyone ever missed someone or something before? Whether the person you miss moved far away or as passed, or if you just saw them a few hours ago, this feeling of loss and separation can be really hard. Even when you miss someone, there are ways to feel connected to and be reminded of them. Today, we will get a chance to read Sun Kisses, Moon Hugs which explores ways to maintain connection, even when those we love are not physically present. We will then get an opportunity to express our feelings creatively, through a unique form of painting."

"Before we begin, I want you to know that this is your window of time. This means that this can be a safe space to notice your thoughts, feelings, and needs. Since this space is your window of time, everything you say or do is voluntary. During this time, there is no right or wrong way to participate or create. I'm going to share some basic instructions, but you get to choose how you want to participate. You can follow along completely, or you may want to do something different, it's completely up to you. During your window of time, you have complete freedom to choose. However you choose to spend this time will be perfectly okay. I am here to support you in any way that I can, so please feel free to ask for what you need."
demonstration:
Steps 1 & 2: Drawing using oil pastels
   
 
  Step 3: Painting with a sponge
   
 
  Step 3: Painting with a brush
   
 
  Step 3: Finger painting

You can introduce the art supplies and share the following creation process/techniques with the participants.


"Before we read the book, I'd like to demonstrate how to use the supplies and how to create. For those of you who wish to create, you'll get to use an oil pastel resist technique with the materials at your place setting, including a watercolor paper, oil pastels and foam paint."


Step 1:
"Using oil pastels, you can create a representation of yourself on one side of the paper and a representation of what or whom you are missing on the other side."

(You may want to create a simple drawing as a demonstration).


Step 2:
"Next, using symbols in nature, from your imagination, symbols or concepts from the story, or anything that is significant to you, you can create a drawing with the oil pastels to represent how you can feel connected even if you are apart. Remember, there is no right or wrong way to create. Anything that you wish to draw and paint will be perfectly fine."

(You can add to the drawing by representing the connection and even encourage participants to share their ideas and suggestions. You may also want to explain and demonstrate how the white oil pastel draws on invisible but stands out against the paint).


Step 3:
"So once you've done your drawing with the oil pastels, you're ready to begin painting. To start, you can lightly wet the paper using the spray bottle. The water helps the colors to spread more easily and allows the oil pastel resist technique to fully pop through the paint. You can apply the foam paint with a brush to resist the oil pastels. Feel free to use your fingers too, but be aware that your hands may be stained for a little while after. You can also use sponges (if available) to apply the paint and add texture. Remember, that a little bit of paint can go a long way."

(You can demonstrate how to spray water, add paint and the final effect of oil pastel resist, how the white shows up as invisible borders, etc.).
opening_circle:
You can prepare the participants for creation through a short discussion. You may wish to remind them that any sharing is optional and if they choose to just observe, that's perfectly okay. Observing is participating.

First, you can invite participants to reflect on and then share about whom or what they may be missing. This can be someone or something they miss sometimes, or even at this moment. You can encourage them to notice how the separation makes them feel.


"Now can you think of an object or symbol or is there something in nature that represents or remind you of the person or thing you miss? Try to notice why this symbol is special to you. What does it say about how you feel about that person or thing? Whatever comes to your mind will be just fine. If you like, you can carry this symbol or image with you and draw it using oil pastels during creation. And it's okay if you cannot think of anything specific. You will have the opportunity to explore this concept more through this workshop."

"When you are ready and if you feel comfortable, I invite you to share by naming who or what you miss and what object or symbol came up for you and why. For example, 'I miss my Dad because he lives across the country. Whenever I see the moon, I think of him because it is our favorite part of nature and he gave me a lunar calendar.'"

 

After participants have shared:
"Thank you for looking into your hearts and sharing about the loved ones you miss. Remember that this love you have for those you care about is inside yourselves and you can feel and share it in all kinds of ways."

setup:
Table setup
   
 
  Foam paint

You can prepare the paint palettes by adding a small mound of foam paint (3-5 colors in total) onto a plate, keeping in mind that a little bit goes a long way. You can always replenish the colors later if needed.

You can lay out the supplies so that each child has easy access to them.

It may be helpful to create a sample in advance to get a feel for the creation process. You can always modify the complexity of the creation process as you see fit.

You have complete freedom to alter or adapt any portion or element of this workshop to cater to your specific group's needs.
warm_up:
You can invite those who wish to partake, to an embodied warm-up. You can share with the children that love can be found everywhere. It is inside each of us; it is also all around us, in this room and in the world. All you have to do is look and see. You can show your participants this video of the embodied art activity starting at the time stamp 6:25.

You can invite the children to stand up in a circle if they feel comfortable. Then, using their body, they can act out different symbols of love. Feel free to lead by demonstrating examples, and inviting the children to follow along. See if you can take your time with each movement so children can connect with the love that is inside and around them.

If you like, you can first ask the children to put their hand on the hearts to see if they can feel their heartbeat and the love they have inside.

Here are some symbols that you can share with children that they can act out (you may want to ask the children if they can think of others):

A heart is a symbol for love:
You can create a little heart with your fingers and hands.
You can hold the heart up to your eyes and look through it at others in the room.

"X" is a symbol for a kiss:
You can make a little "X" with your fingers or hands.
You can create a big "X" with your body; stretch your arms wide and reach up to the sky, then spread their legs wide to create and upside-down "V."

"O" is a symbol for a hug:
You can make a little "O" with your fingers or hands.
You can reach your arms over your head in a curved shape to create a big "O."
You can slowly move your arms (in the "O" shape) in front of you, then cross your arms and wrap them around your body to give yourself a big hug.
creation:
Creation in process  
   
 
Finished creation  

Depending on the wants, needs, and expectations of your group, you can ask the children to follow along and read the story with you, invite them to close their eyes and simply listen to the story, if they feel comfortable doing so, or you may encourage them to gather around you and engage in the words and pictures in the book Sun Kisses, Moon Hugs together.

You can preface the reading by explaining to the children that it’s a story about love and how love is all around us, and that even when someone you love goes away, you can still feel connected to them.

After reading the story, you can ask the children to share if they saw something in the book, to which they felt connected. If time permitting, you can also invite them to share how or what in nature can help them feel connected to the people they love and miss.

Creation:
"This is your window of time to practice respecting and connecting to your thoughts, feelings, visions, and anything else that comes up for you. There is no wrong way create; simply notice your needs and honor your whatever comes up. If this means just sitting and noticing what your heart is feeling or if you need to put your head down, or just observe, that is okay too. Even though you may miss a special person/thing and they are not with you, you can bring them into your heart anytime. By thinking about something that reminds you of them, it can help you to connect to them, even if they are far away."

"When you are ready, you can begin to create a drawing to represent you and the person or thing you miss. Just like in the book, you can connect the two figures using ideas from the book, or your imagination. This can be something in nature like sunshine rays, a tree, rainbow, or something that you have to remind you of this special person or thing. You can then finish your drawing by using the foam paint."


Feel free to offer assistance where you see the need.
closing:
You can invite children to volunteer and share their creations, anything they discovered, felt or experienced during the workshop, or anything else they may wish to share.


Afterwards:
"Thank you all for being here today. Remember that, if we look for it, there are always ways for us to connect to and share our embodiment of love with those we feel far away from. Your participation today, whether you chose to create or not, is a wonderful reminder of how close our loved ones and prized possessions can actually be."
description: To use the concepts and images in the picture book "Sun Kisses, Moon Hugs," to help children learn to identify and express their feelings about separation/loss and develop ways to maintain their sense of connection, comfort and well-being even when loved ones are not physically present.
optional_materials:
• Baby wipes

  • Sponges
introduction:
"Today, we will get a chance to read Sun Kisses, Moon Hugs which explores ways to maintain connection, even when those we love are not physically present. We will then get an opportunity to express our feelings creatively, through a unique form of painting."

"Before we begin, I want you to know that this is your window of time. This means that this can be a safe space to notice your thoughts, feelings, and needs. Since this space is your window of time, everything you say or do is voluntary. During this time, there is no right or wrong way to participate or create. I'm going to share some basic instructions, but you get to choose how you want to participate. You can follow along completely, or you may want to do something different, it's completely up to you. During your window of time, you have complete freedom to choose. However you choose to spend this time will be perfectly okay. I am here to support you in any way that I can, so please feel free to ask for what you need."
demonstration:
Steps 1 & 2: Drawing using oil pastels
   
 
  Step 3: Painting with a sponge
   
 
  Step 3: Painting with a brush
   
 
  Step 3: Finger painting

You can introduce the art supplies and share the following creation process/techniques with the children. Feel free to simplify the creation process to meet the needs of your age group.


"Before we read the book, I'd like to demonstrate how to use the supplies and how to create. For those of you who wish to create, you'll get to use an oil pastel resist technique with the materials at your place setting, including a watercolor paper, oil pastels and foam paint."


Step 1:
"Using oil pastels, you can create a representation of yourself on one side of the paper and a representation of what or whom you are missing on the other side."

(You may want to create a simple drawing as a demonstration. You can explain that it's important to press firmly when using oil pastels; that way, the color will be strong enough to show through when paint is added. You may want to show using white oil pastel, and how it will look invisible on paper, but when paint is added in the next step, something special happens; the image will appear).


Step 2:
"Next, you can add a symbol to represent how you are connected with the person to thing that you miss, even when you're apart. You may borrow symbols or concepts from the book we'll read shortly, use symbols in natures, in your imagination, or anything that is significant to you and the person or thing you miss. Remember, there is no right or wrong way to create. Anything that you wish to draw and paint will be perfectly fine."

(You can add to the drawing by representing the connection. You may also want to explain and demonstrate how the white oil pastel draws on invisible but stands out against the paint).


Step 3:
"So once you've done your drawing with the oil pastels, you're ready to begin painting. To start, you can lightly wet the paper using the spray bottle. The water helps the colors to spread more easily and allows the oil pastel resist technique to fully pop through the paint. You can apply the foam paint with a brush to resist the oil pastels. Feel free to use your fingers too, but be aware that your hands may be stained for a little while after. You can also use sponges (if available) to apply the paint and add texture. Remember, that a little bit of paint can go a long way."

(You can demonstrate how to spray water, add paint and the final effect of oil pastel resist, how the white shows up as invisible borders, etc.).
opening_circle:
"I now invite you to take a moment and see if you can you think of someone or something you miss sometimes. Try to reflect and notice who or what you miss and how it makes you feel."

"Now, try to think about if you have personal item, or if there is something in nature that reminds you of the person or thing you miss? See if you can notice why it's special to you."

If they are comfortable, you can invite the children to share by naming who or what they miss, what object or symbol they came up with and why.

You may want to reassure participants that it is okay if they can't think of anything specific at this time and that they will get to explore this more during the workshop. You can model the sharing in a few words so that it doesn't run too long. For example, "I miss my sister because she and her family live across the country. Whenever I see pink flowers I think of her because they are her favorite."
extra_field: Susan Schaefer Bernardo and Courtenay Fletcher, author and illustrator of Sun Kisses, Moon Hugs, introduce their book, read the book, and introduce the workshop.

title: The Reasons We Smile
objective: This workshop aims to encourage children to remember that even though life can bring them challenges, there are always reasons for them to smile.
materials:
• Sheets of white paper

  • Markers

  • Crayons

  • Colored Pencils
setup: If you wish to prepare your materials beforehand, we recommend that you set out a stack of white paper, a box of crayons, colored pencils, and markers on each table.
warm_up: "First I'd like to invite you to join me in a brief relaxation exercise. For those of you who wish to participate, if you feel comfortable and safe, you can start by closing your eyes. If you prefer to keep them open that's perfectly okay too. The idea is that you feel comfortable and safe. Now I'd like to encourage you to think about a typical day in your life. Rather than focusing your thoughts on everyday worries like the ones just mentioned, try to clear your mind place your focus on simple joys... maybe a friend told you something nice or gave you a surprise treat... maybe you remember when you saw a beautiful butterfly land on a flower right next to you... maybe you got a good grade on a test and you feel proud. Try to think of all the little things that happen throughout the day that are worthy of the biggest smile you can give. Feel free to take a few more minutes to imagine all of those wonderful moments... big and small... that you experience, even in one day, that make you smile. And when you feel ready, please open your eyes."
creation:
"I would now like to now invite you to take a piece of paper and draw a smile. Feel free to make the mouth with teeth as large as you want. You can draw the smile however way you like. If you like, you can color the background too, or leave it blank. It's entirely up to you." 

Next, I'd like to invite you to fill each tooth with words, shapes, symbols, or thoughts that bring you a smile. Remember, there is no wrong way to do this. Anything that makes you smile, big or small will be perfect. It could be your pet, it could be a book, it could be a person, a song, a thought, a dream, a goal, anything you that makes you smile, write or draw it in each tooth. You can have as few and as many things you like."
 

       
   The Reasons We Smile creation     The Reasons We Smile creation
closing:
For the closing, you may give the children an opportunity to share their amazing smile creations and anything they learned, felt or experienced in the process of creating, or anything else they wish to share. Of course, this is purely optional and if no one feels comfortable sharing, it's perfectly okay.

You can invite the children to show their smiles to the group.

You may also wish to consider thanking the children for sharing (if they did) and being bold, creative and thoughtful in thinking about the reason they smile.

"Remember that you are the only one who can see, feel, and appreciate the reasons you have for smiling. Those reasons are all unique, special, and wonderful. It is perfectly normal to  feel like frowning sometimes. I'd like to encourage you to try to shake it off and remember that there are things in your life all around you that can make you smile."
description: Helps to remind the participants that even though life can bring us challenges, there are always reasons for us to smile.
optional_materials:
Optional printable worksheet

You can also facilitate this workshop using a printable worksheet. If you are utilizing the worksheet in lieu of the regular workshop materials, be sure to send the sheet or print copies out for your participants beforehand depending on the setting.

  • The Reasons We Smile: English | Spanish
introduction:
"Sometimes we have an easier time saying what we are unhappy about, than talking about the things that make us happy. For example, 'I don't want to do my homework,' or 'I don't want to wear the clothes my mom wants me to,' or 'I don't like to eat vegetables' or 'I hate to go to sleep at bedtime,' or everyday statements like 'I'm hungry, tired, bored, hot or cold.' All these things can negatively impact our day without us even realizing it.  

"Every day it seems so easy to notice the reasons that make us frown that we often forget that we have plenty of things to smile for. Today, you have an opportunity to take time to appreciate the things, big and small that make us smile."

"Before we begin, I want you to know that this workshop is a window of time for you. This means that this is a safe space to notice your thoughts, feelings, and needs. Since this space is your window of time, everything you say or do is voluntary. I’ll offer a suggested workshop idea, share about the materials we have available, and invite you to create, but there’s no wrong way to do this. It doesn't matter what it looks like. What matters is taking this time to truly honor your thoughts and feelings, however they come out. If you can’t think of anything or draw a blank on what to create or write, feel free to just observe. However you choose to spend this time will be perfectly okay. This is your time. Please ask for what you need, and know that I’m here in support of you."

title: Creating a Safe/Brave Place
objective: This workshop aims to help participants feel a sense of their own power through exploring images of safety, and creating a safe/brave place within themselves.
materials:
• Colored pencils

  • Pencil sharpeners

  • Construction paper (various colors)
setup:
You may wish to prepare the art supplies on the table for easy transition during the workshop. If you are using music, you can cue the song that you will be using.

An open space for the Opening and/or Guided Imagery can be helpful but is not necessary. If an open space is not available, the activities can be done at the table.

You may also consider creating a sample Safe Place in advance to show participants what it can look like. If you choose to do so, we suggest creating a simple sample, so that participants aren't overwhelmed by any "artistic" challenges.
 

Sample table setup
warm_up:
Embodied Art Activity: What Makes You Feel Safe?
For this part, you can invite participants to gather and stand in a circle and space themselves so that they're able to move around without bumping into the person next to them. If you're doing this activity at the table, each person can sit or stand to create their image when it's their turn.

"For those who feel comfortable, we can start our workshop off by using our bodies. I'm going to start off by asking a question, and invite you to think of how we can answer it by using our bodies."

"The question is: 'What makes you feel safe/brave?' Feel free to take a minute to think about what makes you feel safe/brave. When I think of what makes me feel safe, I think of hugs. Hugs make me feel safe, so my image might look like this (you can demonstrate by wrapping your arms around yourself and saying: 'hugs')."

You can invite the participants to repeat your movement and word after you.

"But for you, 'hugs' may not be safe, so your image might look like this (you can hold your arms straight out in front of you as if you're motioning to stop and say: 'Stay away')."

You can invite the participants to repeat the movement and word after you again.

Please note, that you can also show the possible range of images from a small, modest statue, to a large, exaggerated image (see below images).
 

Embodied Art Activity at the Table: "Hugs" (modest) Embodied Art Activity at the Table: "Hugs" (exaggerated)
Embodied Art Activity in a Circle: "Stay Away!" (modest) Embodied Art Activity in a Circle: "Stay Away!" (exaggerated)


You can now invite those who wish to participate, to share their image and word/phrase, and the rest of the group can repeat both parts.
 

Guided Imagery: What Is Your Safe Place?
"For our next activity, I invite you to try and relax and use your imagination to picture a safe/brave place in your mind. Afterwards, you'll get a chance to create your safe/brave place on paper with any of the art supplies you see here. Remember, there is no wrong way to imagine or create your safe/brave place, and you are free to participate fully, partially, or do something else during this time. You have complete freedom to choose."

"Before we start, I'd like to invite you to find a place in the room where you feel most comfortable. This can look like you sitting in a chair, sitting or lying on the floor, standing, or anything in between. Once you get to your comfortable place, feel free to close your eyes if you feel comfortable doing so. Or you can keep them open. However you are most comfortable."

For the most effective guided imagery, we suggest speaking in a soft, slow tone and pausing where it feels right.

The guided imagery can sound something like this:

"If you like, start by taking a deep breath in... then slowly let it out. Whatever is comfortable for you. Now I invite you to feel your feet and give them a squeeze... and let go. I invite you to feel your knees and give them a shake and pause... Feel your shoulders, move them up and down several times... Notice your arms and wiggle them around and pause... How about your hands? Squeeze your hands tightly and let go... you can repeat several times."

"If you feel comfortable doing so, take a deep breath, and begin to envision your safe place."

You can continue by asking any or all of the following questions to aid participants in visualizing their safe place. Please feel free to adapt or add your own prompts to better cater to your specific group.

  • "What does your safe/brave place look like?"

  • "What colors do you see?"

  • "What does your safe/brave place feel like?"

  • "What does your safe/brave place sound like?"

  • "Is it quiet in your safe/brave place?"

  • "What do you hear?"

  • "Are you alone in your safe/brave place?"

  • "If you're not alone, who's with you?"

  • "What are you doing in your safe/brave place?"

  • "Did you bring something with you to your safe/brave place?"

  • "What did you leave behind?"

  • "Is your safe place somewhere you've been before or a place you've made up?"

  • "How does your safe/brave place make you feel?"

"When you're ready, you can open your eyes, move slowly back to your seat, and begin to create your safe/brave place on paper."
creation: Feel free to offer assistance where you see fit. You may wish to give time reminders, if necessary. You may also wish to remind participants that they are free to use whatever material and supplies available and create their safe space creations however way they like. It doesn't matter what it looks like. What's important is that they are taking this time to honor their thoughts and feelings, and creating something that is meaningful to them.
closing:
As you begin the closing, you can let the participants know that this time is for "heart talk," for those who wish to participate. 

It's a time when they can talk about their art. Each participant chooses how they want to talk about their creation. They can share what their art piece means to them, anything they learned, felt or experienced during the creation process, or anything else they may wish to share. They have the option to participate however they'd like, from sharing their story to being a witness and listening to the other stories.

After each participant has a chance to share, you can offer them a "special envelope" or a piece of paper to save their art and keep it protected from other people's eyes and judgments; a safe place for their 'safe place.'

You can also invite the participants to share how they feel now that they've created their 'safe/brave place.'
description: Through exploring images of safety, this workshop can help participants feel a sense of their own power by inviting them to create a safe place within themselves.
tips:
• We have found that it's important that you and any other facilitators, staff, or volunteers in the room participate along with the group, if possible. By modeling your enthusiasm and willingness to participate, you can help build trust, bonding, and make it safer for participants to play and share vulnerable experiences.

  • As an additional strategy, you may want to invite the participants to share about examining their different safety strategies. You can ask questions like: "Which safety strategies have been helpful in the past?" "Which safety strategies aren't serving you anymore?"

  • You can support your participants in understanding that because of trauma, it's completely normal not to feel safe all the time, and that part of healing from trauma can be opening up the possibility for safety. Being gentle and patient, with what can be a slow process, can be helpful.

  • Another helpful tip is to allow the participants to define for themselves their visions of safety and their journey to feeling safe. 

  • If "violent" images come up as safety strategies, having a non-judgmental approach, and encouraging other participants to do the same can help create safety in the group. It's okay if someone uses a strategy that you or the other participants wouldn't use.

  • It's also perfectly okay if participants can't envision a safe place. They can try something out to see if it feels safe and notice what feelings come up for them. They can just play with the supplies, breathe with their hand over their heart, or use this time to write in a journal.

  • As a facilitator, you may have preconceived notions about your role and may have the impulse to help participants to problem-solve, find a safe place, or protect them from feelings they find uncomfortable. However, you can consider seeing your role as providing the space for the participants to acknowledge and validate their feelings and experiences.


Note about introducing embodied art:

You may wish to share with your participants the benefits of moving their bodies in playful and safe ways. Understanding what’s meaningful about movement and body awareness can help participants feel at ease expanding their comfort zones. For more about embodied art workshops and how to introduce them in your groups, please see Introduction to Embodied Art Workshops.
