introduction:
"Before we begin, I want you to know that this workshop is a window of time for you. This means that this can be a safe/brave space to notice your thoughts, feelings, and needs. Since this space is your window of time, everything you say or do is voluntary. I’ll offer a suggested workshop idea, share about the materials we have available, and invite you to create, but there’s no right or wrong way to do this. It doesn't matter what it looks like. What matters is taking this time to truly honor your thoughts and feelings, however they come out. If you can’t think of anything or draw a blank on what to create or write, feel free to just observe. However you choose to spend this time will be perfectly okay. This is your time. Please ask for what you need, and know that I’m here in support of you."

"During this workshop, you will have an opportunity to talk about 'safety' and what it can mean to you. I will invite you to do three activities that can help you create your safe/brave place. You'll have the option to creatively use your body, your mind, and draw something on paper. At the end of the workshop session what is most important is that you trust your own needs to connect to what safety means to you. Everything is voluntary, and observing is participating."

"Throughout this workshop, you are invited to participate, which means you always have the option to pass. Passing can look like you sitting back and watching what goes on or it can look like you participating in only a few activities that you feel comfortable with. It's up to you."

title: River Stories / Historias del Rio
objective: This workshop gives participants an opportunity to use the metaphor of a river to acknowledge their past, notice their resilience and honor their present strength, through the process of visual and embodied art.
materials:
•  
      Optional printable self-led worksheet

    Construction paper (variety of colors)

  • Colored pencils

  • Pencil sharpeners

  • River Stories worksheet handout

  • Pens

You can also facilitate this workshop using this printable self-led worksheet. If you are utilizing this sheet in lieu of the regular workshop materials, be sure to send the sheet or print them out beforehand for your participants depending on the setting.
setup:
River Stories table setup

You are welcome to provide any and as many of the optional material that you see fit.

You can lay out the supplies on the table for easy transition during the group. If you're incorporating music for the visualization and creation, you may want to cue the song that you'll be using.

An open space for the sharing portion is helpful but not necessary. If you have limited space, you can refer to the Tips section below for more info.

If you are re-arranging your room to allow for more movement space, you might want to invite the participants to help you or do it in front of them, so that the transition is not jarring.

It might be helpful for you to create your river art and worksheet ahead of time, so that you can be prepared to demonstrate the sharing process or be a buddy for someone sharing (so that they don't have to share alone).

If possible, you can write the date and the phrase "I am here, in this room, with you." written in large letters on a poster or a chalkboard as a "prompt" so that when participants share, they can look up and see the words (instead of just reading them from the River Stories worksheet).


Video Samples:
Because the sharing part of this workshop has more steps than usual, we recommend watching one or more of the sample videos as a reference for the process. We suggest that you let the group have their own experience (instead of sharing the videos with them). In watching the videos, you will notice how participants have chosen to share in slightly different ways (e.g. using body movements, expressing emotions, using more or less words, etc.). We have included all of these samples, so you see some of the variety that can occur in this workshop.

  • River Stories Intro and Demo

  • River Stories Sample 1

  • River Stories Sample 2

  • River Stories Sample 3

  • River Stories Sample 4

 

As a facilitator, you have complete freedom to alter or adapt any portion or element of this workshop to cater to your specific group's needs.
warm_up:
Starting the River Story with birthday and today's date

 

Before the visualization starts, you can invite participants to choose a piece of colored construction paper that they will use to draw their river. You can invite them to start with their birth date on one end of the paper (the beginning of their river) and end with today's date (the end of their river). They can choose to write this any way they'd like to.

We have found that guided visualizations are most effective when spoken in a soft, slow tone, pausing where it feels right (specifically, after each question to give participants time to visualize their responses).


"I now would like to invite you to join me in a brief visualization. If you prefer to observe, that’s perfectly okay. Observing is participating.”

“For those of you who wish to follow along, try to get yourself in a comfortable position. If you feel safe, you can close your eyes, or keep them open. However way you are most comfortable.”

“Now, take a few deep breaths."

(You can guide participants to breathe in for a count of 5 seconds, hold it for 3 and exhale for 7 seconds, and repeat two or three times).


"Try to imagine your life as a river. You might picture yourself floating above your river and looking down at it or walking along side of it. What does it look like?..." What does the beginning of the river look like?... Where does your river flow quickly and where does it flow slowly?... Where is your river deep?... And where is it shallow?... Does your river have any twists, turns or bends?... Where is it narrow and where is it wide?... What do the banks of your river look like?... Does the water in your river have a color?... Can you see where your river is going?..."

"Sit with your thoughts for a moment and when you're ready, you can open your eyes (if they're closed) and begin to create your river on paper."
creation:
Participants creating their River Stories









 
 
  Sharing the "beginning" of the river









 
 
  One by one, sharing the second event









 
 
  Reaching the "end" of their rivers








 

You can give participants about 30 minutes (or however long you see fit) to create their rivers. If anyone finishes early, you can invite them to journal freely on the back of their river art, take time to sit quietly with their experience, begin to work on their River Stories worksheet to get ready for the sharing option, or anything else that works for them, you and the group.

Feel free to offer assistance where you see the need. You may want to give gentle time prompts such as: "We have about ten minutes to finish up our artwork," which can help participants be aware of their time.

Once participants are done creating their river, you can invite them to the next step.


Sharing Our River Stories: Filling Out the Worksheet
"Now, we'll have the opportunity to share our stories in a special way. For those of you who want to follow along, you can pick three moments from your life that you'd like to acknowledge and honor today. You can be very specific, such as: 'Age 26, we moved to a new home and it was hard.' Or, you can be general, such as: 'Age 26, something new'."

"Remember, just as with any other part of this workshop, sharing is optional, and if you don't feel comfortable sharing, that's perfectly okay. You get to decide if you want to share, what you want to share, and how you want to share it. Here's a worksheet to help get us ready for the sharing."


You can invite participants to fill out the Worksheet.


Sharing Our River Stories: Walking the River
Once everyone who wants to has completed their River Stories worksheet, you can invite the group to bring their creations with their worksheets and sit together, ideally facing the same direction.

It may be helpful for participants to see a physical demonstration of the sharing process, so you may consider being the first person in the first group to share.

You can stand up in front of the group and invite another 1-2 volunteers who also wish to share to stand up with you (see Demo videos above for reference).


"In a moment, I'm going to invite you to share your story with your body, your words, or both."

"How many of you have ever felt like something happened to you but it wasn't seen, heard, or acknowledged the way you would have liked? Today, we will each have the option to share our river with the group, and the group can really see, hear, and acknowledge the person, without any judgment; to really honor each journey."

"You get to choose if you want to share, and no one will share alone unless you want to. The basic structure is that a few people can stand up here together, facing the group. It's your choice if you want to show your river art as you do this."

"Those who are up here, I invite you to imagine that your river is stretched out in front of you, that you are standing at the beginning, at your place of birth, and that the river flows toward the rest of the group. You can then take turns sharing your birth date, followed by 'I was born.' For example, the first person might say: 'August 17, 1985, I was born.' Then, the second person would say: 'June 15, 1971, I was born'."

"Once all the 'beginnings' are shared, the first person can take a step forward and share the first event from your river that you want to honor today. As a reminder, you get to decide how much you want to share with us either with your words or with your body. For example, you could say: 'Age 8, my teacher yelled at me in front of the class.' Or, '1989, I felt embarrassed,' while silently making a movement. And you can demonstrate this by covering your face in an embarrassed way while saying '4th grade'."

"Once everyone has shared their first event, the first person can take another step forward and share their second event. One at a time, the other people standing can take their steps forward and share their second events."

"Once everyone has shared their second event, then each person up here can take a third step and share their third event, one at a time."


River Ending / Group Acknowledgement:
"Once everyone who chooses to has shared their third event, then each person will be invited to step forward one at a time, and say today's date and the sentence: 'I am here, in this room, with you.' We can say this because in addition to honoring everything we've gone through, we also get to come to this present moment in time and space and notice that we're not alone."

"After each person says: 'I am here in this room with you,' the rest of the group says, 'We see you,' all together in response, showing the community of support that we have here."


You can now invite participants to begin sharing their river stories. If you like, after each set of sharing finishes, you can invite the group to acknowledge the courage of the sharers by snapping their fingers. We encourage you to also acknowledge those who honored their desire to participate by observation only.
closing:
"Thank you all for taking this window of time to honor yourself, your journey, and the journeys of others."


You can invite the participants to take a breath or two together, if you see fit.


"Now we can take a moment for anyone who would like, to share about anything that came up for you during this workshop. You can share your art, your feelings, your thoughts, or anything that was meaningful about your experience today."

Optional Closing Questions:

  • Looking back at your river, what did you notice?

  • What made your river twist and turn?

  • How did it feel to share your river?

  • How did it feel to be acknowledged?

  • Where did you notice your strength or resilience today?

  • Where would you like your river to go from today on?
description: Through visual art (drawing) and embodied art (movement), participants are invited to use the metaphor of a river to acknowledge their past, notice their resilience, and honor their present strength.
notes:
With this workshop, it can be very helpful to set up the expectation of confidentiality ahead of time. It can be safer for participants to share if they know that not only will nothing be shared but that they don't have to answer any questions about their experiences.

You might say: "Before we begin, can we make the agreement that we will keep whatever anyone shares confidential? That way, we can each share exactly what we want to, and know that no one, even people in this room, will ever mention it to us unless we bring it up again first."
tips:
• It can be very helpful that you and any other facilitators, staff, or volunteers in the room participate along with the group. By modeling your enthusiasm and willingness to participate, you can help build trust, bonding, and make it safer for other people to play and share vulnerable experiences.

  • If you have limited space, you can encourage participants to make very tiny steps when they walk their river so that the participants still get the experience of moving forward towards the group.

  • If you end up with one person left who wants to share but everyone else has shared already, you or another participant can share your river again so that the one person does not feel alone walking their river. Of course, it's great to also honor the choice of any participants who request to walk their river alone.

  • If anyone in your group feels uncomfortable sharing their birth date, they do not need to share their birth year or age. They can just share the day and month or say whatever feels comfortable to them (for example, "a long time ago" or "at one point in the not too distant past").

  • In case anyone expresses concern, you can let them know that it's okay if different people's rivers don't line up when they share together. For example, one person's river might be in 1990 while another's river is in 2007 even though they are standing side by side. The reasons to share rivers with buddies is so that we can feel support or connection while we share.

  • If you like, you can invite participants to add a sentence or phrase along with "I was born." For example: "August 17, 1985: I was born and welcomed into the world."


Note about introducing embodied art:
You may wish to share with your participants the benefits of moving their bodies in playful and safe ways. Understanding what’s meaningful about movement and body awareness can help participants feel at ease expanding their comfort zones. For more about embodied art workshops and how to introduce them in your groups, please see Introduction to Embodied Art Workshops.
objective_spanish: Este taller permite que los participantes usen un rio como metáfora por medio de un proceso visual y de arte personificado para reconocer su pasado, notar su resistencia y honrar la fortaleza que tienen en el presente.
materials_spanish:
• Papel de Construcción / Cartulina (una variedad de colores)
• Lápices de Color
• Sacapuntas
• Hoja de Trabajo de Historias del Rio
• Pluma/lapicera
timeframe_spanish:
Introducción 5 minutos
Demostración 5 minutos
Comienzo 5 minutos
Preparamiento 10 minutos
Creación 60 minutos
Cierre 10 minutos
Total 01 hora 35 minutos
setup_spanish:
Puedes proveer cualquier material opcional que pienses que es necesario. Puedes organizar los materiales en la mesa para que sea una transición fácil durante grupo. Si incorporaras música para la visualización y creación, es recomendable que prepares la canción que usaras. Tener un espacio abierto para poder compartir es recomendable pero no necesario.

Si tienes espacio limitado, refiere a la sección de consejos para mas información. Si estas reacomodando tu cuarto para permitir movimiento, pide a los participantes que te ayuden o mueve el cuarto en frente de ellos para que no se confundan. Podría ser de ayuda crear tu arte de rio y completar tu hoja de trabajo antes de tiempo para que estés preparado para demostrar como comparatir o para ayudar a otros a compartir (para que no tengan que compartir solos).

Si es posible, escribe en letras grandes la fecha y la frase “yo estoy aquí, en este cuarto, contigo.” En un pizarrón o poster como aviso para que cuando los participantes compartan su arte, ellos puedan ver las palabras.

Muestra de Video: Para compartir en este taller, hay mas pasos de lo usual, y recomendamos que miren uno o mas de estas muestras de video como referencia del proceso. Sugerimos que permitan que el grupo tenga su propia experiencia (en ves de compartir los videos con ellos). En los videos, te darás cuenta como los participantes deciden compartir de maneras diferentes (ej., moviendo el cuerpo, expresando emociones, usando mas o menos palabras, etc.).

Hemos incluido los ejemplos para que puedas ver las variedades que puedan ocurrir en este taller.   Como facilitador, tienes la libertad de cambiar o adaptar cualquier porción o elemento de este taller para abastecer a las necesidades de su grupo.
warm_up_spanish:
Antes de que comience la visualización, puedes invitar a los participantes a que escojan un papel de construcción del color que ellos quieran para luego dibujar su rio. Puedes invitarlos a que comiencen con su fecha de nacimiento en una punta del papel (el comienzo del rio) y el final con la fecha de hoy (el final del rio). Ellos pueden elegir escribirlo de la manera que ellos gusten. Hemos descubierto que las visualizaciones guiadas son mas efectivas cuando guías en un tono suave y lento, pausando donde sientes que es necesario (especialmente, después de cada pregunta para darle tiempo a los participantes para visualizar sus respuestas).  

“Ahora quisiera invitarlos a que participen en una breve visualización. Si prefieres observar, también esta permitido. El observar es participar.”

“Para aquellos que deciden seguirme, traten de ponerse en una posición cómoda. SI te sientes Seguro, puedes cerrar tus ojos, o mantenerlos abiertos. Haz lo que te haga sentir mas cómodo.”

“Ahora, respire hondo unas cuantas veces.”

(Puedes guiar a los participantes a que inhalen hasta la cuenta de 5 segundos, detengan su aire por 2, y saquen su aire por 7 segundos, y repitan esto 2 o 3 veces.)

“Trata de imaginar tu vida como una rio. Quizás te ves flotando sobre el rio y mirándolo o caminando a lo largo de el.

¿Como se ve?

“Como es el principio del rio?

¿Que parte del rio corre rápido y donde corre lento?

¿Que parte del rio es profundo?

¿Donde es poco profundo?

Tu rio tiene giros, vueltas, ¿o curvas?

¿Dónde es angosto y donde es ancho?

¿Como son las orillas del rio?

¿El agua en el rio tiene algún color?

Puedes ver hacia donde va tu rio? “Siéntense con sus pensamientos por un momento, y cuando estés listo, puedes abrir tus ojos (si están cerrados) y comienza a crear tu rio en el pape.”
creation_spanish:
Puedes darles a los participantes alrededor de 30 minutos (o la cantidad de tiempo que tu pienses que es necesario) para crear sus ríos. Si alguien termine antes de tiempo, puedes invitarlos a que escriban libremente atrás de su arte de rio, tomen un momento para sentarse en silencio con su experiencia, comiencen a trabajar en su hoja de trabajo de Historias del Rio para poder compartir, o a hacer cualquier otra cosa que sea de beneficio para ellos y el grupo. Siéntete libre de ofrecer ayuda donde veas que es necesario.

Quizás quieras darles gentiles recordatorios del tiempo que les resta, por ejemplo: “Tenemos alrededor de 10 minutos para terminar nuestra obra de arte,” lo cual permite que los participantes sean conscientes de su tiempo. Una vez que los participantes terminan de crear su rio, puedes invitarlos a seguir el próximo paso.

Compartiendo Nuestras Historias de Rio: Completando el Folleto

“Ahora, tendremos la oportunidad de compartir nuestras historias de una manera especial. Para aquellos que quieren participar, pueden elegir 3 momentos de su visa que quieras reconocer y honrar hoy.

Puedes ser muy especifico, como: ‘A los 26 nos movimos a una casa nueva y fue difícil.’ O puedes ser breve, como: ‘Edad 26, algo nuevo’.” . “Recuerda, al igual como las otras partes de este taller, el compartir es opcional, y si no te sientes cómodo, esta bien.

Tu decides si quieres compartir, que quieres compartir, y como los quieres compartir. Aquí esta un folleto que nos ayuda a prepararnos para compartir.” Puedes invitar a los participantes a que completen la hoja de trabajo. Compartiendo Nuestras Historias de Rio: Recorriendo el Rio Una vez que todos los que quisieron, completaron la hoja de trabajo de las Historias del Rio, puedes invitar al grupo a que traigan sus creaciones y se sienten juntos. Lo ideal seria que se sienten mirando en la misma dirección.

Puede ser de ayuda que los participantes vean una demonstración física del proceso para compartir, considera ser la primera persona en el grupo en compartir. Puedes pararte en frente del grupo e invitar a 1-2 voluntarios que deseen compartir, a que se paren contigo (usa el video de demonstración como referencia).

“En un momento, voy a invitarlos a compartir su historia con su cuerpo, palabras, o usando los dos.” “Cuantos de ustedes han sentido que cuando algo te pasa, ¿no fue visto, escuchado o reconocido como tu querías? Hoy, cada uno tendrá la opción de compartir su rio con el grupo, y el grupo podrá ver, escuchar, y reconocer a la persona sin juzgar, para honrar el camino de cada uno.”

“Tu podrás elegir si quieres compartir, y nadie compartirá solo, almenos que eso sea lo que tu quieres. La estructura básica es que unas cuantas personas se paren en frente juntas, mirando al grupo. Es tu decisión si quieres mostrar tu arte del rio mientras haces esto.”

“Aquellos que están aquí en frente, los invito a que imaginen que su rio se extiende en frente suyo, que tu estas en el principio, en tu lugar de Nacimiento, y que el rio fluye hacia el resto del grupo. Pueden turnarse a compartir su fecha de nacimiento, seguido por ‘Yo nací.’ Por ejemplo, la primera persona podría decir: ‘Agosto 17, 1985, yo nací.‘ Luego, la segunda persona podrá decir: ‘Junio 5, 1971, yo nací’.”

"Una vez que todos los ‘comienzos’ fueron compartidos, la primera persona puede ir aun mas lejos y compartir el primer evento de su rio que quiera honrar hoy. Les recuerdo que ustedes deciden cuanto quieren compartir con nosotros usando palabras o su cuerpo. Por ejemplo, podrías decir: ‘Edad 8, mi maestra me grito en frente de la clase.’ O, ‘1989, sentí vergüenza,” y al mismo tiempo hacienda los movimientos en silencio. también puedes demonstrar lo compartido cubriéndote la cara demonstración que sentiste vergüenza y diciendo ‘4to grado’.”

“Una vez que todos hayan compartido su primer evento, la primera persona puede seguir con el próximo paso y compartir su segundo evento. Uno a la vez, las otras personas que están paradas pueden dar un paso adelante y compartir su segundo evento.”

“Cuando todos compartieron su segundo evento, luego cada persona aquí adelante puede tomar un tercer paso y compartir su tercer evento, uno a la vez.”

Terminando el Rio / Reconocimiento del Grupo “Cuando todos los que decidieron compartir, han terminado de compartir su tercer evento, cada persona será invitada a dar un paso hacia el frente, uno a la vez, y decir la fecha de hoy y la oración: ‘Yo estoy aquí, en este cuarto, contigo.’ Podemos decir esto porque aparte de honrar todo lo que hemos pasado, también pudimos llegar a este preciso momento en este tiempo y espacio y reconocemos que no estamos solos.”

“Después de que cada persona diga: ‘Yo estoy aquí en este cuarto contigo,’ el resto del grupo dirá, ‘Nosotros te vemos,’ todos juntos respondiendo, demostrando la comunidad de apoyo que tenemos aquí.”

Ahora puedes invitar a los participantes a compartir sus historias de rio. Si quieres, después de que terminen de compartir cada serie, puedes invitar al grupo a reconocer la valentía de los que compartieron, por medio del chasquido de dedos. Te animamos que también reconozcas aquellos que honraron su deseo de participar con solo observar.
closing_spanish:
“Gracias a todos por tomar esta ventana de tiempo para honrarse a su mismos, su camino, y el camino de otros.” Si piensas que es necesario, puedes invitar a los participantes a que respiren juntos una o dos veces. “Ahora podemos tomarnos un tiempo para que puedan compartir, si gustan, cualquier cosa que se les haya presentado durante este taller. Puedes compartir tu arte, tus sentimientos, tus pensamientos o cualquier cosa que haya sido significante sobre tu experiencia hoy.”  

Preguntas Opcionales para el Cierre:
•    Mirando hacia atrás en tu rio, de que diste cuenta
•    ¿Que hizo que tu rio tenga vueltas y giros?
•    ¿Como te sentiste al compartir tu rio?
•    Como se sintió el ser reconocido/a?
•    ¿Donde notaste tu fuerza o resistencia hoy?
•    ¿Donde quieres que vaya tu rio desde hoy?
notes_spanish:
Con este taller, puede ser de ayuda el prepara las expectativas de confidencialidad antes de tiempo. Puede ser mas seguro que los participantes compartan si saben que nada de lo que ellos comparten será divulgado pero y que también sepan que no tienen que contestar preguntas sobre sus experiencias.

Puedes decir: “Antes de comenzar, podemos hacer un acuerdo de que mantendremos todo lo que es compartido en confidencia? De esa forma, cada uno puede compartir lo que ellos quieran sabiendo que las personas en este cuarto nunca mencionaron lo que se comparte, al menos que la persona que esta compartiendo lo mencione primero.”
tips_spanish:
• Puede ser de beneficio que cualquier otro facilitador, personal, o voluntario en el cuarto participe con el grupo. Por medio de la demonstración de entusiasmo y de que uno esta dispuesto, puedes crear confianza, un enlace, y hacer que otros se sientan a salvo cuando los participantes jueguen y compartan sus experiencias vulnerables.

• Si tienes espacio limitado, puedes animar a los participantes a que tomen pasos chicos cuando recorrer su rio para que los participantes puedan tener la experiencia de seguir adelante.

• Si solo queda una persona que quiere compartir, tu u otro participante pueden compartir su rio otra vez para que la persona no se sienta sola compartiendo su rio. también es Bueno honrar a las personas que quieren compartir su rio solo.

• Si alguien en tu grupo no se siente cómodo con compartir su fecha de nacimiento, no es necesario que compartan el año en que nacieron o su edad. Otra opción es que compartan el día y el mes o lo que ellos deseen compartir (por ejemplo, “mucho tiempo atrás” o  “En un punto en el pasado no tan distante”).

• Por si alguien pregunta, no importa si los ríos de los participantes no concuerdan cuando comparten juntos. Por ejemplo, el rio de una persona puede tomar lugar en 1990 mientras el rio de otra persona parado a su lado toma lugar en el 2007. El compartir los ríos con un compañero/a es para que sientan apoyo y conexión mientras comparten.

• SI quieres, puedes invitar a los participantes a que agreguen una frase u oración con “Yo nací.” Por ejemplo, “Agosto 17,1985: yo nací y fui bienvenido/a al mundo.”

Nota sobre la introducción del arte expresado: Quizás quieras compartir con los participantes los beneficios de mover sus cuerpos en maneras juguetonas y sanas. Entender lo significativo sobre el movimiento y la conciencia del cuerpo ayuda a que los participantes se sientan cómodos al salir de su zona de confort.

Para mas información sobre talleres de arte expresado y como introducirlos en tu grupo, visita Introduction to Embodied Art Workshops.
optional_materials:
• Markers (in addition to or instead of colored pencils)

  • Metallic markers

  • White colored pencils (or whiteout pens)

  • Relaxing, instrumental music for Visualization and Creation
optional_materials_spanish:
• Marcadores (en adición o como reemplazo de los lápices de color)
• Marcadores Metálicos
• Lápices de color blancos (o plumas de corrector liquido)
• Música instrumental relajante, para la Visualización y Creación
introduction:
"This workshop is all about noticing how you got here and giving others a chance to see you and acknowledge your journey. It's a big deal that we get to be in this room together today."

"Today I'd like to invite you all to think of your lives as a river. Just like a river, our life journey can have twists and turns. We're going to have the chance to notice what we've been through in our past and how we got to be here today by creating art on paper, then physically with our bodies."

"Before we begin, I want you to know that this is your window of time. This means that this can be a safe space to notice your thoughts, feelings, and needs. Since this space is your window of time, everything you say or do is voluntary. During this time, there is no right or wrong way to participate or create. I'm going to share some basic instructions, but you get to choose how you want to participate. You can follow along completely, or you may want to do something different, it's completely up to you. During your window of time, you have complete freedom to choose. However you choose to spend this time will be perfectly okay. I am here to support you in any way that I can, so please feel free to ask for what you need."
introduction_spanish:
“Este taller se trata de notar como llegaste hasta aquí y darles a otros la oportunidad de verte y reconocer to camino. Significa mucho que todos estamos en este cuarto hoy.”

”Hoy quisiera invitarlos a que piensen en su vida como un rio. Como un rio, nuestra vida tambien tiene giros y vueltas. Tendremos la oportunidad de darnos cuenta de todo lo que vivimos en nuestro pasado y ver como llegamos hasta donde estamos hoy por medio del arte en papel, y luego expresarnos con nuestros cuerpos.”

“Antes de comenzar, quiero que sepan que esta es su ventana de tiempo. Eso significa que puedes estar en un lugar seguro para prestarle atención a tus pensamientos, sentimientos, y necesidades. Ya que este espacio es tu ventana de tiempo, todo lo que digas o hagas es voluntario. Durante este tiempo, no hay manera correcta o incorrecta de participar o crear. Compartiré unas instrucciones básicas, pero tu decides como quieres participar. Puedes seguir las instrucciones o puedes decidir hacer algo diferente, es tu decisión. Durante tu venta de tiempo, tendrás la libertad de elegir. Esta permitido pasar este tiempo de la manera que tu quieras. Yo estoy aquí para apoyarte de cualquier manera, así que siéntete libre de pedir lo que necesites.”
demonstration:
Completed self-led worksheet

You can introduce the art supplies and share the following River Stories creation process with the participants. If you've made a sample, you may want to show it for reference.

Feel free to demonstrate any creation elements that you see fit.


"Today, you'll get to use any of the supplies available and create a river that tells the story of your life journey. You can draw your river and its elements however you like."

"Before you draw your river story, you'll have the option to join me in a guided visualization. As you create, I'd like to encourage you to consider the times or events that have shaped your life. The river you are creating on paper can look like what you saw in your mind during the visualization or it could be something new. You can use symbols, words, dates, ages, or anything else you'd like to represent the moments in your life you'd like to honor today. There is no right or wrong way to create your river. It may not even look like a river, and that's perfectly fine."
demonstration_spanish:
Puedes introducir los materiales y comparte el proceso de creación de la siguiente Historia de Rio. Si creaste una muestra, la puedes usar como referencia. Siéntete libre de compartir cualquier elemento de creación que tu creas que es necesario.

“Hoy podrán usar cualquier materiales disponibles para crear un rio que cuenta la historia de tu vida. Puedes dibujar el rio y sus elementos como tu quieras.”

“Antes de que dibujes tu historia del rio, tendrás la opción de participar en una visualización guiada. Mientras trabajas en tu creación, quisiera animarte a que consideres los tiempos y eventos que han moldeado tu vida. El rio que estas creando en el papel puede ser igual al que te imagines durante la visualización o puede ser algo nuevo. Puedes usar símbolos, palabras, fechas, edades, o cualquier otra cosa que represente los momentos en tu vida que valoras hoy. No hay manera correcta o incorrecta de crear tu rio. Puede ser que no parezca un rio, y eso esta bien.”
opening_circle: You can open by inviting anyone who wishes to do so, to share one thing that they experienced today that led up to this moment. For example: "I got on the bus to come here." Or, "I was having a really hard day, and I came to this workshop anyway."
opening_circle_spanish: Puedes comenzar invitando a los participantes a compartir una cosa que hayan vivido hoy para llegar a este momento. Por ejemplo: “me subí a un autobús para llegar aquí.” O, “Estaba teniendo un día muy difícil, pero igual decidí venir a este taller.”

title: Expressive Crayon Warm-Up
objective: This workshop offers participants a simple yet powerful warm-up to safely express any emotions they have been holding inside by scribbling freely.
materials:
• Crayons              

  • Paper (variety of colors)
warm_up:
You have the option to do a brief warm up exercise by inviting the participants to share one or two words that describe how they are feeling right now. It could be any feeling they are experiencing. There is no wrong answer. If no one feels comfortable sharing, that's perfectly okay. You can also skip the warm-up and jump straight into the exercise.

"For those of you who wish to participate, I'd like to invite you to take any piece of paper and any crayon you like and just begin doodling by making random circular motions. Don't worry if you break the crayon or what your doodle looks like. Try to see if you can just let yourself feel the movement of your arm without judging it."

You may give the participants 30-60 seconds to draw circular scribbles. You may find it helpful to participate along with your group so they can see you being playful and relaxed with your scribbles and doodles. This is entirely up to you.

"Now, I'd like to invite you to add to your scribble by picking a new crayon with your other hand and make fast and angular motions. You can use same color crayon or pick a new color. It's entirely up to you. There is no wrong way to do this."

"Now, using both hands at once, try to make either angular or circular motions using the two crayons together."

Once participants have warmed up, you can invite them to take a moment to share anything they'd like to about their experience. Of course, sharing is optional.
creation:
Expressive Crayon depicting anger
Expressive Crayon depicting happiness

To begin, you can invite those who wish to participate to choose a piece of paper, any color they like, or flip their current piece of paper over (if they've done the warm-up).

"I would now like to invite those of you who wish to participate to choose any emotion you like. I'd like to encourage you to pick one that maybe you haven't had permission to feel. For some of you that may be anger, for others it may be grief, aggression, confidence, love, or something else. But again, you have complete freedom to choose any emotion you like."

"Now you can go ahead and choose any crayon you like that best represents that emotion. You may consider going with your first thought; you can always change the emotion or the color later if you like."

"In a moment, I'm going to invite you to express that emotion on the paper in front of you for about two minutes. When we start, I'd like to encourage you to use your crayon to express that emotion on the paper. Think about how you might move your arm to express that emotion. This can look like scribbling or tapping, moving slowly or quickly, or anything else that you feel like doing. Remember, there is no wrong way to do this. Any way you choose would be perfect."

It can be helpful to give examples in the air with a crayon and your own body movements as you say this.

"Don't worry about what it looks like, or even ripping the paper or breaking the crayons. Wherever your emotion takes you, will be perfect. Is everyone ready?"

You can give them as much time as you feel is needed to process their emotion and scribble. Generally, about 2-3 minutes have been enough. Once you feel they've had ample time to scribble, you can invite them to find a pausing place so they can take a brief moment to reflect on what that was like.
closing:
For the closing, you can give the participants an opportunity to share anything they like about their scribbles, their chosen feeling, or whatever they noticed by participating. It can also be helpful to remind them that they are welcome to pass if they don't feel like sharing and that each person's representation of an emotion could be different, and that is okay.

You can end by validating each person's experience, courage and their taking a window of time to honor themselves.
description: In this simple yet powerful warm-up, participants can safely express any emotions they have been holding inside by scribbling freely.
tips:
• This warm-up often works best without music so that participants can connect to their own experiences and different participants can work on different emotions simultaneously without being influenced by the music.

  • If your group has a hard time thinking of emotion words, you can brainstorm words with them ahead of time or have them start with emotions you suggest (like anger, confusion, joy, etc.) and then end with an emotion of their choice.

  • This warm-up works well with emotion-focused workshops or workshops that use crayons.

  • If you have extra time, participants can do additional emotions.


Note about introducing embodied art:
You may wish to share with your participants the benefits of moving their bodies in playful and safe ways. Understanding what’s meaningful about movement and body awareness can help participants feel at ease expanding their comfort zones. For more about embodied art workshops and how to introduce them in your groups, please see Introduction to Embodied Art Workshops.
optional_materials:
You can also facilitate this workshop using a printable worksheet. If you are utilizing the worksheet in lieu of the regular workshop materials, be sure to send a digital copy or print them out for your participants if you are meeting in person.

  • Worksheet: Expressive Crayon Warm-up

  • Book: Nico Draws a Feeling

  • Video: Reading of Nico Draws a Feeling

 

 
Expressive Crayon Warm-up Worksheet
introduction:
Circular Doodles Angular scribbles on
top of circular doodles

This workshop can be used as a stand-alone independent workshop, or as a warm-up for another workshop. If you're using this as a stand-alone exercise, you may wish to introduce the warm-up, the materials, and how this exercise can be an effective short-term release of emotion. You have complete freedom to alter or adapt any part of this workshop to suit your group's needs.

"Before we begin, I want you to know that this workshop is a window of time for you. This means that this is a safe space to notice your thoughts, feelings, and needs. Since this space is your window of time, everything you say or do is voluntary. I’ll offer a suggested workshop idea, share about the materials we have available, and invite you to create, but there’s no right or wrong way to do this. It doesn't matter what it looks like. What matters is taking this time to truly honor your thoughts and feelings, however they come out. Please ask for what you need, and know that I’m here in support of you. If you can’t think of anything or draw a blank on what to create or write, feel free to just play with the materials."

title: River Stories
objective: This workshop gives children and teens an opportunity to use the metaphor of a river to acknowledge their past, notice their resilience and honor their present strength, through the process of visual and embodied art.
materials:
•  
      Optional printable self-led worksheet
       

    Construction paper (variety of colors)

  • Colored pencils

  • Pencil sharpeners

  • River Stories worksheet handout

  • Pens

You can also facilitate this workshop using this printable self-led worksheet. If you are utilizing this sheet in lieu of the regular workshop materials, be sure to send the sheet or print them out beforehand for your participants depending on the setting.
setup:
River Stories table setup


 

You are welcome to provide any and as many of the optional material that you see fit.

You can lay out the supplies on the table for easy transition during the group. If you're incorporating music for the visualization and creation, you may want to cue the song that you'll be using.

An open space for the sharing portion is helpful but not necessary. If you have limited space, you can refer to the Tips section below for more info.

If you are re-arranging your room to allow for more movement space, you might want to invite the participants to help you or do it in front of them, so that the transition is not jarring.

It might be helpful for you to create your river art and worksheet ahead of time, so that you can be prepared to demonstrate the sharing process or be a buddy for someone sharing (so that they don't have to share alone).

If possible, you can write the date and the phrase "I am here, in this room, with you." written in large letters on a poster or a chalkboard as a "prompt" so that when participants share, they can look up and see the words (instead of just reading them from the River Stories worksheet).


Video Samples:
Because the sharing part of this workshop has more steps than usual, we recommend watching one or more of the sample videos as a reference for the process. We suggest that you let the group have their own experience (instead of sharing the videos with them). In watching the videos, you will notice how participants have chosen to share in slightly different ways (e.g. using body movements, expressing emotions, using more or less words, etc.). We have included all of these samples, so you see some of the variety that can occur in this workshop.

  • River Stories Intro and Demo

  • River Stories Sample 1

  • River Stories Sample 2

  • River Stories Sample 3

  • River Stories Sample 4

 

As a facilitator, you have complete freedom to alter or adapt any portion or element of this workshop to cater to your specific group's needs.
warm_up:
Starting the River Story with birthday and today's date

 

Before the visualization starts, you can invite participants to choose a piece of colored construction paper that they will use to draw their river. You can invite them to start with their birth date on one end of the paper (the beginning of their river) and end with today's date (the end of their river). They can choose to write this any way they'd like to.

We have found that guided visualizations are most effective when spoken in a soft, slow tone, pausing where it feels right (specifically, after each question to give participants time to visualize their responses).


"I now would like to invite you to join me in a brief visualization. If you prefer to observe, that’s perfectly okay. Observing is participating.”

“For those of you who wish to follow along, try to get yourself in a comfortable position. If you feel safe, you can close your eyes, or keep them open. However way you are most comfortable.”

“Now, take a few deep breaths."

(You can guide participants to breathe in for a count of 5 seconds, hold it for 3 and exhale for 7 seconds, and repeat two or three times).


"Try to imagine your life as a river. You might picture yourself floating above your river and looking down at it or walking along side of it. What does it look like?..." What does the beginning of the river look like?... Where does your river flow quickly and where does it flow slowly?... Where is your river deep?... And where is it shallow?... Does your river have any twists, turns or bends?... Where is it narrow and where is it wide?... What do the banks of your river look like?... Does the water in your river have a color?... Can you see where your river is going?..."

"Sit with your thoughts for a moment and when you're ready, you can open your eyes (if they're closed) and begin to create your river on paper."
creation:
Participants creating their River Stories









 
 
  Sharing the "beginning" of the river









 
 
  One by one, sharing the second event









 
 
  Reaching the "end" of their rivers








 

You can give participants about 30 minutes (or however long you see fit) to create their rivers. If anyone finishes early, you can invite them to journal freely on the back of their river art, take time to sit quietly with their experience, begin to work on their River Stories worksheet to get ready for the sharing option, or anything else that works for them, you and the group.

Feel free to offer assistance where you see the need. You may want to give gentle time prompts such as: "We have about ten minutes to finish up our artwork," which can help participants be aware of their time.

Once participants are done creating their river, you can invite them to the next step.


Sharing Our River Stories: Filling Out the Worksheet
"Now, we'll have the opportunity to share our stories in a special way. For those of you who want to follow along, you can pick three moments from your life that you'd like to acknowledge and honor today. You can be very specific, such as: 'Age 5, we moved to a new home and it was scary.' Or, you can be general, such as: 'Age 5, something new'."

"Remember, just as with any other part of this workshop, sharing is optional, and if you don't feel comfortable sharing, that's perfectly okay. You get to decide if you want to share, what you want to share, and how you want to share it. Here's a worksheet to help get us ready for the sharing."


You can invite participants to fill out the Worksheet.


Sharing Our River Stories: Walking the River
Once everyone who wants to has completed their River Stories worksheet, you can invite the group to bring their creations with their worksheets and sit together, ideally facing the same direction.

It may be helpful for participants to see a physical demonstration of the sharing process, so you may consider being the first person in the first group to share.


You can stand up in front of the group and invite another 1-2 volunteers who also wish to share to stand up with you (see Demo videos above for reference).


"In a moment, I'm going to invite you to share your story with your body, your words, or both."

"How many of you have ever felt like something happened to you but it wasn't seen, heard, or acknowledged the way you would have liked? Today, we will each have the option to share our river with the group, and the group can really see, hear, and acknowledge the person, without any judgment; to really honor each journey."

"You get to choose if you want to share, and no one will share alone unless you want to. The basic structure is that a few people can stand up here together, facing the group. It's your choice if you want to show your river art as you do this."

"Those who are up here, I invite you to imagine that your river is stretched out in front of you, that you are standing at the beginning, at your place of birth, and that the river flows toward the rest of the group. You can then take turns sharing your birth date, followed by 'I was born.' For example, the first person might say: 'August 17, 1995, I was born.' Then, the second person would say: 'June 15, 2001, I was born'."

"Once all the 'beginnings' are shared, the first person can take a step forward and share the first event from your river that you want to honor today. As a reminder, you get to decide how much you want to share with us either with your words or with your body. For example, you could say: 'Age 8, my teacher yelled at me in front of the class.' Or, '1989, I felt embarrassed,' while silently making a movement. And you can demonstrate this by covering your face in an embarrassed way while saying '4th grade'."

"Once everyone has shared their first event, the first person can take another step forward and share their second event. One at a time, the other people standing can take their steps forward and share their second events."

"Once everyone has shared their second event, then each person up here can take a third step and share their third event, one at a time."


River Ending / Group Acknowledgement:
"Once everyone who chooses to has shared their third event, then each person will be invited to step forward one at a time, and say today's date and the sentence: 'I am here, in this room, with you.' We can say this because in addition to honoring everything we've gone through, we also get to come to this present moment in time and space and notice that we're not alone."

"After each person says: 'I am here in this room with you,' the rest of the group says, 'We see you,' all together in response, showing the community of support that we have here."


You can now invite participants to begin sharing their river stories. If you like, after each set of sharing finishes, you can invite the group to acknowledge the courage of the sharers by snapping their fingers. We encourage you to also acknowledge those who honored their desire to participate by observation only.
closing:
"Thank you all for taking this window of time to honor yourself, your journey, and the journeys of others."


You can invite the participants to take a breath or two together, if you see fit.


"Now we can take a moment for anyone who would like, to share about anything that came up for you during this workshop. You can share your art, your feelings, your thoughts, or anything that was meaningful about your experience today."

Optional Closing Questions:

  • Looking back at your river, what did you notice?

  • What made your river twist and turn?

  • How did it feel to share your river?

  • How did it feel to be acknowledged?

  • Where did you notice your strength or resilience today?

  • Where would you like your river to go from today on?
description: Through visual art (drawing) and embodied art (movement), participants are invited to use the metaphor of a river to acknowledge their past, notice their resilience, and honor their present strength.
notes:
With this workshop, it can be very helpful to set up the expectation of confidentiality ahead of time. It can be safer for participants to share if they know that not only will nothing be shared but that they don't have to answer any questions about their experiences.

You might say: "Before we begin, can we make the agreement that we will keep whatever anyone shares confidential? That way, we can each share exactly what we want to, and know that no one, even people in this room, will ever mention it to us unless we bring it up again first."
tips:
• It can be very helpful that you and any other facilitators, staff, or volunteers in the room participate along with the group. By modeling your enthusiasm and willingness to participate, you can help build trust, bonding, and make it safer for other people to play and share vulnerable experiences.

  • If you have limited space, you can encourage participants to make very tiny steps when they walk their river so that the participants still get the experience of moving forward towards the group.

  • If you end up with one person left who wants to share but everyone else has shared already, you or another participant can share your river again so that the one person does not feel alone walking their river. Of course, it's great to also honor the choice of any participants who request to walk their river alone.

  • If anyone in your group feels uncomfortable sharing their birth date, they do not need to share their birth year or age. They can just share the day and month or say whatever feels comfortable to them (for example, "a long time ago" or "at one point in the not too distant past").

  • In case anyone expresses concern, you can let them know that it's okay if different people's rivers don't line up when they share together. For example, one person's river might be in 1990 while another's river is in 2007 even though they are standing side by side. The reasons to share rivers with buddies is so that we can feel support or connection while we share.

  • If you like, you can invite participants to add a sentence or phrase along with "I was born." For example: "August 17, 1985: I was born and welcomed into the world."


Note about introducing embodied art:
You may wish to share with your participants the benefits of moving their bodies in playful and safe ways. Understanding what’s meaningful about movement and body awareness can help participants feel at ease expanding their comfort zones. For more about embodied art workshops and how to introduce them in your groups, please see Introduction to Embodied Art Workshops.
optional_materials:
• Markers (in addition to or instead of colored pencils)

  • Metallic markers

  • White colored pencils (or whiteout pens)

  • Relaxing, instrumental music for Visualization and Creation
introduction:
"This workshop is all about noticing how you got here and giving others a chance to see you and acknowledge your journey. It's a big deal that we get to be in this room together today."

"Today I'd like to invite you all to think of your lives as a river. Just like a river, our life journey can have twists and turns. We're going to have the chance to notice what we've been through in our past and how we got to be here today by creating art on paper, then physically with our bodies."

"Before we begin, I want you to know that this is your window of time. This means that this can be a safe space to notice your thoughts, feelings, and needs. Since this space is your window of time, everything you say or do is voluntary. During this time, there is no right or wrong way to participate or create. I'm going to share some basic instructions, but you get to choose how you want to participate. You can follow along completely, or you may want to do something different, it's completely up to you. During your window of time, you have complete freedom to choose. However you choose to spend this time will be perfectly okay. I am here to support you in any way that I can, so please feel free to ask for what you need."
demonstration:
Completed self-led worksheet

You can introduce the art supplies and share the following River Stories creation process with the participants. If you've made a sample, you may want to show it for reference.

Feel free to demonstrate any creation elements that you see fit.


"Today, you'll get to use any of the supplies available and create a river that tells the story of your life journey. You can draw your river and its elements however you like."

"Before you draw your river story, you'll have the option to join me in a guided visualization. As you create, I'd like to encourage you to consider the times or events that have shaped your life. The river you are creating on paper can look like what you saw in your mind during the visualization or it could be something new. You can use symbols, words, dates, ages, or anything else you'd like to represent the moments in your life you'd like to honor today. There is no right or wrong way to create your river. It may not even look like a river, and that's perfectly fine."
opening_circle: You can open by inviting anyone who wishes to do so, to share one thing that they experienced today that led up to this moment. For example: "I got on the bus to come here." Or, "I was having a really hard day, and I came to this workshop anyway."

title: Building Resilience / Construyendo Resiliencia
objective: Through the process of guided imagery, watercolor painting and dimensional putty, this workshop aims to help participants learn simple self-regulation techniques by creating a flower painting, which can serve as a calming image and a symbol of strength and resilience.
materials:
• Fresh cut flowers

  • White cardstock

  • Liquid watercolors

  • Rulers

  • Pencils

  • Erasers

  • Scissors
setup:
Building Resilience table setup
 

Before you begin this workshop, you might want to think about how you'd like to gather the fresh flowers. You can take participants on a nature walk to allow them to make a connection with nature and to find a flower that really speaks to them. If this isn't possible, you can bring in various flowers of your own and have the participants choose. You can also substitute flowers with fresh herbs.

If appropriate for your age group, you can print a copy of the Resilience handout for each participant and hand them out at the end of the workshop, or at any point you feel best.

If you're using air-dry putty, you may want to make sure to keep the packages sealed until it's time to create. This will keep the putty fresh and avoid any drying.

You have complete freedom to alter or adapt any portion or element of this workshop to cater to your specific group's needs.
warm_up:
"Before we create, I would like to invite you to join me in a warm-up. Remember, if you prefer to observe or use this time to do something else, that's perfectly okay. There is no right or wrong way to participate."

     
  Meeting your flower and noticing the details







 
 
  Drawing a border
 

 

 

"For those of you who want to follow along, I invite you to find a comfortable position in your chair. Take a deep breath and look around you. Breathe in some fresh, clean air. You are in a safe place and this is your window of time to notice your thoughts, feelings, and your needs."

"Look at the people at your table. We all have a lot in common and we are not alone. If you'd like, I welcome you to look at each person and make eye contact with them and give them a gentle nod or smile. Let's support each other and build a creative and helpful community here. Relax and settle in for some fun."

"Now I invite you to choose a flower. This is your special flower for today's art activity."


Speaking slowly and pausing in between questions, you can guide the participants:

"You are welcome to take a good, slow look at all of its colors and shapes. What do you see? Notice the details in the flower. If you like, you can use a magnifying glass (if available) to get a closer look at the intricate details. What new things did you notice about your flower after looking closer? I also invite you to smell your flower. What kind of smell does it have? What do you think about when you smell it? Does it remind you of anything?"

"As you take the time to notice all of the great things about your flower, I'd like to invite you to think about why you chose the flower you did. Think about all of the ways your flower is unique. Is it strong? Delicate? Colorful? Did you see anything in the flower that that you see in you?"


Drawing A Border:
"I invite you to begin by taking a pencil and ruler to draw a border around the paper you'd like to create on. You can measure the width of the ruler to space your border all around the page. This is to create a build-in frame. You can leave the borders white for now and you'll get a chance to come back to write your affirmations inside of it."


Breathing Techniques and Mindful Meditation:
"Before we draw our flowers, I'd like to give you an opportunity to learn some breathing exercises that you can do when you are going through a difficult time. Breathing exercises can help us calm ourselves down and relax. Whenever you get upset, remember to take three deep breaths. Taking these breaths can help us think more clearly and build resilience."


Before you begin the breathing exercise, you may want to remind participants that they get to choose how they'd like to participate. We have found that guided meditations and relaxations are most effective when spoken in a soft, slow tone, pausing where it feels right.


 

     
  Standing breaths
 
 
  Sitting breaths

 

Standing Breaths:
You can invite participants to stand up with feet placed apart for balance, leaving more than an arm's length between one another. Then, you can guide them through taking three deep breaths while raising their arms up and down at each breath.


Sitting Breaths:
"I now invite you to sit comfortably in a chair, and cross the fingers of both hands together and place them lightly on your belly. You can rest your elbows comfortably along your body... relax and drop your shoulders... if you feel safe, you can close your eyes, or keep them open. However you're most comfortable... Now take a deep breath in and out... notice your belly move up and down as you inhale and exhale."


Flower Meditation: (to continuously flow from sitting/standing breaths)
In a gently tone, you can use some of the prompts below, pausing in between the prompts to allow participants to take in each of them with tenderness. You can invite them to close their eyes if they feel comfortable doing so.

"I invite you to stay focused on your breathing and keeping your body relaxed. Listen to the sounds of the room... Now think about your flower growing tall and strong... Imagine your flower reaching toward the sun... Think of a gentle rain refreshing your flower... Think of all you have in common with your flower... Just like this flower, you are born into this world fresh and pure... You are loving and lovable... Now think about all of the different qualities of your flower and how you are just like it... No matter what is going on around you or happening to you, deep inside you there is always this calm, safe place that you can always find, today and always."
creation:
Building Resilience flower creation in progress

You can now invite those who wish to create their flower to begin. You may need to remind them of the creation process if you see the need and remind them that there is no right or wrong way to create.

Feel free to offer assistance where you see the need.
closing:
You can give participants a chance to volunteer and share their creations, anything they discovered, felt or experienced, or anything else they may wish to share.

Optional closing questions include:

  • "Did you discover anything about yourself?"

  • "Did you learn anything new?"

  • "What is one way you can calm yourself down when you're upset?"

  • "Why is it important to calm yourself when you're upset?"

  • "How are you resilient?"

  • "How have you been resilient in the past?"


"Take a look around and remember, we're not alone. We have a lot in common and we all go through difficult times and we are learning to support ourselves and each other every time we come here."
description: Through the process of guided imagery, watercolor painting, and dimensional putty, this workshop can help participants learn simple self-regulation techniques by creating a flower painting, which can then serve as a calming image, a personal symbol of strength and reminder of our individual resilience.
objective_spanish: A través del proceso de imaginería guiada, pintura liquida y masilla dimensional, este taller tiene como objetivo ayudar a las y los participantes a aprender técnicas simples de autorregulación mediante la creación de una pintura de flores, la cual puede servir como imagen de calma y como símbolo de fuerza y resiliencia.
materials_spanish:
• Flores frescas 
  • Cartulina blanca
  • Pintura liquida
  • Reglas
  • Lápices
  • Borradores
  • Tijeras
timeframe_spanish:
Introducción: 10 min
Demostración: 20 min
Calentamiento: 20 min
Creación: 50 min
Cierre: 10 min
Total: 1:50 hora
setup_spanish:
Antes de comenzar este taller, es posible que quiera pensar en cómo le gustaría recolectar las flores frescas. Puede llevar a las y los participantes a una caminata por la naturaleza para permitirles hacer una conexión con la naturaleza y encontrar una flor que realmente les hable. Si esto no es posible, usted puede traer las flores y hacer que las y los participantes elijan. También puede sustituir las flores con hierbas frescas.

Si es apropiado para la edad de su grupo, puede imprimir una copia del folleto de Resiliencia para cada participante y entregarlo al final del taller, o en cualquier momento que usted sienta que es apropiado.

Si está utilizando una masilla que se seca con el aire, puede ser que quiera asegurarse de mantener los paquetes sellados hasta que sea el momento de usarlos. Esto mantendrá la masilla fresca y evitará que se seque.

Tiene total libertad para alterar o adaptar cualquier parte o elemento de este taller para satisfacer las necesidades de su grupo específico.
creation_spanish:
Pasos para la creación:

"Antes de comenzar a crear, voy a guiarles a través de la imaginación e imaginaremos que somos una flor y esto nos ayudará a prepararnos para crear. También me gustaría compartirles el proceso de creación, así que después de que utilicemos nuestra imaginación podemos ir directo a hacer arte".

Paso 1: Dibujando una flor
"Para comenzar, pueden tomar su flor en su mano y mirarla mientras la dibujan en el papel. Si lo desean, pueden dibujar la flor muy grande para que realmente puedan centrarse en los detalles. No se preocupe si su dibujo no se parece a su flor en particular, recuerden que lo que salga está bien".

Paso 2: Añadiendo Color
"Luego, usando las pinturas liquidas, pueden agregar color a su flor. Pueden usar los colores de su flor o pueden crear nuevos colores. No hay una forma incorrecta de agregar color. Si eligen no agregar ningún color, agregando más detalles a su dibujo también es algo que podrían querer probar".

Paso 3: Agregando Relieve
"A continuación, puede usar la masilla que se seca con el aire para agregar relieve a su pintura. Agregar un borde o detalles divertidos a su flor podría ser algo que tal vez quieran considerar. Pueden usar el pegamento para pegar la masilla".

(Opcional): Puede demostrar cómo la pintura liquida color oro y plata, si es que tiene disponible, se pueden agregar como el último paso del proceso de creación para agregar acentos a la flor. Puede demostrar brevemente cómo aplicar la pintura con un pincel pequeño.

Paso 4: Escribiendo Afirmaciones
"Finalmente, les invitaré a agregar algunas palabras positivas que les den tranquilidad en su dibujo. Pueden escribir algunas afirmaciones o palabras de aliento que puedan ayudarles a superar los momentos difíciles".

(Opcional): Puede compartir el siguiente ejemplo con las y los participantes:
"En la parte superior, pueden escribir: 'Soy tan fresca o fresco como una flor'. En el lado izquierdo, puede escribir: “Tomo tres respiraciones profundas para calmarme”. En el lado derecho, pueden escribir: "Soy amorosa o amoroso y amable". Y en la parte inferior, puedes escribir y terminar esta oración: "Yo soy _________".

"Antes de empezar a crear, me gustaría invitarles a unirse a un calentamiento. Recuerden, si prefieren observar o usar este tiempo para hacer otra cosa, está perfectamente bien. No hay una forma correcta o incorrecta de participar. "

"Para las personas que quieran hacer el calentamiento, les invito a encontrar una posición cómoda en su silla. Respiren hondo y miren a su alrededor. Respiren un poco de aire fresco y limpio. Están en un lugar seguro y esta es su ventana de tiempo para notar sus pensamientos, sentimientos y sus necesidades ".

"Miren a las personas en su mesa. Todas y todos tenemos mucho en común y no estamos solas ni solos. Si lo desean, les invito a que miren a cada persona y hagan contacto visual con ellas y ellos, y les saluden moviendo ligeramente la cabeza o sonriendo. Apoyémonos entre nosotras y nosotros y construyamos aquí una comunidad creativa y útil. Relájense y pónganse cómodas y cómodos para divertirse"

"Ahora les invito a elegir una flor. Esta es su flor especial para la actividad artística de hoy".

Hablando lentamente y pausando entre las preguntas, puede guiar a los participantes:

"Les invito a que observen detenidamente su flor y todas sus formas y colores. ¿Qué ven? Observen los detalles en la flor. Si lo desean, puede usar una lupa (si está disponible) para ver más de cerca los detalles. ¿Qué cosas nuevas notaron sobre tu flor después de mirarla más de cerca? También les invito a oler su flor. ¿Qué tipo de olor tiene? ¿Qué piensan cuando la huelen? ¿El olor les recuerda algo?"

"A medida que se toman el tiempo para notar todos los detalles increíbles de su flor, me gustaría invitarles a pensar por qué eligieron esa flor en particular. Piensen en todas las maneras en las que su flor es única. ¿Es fuerte? ¿Delicada? ¿Colorida? ¿Vieron algo en su flor que ven en ustedes mismas y mismos? "

Dibujando un borde:
"Les invito a comenzar tomando un lápiz y una regla para dibujar un borde alrededor del papel en el que van a crear. Pueden medir el ancho de la regla para espaciar su borde alrededor de la hoja. Esto es para crear un marco. Pueden dejar los bordes en blanco por ahora y tendrán la oportunidad de regresar más adelante a escribir sus afirmaciones dentro de él".

Técnicas de respiración y meditación de atención plena (o mindfulness):
"Antes de que dibujemos nuestras flores, me gustaría darles la oportunidad de aprender algunos ejercicios de respiración que pueden hacer cuando están pasando por un momento difícil. Los ejercicios de respiración pueden ayudarnos a calmarnos y relajarnos. Siempre que sintamos enojo, recordemos tomar tres respiraciones profundas. Tomar estas respiraciones puede ayudarnos a pensar con mayor claridad y construir resiliencia ".

Antes de comenzar el ejercicio de respiración, puede recordarles a las y los participantes que cada quien elige cómo les gustaría participar. Hemos encontrado que las meditaciones guiadas y las relajaciones son más efectivas cuando se hablan en un tono suave y lento, tomando una pausa donde se siente oportuno.

Tomando respiraciones de pie: 
Puede invitar a las y los participantes a ponerse de pie con los pies separados para mantener el equilibrio, dejando más de lo equivalente a la medida de un brazo entre sí. Luego, puede guiarles a través de tres respiraciones profundas mientras levanta los brazos hacia arriba y hacia abajo con cada respiración.

Tomando respiraciones sentadas y sentados:
"Ahora les invito a sentarse cómodamente en una silla, y crucen los dedos de ambas manos y colóquenlos ligeramente sobre su vientre. Pueden apoyar sus codos cómodamente a lo largo de su cuerpo ... relájense y dejen caer los hombros ... si se sienten seguras o seguros, pueden cerrar los ojos o mantenerlos abiertos. Lo que a ustedes les haga sentir más comodidad... Ahora respiren y exhalen profundamente ... observen como su barriga se mueve hacia arriba y hacia abajo cuando inhalan y exhalan ".

Meditación de la flor: (seguida de las respiraciones de pie/sentadas o sentados)
En un tono suave, puede utilizar algunas de las indicaciones que le presentamos a continuación, deteniéndose entre las indicaciones para permitir que las y los participantes las reciban con ternura. Puede invitarlos a cerrar los ojos si se sienten cómodas o cómodos haciéndolo.

"Les invito a que se enfoquen en su respiración y mantengan sus cuerpos relajados. Escuchen los sonidos de la habitación... Ahora piensen como su flor crece alta y fuerte ... Imaginen como su flor crece y se acerca al sol… Imaginen como cae una lluvia suave y como refresca su flor... Piensen en todo lo que tienen en común ustedes con su flor... Al igual que esta flor, ustedes nacieron en este mundo fresco y puro… Ustedes son personas amorosas y les aman ... Ahora piensen en todas las diferentes cualidades de su flor y cómo se parecen a ella ... No importa lo que esté sucediendo a su alrededor o lo que les esté sucediendo, en lo más profundo de ustedes siempre existe este lugar tranquilo y seguro que siempre pueden encontrar, hoy y todos los días."

Ahora puede invitar a que comiencen con su flor las personas que deseen crearla. Es posible que deba recordarles el proceso de creación si ve la necesidad, recordarles que no hay una forma correcta o incorrecta de crear.

Siéntase libre de ofrecer asistencia donde la vea necesaria.
closing_spanish:
Puede darles a las y los participantes la oportunidad de compartir de manera voluntaria sus creaciones, o también cualquier cosa que hayan descubierto, sentido o experimentado, o cualquier otra cosa que deseen compartir.

Las preguntas de cierre opcionales e incluyen:

"¿Descubriste algo sobre ti en este taller?"

"¿Aprendiste algo nuevo?"

"¿De qué manera puedes calmarte cuando estás molesta o molesto?"

"¿Por qué es importante calmarse cuando estamos molestas o molestos?"

"¿Cómo eres resiliente?"

"¿Cómo has sido resiliente en el pasado?"


"Miren a su alrededor y recuerde, no estamos solas ni solos. Tenemos mucho en común y todas y todos pasamos por momentos difíciles y estamos aprendiendo a apoyarnos a nosotras y nosotros mismos y a los demás cada vez que venimos aquí".
