introduction:
"Thank you for being here today. Before we begin, I want you to know that this is your window of time. This means that this can be a safe space to notice your thoughts, feelings, and needs. Since this space is your window of time, everything you say or do is voluntary. During this time, there is no right or wrong way to participate or create. I'm going to share some basic instructions, but you get to choose how you want to participate. You can follow along completely, or you may want to do something different, it's completely up to you. During your window of time, you have complete freedom to choose. However you choose to spend this time will be perfectly okay. I am here to support you in any way that I can, so please feel free to ask for what you need."

"In this workshop we'll have an opportunity to talk about something that is inside all of us. It's something that some of us may notice inside ourselves more than others but once we notice it and understand it, it can be really helpful."

"The topic of today is resilience. What does this word mean? Well, resilience is the inner strength that allows us to keep going even through difficult and challenging times. Resilience is not a trait that some people have and others do not, resilience is an ability that we can all learn and develop."

"Let me give you an example: When Emma was learning to ride her bike, she fell many times, but she kept getting back up until she finally learned to ride without falling. Even though it hurt to fall so many times, Emma was able to keep trying and learned to ride her bike. It took some work for Emma to keep trying; she had to believe in herself, she had to try new ways of balancing and eventually, she did it."

"Here's another example: John was upset that he had to move out of his old home. This meant that he also had to move to a new school, too. He was so angry and he told his mom that he would never go to school again. But, after a few weeks of being scared and going to his new school, he started to make friends and slowly, he began to enjoy it."

"With these two examples, how were these two people showing that they were resilient? Can you think of a time when something happened in your life where you were resilient? I'd like to invite you to think about what you did to get through your difficult situation? Did you ask for help? Did you stay positive? Did you find a way to solve a problem? Did you make a plan? What did you do? Think about this for a moment and remember throughout today that you are strong and capable of getting through things that are difficult."

"As we have a chance to create paintings today we will have an opportunity to solve problems, trust ourselves and our creativity, learn new things and learn something new about ourselves; we all have the power to be resilient."
introduction_spanish:
"Gracias por estar aquí hoy. Antes de comenzar, quiero que sepan que esta es su ventana de tiempo. Esto significa que este puede ser un espacio seguro para que ustedes noten sus pensamientos, sentimientos y necesidades. Ya que este espacio es su ventana, todo lo que digan o hagan es voluntario. Durante este tiempo, no hay una forma correcta o incorrecta de participar o crear. Voy a compartir algunas instrucciones básicas con ustedes, pero pueden elegir cómo quieren participar. Pueden seguirlas al pie de la letra, o puede ser que quieran hacer algo diferente, esto depende completamente de cada una o uno de ustedes. Durante su ventana de tiempo, tienen total libertad para elegir. Como decidan pasar este tiempo estará perfectamente bien. Estoy aquí para ayudarles de cualquier manera que pueda, así que no duden en pedirme lo que necesiten".

"En este taller tendremos la oportunidad de hablar sobre algo que está dentro de todas y todos nosotros. Es algo que puede ser que algunas personas lo notamos más que otras, pero está dentro de cada quien. Una vez que lo notamos y lo entendemos, puede ser realmente útil".

"El tema de hoy es la resiliencia. ¿Qué significa esta palabra? Bueno, la resiliencia es la fuerza interior que nos permite seguir adelante incluso en tiempos difíciles y desafiantes. La resiliencia no es un rasgo que algunas personas tienen y otras no, la resiliencia es una habilidad que todas y todos podemos aprender y desarrollar ".

"Déjenme darles un ejemplo: cuando Emma estaba aprendiendo a andar en bicicleta, se cayó muchas veces, pero se siguió subiendo a la bicicleta hasta que finalmente aprendió a andar sin caerse. Aunque le dolió caer tantas veces, Emma pudo seguir intentándolo hasta aprender a andar en bicicleta. Le costó trabajo a Emma seguir intentándolo; ya que tenía que creer en sí misma, tenía que probar nuevas formas de equilibrio y, finalmente, lo logró ".

"Les tengo otro ejemplo: John estaba molesto porque tuvo que mudarse de su antigua casa. Esto significaba que también tenía que mudarse a una nueva escuela. Estaba tan enojado que le dijo a su mamá que nunca más iría a la escuela de nuevo. Pero, después de unas semanas de estar asustado y estar yendo a su nueva escuela, comenzó a hacer amigos y, lentamente, y comenzó a disfrutarlo".

"En estos dos ejemplos, ¿cómo demostraron estas dos personas que eran resilientes? ¿Se les ocurre algún momento en el que sucedió algo en sus vidas en el que fueran resilientes? Me gustaría invitarles a pensar en ¿qué hicieron para superar esta situación difícil? ¿Pidieron ayuda? ¿Se mantuvieron positivas o positivos? ¿Encontraron una manera de resolver su problema? ¿Hicieron un plan? ¿Qué hicieron? Piensen en esto por un momento y a lo largo del día recuerden que ustedes son fuertes y capaces de superar las cosas que son difíciles ".

"Así como hoy tenemos la oportunidad de crear pinturas, también tendremos la oportunidad de resolver problemas, confiar en nosotras mismas o nosotros mismos y en nuestras creatividades, aprender cosas nuevas y aprender algo nuevo sobre nosotras o nosotros mismos; todas y todos tenemos el poder de ser resilientes".
demonstration:
"During this workshop you will have an opportunity to use different art materials to draw and paint a flower that can represent your resilience. I will give you information about the art supplies and creation process that you can follow completely or you can choose which parts you would like to do or you can just sit and play with the art supplies. You can even choose to create something different. This is your window of time and you can use it however you'd like, even if it's sitting back and observing; as long as you're honoring your thoughts and feelings, you are doing a great job."

"To start us off, I'm going to show you the art materials that are available to use. While I'm doing this, we're going to talk a little more about resilience."

 

Liquid Watercolors:
You can continue the conversation by moving into the watercolor demonstration. If you're using Bingo bottles, you can briefly demonstrate how to apply watercolor onto the paper by gently squeezing, how they can make dots and blend colors, etc. Feel free to demonstrate any creation elements that you see fit.


"As we begin to explore the watercolors, I invite you to choose some colors and put them onto your paper. Notice how the colors begin to soak into the paper and spread around. If you'd like, choose different types of colors and see what happens when you blend them together. When we're working with watercolors, we can also think about how we're able to handle the things in our lives that we can't control. Just like the watercolors soak into the paper and blend into one another, we usually can't control the difficult things that happen to us. All we can do is work with what is given to us and and figure out the healthy ways to deal with it. We will learn some of these skills today. How have you been able to make the best out of a difficult situation?"

 

Air-Dry Putty:
Before you begin, you can open up the packages of the air-dry putty and invite participants to grab a small chunk of any color they'd like.


"If you'd like, take a piece of the putty into your hands and take a moment to feel it. Move it around and squeeze it with one hand, try squeezing it with two hands. How does it feel? If you'd like, smell the putty. What does it smell like?"

"When we talked earlier about resilience we said that it's a person's ability to navigate through when difficult things happen to them. Let's see if we can make a round ball out of the putty (give participants some time to create their balls)."

"Now, imagine that these round balls are us. I invite you to twist, turn, and break the round ball apart (pause and allow time for this)."

"Let's imagine that this twisting, turning, and breaking apart can be all of the difficult things that can happen in our lives. Try to think what kinds of difficult things have you faced?"

"Now, let's shape our putty back into a ball (pause and let participants gather their putty). For some of you with more pieces to pick up, it took a little more time to gather and mold back into place. This is also true about our lives. Let's take a look around and notice that everyone is back to the same ball that they once started with. Inside of all of us, we have the ability to pick up all of the pieces and put ourselves back together again. As we sit here, notice that everything we have gone through in our past is behind us and it's a big deal to be here today. Maybe you're going through something difficult right now and you feel like it will never get better. I hope this can give you a sense of comfort knowing that you are resilient. Resilience is inside of you."

 

     
  Step 1: Drawing the flower

 
 
  Step 2: Adding Colors

 
 
  Step 3: Adding air-dry putty accent

 
 
  Step 4: Writing affirmation

Creation Steps
"Before you have an opportunity to begin creating I will guide us though imagining that we are a flower to help us get ready to create. I'd now like to share the creation process with you, so after we use our imaginations we can jump right into having a chance to make art."


Step 1: Drawing a Flower
"To start, you can take your flower in your hand again and look at it as you draw it on your paper. If you want, you can draw the flower very large on your page so you can really focus on the details. Don't worry if your drawing doesn't look just like your special flower, remember that whatever comes out will be just right."


Step 2: Adding Color
"Then, using the watercolors, you can add color to your flower. You can follow the color(s) of your flower or you can come up with new colors. There is no wrong way to add color. If you choose not to add any color, adding more detail to your drawing can be something you might want to try out."


Step 3: Adding Accents
"Next, you can use the air-dry putty to add accents to your painting. Adding a fun border or details to your flower might be something to consider. You can use the glue to stick the putty on."

(Optional): You can demonstrate how the gold and silver watercolors, if available, can be added as a last step of the creation process to add accents. You can briefly demonstrate how to apply the paint with a small paintbrush.


Step 4: Writing Affirmations
"Lastly, you will be invited to add some positive and calming words to your drawing. You can write some affirmations or words of encouragement that can help you get through difficult times."

(Optional): You can share the following example with the participants:
"At the very top, you can write: 'I am as fresh as a flower.' On the left side, you can write: 'I take three deep breaths to calm myself.' On the right side, you can write: 'I am loving and lovable.' And on the bottom, you can write and finish this sentence: 'I am _________'."
demonstration_spanish:
"Durante este taller, tendrán la oportunidad de utilizar diferentes materiales de arte para dibujar y pintar una flor que pueda representar su capacidad de resiliencia. Les daré información sobre los diferentes materiales de arte y como pueden hacer esta la flor. Recuerden que pueden seguir al pie de la letra esta información o pueden elegir qué partes les gustaría seguir o simplemente pueden sentarse y jugar con los diferentes materiales de arte. Incluso pueden elegir crear algo totalmente diferente. Esta es su ventana de tiempo y pueden usarla como quieran, incluso si se sientan a observar; Mientras estén honrando sus pensamientos y sentimientos, están haciendo un gran trabajo ".

"Para comenzar, les mostraré los materiales de arte que tenemos hoy disponibles. Mientras hago esto, hablaremos un poco más sobre la capacidad de resiliencia".

Pintura liquida:
Puede continuar la conversación hacia la demostración de la pintura liquida. Si está utilizando botellas de bingo, puede demostrar brevemente cómo aplicar la pintura liquida sobre el papel apretando suavemente, también cómo pueden hacer puntos con la pintura y mezclar colores, etc. Siéntase libre de demostrar cualquier elemento de creación que considere oportuno.

"Mientras comenzamos a explorar las pinturas liquidas, les invito a elegir algunos colores y ponerlos en su papel. Observen cómo los colores comienzan a empaparse en el papel y como se extienden. Si lo desean, elijan diferentes tipos de colores y vean qué sucede cuando se mezclan entre sí. Cuando trabajamos con pintura liquida, también podemos pensar en cómo podemos manejar las cosas que no podemos controlar en nuestras vidas. Igual que las pinturas liquidas cuando se empapan en el papel y se mezclan los colores unos con otros, generalmente no podemos controlar las cosas difíciles que nos suceden. Todo lo que podemos hacer es trabajar con lo que se nos da y descubrir las formas saludables de enfrentarlo. Aprenderemos algunas de estas habilidades hoy ¿Ustedes cómo han podido sacar lo mejor de una situación difícil?

Masilla que se seca con el aire:
Antes de comenzar, puede abrir los paquetes de la masilla e invitar a las y los participantes a que tomen una pequeña porción del color que deseen.

"Si quieren, tomen un pedazo de la masilla en sus manos y tómense un momento para sentirla. Muévanla y apriétenla con una mano, ahora intenten apretarla con las dos manos. ¿Cómo se siente? Si desean olerla, huélanla ¿A qué les huele? "

"Cuando hablábamos acerca de la resiliencia, dijimos que es la capacidad de una persona para navegar a través de las cosas difíciles. A ver si podemos hacer una bola redonda con la masilla (dé a los participantes algo de tiempo para crear sus bolas)".

"Ahora, imaginen que estas bolas redondas somos nosotras o nosotros. Les invito a torcer y romper su bola (tome una pausa y de tiempo para esto)".

"Imaginemos que esta torsión y separación pueden ser todas las cosas difíciles que pueden suceder en nuestras vidas. Traten de pensar ¿qué tipo de cosas difíciles han enfrentado?"

"Ahora, hagamos nuevamente una bola con nuestra masilla (haga una pausa y permita que las y los participantes junten su masilla). Para algunos de ustedes con más piezas para recoger, les tomó un poco más de tiempo para reunirlas y moldearlas de nuevo. Esto también pasa en nuestras vidas. Echemos un vistazo alrededor y notemos que todas y todos volvemos a la misma bola con la que empezamos. Dentro de todos nosotras o nosotros, tenemos la capacidad de recoger todas las piezas y volver a armarnos. Mientras estamos aquí sentadas y sentados, notemos que todo lo que hemos vivido en nuestro pasado ya está detrás de nosotros y no es cualquier cosa poder estar hoy aquí. Tal vez estén pasando por algo difícil en este momento y sientan que nunca va a mejorar. Espero que esto les pueda dar una sensación de comodidad sabiendo que son resilientes. La resiliencia está dentro de ustedes ".

title: Expressive Crayon Warm-Up
objective: This workshop offers children a simple yet powerful warm-up to safely express any emotions they have been holding inside by scribbling freely.
materials:
• Crayons              

  • Paper (variety of colors)
creation:
You can begin by inviting the children to pick a feeling word. It can be a feeling word that they've heard already today or it could be a new one. It's okay if the feeling word is the same or different than another person's in this group. Once they've chosen a feeling, you can invite them to choose any color paper they like.

"For those of you who wish to participate, in a moment, you will have the opportunity to choose a crayon color that reminds you of the emotion you've selected and scribble on your paper, drawing as if you were experiencing that feeling right now. You can scribble fast or slow, big or small, whatever feels best to you. It's okay if the crayon breaks or you rip the paper. It doesn't matter at all what it looks like. Anyway you choose to scribble will be perfect. Is everyone ready?"

You can give them as much time as you feel is needed to process their emotion and scribble. Generally, about 2-3 minutes have been enough. Once you feel they've had ample time to scribble, you can invite them to find a pausing place so they can take a brief moment to reflect on what that was like.

Expressive Crayon depicting anger Expressive Crayon depicting happiness
closing:
For the closing, you can give the children an opportunity to share anything they like about their scribbles, their chosen feeling, or whatever they noticed by participating. It can also be helpful to remind them that they are welcome to pass if they don't feel like sharing and that each person's representation of an emotion could be different, and that is okay.

You can end by validating each child's experience, courage and their taking a window of time to honor themselves.
description: This warm-up allows participants to safely explore and express emotions.
tips:
• This warm-up often works best without music so that children can connect to their own experiences and different children can work on different emotions simultaneously without being influenced by the music.

  • If your group has a hard time thinking of emotion words, you can brainstorm words with them ahead of time or have them start with emotions you suggest (like anger, confusion, joy, etc.) and then end with an emotion of their choice.

  • This warm-up works well with emotion-focused workshops or workshops that use crayons.

  • If you have extra time, children can do additional emotions.


Note about introducing embodied art:
You may wish to share with your children the benefits of moving their bodies in playful and safe ways. Understanding what’s meaningful about movement and body awareness can help children feel at ease expanding their comfort zones. For more about embodied art workshops and how to introduce them in your groups, please see Introduction to Embodied Art Workshops.
optional_materials:
You can also facilitate this workshop using a printable worksheet. If you are utilizing the worksheet in lieu of the regular workshop materials, be sure to send a digital copy or print them out for your participants if you are meeting in person.

  • Worksheet: Expressive Crayon Warm-up

  • Book: Nico Draws a Feeling

  • Video: Reading of Nico Draws a Feeling

 

 
Expressive Crayon Warm-up Worksheet
introduction:
This workshop can be used as a stand-alone independent workshop, or as a warm-up for another workshop. If you're using this as a stand-alone exercise, you may wish to introduce the warm-up, the materials, and how this exercise can be an effective short-term release of emotion. You have complete freedom to alter or adapt any part of this workshop to suit your group's needs.

You can begin by inviting the children to brainstorm some emotions. You can prompt them with a question like: "What are some feeling words?" As they share some answers, you may wish to validate their responses and invite them to show what they look like when they feel that emotion. For example, if someone says "happy," you can say, "Show me what 'happy' looks like to you in 3-2-1, go!"

If no one feels comfortable sharing, that's perfectly okay. You have the option to offer emotions suggestions to them.

You may also wish to remind the children that there's no wrong way to show a feeling (as long as you're not hurting yourself or anyone else), and that there are many ways to show each feeling.

After the group has brainstormed a number of feeling words, you may wish to validate them for sharing and introduce the creation part of this exercise.

"Today, you have an opportunity to not only show on your faces what those feelings look like but also on paper with crayons, by creating an amazing art piece that represents your emotion."

"Before we begin, I want you to know that this workshop is a window of time for you. This means that this is a safe space to notice your thoughts, feelings, and needs. Since this space is your window of time, everything you say or do is voluntary. I’ll offer a suggested workshop idea, share about the materials we have available, and invite you to create, but there’s no wrong way to do this. It doesn't matter what it looks like. What matters is taking this time to truly honor your thoughts and feelings, however they come out. If you can’t think of anything or draw a blank on what to create or write, feel free to just observe. However you choose to spend this time will be perfectly okay. This is your time. Please ask for what you need, and know that I’m here in support of you."

title: Building Resilience
objective: Through the process of guided imagery, watercolor painting and dimensional putty, this workshop aims to help participants learn simple self-regulation techniques by creating a flower painting, which can serve as a calming image and a symbol of strength and resilience.
materials:
• Fresh cut flowers

  • White cardstock

  • Liquid watercolors

  • Rulers

  • Pencils

  • Erasers

  • Scissors
setup:
Building Resilience table setup
 

Before you begin this workshop, you might want to think about how you'd like to gather the fresh flowers. You can take participants on a nature walk to allow them to make a connection with nature and to find a flower that really speaks to them. If this isn't possible, you can bring in various flowers of your own and have the participants choose. You can also substitute flowers with fresh herbs.

You can print a copy of the Resilience handout for each participant and hand them out at the end of the workshop, or at any point you feel best.

If you're using air-dry putty, you may want to make sure to keep the packages sealed until it's time to create. This will keep the putty fresh and avoid any drying.

You have complete freedom to alter or adapt any portion or element of this workshop to cater to your specific group's needs.
warm_up:
"Before we create, I would like to invite you to join me in a warm-up. Remember, if you prefer to observe or use this time to do something else, that's perfectly okay. There is no right or wrong way to participate."

     
  Meeting your flower and noticing the details







 
 
  Drawing a border
 

 

 

"For those of you who want to follow along, I invite you to find a comfortable position in your chair. Take a deep breath and look around you. Breathe in some fresh, clean air. You are in a safe place and this is your window of time to notice your thoughts, feelings, and your needs."

"Look at the people at your table. We all have a lot in common and we are not alone. If you'd like, I welcome you to look at each person and make eye contact with them and give them a gentle nod or smile. Let's support each other and build a creative and helpful community here. Relax and settle in for some fun."

"Now I invite you to choose a flower. This is your special flower for today's art activity."


Speaking slowly and pausing in between questions, you can guide the participants:

"You are welcome to take a good, slow look at all of its colors and shapes. What do you see? Notice the details in the flower. If you like, you can use a magnifying glass (if available) to get a closer look at the intricate details. What new things did you notice about your flower after looking closer? I also invite you to smell your flower. What kind of smell does it have? What do you think about when you smell it? Does it remind you of anything?"

"As you take the time to notice all of the great things about your flower, I'd like to invite you to think about why you chose the flower you did. Think about all of the ways your flower is unique. Is it strong? Delicate? Colorful? Did you see anything in the flower that that you see in you?"


Drawing A Border:
"I invite you to begin by taking a pencil and ruler to draw a border around the paper you'd like to create on. You can measure the width of the ruler to space your border all around the page. This is to create a build-in frame. You can leave the borders white for now and you'll get a chance to come back to write your affirmations inside of it."


Breathing Techniques and Mindful Meditation:
"Before we draw our flowers, I'd like to give you an opportunity to learn some breathing exercises that you can do when you are going through a difficult time. Breathing exercises can help us calm ourselves down and relax. Whenever you get upset, remember to take three deep breaths. Taking these breaths can help us think more clearly and build resilience."


Before you begin the breathing exercise, you may want to remind participants that they get to choose how they'd like to participate. We have found that guided meditations and relaxations are most effective when spoken in a soft, slow tone, pausing where it feels right.


 

     
  Standing breaths
 
 
  Sitting breaths

 

Standing Breaths:
You can invite participants to stand up with feet placed apart for balance, leaving more than an arm's length between one another. Then, you can guide them through taking three deep breaths while raising their arms up and down at each breath.


Sitting Breaths:
"I now invite you to sit comfortably in a chair, and cross the fingers of both hands together and place them lightly on your belly. You can rest your elbows comfortably along your body... relax and drop your shoulders... if you feel safe, you can close your eyes, or keep them open. However you're most comfortable... Now take a deep breath in and out... notice your belly move up and down as you inhale and exhale."


Flower Meditation: (to continuously flow from sitting/standing breaths)
In a gently tone, you can use some of the prompts below, pausing in between the prompts to allow participants to take in each of them with tenderness. You can invite them to close their eyes if they feel comfortable doing so.

"I invite you to stay focused on your breathing and keeping your body relaxed. Listen to the sounds of the room... Now think about your flower growing tall and strong... Imagine your flower reaching toward the sun... Think of a gentle rain refreshing your flower... Think of all you have in common with your flower... Just like this flower, you are born into this world fresh and pure... You are loving and lovable... Now think about all of the different qualities of your flower and how you are just like it... No matter what is going on around you or happening to you, deep inside you there is always this calm, safe place that you can always find, today and always."
creation:
Building Resilience flower creation in progress

You can now invite those who wish to create their flower to begin. You may need to remind them of the creation process if you see the need and remind them that there is no right or wrong way to create.

Feel free to offer assistance where you see the need.
closing:
You can give participants a chance to volunteer and share their creations, anything they discovered, felt or experienced, or anything else they may wish to share.

Optional closing questions include:

  • "Did you discover anything about yourself?"

  • "Did you learn anything new?"

  • "What is one way you can calm yourself down when you're upset?"

  • "Why is it important to calm yourself when you're upset?"

  • "How are you resilient?"

  • "How have you been resilient in the past?"


"Take a look around and remember, we're not alone. We have a lot in common and we all go through difficult times and we are learning to support ourselves and each other every time we come here."
description: Through the process of guided imagery, watercolor painting, and dimensional putty, this workshop can help participants learn simple self-regulation techniques by creating a flower painting, which can then serve as a calming image, a personal symbol of strength and reminder of our individual resilience.
optional_materials:
• Newspaper or placemats

  • Air-dry putty

  • Liquid watercolor gold and silver colors

  • Washable markers

  • Bingo bottles (to be filled with liquid watercolors)

  • Brushes

  • Magnifying glass

  • Tacky glue

  • White crayons or oil pastels

  • Resilience handout
introduction:
"Before we begin, I want you to know that this is your window of time. This means that this can be a safe space to notice your thoughts, feelings, and needs. Since this space is your window of time, everything you say or do is voluntary. During this time, there is no right or wrong way to participate or create. I'm going to share some basic instructions, but you get to choose how you want to participate. You can follow along completely, or you may want to do something different, it's completely up to you. During your window of time, you have complete freedom to choose. However you choose to spend this time will be perfectly okay. I am here to support you in any way that I can, so please feel free to ask for what you need."

"In this workshop we'll have an opportunity to talk about something that is inside all of us. It's something that some of us may notice inside ourselves more than others but once we notice it and understand it, it can be really helpful."

"The topic of today is resilience. What does this word mean? Well, resilience is the inner strength that allows us to navigate through difficult and challenging times. Resilience is not a trait that some people have and others do not, resilience is an ability that we can all learn and develop."

"As we have a chance to create paintings today we will have an opportunity to solve problems, trust ourselves and our creativity, learn new things and learn something new about ourselves; we all have the power to be resilient."
demonstration:
"During this workshop you will have an opportunity to use different art materials to draw and paint a flower that can represent your resilience. I will give you information about the art supplies and creation process that you can follow completely or you can choose which parts you would like to do or you can just sit and play with the art supplies. You can even choose to create something different. This is your window of time and you can use it however you'd like, even if it's sitting back and observing; as long as you're honoring your thoughts and feelings, you are doing a great job."

"To start us off, I'm going to show you the art materials that are available to use. While I'm doing this, we're going to talk a little more about resilience."

 

Liquid Watercolors:
You can continue the conversation by moving into the watercolor demonstration. If you're using Bingo bottles, you can briefly demonstrate how to apply watercolor onto the paper by gently squeezing, how they can make dots and blend colors, etc. Feel free to demonstrate any creation elements that you see fit.


"As we begin to explore the watercolors, I invite you to choose some colors and put them onto your paper. Notice how the colors begin to soak into the paper and spread around. If you'd like, choose different types of colors and see what happens when you blend them together. When we're working with watercolors, we can also think about how we're able to handle the things in our lives that we can't control. Just like the watercolors soak into the paper and blend into one another, we usually can't control the difficult things that happen to us. All we can do is work with what is given to us and and figure out the healthy ways to deal with it. We will learn some of these skills today. How have you been able to make the best out of a difficult situation?"

 

Air-Dry Putty:
Before you begin, you can open up the packages of the air-dry putty and invite participants to grab a small chunk of any color they'd like.


"If you'd like, take a piece of the putty into your hands and take a moment to feel it. Move it around and squeeze it with one hand, try squeezing it with two hands. How does it feel? If you'd like, smell the putty. What does it smell like?"

"When we talked earlier about resilience we said that it's a person's ability to navigate through when difficult things happen to them. Let's see if we can make a round ball out of the putty (give participants some time to create their balls)."

"Now, imagine that these round balls are us. I invite you to twist, turn, and break the round ball apart (pause and allow time for this)."

"Let's imagine that this twisting, turning, and breaking apart can be all of the difficult things that can happen in our lives. Try to think what kinds of difficult things have you faced?"

"Now, let's shape our putty back into a ball (pause and let participants gather their putty). For some of you with more pieces to pick up, it took a little more time to gather and mold back into place. This is also true about our lives. Let's take a look around and notice that everyone is back to the same ball that they once started with. Inside of all of us, we have the ability to pick up all of the pieces and put ourselves back together again. As we sit here, notice that everything we have gone through in our past is behind us and it's a big deal to be here today. Maybe you're going through something difficult right now and you feel like it will never get better. I hope this can give you a sense of comfort knowing that you are resilient. Resilience is inside of you."

 

     
  Step 1: Drawing the flower

 
 
  Step 2: Adding Colors

 
 
  Step 3: Adding air-dry putty accent

 
 
  Step 4: Writing affirmation

Creation Steps
"Before you have an opportunity to begin creating I will guide us though imagining that we are a flower to help us get ready to create. I'd now like to share the creation process with you, so after we use our imaginations we can jump right into having a chance to make art."


Step 1: Drawing a Flower
"To start, you can take your flower in your hand again and look at it as you draw it on your paper. If you want, you can draw the flower very large on your page so you can really focus on the details. Don't worry if your drawing doesn't look just like your special flower, remember that whatever comes out will be just right."


Step 2: Adding Color
"Then, using the watercolors, you can add color to your flower. You can follow the color(s) of your flower or you can come up with new colors. There is no wrong way to add color. If you choose not to add any color, adding more detail to your drawing can be something you might want to try out."


Step 3: Adding Accents
"Next, you can use the air-dry putty to add accents to your painting. Adding a fun border or details to your flower might be something to consider. You can use the glue to stick the putty on."

(Optional): You can demonstrate how the gold and silver watercolors, if available, can be added as a last step of the creation process to add accents. You can briefly demonstrate how to apply the paint with a small paintbrush.


Step 4: Writing Affirmations
"Lastly, you will be invited to add some positive and calming words to your drawing. You can write some affirmations or words of encouragement that can help you get through difficult times."

(Optional): You can share the following example with the participants:
"At the very top, you can write: 'I am as fresh as a flower.' On the left side, you can write: 'I take three deep breaths to calm myself.' On the right side, you can write: 'I am loving and lovable.' And on the bottom, you can write and finish this sentence: 'I am _________'."

Objective:
To provide Window's facilitators with a new way to support participants and engage community through the art of storytelling utilizing digital media. A toolkit, resources and information about the benefits to participants are included.


Introduction:
Digital storytelling is the modern expression of the ancient form of storytelling. Storytelling can be regarded as one of oldest healing arts and forms of communication. Storytelling can enable us to communicate, teach, make meaning of experiences, to inspire and encourage, pass on wisdom and make meaningful connections to ourselves and others.

Digital media is a creative, powerful and deeply engaging way to share our stories. Through sharing their stories, participants and allies are empowered to raise their voices, creating awareness and a ripple effect that moves people to action in their own lives and in their communities.

 

Materials:
With the help of Windows facilitators, AWBW has created a toolkit with tips, suggestions, and guidelines including suggested Windows Workshops to get you started. Click here to download the toolkit.

  • Digital stories can be captured through many types of digital media including, but not limited to: computers, tablets, smart phones, digital cameras, video cameras, etc.

  • How you tell your stories has endless possibilities by combining various images and/or audio. This includes digital images such as photographs, artwork, text, clip art, video, etc. and digital audio including voice, narration, music, sounds, and sound effects.

 

Does AWBW offer resources and support for digital storytelling?
In addition to the comprehensive toolkit provided, AWBW offers the following resources to support your digital storytelling process:
 

  • Digital Storytelling Toolkit

  • Access to funding -- up to $20 per year for apps to create your story with digital media.

  • Use of a dedicated YouTube channel for digital storytelling.

  • iPad loan, when devices are available.

  • Technical support from AWBW program staff (appointment may be necessary).

  • Inspiration and ideas through the Windows workshops and curriculum.

 

How will participants feel empowered by creating a digital story?
Even while maintaining anonymity, seeing their personal art and stories shared publicly and in this innovative way can create a sense of pride and self-worth that can be empowering in many ways. Some of these ways are:
 

  • Affirms and validates their story of survival, wisdom and hope.

  • Confirms they have wisdom to share with others and educate the community.

  • Builds a community of support in discovering they are not alone.

  • Provides a sense of purpose by giving back.

  • By sharing individual experience and unique voice, myths and stereotypes can be broken and free participants to create life in their own vision.

  • Through sharing their art and stories, other survivors are inspired to break the silence.

title: Permission Canvas
objective: This workshop aims to give children "permission" to do something they have been longing to do, to change a habit, or let go of something they've been hanging onto.
materials:
•    
      Sample art supply materials
       
     
      Optional printable self-led worksheet

    Canvas or cardstock (6" x 6" pieces work well)

  • Paint

  • Brushes

  • Mod podge

  • Cake doilies

  • Scrapbook paper

  • White glue

  • Magazines (we suggest Oprah, Nat Geo or travel magazines as they tend to have more inclusive words and imagery)

  • Sponges (to make texture in paint)

  • Foam brushes or Brayers

  • Bubble wrap

  • Sharpies (ultra fine & regular would be ideal)

  • Scissors

  • Stamps & ink pads

  • Writing paper

  • Permission Canvas Handout

  • Journaling Questions

  • Paper Dolls Template

Please note that some of the decoration material are optional and can be used in lieu of others. Feel free to provide what suits your age group's needs.

You can also facilitate this workshop using this printable self-led worksheet. If you are utilizing this sheet in lieu of the regular workshop materials, be sure to send the sheet or print them out beforehand for your participants depending on the setting.
setup:
Completed Permission Canvas
"... Just breathe"
   
 
  Completed self-led worksheet

You can print words and phrases that can be collaged onto the canvases by the children. For example: "They gave themselves permission to," "They decided to," "They let ______ go," or any other words or phrases that may be better suited to your specific group.

If applicable to your group, you can print copies of the optional words, statements, women and men silhouettes templates in advance.

Once you print them, you can also cut the words out (see images for reference).

If you're unable to print these, you can write them on a board and invite children to select the ones that apply to them and write it down instead of collage it.

You can print out the paper doll templates for all the children, but please be mindful that there is not "one" body shape. If children wish to draw their own body template, that's great, and it might be empowering for them. 

You can also print the journaling questions (one copy per child, plus some extras).

You may wish to create a sample in advance to get the feel for the creation process, as well as to show children what the finished art piece can look like. If you choose to do so, we suggest creating a simple sample using only the material you're providing so that children aren't overwhelmed by any "artistic" challenges.

As a facilitator, you have complete freedom to alter or adapt any portion or element of this workshop to cater to your specific group's needs.
creation:
Ripping magazine cutouts for a unique collage finish.
   
 
  Using Mod Podge to glue on mixed-media materials

You can now invite the children to dive in and start creating. You can suggest that they paint the background of their canvas first, and then think about their permission phrase while the paint dries. Since this is a "mixed media" project, they can blend a variety of techniques when creating their art: paint, stamping, and/or collage.

"I encourage you to give yourself permission to create your canvas in whatever way that you wish. You can collage, paint, or simply have an abstract background. You might want to add a person as a focal point of your art. You can use the doll template as a guide, and collage to create clothing from different scrapbook patterns. You can also draw your person freehand or find a magazine image that represents the future you want to create. Whatever you wish."

"You can begin by choosing one permission phrase that is most meaningful to you. Are you giving permission to take more time out for yourself in the future? Maybe you are deciding to spend more quality time with your children? Or perhaps you want to finally tackle that dream or goal you have not yet gotten around to. You fill in the blank. Once you've decide, you can collage the statement onto the background or you can paint to write your phrase directly on the canvas. Since the canvas is focusing on the future that you want, I encourage you to keep your wording optimistic and affirmative."

If some of the children finish earlier than others, you can invite them to look back at their journaling questions. They can answer questions they did not answer previously, or they can journal about their creation. They might also create another canvas, doodle, or draw. Feel free to guide the children as you see fit.
closing:
You can close by inviting the children to share their canvases with the group and anything they discovered about themselves while creating. They can also share their permission phrase out loud. If there's time, you have the option to use "echo listening" where other children repeat the phrase back to the children. Echo listening is a form of listening which is structured to be completely non-judgmental. After listening to the children read their piece, everyone in the room can simply repeat at least one thing they remember the person saying, word for word, so that they hear the entire room "echo" their words to them, rather than judging them. It is one structured way to use supportive listening and ground the vision of the children.

You can also invite the children, if they feel comfortable doing so, to display their canvas somewhere that they will be able to see it everyday, as encouragement and inspiration to look towards the New Year with and hope.

Of course, as with any part of this workshop, sharing is optional and if no one feels comfortable sharing, that's perfectly okay.
 

Completed Permission Canvas Completed Permission Canvas
description: This workshop can give participants permission to do something they have been longing to do, to change a habit, or let go of something.
tips: If a canvas is inaccessible to you, you can also use thick watercolor paper or thick card stock.
optional_materials:
• Pre-typed Words template

  • Pre-typed Statements template

  • Women's Silhouettes template

  • Men's Silhouettes template
introduction:
This workshop was written for the New Year's, but it can be used at any time during the year. The "New Year" doesn't have to be the new calendar year, it could be a "new year" of transition, hope, commitment, or any other "beginning" in a child's life. Please feel free to alter the wording of the introduction as you see fit.

"New Year's is a time of the year that symbolizes renewal and rebirth. It's also an opportunity for us to invite ourselves to say goodbye to the concerns and problems of the past year, and prepare for a new and healthy beginning. We can focus on the things that we want more of in our lives, and look forward to the coming months with more hope, enthusiasm, and an open heart."

"Today, you'll have an opportunity to transition into the New Year in a positive way. You'll have a chance to notice how it would feel to let go of something or someone who is holding you back in your life or a habit you wish to break."

"Afterwards, if you wish to, you can give yourself permission to think about something you really want to accomplish, or a healthy habit you would like to take on. It could be learning a new instrument, creating stronger bonds with family and friends, or anything else you wish to do that can help redirect your focus from negative things, to positive things. Through journaling and painting, you will have a chance to create a canvas that gives you the affirming permission to do whatever you choose in the future."

"Before we begin, I want you to know that this is your window of time. This means that this can be a safe space to notice your thoughts, feelings, and needs. During this time, there is no right or wrong way to participate or create. I'm going to share some basic instructions, but you get to choose how you want to participate. You can follow along completely, or you may want to do something different, it's completely up to you. During your window of time, you have complete freedom to choose. I am here to support you in any way that I can, so please feel free to ask for what you need."
demonstration:
You can paint brayer or sponge brush, then roll the paint on the bubble wrap.
Stamp bubble wrap to your canvas to give an artsy background.

You may wish to take a few minutes to explain the material to the children.

Depending on which materials you're using, you might wish to:

  • Demonstrate how to use the materials to create textures and unique effects. You can show how to use a foam brush, sponge or brayer for blending and layering paint on bubble wrap and then transferring to canvas to create a polka dot effect.

  • Show how to use materials to create textures, shapes and tone on tone effects, by using a light dabbing motion.

  • Explain how Mod Podge can be used as glue for collaging, or as a coating to finish their art.


If you have a sample, this may be a good time to pass it around the room.
opening_circle:
Journal Questions:
You can open by inviting the children to fill in the journal questions. They can write directly on the template or on a separate sheet (if available). You may wish to reassure the children that their writing is for themselves and they won't be reading their answers out loud, unless they want to. You can also remind them that they can skip questions that don't work for them, but encourage them to try to look at each question with curiosity. This is their "window of time" to be present to whatever surfaces and let go of any blame or shame that may come up.

You may also wish to encourage children to take special care in coming up with their permission phrase(s) and creating a positive focus for the "New Year." This expression can be something as simple as giving themselves permission to just breathe, or as significant as changing jobs or starting a new relationship. Some ideas for their canvases are: "They gave themselves permission to let love in" or "They decided to go back to school."

If you like, you can play soft relaxing music in the background during the creation process. This is entirely up to you. Also, depending on the age group, you also have the option to invite the children to share the permission phrase they choose and you can write it for them.

Group Sharing:
Once children have had ample time to fill in the journal questions, you can then invite them to pick one of their answers to the journal questions, and if they feel comfortable, to share with the whole group, emphasizing that sharing is voluntary. They can also share what it would feel like to let go of a thought, a person or a habit that no longer supports them. Or they can share one of their permission phrases and why it would be important to embrace this. And if no one feels comfortable sharing, that's perfectly okay. You can skip to creation.

title: Footprints in the Sand
objective: This workshop gives participants an opportunity to reflect on their life, the good moments and challenges they've had to overcome, and create a sand painting that represents their journey.
materials:
• Colored sand (can be purchased at Discount School Supply)

  • White glue (Elmer's glue)

  • Glue sticks

  • Heavy black construction paper

  • Colored construction paper

  • Colored pencils

  • Toothpicks
setup:
Sample supplies and table setup
 

You are welcome to provide any and as many of the decorative material as you like.

If you see the need, you can cover the tables with newspaper or tablecloths to protect them against glue, sand, etc.

You may want to print a copy of the Native American Sand Painting background handout to share with the participants, if you see fit.

Depending on the sand manufacturer packaging, you may feel the need to transfer each color sand into smaller plastic containers.

You have the option to punch small footprints, using the footprint hole puncher, out of different color construction paper; plenty for each participant.

It may be helpful to create a small sample in advance to show participants what the finished art piece can look like. If you choose to do so, we suggest creating a basic sample and using only the material you're providing, so that participants aren't overwhelmed by any "artistic" challenges.

You have complete freedom to alter or adapt any portion or element of this workshop to cater to your specific group's needs.
creation:
Sample sand painting

You can now invite those who wish to create to begin doing so. You may wish to remind participants that there is no right or wrong way to create. They are free to draw anything, and use any colors that they like. This is their story and their window of time.

It doesn't matter what it looks like. What's important is that they are taking this time to honor their life journey and creating something that is expressive and meaningful to them.

Some participants may need help with certain creation elements, so feel free to offer assistance where you see the need.
closing:
You can give participants a chance to share their sand painting and the story it tells, anything they discovered or experienced during creation, or anything else they may wish to share. This can be a very powerful art project and participants can come away with a stronger sense of their personal journey, and a look at how far they've traveled.

If no one feels comfortable sharing, that's perfectly okay. You can reinforce that when we take time to explore our own personal story, we can learn so much from them.
description: Gives participants an opportunity to learn new ways of telling their story. Through using the technique of sand painting, inspired by a Native American tradition, participants will use symbols to tell a story they would like to share.
optional_materials:
• Footprint hole puncher

  • Newspaper tablecloths

  • Native American Sand Painting background handout

  • Paper plates (1 per table to collect unused and loose sand)
introduction:
If you see fit, you can share the Native American Sand Painting background handout with the participant. You can read it to them, or print a copy for each participant to read on their own. It's entirely up to you.
 

"Today, you will have an opportunity to think about your life journey, places you've been, things you've experienced, and create a painting that tells the story of your life, however you wish to tell it."

"Everyone's experiences are different. Some things that happen to us can be happy, exciting or fun and sometimes things that happen can be sad or difficult. What we are going to do is tell a story in a simple way using symbols and words. Your story can be anything you want it to be. You can decide where your story starts and where you want it to go."

"This project has been inspired by the Native American art form known as sand painting. In the Native American tradition, sand paintings were created to tell stories. Today, you'll get a chance to use sand painting to tell the story of your journey."

"Before we begin, I want you to know that this is your window of time. This means that this can be a safe space to notice your thoughts, feelings, and needs. Since this space is your window of time, everything you say or do is voluntary. During this time, there is no right or wrong way to participate or create. I'm going to share some basic instructions, but you get to choose how you want to participate. You can follow along completely, or you may want to do something different, it's completely up to you. During your window of time, you have complete freedom to choose. However you choose to spend this time will be perfectly okay. I am here to support you in any way that I can, so please feel free to ask for what you need."
demonstration:
Sketching symbols from their story
 
 
  Outlining symbols with glue
 
 
  Sprinkling sand
 
 
  Adding footprints
 
 
  Mapping out the journey
 
 
  Finished sample

You can introduce the art supplies and share the following creation steps with the participants. If you've made a sample in advance, this may be a good time to share it for reference.

You may also consider demonstrating some of the creation steps, as you see the need. Specifically, steps 2-4 below (adding colored sand).


Step 1:
"You can begin by taking two pieces of black construction paper and using a glue stick, glue them together, one on top of the other. This makes the paper stronger and can prevent the paper from wilting when applying the amount of glue that this workshop requires."


Step 2:
"Next, you can take a light colored pencil and begin to sketch out your life journey, by drawing anything that has been a part of that journey. For example, if a playground is part of your journey as a child, and that's a place you liked going to, you can draw a swing-set or a teeter-totter. Maybe the beach is somewhere you love going to now, so you can draw an ocean anywhere you like on the paper. You can think about where you would like your story to begin; it could be at a park, the forest, a playground, your childhood home, or anywhere that you like. You can then think about where you want to go next. Maybe it's sunny out, or maybe it's cold and raining, maybe there's snow on the ground. You can add to your story by drawing however many symbols that are part of your life journey. There is no right or wrong way. Anything you choose to draw that represents the important things in your life will be perfect."


Step 3:
"Next, you get to paint your drawing using colored sand. To do this, you can first gently squeeze white glue to outline or fill in each element of your drawing (basically use the drawing as an outline for the glue). You can then choose any color sand that you like for each item, and sprinkle the sand on top of the glue. So for trees, you can sprinkle green sand on the leaves. It's probably best to squeeze glue then add your choice of color sand to one item at a time, to prevent the glue from drying up."

"You can even mix some sand of one color with some of sand of another color to come up with a new color. Feel free to have fun and get as creative as you like with the sand."

"Once you've painted your drawing with sand, you can lift the paper to dump any loose sand into the paper plate. If there are any gaps showing white glue, you can fill it by simply adding more sand."


Step 4:
"Once you're done with the sand painting, you can use the footprint shapes (if available) and glue them anywhere on the paper to show the path you have walked. You can use any color and as many different colors of footprint shapes that you like."

If you're not providing footprint shapes, you can invite the participants to either draw them, or draw a road, or river, or anything else that could symbolize a path/timeline.
opening_circle:
You can give participants a chance to journal about their life journey. You are welcome to use our suggested prompts below, or your own.

  • "My journey begins with ___________ ."

  • "I would like my journey to lead to __________ ."

title: Me Dolls
objective:
"All About Aubrey"

To give children a creative way to voice a story about the “me” inside them; to provide them a safe space and freedom to explore and express their feelings in an imaginative, fun and creative way.

Note:

This workshop is more complex than most, and for young children, it will take a lot of one-on-one assistance

Materials:
Sculpey (One 8-pound box for a group of 10 will be more than enough.) See sculpey.com for ordering info or local arts/crafts stores.
Push molds of faces, hands, feet - (See sculpey.com or midwestclay.com, or some may be available at local arts/crafts stores.)
Various rubber stamps with letters, numbers, textures, etc. (Available at local arts and craft stores)
Acrylic paints (assorted colors)
Spray or paint-on sealer in matte or gloss to protect the painted sculpey (such as Plastercraft acrylic spray finish in matte or glossy)
Assorted craft wire (18 only if pliable, 20 to 22 gauge, any thicker will be difficult to bend and the sculpey will break. Also adults will need to help start the wire so children can then put the beads on and an adult will need to finish off each piece of wire. The end result is great, but time and staff may not allow this version. Use alternate below.)

 
"Me Dolls" samples.  


EASIER ALTERNATIVE TO WIRE: Pipe cleaners, ribbon, yarn or stretchy cord
Assorted beads (plastic, metal, wood, etc)
Tools for working with the sculpey:

FOR ADULT HELPERS:
Toothpicks (for making holes in the face and body for the wire to pass through to connect parts together)
Handout about where to make holes to attach head and limbs

FOR CHILDREN:
Popsicle sticks (for smoothing, cutting the clay, etc.)

For baking the sculpey:
Toaster oven(s) (Due to toxic fumes from the clay, toaster oven should be one dedicated for non-food use)
Tongs, potholders, yimer

 

 

For painting the sculpey:
Paint brushes in various sizes from small detail to larger widths
Paint trays to collect desired colors of paint

 
  All Pieces Painted

Water cups
Paper towels
Cup or container to collect desired beads
For working wire, beads, ribbon:
Pliers/wire cutters
Scissors
ZipLock plastic bags for each artist to store gathered beads and parts for each doll for the next session (if more than 1 session)
Permanent marker to mark each artist's name on the bags

Timeframe
Total: Two 2-hr sessions
Intro & Sharing: 30 minutes
Creation: 60 minutes
Closing: 30 minutes

Advance Prep Tips:
Since this is a complex project, it can help speed things along if hands and feet are pre-made and baked ahead of time for the children to use, since these are more difficult and time-consuming to make and will give the children more time to focus on faces and bodies. When you are making a lot of hands and feet, you might find the sculpey is sticking inside the molds. If this happens, it can speed things up if you roll the right-sized balls of sculpey, put them in the refrigerator to chill, and then press the cold clay into the mold. It will pop out more easily if it's cold.
Age Range/Adult to Child Ratio:
For ages 7 and up / 1 adult to 5 children
NOTE: You may want an extra pair of hands designated specifically to help with the just the baking, otherwise make sure to have a timer handy to avoid overcooking the sculpey!

   
More "Me Dolls" Creations.    

Opening Circle:Start by talking about dolls. You might want to share several different sample dolls. Ask the children if they have a favorite doll or action figure. Explain that today they're going to make a new kind of doll called a Me Doll. This kind of doll is different from others because its not one you play with, but one that is more like art. A Me Doll is an art doll and a Me Doll is all about the “me” inside. Every Me Doll is different and every one is special, just like each one of us is special. Your Me Doll doesn't even have to look just like you if you don't want. Some may be about laughing, some about being happy, some about being angry or even sad. Your Me Doll can say and look like whatever you want it to.

What kind of Me Doll do you want to make today? Let's practice looking for our Me Doll face right now. We're going to pass around the mirror and when it's your turn, hold the mirror up right in front of your face. When you can make the face that your Me Doll is feeling, then put the mirror down and show us. Then pass the mirror to the next person. If the feeling your face is making has a name, you can share that if you like. Don't be afraid to share any kind of face you want to.

Demonstration:
Now show the children one way of making a face with clay by using a push mold face. You might want to stretch it or mold it into different expressions. You can also make a face yourself to show them they have different ways to make their doll. You might even want to make a "mistake" and smoosh it up and start over. Show them the pre-made hands and feet so that they will see what the look like and to give an idea of the general size of dolls. Next explain that once their face and body parts are done, the sculpey needs to bake. Show a sample piece that is baked and how it has hardened. (Please allow at least 10 minutes per hand/foot when calculating your prep time with sculpey push molded shapes, plus baking. You can bake them all at once.)

 

Creation:
Play some nice music.

 

 

Pressing clay into the mold.
Pulling clay out of the mold

 

Part 1: Making sculpey heads and bodies.
Have the children start creating their dolls by experimenting with the push molds, free forming the clay, using stamps for words or textures, etc. Adults may need to assist with the push molds. Adults will need to make the holes in the body and face parts to allow for the wire or cord to pass through. Don't make the holes too close to the side or they may break. Leave at least 1/4" if possible. Make a clean pass through with the toothpick from front to back and clean up the hole by smoothing any rough edges of clay and make sure the hole is clean of debris.

Part 2: Baking the sculpey.
Start to collect finished sculpey pieces as they are ready and bake in toaster oven at 300 degrees for approx. 7-10 minutes based on thickness of clay. Allow pieces to cool completely before painting. Keep these in a separate area for cooling - at least 10 minutes!

Part 3: Painting the sculpey.
Next, the cooled sculpey doll parts can be painted using acrylic paint. Pass out the pre-baked hands and feet to each child. When the paint is dry, spray with a sealer according to manufacturer directions.

Part 4: Wiring and beading
While the doll parts are drying, have each child choose wire or alternate and select beads for connecting head, body, arms, legs and other ornamentation as desired, such as charms, bits of chain, etc. When doll parts are dry, begin to wire and bead. Adults will need to do most of this part, but the children are usually excited about stringing their own beads. Adults will have to loop the wire end through the hole and twist it around itself about 3 or 4 times to secure, cutting off the excess wire with wire cutters. Remember if you are using wire not to twist the wire too tightly against the sculpey or it might break or rub the paint off. There should be a little flex space to allow for posing the doll into its final position.

Part 5: Naming the Me Doll
Giving the doll a name makes it special and may free up the discussion about what this doll represents to each child. Be sure to write down the name and any words that go with each doll for each child.
 

   
Painting the base color   Adding a highlight color with
a dry brush		   Painting completed

Closing:
Have each child introduce their Me Doll. Ask them to share anything that this Me Doll might like to say.

 

Tips:
• If wire can't be used because of safety concerns, ribbon or embroidery floss also works well.
• The details of the mold will be clearer if you put the clay in the mold and then put it in the freezer for ten minutes.

title: Me Dolls
objective:
One leader shares her "Me Doll" named "Addie."

To give voice to the hopes, dreams, screams, and messages of survival and healing that make each survivor's journey unique.  By exploring different messages and themes within each woman's experience, each artist can reach within and create a dolls that is all about the "me" perhaps no one has heard or seen before, a doll that will reach out with humor and whimsy to celebrate her strengths
and claim a violence-free future. 

Note:
This workshop is more complex than most, and may take a lot of one-on-one assistance.

 

 

 

 
Promise, by anonymous.    

 

 

 

 

Materials:
Sculpey (One 8-pound box for a group of 10 will be more than enough.)  See sculpey.com for ordering info or local arts/crafts stores.
Push molds of faces, hands, feet - (See sculpey.com or midwestclay.com, or some may be available at local arts/crafts stores.)
Various rubber stamps with letters, numbers, textures, etc. (Available at local arts and craft stores)
Acrylic paints (assorted colors)
Spray or paint-on sealer in matte or gloss to protect the painted sculpey (such as Plastercraft acrylic spray finish in matte or glossy)
Assorted craft wire (18 only if pliable, 20 to 22 gauge, any thicker will be difficult to bend and the sculpey will break.  Note: an easier alternative to wire is to use pipe-cleaners, ribbon, yarn or stretchy cord.
Assorted beads (plastic, metal, wood, etc)
Assorted Ribbon  (on the thin side for hanging the dolls if desired)

Tools for working with the sculpey:
Toothpicks (for making holes in the face and body for the wire to pass through to connect parts together)
Popsicle sticks (for smoothing, cutting the clay, etc.)
Handout about where to make holes in the doll to attach limbs and head

 

 

 

For baking the sculpey:
Toaster oven(s) (Due to toxic fumes from the clay, toaster oven should be one dedicated for non-food use)

Tongs, potholders, timer

 
  The Key-per, by MFW

For painting the sculpey:
Paint brushes in various sizes from small detail to larger widths
Paint trays to collect desired colors of paint
Water cups
Paper towels
Cup or container to collect desired beads
For working wire, beads, ribbon:
Pliers/wire cutters
Scissors
ZipLock plastic bags for each artist to store gathered beads and parts for each doll for the next session (if more than 1 session)
Permanent marker to mark each artist's name on the bags

Timeframe:
Total: Two 2-hr sessions
Intro & Sharing: 30 minutes
Creation: 60 minutes
Closing: 30 minutes

Advance Prep Tips:
Since this is a complex project, it can help speed things along if hands and feet are pre-made and baked ahead of time for the women to use, since these are more difficult and time-consuming to make and will give the participants more time to focus on faces and bodies.  When you are making a lot of hands and feet, you might find the sculpey is sticking inside the molds.  If this happens, it can speed things up if you roll the right sized balls of sculpey, put them in the refrigerator to chill, and then press the cold clay into the mold.  It will come out more easily if it's cold.

 
"Me Dolls" Samples  

Opening Circle:
A doll may be a small representation of a human being or a fantasy character, but it carries with it something much more important than form; its soul.  The Me Doll is a type of contemporary art doll which reflects some aspect of self.  They represent the survivor's search for meaning.  Today you'll be able to creature your own Me Doll that is a unique work of art that claims its own existence, no matter what the medium or the message.  It may touch your heart and also provoke surprisingly intense reactions.  Just as each of us exists and has a reality waiting to be expressed, the Me Dolls allow a safe and creative way to explore and express our feelings in sometimes unexpectedly delightful, humorous, or even painful ways.  It's important to remember to respect your feelings, even the darker more painful ones.  It's OK to laugh, and it's also OK to cry.  Allow your doll to carry the emotion with you because she is an expression of you.  Each unique doll you make will allow you to voice an aspect of your extraordinary journey of survival.  The Me Doll may end up looking very different from how you first intended or expected but remember do not be afraid to let go and see what's going to come out of this process.  The doll may or may not look anything like your own physical self, but that's because it's a representation of that part of "me" inside that the artist is allowing to find expression. 
 

 

 

Relaxation & Reflection:

 
  Yada, by anonymous.

Take a few minutes to relax.  Get settled comfortably in your seat, take a couple deep breaths, pick up a piece of sculpey, close your eyes if you feel comfortable.  Just focus on the "me" inside.  How are your feeling at this moment?  Can you picture a facial expression, posture or color that represents this moment?  Take a few minutes to think about your feelings.  Work them into the clay as you reflect.  Feel the sculpey give and form different random shapes as your hands start to get the feel of it.  Are there feelings you haven't felt comfortable expressing?  Is there something you've always wanted to say but held it inside?  Would you like to let your "me doll" speak for you?  What would she say?  Think of her face, her body.  Think about her hands, feet.  When you're ready slowly open your eyes, and begin to create.
(Note: working with the clay during the relaxation will warm up the clay and make it too sticky to use in the molds.  Have the women use only half their clay during the relaxation, so the other half can stay cool and ready to use in the molds) 

Demonstration:
You will want to take a few minutes to explain the use of the push molds.  Make a sample face mold, then begin to modify the features explaining that the artist may wish to use the face right from the mold or use it as a starting point to personalize their own face.  Remind them they are free to form their very own parts without the use of the molds as well.  Explain that they will need to put holes in each part with a toothpick so that all parts can be connected with wire.  These holes should be placed about 1/4" from the edge, not too close or the sculpey will break.  Pass the toothpick through from front to back and make sure the hole is clear of debris and smooth on the back side.  Next explain that the sculpey needs to bake.  Show a sample piece that is baked.  Remind the women that they will need to place holes in the pieces if they wish to connect them with wire and beads later.     

Creation:
Play some nice music.

 
Pressing clay into the mold.  

Part 1:  Making sculpey heads and bodies.
Have the women start creating their dolls by experimenting with the push molds, free forming the clay, using stamps for words or textures, etc. 

Part 2: Baking the sculpey.
Start to collect finished sculpey pieces as they're available, checking frequently for those who have more pieces ready for baking.  Bake in toaster oven at 300 degrees for appox. 7-10 minutes based on thickness of clay.  Allow pieces to cool completely before painting. (About 10 minutes) 

 

 
Pulling clay out of the mold.  
 
All pieces completed.  

Part 3: Painting the sculpey.
Next, the baked sculpey doll parts can be painted using acrylic paint.  When the paint is dry, spray with a sealer according to manufacturer directions.  

Part 4: Wiring and beading
While their doll parts are drying, have each woman choose wire and select beads for connecting head, body, arms, legs and other ornamentation as desired, such as charms, bits of chain, etc.  When doll parts are dry, begin to wire and bead.  There are many different and creative ways to use the wire, but some may find it frustrating at first.  Cut the wire a little longer than needed to allow for wrapping and coiling if desired.  To avoid frustration, show the women the basic way to loop the wire end through the hole and twist it around itself about 3 or 4 times to secure.  They may choose to hide this part by sliding a bead over it, or simply let it show.  They may wish to curl the excess wire using the wire tool instead of cutting off with the wire cutters.  They may choose to use ribbon in the doll's head by which to hang it, or they may use wire.  Encourage them to try their own creative solutions too.  Remember to tell the women not to twist the wire too tightly against the sculpey or it might break or rub off the paint.  There should be a little flex  space to allow for posing the doll into its final position. 

Part 5:  Naming the Me Doll
Giving the doll a name brings a deeper meaning and may free up the discussion about what this doll represents to each artist.
 

 

    
Painting the base color.   Adding a highligt color with a dry brush.   Painting completed with 2 layers.

Closing:
Have each woman share about the process of making her Me Doll and introduce it and what it is saying about the "me" inside of her. 

 

Tips:
To save time, leader Katie Gilbertson and Nuvia Garcia of Alternatives to Domestic Violence used Shrinky Dink paper to create hands and feet for their Me-Dolls.
