title: New Year Wishing Well
objective: This workshop gives participants an opportunity to focus on the new year and filling it with their hopes and wishes, through the creation of a Wishing Well.
materials:
• Super Sculpey polymer clay

  • Toaster Oven

  • Scissors

  • Hole punch

  • Paper drinking cups (one for each participant)

  • Pipe cleaners

  • Colored tissue paper (variety of colors including earth tones)

  • Mod Podge (you can make your own with a solution of 1/2 water 1/2 white glue)

  • Thick paint brushes

  • Paper towels

  • Permanent markers

  • Brown paper grocery bags
setup: You may wish to create a sample wishing well in advance to get the hang of the creation process, if you don't have experience with the material. It may also serve as a good sample for participants to look at. To make it easier for the participants to choose colors, you may also want to break up the pieces of Sculpey. This is entirely up to you. You have complete freedom to adapt or alter any portion of this workshop to cater to your group's needs.
warm_up:
"Before we begin, I would like to invite you to take a moment to think about your wishes or hopes for your new life. Feel free to be as creative as you like. It could be anything. You could wish for more time with your children, you can wish for a better job, a better living situation, or it can be an item you can buy. It could be anything you wish to have or be to start your new year."

You may wish to give participants a few moments to reflect.

"Now, I'd like to invite you to choose the clay in a color that you feel represents one of your wishes. I'd like to encourage you to trust your gut feeling and select any color that speaks to you."

"As you take the clay, feel free to begin to play with it, squish it in your hand over and over."

"If you wish to join me in a brief mediation exercise, I'd like to invite you to close your eyes with your feet on the floor. If you wish to keep your eyes open, that works just as well. The idea is that you feel safe and comfortable where you are. If you wish to just observe, that is perfectly okay. You are free to do whatever pleases you."

"For those who'd like participate, you can start by taking a deep breath in, a deep positive and loving breath for your whole body. Now exhale that breathe all the way from the bottom of your feet. You may take this moment to think about wishes and all of your hopes for the future as you breathe in positive breath and exhale any tension or stress and worry out of your body."

"Try to think about the door to the new year opening to a realm of possibilities; possibilities for a new life; a new beginning. Take a deep breath in as you see the door opening to your new year... now exhale. As you look through the door, I'd like to encourage you to feel a comforting new you welcoming and embracing you into this new year. Try to focus on your wishes. Your wishes may be as fun, simple or elaborate as you want. Wish whatever crazy thing you want for your life. Take a deep breath in for that first wish you thought of, and exhale a deep love for that wish."

"Now, try to think about any other wishes you have for your new year. Feel free to take as much time as you need to sit in the moment and listen to wishes from your heart."
creation:
Two Wishing Wells with stones inside
 

You can now invite the participants to begin creating. You may wish to remind them to choose colors that represent their wishes. They can choose as many colors as they like. You may also wish to remind them that a pinch of each color is all they will need to create each stone.

Once participants are done creating their wishing well stones, you may begin to bake them.


Baking:
To bake, you can use a thick piece of paper or brown paper grocery bag to line the toaster oven tray. You may also use a foil-lined cookie sheet.

Please be mindful that even the outer surface of the toaster oven can get very hot!

You can bake the Sculpey at 275°F for 15 minutes (for each ¼ inch of clay thickness).

Please allow about 10 minutes for the stones to cool before handling them.

 

While the stones are baking, participants can create their well.

Creating the Well:
Using the tissue paper and Mod Podge, participants can take a paper cup and decorate it any way they choose. They can cut, rip or tear shapes and pieces of the tissue paper and use the Mod Podge to help layer the pieces all the way around the cup. If participants choose, they can add glitter, ribbons, foam stickers, pom poms and any embellishments provided. You may wish to remind them that they are free to use any of the material to decorate their well. It doesn't matter what it looks like. This is theirs and however they wish to decorated it will be perfect.

After decorating, participants can punch two holes across from each other near the top of the cup and attach the pipe cleaners for the handle by looping the pipe cleaner.

Finally, you can give participants the option to place blue crumpled up tissue inside the cup to look like water to keep their wishing stones.
closing: For the closing, you may give the participants an opportunity to share their amazing Wishing Wells, what wishes their stones represent, what they felt or experienced in the process of creating, or anything else they wish to share. Of course, this is purely optional and if no one feels comfortable sharing, it's perfectly okay.
description: This workshop uses the soothing and often cathartic exercise of working with Sculpey clay to create stones for a new year's Wishing Well, which they will also create!
optional_materials:
• Glitter

  • Sequins

  • Yarn

  • Embellishments of your choice

 

Additionally, you can also facilitate this workshop using a printable worksheet. If you are utilizing the worksheet in lieu of the regular workshop materials, be sure to send a digital copy or print them out for your participants if you are meeting in person.

  • Wishing Well Workshop Worksheet

 

 

My Wishing Well Worksheet
introduction:
"Did you know the word 'January' comes form the Latin word meaning 'the door to the year?'"

"Today we'll have an opportunity to think of this door, and what we want to open the new year to. I'm going to invite you to think about the next steps you will be taking in your lives, whatever they may be, in a fun and creative way, by making a New Year Wishing Well. You will have an opportunity to create something meaningful that symbolizes your hopes and wishes for the new year."

"Before we begin, I want you to know that this is your window of time. It's a time for you to focus on your thoughts, needs and feelings. During this time, there is no wrong way to participate or create. I'm going to share some basic instructions, but you get to choose how you want to participate. You can follow along completely, partially, or you may want to do something entirely different, it's completely up to you. During your window of time, you have complete freedom to choose. I am here to support you in any way that I can, so please feel free to ask for what you need."
demonstration:
Step 1-2: Making the "snake"  
   
   Step 3: Rolling up the snake into a ball  
   
   Step 4: Rolling the ball into bigger snake  
   
    Step 5: Squishing the ball into a stone  
   
   A finished wishing stone  

You can demonstrate how to make swirly or marbled stones out of Sculpey before the relaxation. This way, the participants can jump right into creation.

To demonstrate, you may guide the participants through the following steps (see images for references):

Step 1: (Creating the Stone)
You can choose at least two colors. You may wish to remind the participants that they have complete freedom to choose any and as many colors as they like. It doesn't matter what it looks like. A pinch of each color is enough to make the stones.

Step 2:
You can take each color and roll it into a "snake."

Step 3:
Next, you can wrap each "snake" around each other like a candy-cane and twist together, then roll it into a ball.

Step 4:
Now, you may roll the ball out into a larger "snake" until the colors are blended just the way you want them.

Step 5:
Finally, you can roll the "snake" into a ball, then flatten the ball into the shape of stone you like. If you want, you can repeat steps 4 and 5 to create a more marbled effect.

The next step is to bake the stones. You can certainly bake your sample stone now (see creation section for baking instructions). But we recommend skipping to relaxation, as baking takes time and the demonstration is really to show participants how to work with the Sculpeys.

title: Teen Red Flag Banners
objective: This workshop aims to help teens learn to identify red flags and warning signs of a potentially abusive relationship and utilize their past experiences to create a vision for a healthy relationship in the future.
materials:
Optional printable worksheet

  • Red cardstock (or construction paper)

  • Large flag template

  • Small flag templates

  • Glue sticks

  • Scissors

  • Magazines (Oprah, Nat Geo and travel magazines tend to have more inclusive words and imagery)

  • Permanent markers (dark colors and/or metallics)

  • Ribbon / yarn

  • Red Flags of Abusive Relationships handout

  • Teen Dating Violence Resources handout

  • Pens

You can also facilitate this workshop using this printable worksheet. If you are utilizing the worksheet in lieu of the regular workshop materials, be sure to send the sheet or print copies out for your participants beforehand depending on the setting.
setup:
Cutting out your group project template
 
 
  Cutting out your individual project template
 

You can facilitate this workshop as a team project, individual project, or both. You can provide either the small flags, large ones or both. It's entirely up to you.

You can print or copy flag templates onto red cardstock or construction paper. Or, you can hand out multiple templates and allow participants to trace.

To save time during the workshop, you may want to pre-cut the flags. You can give participants an opportunity to create more than one flag, so you may want to print the amount of flags accordingly.

You can print out one copy of the Red Flags of Abusive Relationships handout and Teen Dating Violence Resources handout for each participant. 

You may want to read through the Red Flags handout and highlight the bullet points you'd like to cover. You may also choose to do this workshop in two sessions, if you see fit.

It may be helpful to create a sample in advance to show participants what it can look like. If you choose to do so, we suggest creating a very basic demo sample so that participants aren't overwhelmed by any "artistic" challenges.

You have complete freedom to alter or adapt any portion or element of this workshop to cater to your specific group's needs.
creation:
Part 1: Writing out the red flags
 
     
  Part 3: Collaging
 
 
  Part 4: Placing a ribbon and gluing the inside of the flag
 
 
  Tying a knot between the flags

You can now invite those who wish to do so, to begin creating their red flags banner(s). If time permits, you can give participants a chance to make as many flags as you see fit.

The time you choose to allocate to each part is completely up to you. It may be helpful to give participants gentle time reminders to keep your workshop on track.

You may wish to remind participants that there is no right or wrong way to create or participate. They are free to use this time however they like.


Part 1: Writing Down the Red Flags
To begin, participants can cut out a red flag (if not done in advance) and on one side, write down the warning signs they've experienced in any past relationships. They can use any color markers that they like. They can write words, draw symbols, or whatever they like. They can refer to the Red Flags of Abusive Relationships handout in opening circle, if they wish. These flags can serve as a reminder of what they should look out for in the future.


Part 2: Collaging
Once they're done with their journaling, participants can turn the flag over and begin decorating the other side of their flag(s). They get to use the collage material and any of the art supplies available to express their vision of a healthy relationship and the most important things they wish to have in their future relationship.


Part 3: Putting It All Together
Participants can place a piece of ribbon on the inside of their completed flag along the center seam, apply glue to the inside and fold the flag in half (over the ribbon). They can then add beads (if available) and/or tie a knot at each end of the ribbon.

If creating more than one personal flag, participants can use a larger piece of ribbon, and apply the above steps to as many flags as they've created. Ideally, they would leave some space in between each flag. They can tie a knot and/or add beads (if available) between each flag, if they choose.

If this is a group project, you can invite participants to attach their flag(s) along the large piece of clothesline or ribbon following the same folding/gluing steps as above. They can then add either a knot or a bead before the next flag, so it can be hung up and displayed (if participants choose to do so).
closing:
You can give participants a chance to volunteer and share their red flag banners, some of the red flags they wrote about and why they chose the images on their collages to represent what they believe makes a healthy relationship, or anything else they may wish to share.

You can reinforce the importance of paying attention to red flags and remind them that they deserve and are worthy of a healthy relationship.

If this was a group project, you can invite participants to volunteer and help hang the banner.

You can end by thanking them for their resiliency and for their courage to be here today.

       
"Never underestimate a woman's intuition."         "It's a relationship that makes your eyes sparkle."
description: This workshop gives teens an opportunity to identify "red flags", or warning signs, of an abusive relationship.
notes:
You may also choose to do this workshop in two sessions.

First session: Discussing red flags using handout and creating on one side of the flags.
Second session: Discuss what healthy relationships look like and create collage side.
tips:
Note to facilitators:

  • Teens tend to learn about relationships from the adults they live with, social media, the internet and their friends. As adults, we have the responsibility to be open to discussing relationships with teens, to hear their questions with respect and give them real answers. Being honest without judgment, no matter what they share with us can goes a long way in making you a child's or a teen's "safe adult."

  • While you may feel like you can't be both a friend and an advocate to the teens, keep in mind that all you need to be is their trusted adult.
optional_materials:
• Beads

  • Twine / string / clothesline (for group project)
introduction:
"Teen dating violence isn’t an argument every once in a while, or a bad mood after a bad day, it is a pattern of controlling behavior that someone uses against a girlfriend or boyfriend."

"Abuse can cause injury and even death, but it doesn’t have to be physical. It can include verbal and emotional abuse, constant insults, isolation from family and friends, name calling, controlling what someone wears, and it can also include sexual abuse."

"Teen dating violence can be very difficult to identify. Have you ever had that gut feeling that something wasn't right? Have you ever thought, 'I saw all the writing on the wall and looked the other way'?"

"Often times we fail to see what is right in front of our face. We know it's there, however we don't really see it. Red flags are intuitive warnings that let us know something is wrong. All too often we silence that little voice inside of ourselves that warns us of a potential danger. Abusive people are skilled at manipulating us into believing them and doubting ourselves."

"Over time, abusers may convince us to automatically defer to what they think and want and to disregard our own needs, wants and opinions. Today, we'll have a chance to take a look back at the red flags and then create our own red flags to honor and allow our inner voice, needs and desires to be heard. We can save ourselves a lot of frustration and pain in the future by practicing identifying our red flags. During this workshop you will also have an opportunity to notice the things you want in your future relationships."

"Before we begin, I want you to know that this is your window of time. This means that this can be a safe space to notice your thoughts, feelings, and needs. Since this space is your window of time, everything you say or do is voluntary. During this time, there is no right or wrong way to participate or create. I'm going to share some basic instructions, but you get to choose how you want to participate. You can follow along completely, or you may want to do something different, it's completely up to you. During your window of time, you have complete freedom to choose. However you choose to spend this time will be perfectly okay. I am here to support you in any way that I can, so please feel free to ask for what you need."
demonstration:
You can introduce the art supplies and share and demonstrate any creation elements and/or techniques that you see fit (Ex: how to collage, etc). If you've made a sample, you may want to show it for reference.

A personal Red Flag Banners creation with knots in between each flag
opening_circle:
You can open by passing out the Red Flags of Abusive Relationships handout and go over it as a group. You can invite the participants to share any thoughts about red flags, they can share personal experiences (that happened to them or someone they know), thoughts about how this issue is portrayed in the media (i.e. Rihanna and Chris Brown), and/or what the handout made them think about.

If applicable, feel free to identify and explain how what they shared can an example of a red flag of a specific type of abuse. For example, if a participant shares: “I knew something was off when he/she said that I should not talk to boys/girls at parties."  Just because you are talking to someone doesn't mean you two are hooking up. This is an example of excessive jealousy.

Of course, sharing is optional, and if anyone doesn't feel comfortable sharing, that's perfectly okay.

title: Resiliency Rainsticks
full_name: Susan Schaefer Bernardo and Courtenay Fletcher
objective: This workshop aims to help families focus on healthy ways to express their feelings and work together to create a rainstick that represents their resilience.
materials:
•      

    Rainstick kits

  • The Rhino Who Swallowed a Storm book (by LeVar Burton and Susan Schaefer Bernardo)

    • Video: Reading of The Rhino Who Swallowed a Storm (from space!)

  • Rainstick Kit Instructions handout

  • Small beads

  • Tissue paper

  • Construction paper (variety of colors)

  • ModPodge (or a homemade solution of half white glue/half water)

  • Paint brushes

  • Permanent markers

  • Oil pastels (CrayPas)
setup:
You are welcome to provide any and as many of the decorative material as you like.

You can lay out the supplies so that each participant/family has easy access and ample room to create.

You can print a copy of the Rainstick Instructions handout for each participant.

If you'd like, you can also print the optional Rhino journaling sheet for each participant.

If you choose to not go with the rainstick kit and create your own, you can pre-cut aluminum foil sheets down to a size that fits the cardboard tubing you're providing (see Demonstration). The aluminum sheets will be used to create the coils for the inside of the rainsticks.

A less expensive alternative to ModPodge is to create a homemade solution of half white glue, half water. You may need to provide individual cups of this solution for each participant/family.

It may be helpful to create a sample in advance to show participants what the finished art piece can look like. If you choose to do so, we suggest creating a very basic demo sample and using only the material you're providing, so that participants aren't overwhelmed by any "artistic" challenges.

While this workshop is focused on families creating one collaborative art piece, you can easily modify it for individual creation.

You have complete freedom to alter or adapt any portion or element of this workshop to cater to your specific group's needs.
warm_up:
If you're providing the journaling sheets option, you can pass them out and invite participants to journal their responses to the following prompts. You may want to pause in between each prompt to allow participants to journal.


"Before we create, I'd like to invite you to take a few minutes to think to yourself and with your family. In the story, Rhino was told by the whale to 'sing his own song.' What do you think this means? How do you sing your own song and express your feelings?"

"When you are going through rough times as a family what are some of the things that you do together to bring comfort and hope? What do you do individually to help the family?"

"Rhino had many friends show up to help him out. Who can you and your family go to for help? Asking for help is a sign of strength, it shows that we are resilient."

"For those of you who wish to create, I'd like to encourage you to think about how you want to decorate your rainstick. What words, pictures, and/or symbols do you want to put on it? Do you want to put reminders about how to safely express your feelings? How about writing down those people in your life that you can call when you need help? What colors will you choose? What materials will you use?"

(For family creations):
"You might also want to think about giving each other roles as you create your rainsticks. You can think about tasks that can make things run more smoothly. For example, older family members (adults and/or older children) can be in charge of cutting and younger family members can be in charge of choosing colors and gluing. However you want to split up jobs is up to you, as long as you're creating together, you are on the right track. Any questions before we begin?"
creation:
You can now invite those who wish to create their rainsticks to begin. You may want to remind the that there is no right or wrong way to create or participate. They can use the art supplies however they like.

You can refer them to the Rainstick Kit Instructions handout for the step-by-step creation process.

Feel free to offer assistance where you see the need.
 

         
Decorating using decoupage   Adding embellishments   Adding words to the rainstick
closing:
You can invite the participants to volunteer and share their rainstick creations, the sound it can make, anything they discovered, felt or experienced during creation, or anything else they may wish to share.

You can also opt to ask those who wish to share one or two of the following questions:

  • "How did if feel for the family to work together?"

  • "Did their different roles help out during the activity?"

  • "What ways could they have been improved?"

  • "What are some ways that you can express your feelings to your family to help them understand you more?"

  • "How can knowing our roles help out when we are going through the storms or rough times in our lives?"

  • "Now that your rainsticks are finished, how will you use them to remind you of your family's strength?"


Rainstick Ceremony Closing Option:
For those who wish to partake, you can invite one participant/family to volunteer and start by playing their rainstick. After about 30 seconds or so, you can invite another participant/family to join, then the next, then the next, etc.

As the sounds get louder, you can ask the participants to look around the people in their family and share:

"Working together as a family to make it through the rough times can be hard. I encourage you to allow these rainsticks to be a reminder that together, you are strong enough to make it through the storm."
 

Participants engaging in Rainstick Ceremony
optional_materials:
• Rhino Journaling handout

  • Rubber bands

  • Raffia

  • Ribbon

  • Feathers

  • Your choice of embellishments


Alternative Rainstick Creation Option (not using the kit):

  • Cardboard mailing tubes (or gift wrap rolls, toilet paper rolls)

  • Aluminum foil (to create coils for inside the tubes)

  • Pipe cleaners

  • Foam sheet squares (to seal the ends of the cardboard tube)

  • Rubber bands
introduction:
Resiliency Rainstick creation
   

"Before we begin, I want you to know that this is your window of time. This means that this can be a safe space to notice your thoughts, feelings, and needs. Since this space is your window of time, everything you say or do is voluntary. During this time, there is no right or wrong way to participate or create. I'm going to share some basic instructions, but you get to choose how you want to participate. You can follow along completely, or you may want to do something different, it's completely up to you. During your window of time, you have complete freedom to choose. However you choose to spend this time will be perfectly okay. I am here to support you in any way that I can, so please feel free to ask for what you need."


(If you've made a sample, you can show it for reference).


"Today, we'll have an opportunity to create something special with our families. They are called rainsticks. How many of you have heard of a rainstick? Rainsticks are long hollow tubes that have small beads and other things in them. When you lift the tube upright, the sounds that come out sound like rain falling. Rainsticks were invented and used by the Aztecs. When played, they were believed to bring rainstorms, but today, we are going to make them to remind us of our strength. Any questions before we start?"
demonstration:
Step 1
 
  Step 2
 
  Step 3
 
  Step 4 & 5

You can introduce the art supplies and share the following creation steps with the participants. Feel free to demonstrate any creation elements that you see fit (Ex: decoupage techniques, etc.).


 

Rainstick Kit Creation:
If you're using the rainstick kit option, you can pass out the instructions handout and share/demonstrate the following steps with the participants.

 

Step 1:
Using your finger, you can pop up the triangles on a white rectangular paper so the triangles are standing upright at approximately 90 degrees.


Step 2:
Roll the white paper into a cylinder with the triangles pointing inward, then slide the white paper tube into the brown cardboard tube.


Step 3:
Choose a foam end cap and wrap it around one end of the tube, then secure the cap with a rubber band.


Step 4:
Pour beads (about 2 tablespoons should be enough) into the open end of the rainstick.


Step 5:
You can use another rubber band to attach a foam cap to the open end of the tube, then turn your rainstick end over end to hear the simulated sound of falling rain.


Step 6:
You can use any of the art supplies available (markers, oil pastels, tissue paper, and/or any other embellishments) and decorate the rainsticks however way you like.


 

Alternate Rainstick Creation:
If you choose not to go with the rainstick kit option, you can follow these steps to create.

 

     
  Sheet of aluminum

 
 
  Step 1

 
 
  Step 2

 
 
  Step 3


 

Step 1:
Use a piece of aluminum foil and fold it horizontally into about a half-inch strip.


Step 2:
Cut pipe cleaners into about 2" pieces and twist them around the foil.


Step 3:
Make a spiral with the foil using your fingers.


Step 4:
Insert the foil spiral into your cardboard tube. The foil spiral allows the beads to fall slowly, helping create the rain sound.


Step 5:
Close one end of the rainstick to make sure the beads stay inside.


Step 6:
Put in a handful of beads into the tube, and check the sound to make sure it's pleasing to you. If not, you can add or remove beads to get the desired effect.


Step 7:
Seal the tube using paper or another type of seal.


Step 8:
Wrap the tube using decorative paper.


Step 9:
You can use any and as many of the art supplies available and decorate the rainstick however way you like.
opening_circle:
For the opening exercise, you can start by reading The Rhino Who Swallowed A Storm to the group.


"The book I'm going to read is called, The Rhino Who Swallowed A Storm. In the story, we meet Rhino, and he is going through a hard time. As I'm reading, I'd like to invite you to listen very closely and see if you have anything in common with Rhino and his friends. If you prefer to just observe, that's perfectly okay. Observing is participating."


After reading the story, you can follow up with one or more of the following opening activities. Feel free to pick the one(s) that best suits your group.


For Older Participants / Families with Younger Children

Embodied Experience - Be the Storm (Shake, Shimmy and Stomp in the Muck):
You can invite participants to either stand up in front of their chairs or in a circle. You can discuss how Rhino was faced with a storm. You can ask: "What did the storm mean?" Or about the different things they saw in the book and the different sounds that come along with them like wind, rain, lightning and thunder. You can invite those who wish to partake in the exercise to move their bodies in the wind, make sounds of rain and lightning by clapping softly and loudly; make booking sounds and thunder and stomp in the mud that all the rain has created.

Whale Breathing:
You can invite participants to visualize a whale spouting out and then taking in the breath you need to dive deep into the storm, facing it and rising joyfully above the experience. Whale breathing can be good when we are faced with hard times. This kind of breathing can help us calm down when we are feeling stressed.


For Older Participants / Families with Older Children

Full Circle Sharing - Weather Forecast:
You can ask: "If you were the weather, how would you describe how you're feeling today?" For example, some might respond: "I feel sunny and bright today because I'm excited for art." Or, "I feel dark and cloudy because I'm sleepy."

Take A Deeper Look Inside This Book:
On the last page of the book, there are questions you can ask the group. Some include:

  • "At the beginning of the book, Mica Mouse is scared by a thunderstorm. Can you think of a time you have been frightened? What did you do?"

  • "At the beginning of the book, swallowing a storm is a metaphor for holding in your feelings. Have you ever had emotions swirling inside of you like a tornado? What are some ways you let them out?"

  • "Rhino meets many helpers on his journey. Who helps and encourages you and your family? How do you help others?"

  • "Mica feels better after reading a book with her papa. What books or activities comfort you and make you feel better?"

title: Claiming Who I Am
objective: This workshop gives children an opportunity to dispose the negative messages they receive, and create an art piece that allows them to claim and celebrate their unique identities.
materials:
Optional printable worksheet

  • People shapes template

  • Construction paper / cardstock (variety of colors)

  • Multi-cultural cardstock

  • Round circles (cut out from construction paper; variety of colors)

  • Markers

  • Scissors

  • Glue

  • Small buckets (or cans; for disposal of negative messages; 1 per table)

You can also facilitate this workshop using this printable worksheet. If you are utilizing the worksheet in lieu of the regular workshop materials, be sure to send the sheet or print copies out for your participants beforehand depending on the setting.
setup:
Sample table setup

 

You are welcome to provide any and as may decorative material that you like (oil pastels, colored pencils, etc.).

You can print copies of the people shape template onto a diverse range of multi-cultural cardstock (1 per child). For younger children, you may want to cut the shapes out in advance.

You may also consider cutting out a variety of colors circles in advance, enough for each child to choose their preferred color.

It may be helpful to create a sample in advance to get a feel for the best supplies and creation process for your group. If you choose to do so, we suggest creating a basic demo sample so that children aren't overwhelmed by any "artistic" challenges.

It may be helpful to write the creation steps on a board.

You have complete freedom to alter or adapt any portion or element of this workshop to cater to your specific group's needs.
creation:
Sample creation

You can now invite those who wish to create to choose a circle and person outline that they connect with and begin creating their person.

You may wish to remind them that there is no right or wrong way to create. They are free to use this time however they wish and create however it feels right for them.

Feel free to offer assistance where you see the need.
closing:
You can invite the children to volunteer and share their Claiming Who I Am creations, anything they discovered, felt or experienced during creation, or anything else they may wish to share.

You can also give them a partnered sharing option:

         
          Final Creations

"As we bring this workshop to a close, I'd like to give you a chance to share with a partner about this experience. During this process, I encourage you to make it less of a conversation and more of a time to be heard and to witness. As a speaker, try to think about the questions and how you want to share. As a listener, try to think about some non-verbal ways that you can show your partner that you’re listening. For those of you who wish to follow along, take a moment to find a partner in the group. Among yourselves, you can choose who will speak first. You can take about two minutes each to share."

"Here are a few questions you might want to think about when it’s your turn to speak:"

  • "How was this experience for you?"

  • "How can you continue to transform the negative messages that you receive?"

 

Feel free to close out the workshop however way it best suits you and your group.
optional_materials:
• Oil pastels (CrayPas)

  • Colored pencils
introduction:
"Today we will have an opportunity to celebrate our community and ourselves by creating artwork that shares our unique identities. We will get to  create artwork to represents person we are and the unique qualities we have. The name of this workshop is called, Claiming Who I Am."

"Before we begin, I want you to know that this is your window of time. This means that this can be a safe space to notice your thoughts, feelings, and needs. Since this space is your window of time, everything you say or do is voluntary. During this time, there is no right or wrong way to participate or create. I'm going to share some basic instructions, but you get to choose how you want to participate. You can follow along completely, or you may want to do something different, it's completely up to you. During your window of time, you have complete freedom to choose. However you choose to spend this time will be perfectly okay. I am here to support you in any way that I can, so please feel free to ask for what you need."
demonstration:
You can introduce the art supplies and share the following creation steps with the children. Feel free to demonstrate any creation elements and/or techniques that you see fit.


Step 1:
"First, you will get a chance to get rid of all of the negative messages that you've received, because they no longer serve or support you. You'll get to write down all of those words and phrases you've heard or even told yourself onto a piece of paper. Then, you'll get to rip them up and throw them in the trash."


Step 2:
"Next, you'll get to choose the color of circle that you most relate to. This circle represent your core."


Step 3:
"You can then choose any words, phrases, colors and/or symbols that represent who you are at your core and add them to the circle in any way that you choose."


Step 4:
"Next, you can choose a person outline that you most relate to and add features on them that best represent you. You can use any color construction paper and cut out and glue on clothes, hair, glasses, and/or any other elements you like."


Step 5:
"Finally, you can glue the core circle onto your person. The center might be a good spot for this, but you're welcome to place it anywhere you like. There is no right or wrong way to create. You have complete freedom to decorate your person however way you like to honor and celebrate all your wonderful qualities."
 

               
Writing down negative messages   Ripping them up   Throwing negative messages away
 
   
Adding words, phrases, colors and/or
symbols to a circle of your choice to
represent who you are		   Creating clothes and glue them down   Adding your circle to the center
of your person
opening_circle:
Part 1:
"On the piece of paper that you have in front of you, I'd like to invite you to take some time to write down all of the words and phrases that you've heard from other people and/or ones you've even told yourself. Remember, there is no right or wrong way to do this, you can write the words and phrases big, small or however you want to write them."


Feel free to give the children as much time as you see fit. It may be helpful to give them gentle time reminder as you're getting ready to proceed to the next step.

If time permitting, you can invite participants to reflect on and share, if any feel comfortable doing so, how they felt when they heard these messages, where the messages came from, and/or how they have proven those messages wrong.


Part 2:
"Thank you for taking the time to write down your thoughts. Holding your papers in your hands, let’s take a moment to let these messages in with a deep breath and let them all out with an exhale."

"You'll now get a chance to release these negative messages because they no longer serve you. With your papers in your hands, I’d like to invite you to just rip those messages right up. You can rip them in half, or into as many pieces as you like. However way it feels right for you. As you’re ripping, I encourage you to envision all of those messages being released from your mind."

"At the center of your tables, you’ll notice a small bucket (bin). When you’re ready, I'd like to invite you to go ahead and throw all of those message into the bin. If you don’t feel comfortable releasing your messages in this way, feel free to take them with you and release them in your own way when you’re ready."

title: Self-Care Touchstones for Trauma Professionals / Ejemplo de Piedras de Auto-Cuidado Terminadas
objective:
Completed Self-Care Touchstones

As trauma service professionals we must integrate self-care into our lives to be well and to be effective. In this workshop participants will learn about Olga Phoenix's ground breaking work on this subject and explore six dimensions of self-care necessary for life balance through the creation Self-Care Touchstones.

About the Author: This variation of the Touchstones workshop was created by Olga Phoenix, MPA, MA, a survivor of domestic violence and an internationally recognized expert and speaker on the topics of Vicarious Trauma, Compassion Fatigue, Secondary Traumatic Stress, and Trauma-Informed Services, as well as personal and organizational cultures of Sustainability, Self-Care, and Wellness.

This video of Olga sharing about how the self-care wheel saved her life.
materials:
• Writing Pens

  • Double-sided Self-Care & Life Balance Wheel Blank Wheel (English) (Spanish)

  • Six clear round glass stones ( we use 1 1/4" or 1/2") per participant (Stones are available at craft stores, garden stores and online, be sure to buy clear and not iridescent stones. We have also purchased stones at wholesalersuscinc.com. Make sure to buy the clear, non-iridized stones.)https://awbw.org/durational-art-supplies/

  • Card stock in various colors cut into circles in the same dimension as the stones (We use 1 1/4" or 1/2" EK Tools Circle hole punchers which are available on Amazon.com).  

    • If you don't want to use colored cardstock, you can also create your own designs! One way to do this is to utilize acrylic or watercolor paints and paper. You can paint different colors onto the paper, let it dry, and then punch the circles. We've found painting random colors onto the paper works great and can create fun, unique color mixing designs.

  • Clear tacky glue in bottles with a tip

  • Paper Towels

  • Music for reflection and creative time

  • Optional: 3"x4" sheer bags (Can be purchased at craft stores or online at Papermart.com)

 

 

Journaling on the blank wheel

Options for art making:

  • Permanent markers (Fine and/or extra fine)

  • Sharpie Paint Pens with Extra Fine Point

  • Colored pencils - white (Prismacolor brand ONLY) for dark colored paper

  • Silver origami paper - click here to see an instructional video. You can purchase the paper here.

  • Ballpoint pens in various colors
warm_up:
Blank Self-Care & Life Balance Wheel Journaling:

 

 

Invite participants to turn Self-Care & Life Balance Wheel over to reveal the blank wheel.

Now, we will take some time to take a long hard look at the Wheel’s six dimensions and realistically and honestly assess your current situation, where would you like to go.

You will have the next sixteen minutes to reflect on/write about these needs for yourself. Use the blank space in each dimension of the wheel to jot down any words, shapes, colors, images or symbols that come up. There is no right or wrong way to do this journaling exercise. You can write sentences, words, lists, draw symbols, shapes, or anything else you like. Just allow your thoughts to flow onto your paper without judgment. What you write does not have to make sense to anyone but you! It is also fine to just sit quietly and notice what comes up. Remember this is your window of time to connect with yourself and what's meaningful for you.

  1. "Looking at the Physical Dimension of your life, what are the activities that work well for you currently? What are the things you would like to do more of? Less of? Any specific activities you would like to try from the Physical Dimension of the Wheel? Give 2 minutes for this.

  2. Looking at the Psychological Dimension of your life, what are the activities that work well for you currently? What are the things you would like to do more of? Less of? Any specific activities you would like to try from the Psychological Dimension of the Wheel? Give 2 minutes for this.

  3. Looking at the Emotional Dimension of your life, what are the activities that work well for you currently? What are the things you would like to do more of? Less of? Any specific activities you would like to try from the Emotional Dimension of the Wheel? Give 2 minutes for this.

  4. Looking at the Spiritual Dimension of your life, what are the activities that work well for you currently? What are the things you would like to do more of? Less of? Any specific activities you would like to try from the Spiritual Dimension of the Wheel? Give 2 minutes for this.

  5. Looking at the Emotional Dimension of your life, what are the activities that work well for you currently? What are the things you would like to do more of? Less of? Any specific activities you would like to try from the Emotional Dimension of the Wheel? Give 2 minutes for this.

  6. Looking at the Professional Dimension of your life, what are the activities that work well for you currently? What are the things you would like to do more of? Less of? Any specific activities you would like to try from the Professional Dimension of the Wheel? Give 2 minutes for this."
creation:
"Whenever you're ready, I invite you to begin creating your Self-Care Touchstones. You can make one for each of the six dimensions of the wheel, one for all of the dimensions or anything in between. As you create, remember to create your Touchstones in any way that feels right to you. You can create an image or symbol, use colors or words, or any combination you choose. Listen to your heart - what words, shapes, colors will best support you? Whether it seems too big to be possible or too small to be important, honor whatever comes to your mind."

In the last 5 minutes of the creation process, turn down the music, give a time warning, and let them know that they will have an opportunity to share anything about their Touchstone(s) and how they might use them, if they would like.
closing:
Invite participants to share anything they want to about their Self-Care Touchstones, what they mean to them and any discoveries they made. You might encourage the participants to think about and share how/if they want to use their Touchstones in their everyday lives.

Remind the participants that: "In order for the Self-Care & Life Balance Wheel to work, it needs to be preventative and sustainable. It means that we cannot put a copy of the Wheel on our wall at work and expect to never experience the effects of vicarious trauma. The Wheel, rather, needs to become an integral part of our life. Which is why we made Self-Care Touchstones to serve as tangible reminders!"

Reminder for participants: "This process does not end today; you can reflect back on it anytime. Encourage participants to continue to explore the six dimensions of self-care necessary for life balance and create new Self-Care Touchstones to represent those needs. They are worth it!

Congratulations! You have started your new beautiful transformational journey to Self-Care and Wellness, as well as a Joyful and Cherished Life, FREE of Vicarious Trauma!"

tips:
Optional Activity 1: Addressing Fear:

I invite you to take a long hard look at the Wheel’s SIX DIMENSIONS and realistically and honestly assess your current situation, where would you like to go, how do you picture your VT-Free Life and will take to maintain it. The questions below will help you with this process. Use the blank space under each question to jot down your thoughts, ideas, comments, answers as they come up.

  1. Examine the Wheel closely, then mindfully and non-judgmentally listen to your body and mind, and write down the thoughts that come.

  2. What are your hopes and goals in regards to this new Self-Care and Wellness Journey?

  3. What are your fears about this new Self-Care and Wellness Journey?

  4. What do you already know about your life and work habits that require your immediate attention?

  5. How does your life feel? What seems to be working well? What seems to be challenging?


Fantastic work answering the 1st set of questions!! It‘s often very difficult to reflect on our fears, goals, and aspirations. One of the reasons being that human psyche really dislikes CHANGE, and we often hear the voice of INNER CRITIC especially loudly when we are getting ready to start a NEW JOURNEY, no matter how exciting or promising it is. Whatever FEELINGS you might be experiencing at the moment-welcome them! Say: „Hello, dear feeling, I know you are here and present. I welcome you, because you are important to me“. Your psyche‘s resistance to change usually lessens, at least a tiny bit, when it‘s validated and welcomed. And that‘s all we need to proceed!:)

Optional Activity 2: Supporters and Saboteurs:

  1. On a journey like this, it‘s HUGELY important to have a SUPPORTIVE FRIEND. Your therapist, your partner, your best friend, your co-worker, your supervisor, even a loving presence of imaginary INNER FRIEND can do the trick! As long as feel like you are not alone on this journey it all that counts! Who is your current support group? Who would you like to enlist to become a part of your support group? Think about the concept of INNER FRIEND and see if you can find one within.

  2. After you identified your SUPPORT GROUP, it‘s valuable to reflect on your SABOTEURS. It could be your inner critic, an unsupportive colleague, your overly packed schedule, or even an unhealthy habit. Here it‘s important to reflect on the fact that no matter who or what your saboteurs are, YOU and your SUPPORT GROUP can tackle them in NO TIME!

  3. Now, with SUPPORT GROUP identified, and SABOTUERS exposed, let‘s think about your reasons behind getting this Kit in the first place? What is motivating you to seek information about Vicarious Trauma Prevention and Solutions to Living FULL JOYFUL AND MEANINGFUL LIFE?


Excellent job on dismantling BARRIERS and identifying SOLUTIONS! Now, we come prepared to creating our personal SELF-CARE AND LIFE BALANCE WHEEL and our own SIX DIMENSIONS OF VICARIOUS TRAUMA-FREE LIFE!
