closing: For the closing, you may give the children an opportunity to share their amazing flags and anything they learned, felt or experienced in the process of creating, or anything else they wish to share. Of course, this is purely optional and if no one feels comfortable sharing, it's perfectly okay.
optional_materials:
You can also facilitate this workshop using printable worksheets. If you are utilizing the worksheets in lieu of the regular workshop materials, be sure to send a digital copy or print them out for your participants if you are meeting in person.

  • Flying Tall Worksheet (English)

  • Flying Tall Worksheet (Spanish)

   
Flying Tall Worksheet (English)     Flying Tall Worksheet (Spanish)
introduction:
"Today, you will have an opportunity to reflect on your strengths and your good qualities. We each have unique strengths. Different people have different strengths, and everyone is strong in their own way. There is no right or wrong way to be strong. Your own personal understanding of strength is what matters here today. Everyone has had times when they felt strong and when they felt weak. You will have a chance to create a personal flag that celebrates and represents how strong you are, so the next time you feel down, you can have something to remind you of all the incredible strength you hold inside you. The name of this workshop is called 'Flying Tall.'"

"Before we begin, I want you to know that this workshop is a window of time for you. This means that this can be a safe space to notice your thoughts, feelings, and needs. Since this space is your window of time, everything you say or do is voluntary. I’ll offer a suggested workshop idea, share about the materials we have available, and invite you to create, but there’s no right or wrong way to do this. It doesn't matter what it looks like. What matters is taking this time to truly honor your thoughts and feelings, however they come out. If you can’t think of anything or draw a blank on what to create or write, feel free to just observe. However you choose to spend this time will be perfectly okay. This is your time. Please ask for what you need, and know that I’m here in support of you."
demonstration: You may wish to take a moment to show your flag sample (if you've created one) and briefly explain the material and how to assemble and mount the flag.
opening_circle:
You may open by inviting the children to a brief discussion on what strength means. Of course, this is optional for both you and them, but sharing their thoughts can help inspire them to be more connected with themselves through the creation process.

If you choose to incorporate a brief discussion, you're welcome to use some of these questions as prompts or any of your own.

"I'd like to invite you to think about what strength means to you. Is it about how many pounds you can lift? Or does it mean something more than that? For example, one kind of strength is being reliable. Another kind of strength is making good decisions. Another kind of strength is showing kindness."

"As you can see from our discussion, there are all kinds of ways to think about strengths. Remember, there is no right or wrong way to feel strong. Whatever it means to you, is perfect."

"I'd like to encourage you to think of a time when you felt strong. A time when you used your strengths to get through something. Can you think of a time you were strong in a 'big' way? What about a time you were strong in a 'small' way? There are different shapes and sizes of strengths, too."

"If you feel comfortable, I'd like to invite anyone who wishes to share some of the different ways a person can be strong."

title: Introduction to Journaling for Adults
objective:
Many of the AWBW workshops include a journaling component, but did you know you may build an entire workshop around journaling? Working from prompts or simply free writing, participants can journal their feelings and decorate the journal cover as a creative exercise.

The therapeutic benefits of journaling are numerous. A groundbreaking study of the physiological effects of writing appeared in the Journal of the American Medical Association (Vol. 281, No. 14) and found that “writing helped patients get better, and also kept them from getting worse.”

Source: American Psychological Association

Journals are available at Discount School Supply, Amazon, and at other retailers.


When inviting participants to journal, we suggest offering them a Window of Time:

"Before we begin, I want you to know that this workshop is a window of time for you. This means that this can be a safe space to notice your thoughts, feelings, and needs. Since this space is your window of time, everything you say or do is voluntary. I’ll offer a suggested workshop idea, share about the materials we have available, and invite you to create, but there’s no right or wrong way to do this. It doesn't matter what it looks like. What matters is taking this time to truly honor your thoughts and feelings, however they come out. If you can’t think of anything or draw a blank on what to create or write, feel free to just observe. However you choose to spend this time will be perfectly okay. This is your time. Please ask for what you need, and know that I’m here in support of you."

Here are some techniques, tips and journaling exercises:


BASIC TECHNIQUES:
Journal therapy consists of many techniques or writing exercises. In all journal therapy techniques, the writer is encouraged to date everything, write quickly, keep writings and always express their complete truth. Some journal therapy techniques are:

Sprint:
In the sprint technique, catharsis is encouraged by writing about anything for a designated period, such as for five minutes or for ten minutes.

Lists:
In the list technique, the writer writes any number of connected items in order to help prioritize and organize.

Captured Moments:
In the captured moments technique, a writer attempts to completely describe the essence and emotional experience of a memory.

Unsent Letters:
The unsent letters technique attempts to silence a writer’s internal censor.

Dialogue:
In the dialogue technique, the writer creates both sides to conversation involving anything, including but not limited to, people, the body, events, situations, time etc.

Feedback Loop (Reading Aloud):
The feedback technique is important to journal therapy, in that feedback (reading aloud) makes the writer aware of their feelings.

 

TIPS:

Be Spontaneous:
Just grab a pen. Jot down a few words or a few pages. Be free.

Be Ritualistic:
Create a special setting for your writing. Light some scented candles. Write slowly. Let the moment fill you.

Be Formal:
Make a writing date with yourself and stick to it.

Be Emotional:
If you are in an emotional crisis or simply overflowing with feelings, carry your book with you. Use it throughout your day. Fill as many pages as you need.

Be Specific:
You may have a special challenge, issue or event you want to address. Celebrate and honor your life’s turning points in writing.

Source: Woman's Book of Changes ©1998 Tools With Heart, LLC


JOURNALING PROMPS FOR ADULTS:

  • Free write (no instruction… whatever comes to mind).

 

COMPLETE THE SENTENCE:

  • I feel…

  • If you really knew me…

  • I am…

  • I believe…

  • I want you to know…

  • Where I am…

  • Where I’m going…

  • My story…

  • Things that make me smile…

  • If my body could talk…

  • Things I’d like to say "yes" to…

  • Things I’d like to say "no" to…

  • The words I need to hear…

  • What brings me joy…

  • My physical needs…

  • My emotional needs…

  • I wish someone knew that…

  • Today I’m grateful for…

  • Today I’m afraid that…

  • Today I’m angry about…

  • Today I need to remember…

  • Today I plan to change…

  • Today I am happy that…

  • If anything were possible, my life would look like…

  • Today I open my heart to…

  • Today I give myself permission to write about anything…

  • Tomorrow I will imagine…

  • Tomorrow I intend to…

  • I would rather…

  • I will shift my point of view to live more fully by…

  • Who Am I: Today, I am/Yesterday I was/I am becoming…

  • The parts of myself I show to others…

  • The parts of myself I hide from others…

  • My authentic self is…

  • What the present moment offers me is…

  • What’s going on right now is…

  • I feel seen and heard when…

  • Three Blessings: One good thing that happened today/How it happened/Why it happened…

  • A gratitude letter…

 

STRUCTURED WRITING:

  • Write a 1-page personal biography focusing on your strengths.

  • Write about a time you were strong.

  • Write about something you overcame.

  • Choose a quote and have participants write a response to it.

  • Write an “Unsent Letter” to someone… or to yourself.

  • Write a “Love Note(s)” to yourself.

  • Write a prayer.

  • Write a poem.

 

You can download a PDF copy of this guide here.

title: Take a Break, Self Regulate!
objective: This workshop aims to give children an opportunity to discuss the importance of taking breaks and create dice that can help them practice self-care in a fun way.
materials:
• Dice template (2 per participant). Click here to download.

  • Paper or journals for journal excerise

  • Colored Pencils

  • Pencils

  • Markers

  • Transparent tape

  • Glue sticks

  • Scissors

  • White board or paper for group chart and steps for creation

  • Self-Regulation Prompts
setup:
Here are some articles that give great insight about the importance of taking breaks:

  • How Kids Learn Better By Taking Breaks

  • "Brain Breaks" Increase Activity, Educational Performance in Elementary Schools

  • Why Students Need "Brain Breaks"& How You Can Help

  • The Importance of Taking a Break

You may wish to prepare materials for each participant. Depending on their age and their abilities, you may want to pre-cut the box template so children can easily go from writing/drawing straight into the creation portion of the workshop.

You may consider writing each step for the creation process and display it so all the children can easily see it.

For the discussion section, you may wish to prepare your "T" chart in advance. On one side of the "T" you can write: "How we take breaks" and on the other side: "Why we take breaks."

It can be helpful if you could create a sample dice (both) to show the children so they can see what they look like. If you choose to do so, we suggest creating a simple one so that children won't feel overwhelmed with any "artistic" challenges.
warm_up:
“I would now like to invite you to take a moment to think about our discussion. Now that we know a little more about what breaks are, how and why we take them, I’m going to invite you to journal about this question: 'How would you like to take breaks in the future?' I’m going to give you about ten minutes to write in a journal or on a piece of paper. During this time, you're invited to make a list of different activities you can do during your breaks. Think about the different times throughout your day and how your breaks might be different depending on where you are. You might have more time in some parts of your day, and in some, you might have less. Since this is your Window of Time, journaling can look however you want it to look, there is no right or wrong way. I invite you to write words, shapes, symbols, or any other way you would like to do this activity."

"Does anyone have any questions before we start? When we begin, I’ll be giving your time reminders. When the time is over, I will invite you to begin creating your dice. Any questions about journaling or creating before we begin? Let’s begin.”

You may wish to give time reminders through the writing process. You can remind the children that they are welcome to refer to the chart you created as well as utilize the time in however way they feel comfortable. When time is up, you can invite them to create their dice.
creation:
You may wish to remind the children about the steps for creation. If you've written the instructions on a board, you can refer them where you wrote out the steps for them so they can refer to them during the creation part of the workshop. You can also give the children time reminders throughout the entire process.
 

Step 1: Capturing Ideas

  • "On the 1st die template, you can write, draw, and color your different break ideas."

  • "On the 2nd die template, you can write down 6 different time intervals you would like to take a break. You can even create a "You choose" option where you get to choose a time when the dice lands with this side face up."

  • "As you create, you can think about the questions in the introduction."
     

Step 2: Cutting

  • "When you’re finished writing and/or drawing, you can cut around the outer lines of the boxes. You should end up with one piece that looks like a lowercase 't'."
     

Step 3: Folding

  • "You can fold along each of the lines to create a cube."
     

Step 4: Gluing and Taping

  • "Using a glue stick, you can glue each of tab to keep the cube in place."

  • "Use clear tape to close secure the edges."
closing:
“Today we had a chance to talk about the importance of taking a break and how we can take breaks to help us throughout our day. I would like to give you a chance to share your feelings. For anyone who wishes to share, how did it feel to talk about taking breaks? Did you learn anything new? How will you use your dice? Any volunteers that would like to share?"

“Now that we had the chance to hear from everyone that wanted to share with us, I would like to invite anyone who would like to join in on rolling our dice together as a group. Now that you have these dice, I encourage you to continue to practice taking breaks. Share this with your family, your friends, and anyone else that may need help thinking of great ways to take a break. Thank you all for being here today. I appreciate all of you for taking the time to think, create, and participate in a way that was comfortable for you.”
optional_materials:
You can also facilitate this workshop using printable worksheets. If you are utilizing the worksheets in lieu of the regular workshop materials, be sure to send a digital copy or print them out for your participants if you are meeting in person.

  • Take a Break, Self-Regulate Worksheets (English and Spanish)

  • "50 Ways to Take a Break" handout by Karen Horneffer-Ginter, Ph.D. Click here to download.

  • "AWBW 50 Ways to Take a Break" handout in English and Spanish

   
Take a Break, Self-Regulate Worksheet (English)     Take a Break, Self-Regulate Worksheet (Spanish)
introduction:
“Thank you for being here today. Before we begin, I want you to know that this is your Window of Time. It's a time for you to notice your thoughts, needs and feelings. During this time, there is no right or wrong way to participate or create. I'm going to share some instructions, but you get to choose how you want to participate. You can follow along completely, or you may want to do something different, it's completely up to you. During your Window of time, you get to choose. I am here to support you in any way that I can, so please ask for what you need. Any questions before I begin?"

“Today, we have an opportunity to talk about taking breaks. We will get a chance to talk about what taking breaks mean, how we take them, and how they can be helpful in our lives. After our discussion, we will get a chance to write. You will then be invited to use your writing to create dice that you will be able to use when taking breaks in the future."
demonstration:
“In a moment, we'll open with a discussion about taking breaks. Then, I’m going to invite you to write anything that's on your mind in your journal or on a piece of paper. After that, you’ll have some time to create your dice. Since I'm going to invite you to move straight from writing into creating, I’m going to first share with you about the art materials that you can use."

“On your tables, you see that you have markers, colored pencils and regular pencils to use."

"You also have two pieces of thicker paper that you can write on and draw on, then put together to create two boxes, which will be your dice. Each page has 6 squares in it. I’m going to talk about each one separately."

 

Step 1: Capturing Ideas

  • Dice #1: "Each of these will become one die. One die is for you to write and/or draw 6 different ways you can take a break. You can use the list we'll create for ideas, come up with your own, or a combination of both. You're invited to use words, shapes, and/or symbols to represent your breaks. For example, you can draw yourself taking a walk or reading a book, or you can just draw a shoe or a book to represent these things. Remember, there is no right or wrong way to take a break. These dice are for you so feel free to create it however way it works for you."

  • Dice #2: "The second die can be used to tell you how long to take your break. So when you roll both of the dice, two of the dice faces will show the break and the other will show how long to take that break. You can write down 6 different time intervals (Ex: 20 minutes) that you would like to take a break. You can even create a "You choose" option where you get to choose a time when the dice lands with this side face up."

Die #1: How to take a break Die #2: How long to take a break


Step 2: Cutting

  • "When you’re finished writing and/or drawing, you can cut around the outer lines of the boxes. You should end up with one piece that looks like a lowercase 't'."
     

Cutting out the die template

 

Step 3: Folding

  • "You can now fold along each of the lines to create a cube."
     

Folding the dice into a cube

 

Step 4: Gluing and Taping

  • Using a glue stick, you can glue each of tabs keep the cube in place.

  • You can use clear tape to close make the final edges.
     

        
Gluing   Taping


If you've created a sample in advance, you can show it to your participants so they can see how the dice will look when they're done.
opening_circle:
You can begin the discussion by posing the questions below. Based on the ages of your group, you can modify the questions for better understanding or deeper insight.

An option for this section is to first pose a question to the group, then invite participants to get into groups to discuss further. You can give them the opportunity to practice timed listening and sharing. After the paired sharing, you can ask for volunteers to share what they learned from one another. When practicing paired listening, you may wish to remind participants to only share what they personally shared in the group and not to share information they heard from their partner unless given permission from their partner.

You can keep a running list of what participants share so they can refer to it when they create their dice, using a "T" chart. The left side can be titled "How we take a break" and the right, "Why we take a break."

Questions for Discussion:

  • When you think about the word break, what comes to mind?

  • What does taking a break mean to you?

  • How do we usually take breaks?

  • Why do we take breaks?

  • How can breaks be helpful?

    • Breaks can help us when we are physically tired and we need to let our bodies rest.

    • We can use breaks to calm down when we are having big feelings.

      • Angry

      • Excited

      • Anxious

      • Nervous

  • Breaks can be small gifts to ourselves when we have been working hard for a long periods of time.

  • Breaks can help our brain take a rest.
     

"Now that we have a list of the different ways that we can take breaks, let's think about when it's a good idea to take them. Sometimes when our bodies are tired, it can be a good time to take a break. But can you think of any other times it can be good to take a break?"

Feel free to offer suggestions if you wish participants are having a hard time coming up with ideas.

title: The Diamond Inside Me
objective: This workshop provides an opportunity for children to embrace their value by recognizing the people around them that make a positive impact in their lives, and creating a symbolic art piece that represents those relationships.
materials:
•     
      Supplies and sample table set-up

    Diamond Inside Me template

  • Markers and/or colored pencils

  • Plain paper (for the warm-up exercise)

  • Pens and/or pencils
setup:
You can watch the "Priceless Stones" video or read the transcript (simple version for younger children) in advance. If possible, you can show the children this video during the Introduction, or you can print either the transcript or simple version of the video for the children to read.


You have two creation options:

Option 1: (Simple version for younger children)
You can print copies of the Diamond Inside Me template for each participant and invite the children to decorate it using markers and/or color pencils (see Demonstration for details).


Option 2: (for older children and teens)
If you choose to incorporate collaging into your workshop, you can provide larger construction papers for each participant to use as a canvas (please note, the diamond in the left example image has since been redesigned). You may also use the template and invite the children to use that as a collaging canvas. It's entirely up to you.
 

Option 1: Using the template Option 2: Using collaging option


It may be helpful to create a sample in advance to show children what the finished art piece can look like. If you choose to do so, we suggest creating a simple sample and using only the supplies you're providing so that children aren't overwhelmed by any "artistic" challenges.

As a facilitator, you have complete freedom to alter or adapt any portion or element of this workshop to cater to your specific group's needs.
warm_up: “I now invite you to take some time to write or sketch (quickly draw) some things you like/value about yourself, along with some people whom help make you and your life better.”
creation:
You can now invite those who wish to create to begin doing so. You may wish to remind the children that there is no right or wrong way to create. There is no pressure to finish in the time given; this is an exploration that children can always take home and finish as they think of more things they like/value about themselves and more people that support them in a positive way/ help them feel positive.

If you are giving them the collaging option, you may need to allocate a little more to the creation portion.

Depending on the age group some children may need help with certain creation elements, so feel free to offer your assistance where you see the need.
closing:
You can invite any children who wish to do so, a chance to share their amazing art piece, anything they learned, felt or experienced during the creation.

Again, we encourage popcorn style so people are able to opt-in instead of possibly feeling pressure to share. If applicable, you can remind the children that they can continue working on their drawings (or collages) as they think of new things they like/value about themselves and other supportive people in their lives. Or, you can invite them to come back to this artwork later to be reminded of who they are and who is helpful in their lives.
optional_materials:
• Oil pastels (CrayPas)

  • Magazines (for collaging; Oprah, Nat Geo and travel magazines tend to have more inclusive words and imagery)

  • Construction paper (for collaging; any size; any colors)

  • Glue sticks (for collaging)

  • Computer, tablet, etc. (to show "Priceless Stone" video)
introduction:
"Before we begin, I want you to know that this is your window of time. This means that this can be a safe space to notice your thoughts, feelings, and needs. Since this space is your window of time, everything you say or do is voluntary. During this time, there is no right or wrong way to participate or create. I'm going to share some basic instructions, but you get to choose how you want to participate. You can follow along completely, or you may want to do something different, it's completely up to you. During your window of time, you have complete freedom to choose. However you choose to spend this time will be perfectly okay. I am here to support you in any way that I can, so please feel free to ask for what you need."

You can continue by sharing the “Priceless Stones” story either by showing the video, or by inviting the children to read the "Priceless Stones" handout (transcript or simple version).

You can also invite the children to read out loud, popcorn style (anyone can take a turn when they want to, as long as they do not interrupt another person). We encourage this form of reading so that no one has to read, or say pass, if they don’t feel comfortable doing so.
demonstration:
Diamond surrounded by participant's positive qualities and people in their lives whom validate those qualities


 

You can introduce the art supplies and go over the basic creation steps (whichever option you are providing) with the children.


Option 1: (Using the Template)
Children can decorate the diamond using any colors shapes, symbols or words that best represent those qualities about themselves that they value.

Once they're done decorating the diamond, they can surround the diamond with representations of people whom children feel good when they're around them, and see the "diamond" that's inside them. They could be family, friends, teachers, etc. These are the people whom encourage the children and help make them feel happy.

Children can represent one, or as many people around them as they like.

 

Option 2: (Collaging)
You can either use the template or larger construction paper and invite the children to go through the magazines and cut out an images and/or word that best represents their positive qualities (in place of the diamond), glue it onto the center of the page and surround it with images and/or words that represent the people in their lives.

Feel free to demonstrate any creation elements that you see fit.
opening_circle: You can invite anyone who feels comfortable doing so, to briefly share something they like/value about themselves. Again, we encourage popcorn style so people are able to opt-in instead of possibly feeling pressure to share.

Puede invitar a cualquier persona que desee compartir y darle la oportunidad de mostrar ya sea su increíble obra de arte, cualquier cosa que hayan aprendido, sentido o experimentado durante la creación.

Una vez más, alentamos el estilo de las palomitas de maíz para que las personas puedan optar por participar, en lugar de posiblemente sentir la presión de compartir. Si existe la posibilidad, puede recordarles a las y los participantes que pueden continuar trabajando en sus dibujos (o collages) a medida que piensen en cosas nuevas que les gustan o valoran sobre su persona y otras personas que les apoyan en sus vidas. O bien, puede invitarles a las y los participantes a volver a esta obra de arte más tarde para recordar quiénes son y quiénes les ayudan en sus vidas.

  • Magazines (for collaging; Oprah, Nat Geo and travel magazines tend to have more inclusive words and imagery)

  • Construction paper (for collaging; any size; any colors)

  • Glue sticks (for collaging)

  • Computer, tablet, etc. (to show "Priceless Stone" video)

Pasteles al óleo (CrayPas)

introduction:
"Before we begin, I want you to know that this is your window of time. This means that this can be a safe space to notice your thoughts, feelings, and needs. Since this space is your window of time, everything you say or do is voluntary. During this time, there is no right or wrong way to participate or create. I'm going to share some basic instructions, but you get to choose how you want to participate. You can follow along completely, or you may want to do something different, it's completely up to you. During your window of time, you have complete freedom to choose. However you choose to spend this time will be perfectly okay. I am here to support you in any way that I can, so please feel free to ask for what you need."

You can continue by sharing the “Priceless Stones” story either by showing the video, or by inviting the participants to read the "Priceless Stones" handout.

You can also invite the participants to read out loud, popcorn style (anyone can take a turn when they want to, as long as they do not interrupt another person). We encourage this form of reading so that no one has to read, or say pass, if they don’t feel comfortable doing so.
introduction_spanish:
"Antes de comenzar, quiero que sepan que esta es su ventana de tiempo. Esto significa que este puede ser un espacio seguro para que noten sus pensamientos, sentimientos y necesidades. Dado que este espacio es su ventana de tiempo, todo lo que digan o hagan es voluntario. Durante este tiempo, no hay una forma correcta o incorrecta de participar o crear. Voy a compartir algunas instrucciones básicas, pero pueden elegir cómo quieran participar. Pueden seguirlas al pie de la letra o quizás prefieran hacer algo diferente, depende completamente de cada quien. Durante su ventana de tiempo, tienen total libertad para elegir. Cual sea su elección de pasar este tiempo estará perfectamente bien. Estoy aquí para ayudarles de cualquier manera que pueda, así que por favor no duden en pedirme por lo que necesiten."

Puede continuar compartiendo la historia de "La piedra invaluable", ya sea mostrando el video o invitando a las y los participantes a leer el folleto de "La piedra invaluable."

También puede invitar a las y los participantes a leer en voz alta, al estilo de las palomitas de maíz (cualquiera puede tomar un turno cuando lo desee, siempre y cuando no interrumpa a otra persona). Alentamos esta forma de leer para que nadie tenga que leer, o decir pase, si no se sienten cómoda o cómodo haciéndolo.
demonstration:
Diamond surrounded by participant's positive qualities and people in their lives whom validate those qualities


 

You can introduce the art supplies and go over the basic creation steps (whichever option you are providing) with the participants.


Option 1: (Using the Template)
Participants can decorate the diamond using any colors shapes, symbols or words that best represent those qualities about themselves that they value.

Once they're done decorating the diamond, participants can surround the diamond with representations of people whom they feel good when they're around them, and see the "diamond" that's inside them. They could be family, friends, teachers, etc. These are the people whom encourage the participants and help make them feel happy.

Participants can represent one, or as many people around them as they like.

 

Option 2: (Collaging)
You can either use the template or larger construction paper and invite the participants to go through the magazines and cut out an images and/or word that best represents their positive qualities (in place of the diamond), glue it onto the center of the page and surround it with images and/or words that represent the people in their lives.

Feel free to demonstrate any creation elements that you see fit.
demonstration_spanish:
Puede presentar los materiales de arte y repasar los pasos básicos de creación (cualquiera de las opciones que decida hacer) con las y los participantes.

Opción 1: (Uso de la plantilla)
Las y los participantes pueden decorar el diamante utilizando colores, formas, símbolos o palabras que mejor representen las cualidades que cada quien valora de su persona.

Una vez que terminen de decorar el diamante, las y los participantes pueden rodear el diamante con representaciones de personas con quienes se sienten bien cuando están cerca de ellas, y ver el "diamante" que está dentro de esas personas. Pueden ser familiares, amigas, amigos, maestras, maestros, etc. Estas son las personas que alientan a las y los participantes y les ayudan a sentirse felices.

Las y los participantes pueden representar a una o tantas personas a su alrededor como deseen.

Opción 2: (Collage)
Puede usar la plantilla o un papel de construcción más grande e invitar a las y los participantes a que revisen las revistas y recorten las imágenes y / o palabras que mejor representan sus cualidades positivas (en lugar del diamante), las pueden pegar en el centro de la página. y rodéelo con imágenes y / o palabras que representen a las personas en sus vidas.

Siéntase libre de demostrar cualquier elemento de creación que considere adecuado.
opening_circle: You can invite anyone who feels comfortable doing so, to briefly share something they like/value about themselves. Again, we encourage popcorn style so people are able to opt-in instead of possibly feeling pressure to share.
opening_circle_spanish: Puede invitar a alguien del grupo que se sienta cómoda o cómodo, para que comparta brevemente algo que les guste / valoren sobre su persona. Una vez más, alentemos el estilo de las palomitas de maíz para que las personas puedan optar por participar, en lugar de posiblemente sentir la presión de compartir.

title: Your Wellness Matters Shrinky Dinks
objective: This workshop offers a safe and creative way for children to explore the need and meaning of wellness in order to practice self-care.
materials:
• Shrinky Dink material (Ruff-N-Ready)

  • Wellness templates (click here to download)

  • Permanent markers

  • Colored pencils

  • Scissors

  • Hole punch

  • Toaster oven

  • Brown grocery paper bags or cookie sheets (for baking)

  • Ribbon or craft wire
setup:
You may need to print enough photocopies of the various templates for all the children.

It would be most efficient to pre-cut the Shrinky Dink film into 3 1/2 x 4 inch squares to fit the size of our template.

You may consider trying this project in advance so you have some samples to share, or if you have never used the Shrinky Dink materials you may also want to get a feel for how the Shrinky Dinks cook. It can be fun to watch them shrink!

If you choose to create one in advance, we suggest keeping it as simple as possible so as not to overwhelm the children with an artistic challenge.
warm_up:
You may do this meditation/relaxation exercise, or one of your own. We have found that speaking in a soft, calming tone and pausing where it feels right is most effective.

"Before we begin creating our Shrinky Dinks, I'd like to invite you to join me in a brief mediation exercise. Of course, this is optional. If you choose to use this time to observe or do something else, that's perfectly okay."

"For those who wish to participate, if you're comfortable, I welcome you to close your eyes. You can also keep them open and fixate on an object or look around. However you feel comfortable, works just fine. If you're sitting in a chair, I invite you to place your feet on the floor and to feel your back against the chair."

"Slowly, try to focus on your breathing... such as the air flowing into your nostrils and out of your mouth, or your belly rising and falling as you inhale and exhale."

"Now, I'd like to invite you to think about the questions we asked earlier. What does taking care of yourself look like? Is it a happy thought? Is it a calm thought? If your mind starts to race, it's okay. Try to return your focus to your breathing."

"I welcome you to take one more deep breathe... exhale, and when you're comfortable, you can open your eyes and return to the moment."
creation:
If you've created a Shrinky Dink in advance, you may wish to show it as an example.


Step 1: Designing
"For those of you who wish to create your special Shrinky Dink, you can begin by choosing one of the wellness templates in front of you. If you don't like any of the templates, you are also welcome to create your own design that's the same size. I'd like to encourage you to think about any words, symbols, or colors that you connect with as you reflect on your wellness. You can use any of the materials to trace the image on the Shrinky Dink and color it however way you wish."

"Please note that colored pencils work on the rough side of the Shrinky Dink and Sharpies can work on both sides."

Step 2: Cutting out
"When you are finished coloring, you may cut out your shape with scissors. In a moment, you'll have the opportunity to bake them and once they're baked, you can't alter them."

Step 3: Optional hole-punch
"If you would like to add ribbon or wire to your Shrinky Dink, to maybe use it as a necklace, bracelet or hang it on a wall, you can now use a hole-puncher to punch a hole where you want the ribbon to go."

Step 4: Preparing to Bake
"Now, your wellness Shrinky Dink is ready to bake."

Depending on the age group, you may feel the need to assist the children with the prepping and baking. To prepare, you can place the pieces onto a cut out piece of brown paper bag or cookie sheet, with the shiny side facing up. This will help prevent the plastic from folding onto itself. The Shrinky Dink pieces should not be touching, as they may stick together when baking.

Step 5: Baking
You can place the wellness Shrinky Dinks in the oven at 300°F for 1-3 minutes.

Please be mindful that if you're using a toaster oven, even the outer surface can get very hot!

The heat initially causes the plastic to fold. You can continue to bake the pieces until they flatten. If you remove the tray or paper bag prematurely, you can still place it back in the oven to finish baking.

Step 6: Cooling
Once they've baked, you can removed them from the oven and let them cool down. This usually takes another 1-3 minutes.

Step 7: Adding Ribbon (optional)
Those who have punched a hole in their wellness Shrinky Dink, can now use ribbon or wire and loop it through the hole. You can invite the children to add beads now, if you've chosen to use them.
closing:
For the closing, you can invite the children to share how it felt to focus on their own wellness during the workshop. They may wish to share their thoughts, their process, or even how they may take steps to care for themselves. If they want to share one word, great. If they don't want to share at all, that's great too.

Once sharing is complete, you may wish to remind the children that their "wellness" window of time doesn't need to end when the session ends. Learning and practicing self-care is a muscle, and this workshop may be the foundation for further growing in wellness.
optional_materials:
• Beads

  • Soothing music

  • Explore 28 pages of fun and creative Shrinky Dink templates here!
introduction:
"Today you are going to have an opportunity to create a Shrinky Dink while you reflect on your needs, your wellness, and your self-care. How you take care of yourself may look different for each of you, and that is okay. Some of you may think of snuggling a puppy, reading a book, or taking a nap. For others, taking care of yourself may mean taking five minutes to do nothing. Whatever it means to you, will be perfect. During this workshop, I'd like to encourage you to recognize and identify those things in order to start practicing self-care."

"Before we begin, I want you to know that this workshop is a window of time for you. This means that this is a safe space to notice your thoughts, feelings, and needs. Since this space is your window of time, everything you say or do is voluntary. I’ll offer a suggested workshop idea, share about the materials we have available, and invite you to create, but there’s no wrong way to do this. It doesn't matter what it looks like. What matters is taking this time to truly honor your thoughts and feelings, however they come out. If you can’t think of anything or draw a blank on what to create or write, feel free to just observe. However you choose to spend this time will be perfectly okay. This is your time. Please ask for what you need, and know that I’m here in support of you."
opening_circle:
"For those of you who wish to participate, I'd like to invite each of you to begin thinking about what wellness or self-care looks like for you. Perhaps think of the following:"

  • "What does it look like to take care of yourself?"

  • "What makes you feel happy?"

  • "What makes you feel calm?"
     

You have complete freedom to prompt them any way you wish. The idea is that the children have an opportunity to think about what self-care means to them.

title: Creating a Safe/Brave Place / Creando Un Lugar Seguro/Valiente
objective: This workshop aims to give children an opportunity to learn that they have the capacity within them to create healing images, and a voice in feeling safe.
materials:
Safety Picture Making supplies

Picture Making: (for children under 7)

  • Non-toxic marker

  • Construction paper (to draw on)

  • Permanent marker (for name writing)

  • Large envelopes (to keep the art piece protected)

 


 

    
  Collage-Making supplies

Optional Collage Making: (for children over 7)

  • Glue stick (one for each child)

  • Appropriate magazines (Oprah, Nat Geo and travel magazines tend to have more inclusive imagery)

  • Construction paper

  • Scissors (one for each child)

  • Large envelopes
setup:
For the Opening and Relaxation, it is ideal for each participant to be on the floor on their own mat or piece of carpet. This way they have a defined space, a boundary for their body in which to relax and feel safe. But this is not necessary. This workshop can be done entirely at the table.

You may consider creating a sample in advance to show the children what the final art piece can look like. If you choose to do so, we suggest creating a simple sample using only the material you're providing, so children aren't overwhelmed by any "artistic" challenges.

Please note that elements of this workshop can differ depending on the age group you're working with. As a facilitator, you have complete freedom to alter or adapt any portion or element of this workshop to cater to your specific group's needs.
warm_up:
You can begin the warm-up with the Wiggle Down exercise. If you've chosen to incorporate dream pillows into your workshop, you can pass them out during this time, so that anyone who wishes and feels safer to do so, can hold them during the exercise. You can invite the children to find a comfortable spot and begin the exercise.
 

Wiggle Down exercise:
"I now invite you to join me in a short warm-up exercise. If you prefer to just watch, or do something else during this time, that's perfectly okay."

"For those of you who wish to participate, I invite you to wiggle your toes... now take a deep breath... and relax your toes."

"Wiggle your legs... now take a deep breath... and relax your legs."

"Wiggle your tummy... now take a deep breath... and relax your tummy."

"Wiggle your shoulders... now take a deep breath... and relax your shoulders."

"Finally, wiggle your arms and hands... now take a deep breath... and relax them."

"Now, if you wish to participate, I invite you to imagine a peaceful and quiet place where you can feel safe. You might imagine floating on a cloud, or on a tropical island, in a tree house, or walking in a beautiful forest, or lying on a bunch of soft pillows. Whatever comes to your mind when you think of a safe place will be perfect. Try to think of what that place looks like. What does it smell like? Is anyone there with you that makes you feel safe? What does the place feel like? Have you been to this place before or is it in your imagination? Whatever comes to your mind will be perfect."

"And when you are ready, you can come back to this moment and begin creating your safe/brave place.
creation:
"Now, I invite you to create on the paper. You can draw images, symbols, write words, or anything that comes to mind about your safe/brave place and feeling safe."

If you've chosen to incorporate collage into the creation process, you can invite the children to begin looking through the magazines, cutting out words and images that represent their vision of a 'safe place' and collage them onto the construction papers.

Depending on the age group, some children may need assistance. Please feel free to offer assistance where you see the need.

For older kids you can use the Safe Place handout, if you see fit.
 

        
Child creating their safe place   Sample safe place creation
closing:
For the closing, you can invite the children to share their Safe/Brave Place creations, what it means to them, or anything else they may wish to share. Of course, sharing is optional and if no one feels comfortable sharing, that's perfectly okay.

You can also give each child who chose to create, an envelop to keep their creations protected.
tips:
Please be mindful that often times when adults make judgments or labels about children's art work, children can learn not to trust art and its healing process. It could be a deep blow to their self-esteem and damage how they feel about themselves and their art.

We suggest using a pleasant voice tone and being authentic when you respond to each child. Children know when adults are not being true to their feelings, especially children who have experienced trauma. These children can have a special radar that can make them hyper-sensitive to adults. This is a defensive tactic that may have kept them safe in the past. Now, we have a window of time with them and an opportunity to show that adults can be safe and authentic.

You may also want to be mindful of what you, or other children say about their art, especially during the sharing segment. For example, judgmental questions such as: "What's that supposed to be?" or "That's nice, pretty, dark, bright, etc." should be avoided. Instead, you can say: "If you want to, I'd love to hear about your drawing," or "Awesome, brilliant, fantastic, etc." would be more appropriate statements that can be made about the art. Children may need verbal support from you in order not to 'crush' or judge another child's work. Remember some of these kids may not be used to hearing praise or non-judgmental comments before now.
objective_spanish: Este taller da una oportunidad a que los niños aprendan que tiene la capacidad de crear imagines sanadoras y que tienen el poder de sentirse seguros.
materials_spanish:
• Marcadores no tóxicos
• Papel de construcción (para dibujar)
• Marcadores permanentes (para escribir el nombre)
• Sobres grandes (para proteger el arte)
• Barra de pegamento (uno por niño)
• Revistas apropiadas (Oprah, Nat Geo y revistas de viajes tienen imágenes inclusivas)
• Papel de construcción
• Tijeras (uno por niño)
• Sobres grandes
timeframe_spanish:
Introducción 5 minutos
Demonstración 5 minutos
Comienzo 15 minutos
Preparamiento 15 minutos
Creación 30 minutos
Cierre 10 minutos
Total 01 hora 20 minutos
setup_spanish:
Es importante que cada participante este en su propia colchoneta o alfombra durante el Comienzo y la Relajación. Aunque no es necesario, esto permite que tengan su propio espacio y un límite donde puedan relajarse y sentirse seguros/valiente.

Otra opción en hacer el taller en la mesa. Si consideras preparar un ejemplo para mostrarles a los niños como se puede llegar a ver su arte, es importante que lo hagas con materiales que les proveerás a ellos para que no se sientan limitados.

Tome en cuenta que el taller se puede adaptar dependiendo al rango de edad de los niños que participaran en el taller. Como facilitador/a, tienes la libertad de cambiar o adaptar cualquier parte o elemento del taller tomando en cuenta las necesidades de tu grupo.
warm_up_spanish:
Puedes preparar al grupo para el taller usando el ejercicio de “Movimiento”. Si decides incorporar las almohadas sonadoras, puedes repartirlas durante este tiempo para aquellos que las necesiten para sentirse cómodos y seguros. Invita a los niños a que encuentren un lugar cómodo y comienza el ejercicio.  

Ejercicio de Movimiento: "Ahora te invito a que me acompañes en un ejercicio para prepararnos para el taller. Si no quieres participar, también puedes observar o hacer otra cosa durante este tiempo.” “Para aquellos que desean participar, los invito a que muevan las dedos de los pies.. ahora respiren hondo… y relajen los dedos de los pies.” “Mueve tus piernas… ahora respira hondo… y relaja tus piernas.”

“Mueve tu estomago… ahora respira hondo… y relaja tu estómago.”

“Mueve tus hombros… ahora respira hondo… y relaja tus hombros.” "Por último, mueve tus brazos y tus manos… ahora respira hondo.. y relájalos.”

"Si decides participar, te invito a que imagines un lugar Seguro y silencioso. Por ahí te imaginas flotando en una nube, en una isla tropical, una casa de árbol, caminando en un hermoso bosque o acostándote sobre almohadones cómodos. Trata de imaginarte los detalles del lugar. Como huele? Estas con alguien que te hace sentir a salvo? Como se siente el lugar? Ya has visitado este lugar o solo lo estas imaginando?” “Cuando estés listo, puedes comenzar a crear tu lugar seguro”
creation_spanish:
“Ahora te invito a que empieces a crear tu lugar Seguro/Valiente en el papel. Puedes dibujar imágenes o símbolos. También puedes escribir palabras que se te vengan a la mente cuando piensas en estar en tu lugar seguro.”

Si has decidido incorporar la creación de collages, invita a que los participantes empiecen a buscar fotos en las revistar, y cortar palabras e imágenes que representan su visión de ‘un lugar seguro’ y que las peguen en forma de collage en papel de construcción. Asegúrate de ofrecer asistencia si el grupo lo necesita.

Si es apropiado, reparte el Safe Place Handout, para los niños mayores.
closing_spanish: Durante el cierre del taller, invita a que compartan sus creaciones de su Lugar Seguro, que significa para ellos, y cualquier otra cosa que quieran compartir. Recuerda que el compartir es opcional. También puedes proveer sobres para que los niños guarden sus creaciones.
tips_spanish:
Recuerda que a veces cuando los adultos hacen comentarios sobre el arte de los niños, puede afectar la confianza en el arte y el proceso de sanidad.

Puede dañar su auto-estima y afectar como se sienten sobre su arte y sobre ellos mismos. Sugerimos que uses una vos agradable  y que seas autentico/a cuando hablas con los niños. Ellos son sensibles a las reacciones de los adultos, más si han pasado por un trauma y pueden dares cuanto cuando un adulto no es sincere con sus sentimientos. Tenemos una oportunidad de demostrarles que los adultos pueden ser seguros y auténticos.

Es importante que También tengas cuidado con lo que tu u otros niños dicen cuando los niños compartan su arte. Preguntas con críticas tal como “que ese so?” o “eso es lindo, oscuro, etc.” debes evitarlas. Puedes decir: “si quieres, me encantaría escuchar sobre tu creación” o “brillante, fantástico, etc.” sería más apropiado.

Los niños necesitaran que alguien los aconseje sobre los comentarios apropiados cuando hablan de la creación de otro participante. Algunos niños pueden no estar acostumbrados a escuchar elogios sobre su arte.
optional_materials:
You can also facilitate this workshop using printable worksheets. If you are utilizing the worksheets in lieu of the regular workshop materials, be sure to send a digital copy or print them out for your participants if you are meeting in person.

  • Creating a Safe Place

  • Creating a Safe/Brave Place

  • Creating a Safe/Brave Place (Cut-out Version) / Crear un Espacio Seguro/Valiente

  • Safe Place Handout (for older children)

  • Clear contact paper (optional for any age group)

  • Glitter glue

  • Fun stickers

  • Color pencils

  • Crayons / CrayPas

 

       
Creating a Safe Place Worksheet     Creating a Safe/Brave Place     Creating a Safe/Brave Place Worksheet
      Worksheet     (Cut-out Version) | English & Spanish
optional_materials_spanish:
• Papel adhesivo (opcional para cualquier rango de edad)
• Folleto de Un Lugar Seguro (para los niños más grandes)
• Pegamento con brillo
• Calcomanías divertidas
• Lápices de color
• Crayones / Crayones de aceite
introduction: "Before we begin, I want you to know that this workshop is a window of time for you. This means that this can be a safe/brave space to notice your thoughts, feelings, and needs. Since this space is your window of time, everything you say or do is voluntary. I’ll offer a suggested workshop idea, share about the materials we have available, and invite you to create, but there’s no right or wrong way to do this. It doesn't matter what it looks like. What matters is taking this time to truly honor your thoughts and feelings, however they come out. If you can’t think of anything or draw a blank on what to create or write, feel free to just observe. However you choose to spend this time will be perfectly okay. This is your time. Please ask for what you need, and know that I’m here in support of you."
introduction_spanish: “Antes de que comencemos, quiero que sepan que este taller es un tiempo para ti mismo donde puedes estar a salvo mientras le prestas atención a tus pensamientos, sentimientos, y necesidades. Todo lo que digas o hagas es por u propia voluntad. Ofreceré una idea general del taller, los materiales que tenemos disponibles, y te invitare a que crear. No hay manera correcta o incorrecta de crear. Lo importante es que tomes el tiempo de honrar a tus pensamientos y sentimientos, y que los expreses de la manera que tú quieras. SI no sabes que dibujar, crear, o escribir, puedes observar. Tu elijes como quieres usar este tiempo porque es tu tiempo. Puedes pedirme lo que necesites, y recuerda que estoy aquí para apoyarte.”
demonstration:
You can take a moment to explain the material and how to use them, if necessary.

If you are incorporating collage into your workshop, you can explain to the children that they can cut images out of magazines using scissors, or cut them out by hand, which can create a cool effect.
demonstration_spanish:
Si es necesario, explica los materiales y como usarlos. Si incorporaras la creación del collage, explícale a los niños que puedes cortar imágenes de las revistas usando tijeras o a mano. Comienzo Puedes comenzar con invitar a que los niños participen en una discusión opcional.

“Que significa sentirse seguro/valiente? Cómo te sientes seguro/valiente? Si te sientes cómodo te invito a que compartas lo que te hace sentir seguro/valiente. También está permitido el no querer compartir, porque a veces compartir no te hace sentir seguro.”  

Almohadas Sonadoras Opcionales: Es posible que los niños más pequeños necesiten tener algo en sus manos mientras se imaginan su lugar seguro. Algunos niños tienen dificultad en enfocarse y escuchar por un tiempo prolongado, así que necesitaran hacer algo con sus manos. Puedes usar peluches o crear “almohadas sonadoras” para cada niño. 

Las almohadas son pequeñas bolsas rellenadas con arroz. Deben ser exactamente iguales. También puedes usar aceites esenciales como lavanda para aromatizarlas.

Crear las almohadas es opcional. Si decides hacer almohadas para cada niño, explícales que son para ellos y que se pueden quedar con ellas. Las almohadas son una ayuda y un recuerdo de que pueden tener un tiempo seguro.
opening_circle:
You can open by inviting the children to an optional discussion.

"What does it mean to feel safe/brave? How do you feel safe/brave? I invite anyone who feels comfortable, to share what makes you feel safe. It’s okay if you don’t feel like saying anything because sometimes sharing doesn't feel safe.” 
 

Optional Dream Pillows:
For young children, it can be helpful if they have something to hold onto as they imagine their safe place. They may need something to do with their hands. For some kids, it might be difficult to focus and just listen for a long time.

You can use stuffed animals or make “dream pillows” that they can keep. Dream pillows are small bean bags filled with rice. All the pillows are exactly the same size, shape, and color. You can scent them with geranium and lavender essence oil.

This is purely optional. If you choose to create dream pillows for the children, you can explain at the beginning that they get to take their dream pillow with them. It can be helpful to carry something nurturing with them, a reminder of having that safe time.

title: Take a Break, Self-Regulate!
objective: This workshop aims to give participants an opportunity to discuss the importance of taking breaks to self-regulate and create dice that can help them practice self-care in a fun way.
materials:
•

    Dice template (2 per participant). Click here to download the template.

  • Paper or journals for journaling activity

  • Colored pencils

  • Pencils

  • Markers

  • Transparent tape

  • Glue sticks

  • Scissors

  • White board or paper for group chart and steps for creation

  • Self-Regulation Prompts
setup:
Here are some articles that give great insight about the importance of taking breaks:

  • 5 Science-Backed Ways Taking a Break Boosts Our Productivity

  • Why and How You Should Take Breaks at Work

  • The Importance of Taking a Break

  • How Do Work Breaks Help Your Brain? 5 Surprising Answers


You may wish to prepare materials for each participant. Depending on their age and their abilities, you may want to pre-cut the box template so participants can easily go from writing/drawing straight into the creation portion of the workshop.

You may consider writing each step for the creation process and display it so all participants can easily see it.

For the discussion section, you may wish to prepare your "T" chart in advance. On one side of the "T" you can write: "How we take breaks" and on the other side: "Why we take breaks."

It can be helpful if you could create a sample dice (both) to show your participants so they can see what they look like. If you choose to do so, we suggest creating a simple one so that participants won't feel overwhelmed with any "artistic" challenges.
warm_up:
“I would now like to invite you to take a moment to think about our discussion. Now that we know a little more about what breaks are, how and why we take them, I’m going to invite you to journal about this question: 'How would you like to take breaks in the future?' I’m going to give you about ten minutes to write in a journal or on a piece of paper. During this time, you're invited to make a list of different activities you can do during your breaks. Think about the different times throughout your day and how your breaks might be different depending on where you are. You might have more time in some parts of your day, and in some, you might have less. Since this is your Window of Time, journaling can look however you want it to look, there is no right or wrong way. I invite you to write words, shapes, symbols, or any other way you would like to do this activity."

"Does anyone have any questions before we start? When we begin, I’ll be giving your time reminders. When the time is over, I will invite you to begin creating your dice. Any questions about journaling or creating before we begin? Let’s begin.”

You may wish to give time reminders through the writing process. You can remind participants that they are welcome to refer to the chart you created as well as utilize the time in however way they feel comfortable. When time is up, you can invite them to create their dice.
creation:
You may wish to remind participants about the steps for creation. If you've written the instructions on a board, you can refer the participants where you wrote out the steps for them so they can refer to them during the creation part of the workshop. You can also give participants time reminders throughout the entire process.
 

Step 1: Capturing Ideas

  • "On the 1st die template, you can write, draw, and color your different break ideas."

  • "On the 2nd die template, you can write down 6 different time intervals you would like to take a break. You can even create a "You choose" option where you get to choose a time when the dice lands with this side face up."

  • "As you create, you can think about the questions in the introduction."
     

Step 2: Cutting

  • "When you’re finished writing and/or drawing, you can cut around the outer lines of the boxes. You should end up with one piece that looks like a lowercase 't'."
     

Step 3: Folding

  • "You can fold along each of the lines to create a cube."
     

Step 4: Gluing and Taping

  • "Using a glue stick, you can glue each of tab to keep the cube in place."

  • "Use clear tape to close secure the edges."
closing:
“Today we had a chance to talk about the importance of taking a break and how we can take breaks to help us throughout our day. I would like to give you a chance to share your feelings. For anyone who wishes to share, how did it feel to talk about taking breaks? Did you learn anything new? How will you use your dice? Any volunteers that would like to share?"

“Now that we had the chance to hear from everyone that wanted to share with us, I would like to invite anyone who would like to join in on rolling our dice together as a group. Now that you have these dice, I encourage you to continue to practice taking breaks. Share this with your family, your friends, and anyone else that may need help thinking of great ways to take a break. Thank you all for being here today. I appreciate all of you for taking the time to think, create, and participate in a way that was comfortable for you.”
optional_materials:
You can also facilitate this workshop using printable worksheets. If you are utilizing the worksheets in lieu of the regular workshop materials, be sure to send a digital copy or print them out for your participants if you are meeting in person.

  • Take a Break, Self-Regulate Worksheets (English and Spanish)

  • "50 Ways to Take a Break" handout by Karen Horneffer-Ginter, Ph.D. Click here to download.

  • "AWBW 50 Ways to Take a Break" handout in English and Spanish

   
Take a Break, Self-Regulate Worksheet (English)     Take a Break, Self-Regulate Worksheet (Spanish)
introduction:
“Thank you for being here today. Before we begin, I want you to know that this is your Window of Time. It's a time for you to notice your thoughts, needs and feelings. During this time, there is no right or wrong way to participate or create. I'm going to share some instructions, but you get to choose how you want to participate. You can follow along completely, or you may want to do something different, it's completely up to you. During your Window of time, you get to choose. I am here to support you in any way that I can, so please ask for what you need. Any questions before I begin?"

“Today, we have an opportunity to talk about taking breaks. We will get a chance to talk about what taking breaks mean, how we take them, and how they can be helpful in our lives. After our discussion, we will get a chance to write. You will then be invited to use your writing to create dice that you will be able to use when taking breaks in the future.”
demonstration:
“In a moment, we'll open with a discussion about taking breaks. Then, I’m going to invite you to write anything that's on your mind in your journal or on a piece of paper. After that, you’ll have some time to create your dice. Since I will invite you to move straight from writing into creating, I’m going to first share with you about the art materials that you can use."

“On your tables, you see that you have markers, colored pencils and regular pencils to use."

"You also have two pieces of thicker paper that you can write on and draw on, then put together to create two boxes, which will be your dice. Each page has 6 squares in it. I’m going to talk about each one separately."

 

Step 1: Capturing Ideas

  • Dice #1: "Each of these will become one die. One die is for you to write and/or draw 6 different ways you can take a break. You can use the list we'll create for ideas, come up with your own, or a combination of both. You're invited to use words, shapes, and/or symbols to represent your breaks. For example, you can draw yourself taking a walk or reading a book, or you can just draw a shoe or a book to represent these things. Remember, there is no right or wrong way to take a break. These dice are for you so feel free to create it however way it works for you."

  • Dice #2: "The second die can be used to tell you how long to take your break. So when you roll both of the dice, two of the dice faces will show the break and the other will show how long to take that break. You can write down 6 different time intervals (Ex: 20 minutes) that you would like to take a break. You can even create a "You choose" option where you get to choose a time when the dice lands with this side face up."

Die #1: How to take a break Die #2: How long to take a break


Step 2: Cutting

  • "When you’re finished writing and/or drawing, you can cut around the outer lines of the boxes. You should end up with one piece that looks like a lowercase 't'."
     

Cutting out the die template

 

Step 3: Folding

 

  • "You can now fold along each of the lines to create a cube."
     

Folding the dice into a cube

 

Step 4: Gluing and Taping

  • Using a glue stick, you can glue each of tabs keep the cube in place.

  • You can use clear tape to close make the final edges.
     

        
Gluing   Taping


If you've created a sample in advance, you can show it to your participants so they can see how the dice will look when they're done.
opening_circle:
You can begin the discussion by posing the questions below. Based on the ages of your group, you can modify the questions for better understanding or deeper insight.

An option for this section is to first pose a question to the group, then invite participants to get into groups to discuss further. You can give them the opportunity to practice timed listening and sharing. After the paired sharing, you can ask for volunteers to share what they learned from one another. When practicing paired listening, you may wish to remind participants to only share what they personally shared in the group and not to share information they heard from their partner unless given permission from their partner.

You can keep a running list of what participants share so they can refer to it when they create their dice, using a "T" chart. The left side can be titled "How we take a break" and the right, "Why we take a break."

Questions for Discussion:

  • When you think about the word break, what comes to mind?

  • What does taking a break mean to you?

  • How do we usually take breaks?

  • Why do we take breaks?

  • How can breaks be helpful?

    • Breaks can help us when we are physically tired and we need to let our bodies rest.

    • We can use breaks to calm down when we are having big feelings.

      • Angry

      • Excited

      • Anxious

      • Nervous

  • Breaks can be small gifts to ourselves when we have been working hard for a long periods of time.

  • Breaks can help our brain take a rest.
     

"Now that we have a list of the different ways that we can take breaks, let's think about when it's a good idea to take them. Sometimes when our bodies are tired, it can be a good time to take a break. But can you think of any other times it can be good to take a break?"

Feel free to offer suggestions if you wish participants are having a hard time coming up with ideas.

title: A Window of Healing Workshop Series
objective:
In 2016, A Window Between Worlds (AWBW) collaborated with Bridges to Healing (BTH), a counseling and training center, to create and facilitate a six-month series of art workshops. The goal was to provide trauma survivors with a window of time where they can feel safe and supported within a community of survivors while discovering a renewed sense of themselves through creative expression.

The staff at BTH who created this series are all therapists who are also AWBW Facilitators. The monthly themes were sequenced so they intentionally build upon each other to facilitate healing and empowerment. The series identified six different themes to support survivors in moving through the trauma cycle, starting with the acute crisis and working towards healing and integration and culminating in envisioning a hopeful future. After creating the themes, BTH staff combed through the AWBW curriculum and identified workshops that would support each theme. Then BTH and AWBW staff facilitated bi-monthly workshops for six months, focusing on one theme each month. Two art workshops were facilitated each month that focused on that one particular topic, the idea being that learning is proactive and repetition will help support integrating the learning. Each workshop session was structured so the participants first had an opportunity to participate in the art workshop. Time was set aside at the end of each group session to provide a psychoeducation aspect to the workshop. The goal being that having a piece of psychoeducation at the end of each workshop will enable participants to connect the dots regarding the theme of the art workshop and have a better understanding regarding the challenges they face as trauma survivors as well as knowledge around their strength, coping abilities, external and internal resources, so they are often better able to address challenges and trauma triggers, gain a since of control, and increase their ability to work towards emotional and psychological wellness. Which dovetails with the trauma-informed care principal of sharing information with survivors about trauma and trauma responses so they are able to integrate that information into their lives to mitigate the effect trauma has on their lives.

We welcome you to utilize any aspect of the Window of Healing workshop series with your participants. As with any AWBW art workshop, you have the freedom to follow the sequence, pick out elements to utilize independently, or any other way that best meets the needs of you participants. Often there are several options for possible workshops to facilitate for any given theme. This is intentional as the series was created to provide structure and also flexibility. All of the handouts that were utilized when presenting the psychoeducation aspect of each workshop are attached below. It's completely up to you if you want to utilize the handouts to help you prepare for the workshop psychoeducation part of the workshop. During the six-month pilot all of the handouts were given to the participants. We welcome you to do the same, or use them to inform what you present or not utilize at all. Some of the workshops also have additional activities that are available if you opt in to use them as they are all optional.

While the series was created to specifically address trauma you are welcome to facilitate the series with a different focus such as grief and loss, or forgiveness.


Theme 1: Safety and Self-regulation

  • Workshop 1: Do Enter Door Hanger

    • Psychoeducation: Creating Safe Boundaries for Self

    • Handouts:

      • Do Enter Journaling Sheet

      • Setting Healthy Boundaries

  • Workshop 2: Creating a Safe/Brave Place

    • Psychoeducation: Grounding and Relaxation

    • Handouts:

      • Definition of Trauma and Regulation

      • Coping Strategies to Helping You Feel Safe

         

Theme 2: Strengths and Positive Self-image

  • Workshop 1: My Butterfly or The Lotus Flower or  I Am Strong Because

    • Psychoeducation: Knowing My Strengths

    • Handouts:

      • My Personal Strenghts

      • Resilence

    • Additional Activity (optional): Create 3 post-it note affirmations you can put around the house to remind you of positive self-talk.

  • Workshop 2: Funeral for All the Labels I Believed to be True About Me

    • Psychoeducation: Societal Labels, Messages You Received About Yourself from Others and Strengthening Positive Self-Image

    • Handouts:

      • 7 Steps to Positive Self Talk

    • Opening Activity (optional): List societal labels from group on flip chart to shred

       

Theme 3: Identifying and Honoring Feelings

  • Workshop 1: Stories of the Heart

    • Psychoeducation: Being Present, Nature of Feelings (they go away after being felt).

    • Handouts:

      • Feelings Faces Chart

      • Understanding Your Feelings

  • Workshop 2: Putting Myself Back Together

    • Psychoeducation: Negative and Positive Feelings can exist together, it can be a choice to let go or transform negative feelings.

    • Handouts:

      • Feelings Faces Chart

      • Connecting With Your Feelings

         

Theme 4: Exploring Relationships and Building Support Networks

  • Workshop 1: Examining Relationships Collage or Warm Fuzzy or Helping Hands, Healing Hands

    • Psychoeducation: Setting Boundaries & Creating a Community of Support

    • Handouts:

      • Setting Healthy Boundaries

      • Building a Personal Support Network

  • Workshop 2: Loving Relationships Charms

    • Psychoeducation: Defining and examining healthy and balanced boundaries and relationships.

    • Handouts:

      • Creating a Healthy and Balanced Relationship Writing Prompt

      • Healthy Boundaries

         

Theme 5: Healing and Integration

  • Workshop 1:  Permission Canvas

    • Psychoeducation: Being willing and prepared to be committed to the healing process.

    • Handouts: The Decision to Heal

  • Workshop 2: River Stories

    • Psychoeducation: The healing power of integrating the past and present.

    • Handouts: Healing and Integration

       

Theme 6: Envisioning a Brighter Future and Celebrating Joy and Gratitude

  • Workshop 1: Vision Boards or Journey Footprints

    • Psychoeducation: Identifying were you came from and where you want to go.

    • Handouts: Why Your Story Matters

  • Workshop 2: Thank Me Card or The Reasons We Smile

    • Psychoeducation: Exploring how celebrating and mindfully focusing on joy and gratitude can positively impact our happiness and all aspects of our lives.

    • Handouts:

      • The Benefits of Gratitude

      • 7 Strategies for Cultivating Gratitude
