title: A Window to Your Soul: Community Tile Wall Project
objective:
This workshop invites participants to reflect on someone/something they go to for inspiration, create art to represent it and add it to a community art piece.

Note from the author: This workshop will allow the participants to share a glimpse of who they are by reflecting on a person, a place or an object of importance. They can give the world a glimpse of something they are carrying that can weigh heavy on them, or a thing that they can turn to for inspiration and motivation. This workshop aims to help participants find commonalities in their stories and experiences. By the end of this workshop, a community tile wall can help portray the message of “There is no us, and them, only us." One in unity.
materials:
• Window to Your Soul worksheets (2 pages- landscape and portrait orientation)

  • 4" x 5" cardstock

  • Video of Fabian introducing A Window to Your Soul (begins at 1:15)

  • Color pencils

  • Markers

  • Pastels

  • Graphite pencils

  • Masking tape

  • Painter's tape

  • Empty wall space or large presentation board to display art.
setup:
• Print both pages of A Window to Your Soul worksheets for each participant. (They can choose which orientation the want.)
  • Create samples of a completed worksheet and final tile to share with participants.
  • Write down the agenda for the day:
    • Step 1: Worksheet
    • Step 2: Paired Sharing
    • Step 3: Create Your Tile
    • Step 4: Brining Our Art Together
  • Find a blank wall or presentation board to display participants' artwork.

If you’d like we you can have a sample of a previous work done by other (incarcerated) or participants. If you would like to make one yourself as to have for as a sample that would only help bring connection and openness for those participants.

Note: If working with participants who are institutionalized, all supplies should be counted thoroughly with an inventory list and ready to hand out as needed as to help keep track of what is being used. Materials should be spread out visually on a separate table if placing supplies on their table is not available due to space. Temptation for these incarcerated participants to gain an art tool is at hand, for they are limited in the institutions. Explain on the importance of this group and materials are ours and in order to continue having these groups we all need to care for our materials being returned and accounted for, be mindful in delivery not judgmental).
 

Worksheet with art space in portrait orientation.

Worksheet with art space in landscape orientation.
warm_up:
Worksheet:
Hand out the worksheets for each participant.

"To open up the space to our energy, I'm going to offer something for you to think about. When I give you the prompt, I'll invite you to sit for a moment to think about it and let it soak in. Something might automatically come to mind or it might take you a few minutes to think of something, however long it takes is fine. Your worksheets are here to guide your thoughts and the design of your final art piece.

"Today I invite you to think of a person, place, or thing that you go to for inspiration. You might also think about someone/something you would like to revisit to work on something that's been holding you back. I'll give you about 15 minutes to think and fill in your worksheet. I'll be giving you time reminders throughout this process."

Paired Sharing:
"I'm going to invite you to find a partner that you'd like to work on this next section with." Give participants a moment to find their partners.

"Now that you have your partner, decide who will speak first and who will listen. Each of you will have 2 minutes to be the speaker and 2 minutes to be the listener. I will give you time reminders and letting you know when to switch from listener to speaker. During your time as a speaker, you can share anything that came up for you when you thought about the prompt. You can even share about what you are planning to create for your final art piece. As a listener, try not to make this process a discussion, your role is to listen and witness what is being shared with you. Any questions before we begin?"

Bring the group back together and if time permits, ask for a few volunteers to share what they shared or what is coming up for them during this time. To honor confidentiality, ask participants not to share what anything their partner shared with them.
creation: Invite participants to begin creating on their cardstock. Give gentle time reminders.
closing:
Completed tile wall.

Putting Our Art Together:

Bring participants back to the group space. Invite them to sit with their art for a moment and think about what came up for them. Before participants share, ask them if it's OK for you to add their creation to the community display.

After all volunteers have shared, ask those who didn't share if they would like to add their art to the community piece. Once the collection is complete, invite participants to take it all in. You can ask them to notice similarities they noticed from what was shared or from what they are seeing on display.

As you close the workshop, point to the wall and let participants know that it represents that there is no us and them, only us. Thank all participants for showing up and participating in all of the ways they did. If you will be leaving the artwork on display, make sure it's OK with participants who contributed their art. Give them the option to leave it up or take it with them.
introduction:
Fabian demonstrating the window to your soul.

See Fabian introduce A Window to Your Soul in this video (begins at 1:15). You can use this for your reference and/or you can show it to participants.

“I’d like to welcome you today and introduce myself (and my organization and/or why I do this work, etc). Before we begin, I want you to know that this is your Window of Time. It's a time for you to notice your thoughts, needs and feelings. During this time, there is no right or wrong way to participate — even observing is participating. You can follow along completely or you may want to do something different, it's completely up to you. During your Window of Time, you get to choose. I am here to support you in any way that I can, so please ask for what you need. Any questions before I begin?

Point out the rough outline of the workshop for participants to refer to throughout the workshop:

  • Step 1: Worksheet
  • Step 2: Paired Sharing
  • Step 3: Create Your Tile
  • Step 4: Bringing Our Art Together (Closing)

Hold the cardstock up and ask participants what they see. Wait a few minutes to gather feedback. Place the cardstock on your chest and say that this is a window to their soul.

"Today's workshop is called, A Window to Your Soul. We will be starting off with a discussion where I will be inviting you to think about a something. I'll be giving you a worksheet to gather your thoughts and to practice by sketching what your final art piece will look like. You will have the opportunity to discuss your thoughts with a partner during a paired sharing exercise and prepare to make your tile."
demonstration:
Go over the different art materials that are available to the participants. Show them samples of the completed worksheet and final tile. Remind participants of the agenda for the day.

  • Step 1: Worksheet
    • The worksheet can be used to sketch out the final design. Invite participants to design their artwork in portrait or landscape orientation. See examples to the right.
  • Step 2: Paired Sharing
    • You will be invited to find a partner and discuss what you came up with and talk about your final design.
  • Step 3: Creating Your Tile
    • On the cardstock/canvas, you will create your final design
  • Step 4: Bringing Our Art Together (Closing)
    • We will bring the group back together and bring our art together on the wall.
       
Tile in portrait orientation. Tile in landscape orientation.
extra_field:
Fabian Debora

This workshop was created by Fabian Debora, Windows Facilitator and artist. He created this workshop for those who are currently incarcerated, however, we invite you to use it in any setting. Please contact your Program Manager for support with specific adaptations. To check out more of Fabian's art workshops and supporting individuals experiencing incarceration click here.

title: What's Beyond the Brick Wall?

materials:
Note: Ask the institution what can be brought in, it varies according to the detention center.

  • Template 1 - Brick Wall

  • Template 2 - Personal Brick

  • Template 3 - Beyond the Brick Wall

  • Large paper for displaying creation steps and closing prompt

  • Odorless markers

  • Colored pencils

  • Pencils

  • Pre-cut magazine images and words

  • Non-toxic glue

  • Non-toxic fabric paints

  • Paper towels
Brick Wall (template 1) Personal Brick (template 2) Beyond the Brick Wall (template 3)
setup:
• Print the all three templates on cardstock for durability:
        Template 1 - Brick Wall
        Template 2 - Personal Brick
        Template 3 - Beyond the Brick Wall

  • Create a couple of simple samples of each template.

  • Write the creation steps and closing prompt on separate large papers to display during the workshop.
    Creation Steps:
    Step 1: Filling in the brick wall (using template 1)
    Step 2: Removing a brick (using template 2)
    Step 3: Beyond the brick wall (using template 3)

    Closing Prompt:
    Once I take a look at these bricks such as ________, then my vision is clear. What's beyond the wall is _______.
warm_up:
"Today we have an opportunity to explore the bricks that we, others, society, and circumstances place before us. I'll invite you to start thinking about the bricks that make up the wall in front of you right now. Could it be the educational system, your environment, or could it even be your household? What else comes to mind? Would anyone like to share about what comes up for them when they think about these bricks"

Give participants some time to think about these questions. You can also ask questions to get them thinking about placement of their barriers/bricks they will be adding to the brick wall template. Do you want to put the "heaviest" bricks on the bottom, in the center, staggered throughout or somewhere else completely?
creation:
"Now that we've talked about some of the things locking us up and keeping us from our goals and future, it's time to add them all to our brick wall." Throughout the creation process, continue to offer verbal reassurance and remind them that nothing is impossible. Refer to the steps written on the large paper.

Step 1: Filling in the brick wall (template 1)
"I invite you to start filling in your brick wall (using the brick wall template) with all of those 'bricks' you've identified for yourself. You can write words or draw symbols of all those things that make you feel trapped."

Step 2: Removing a brick (template 2)
"You are invited to choose one brick to focus on removing today from the wall barrier. Sometimes it helps to start with the easiest brick to remove. Which brick would be the most realistic for you to remove from the wall barrier? You don't have to pick the easiest brick. Maybe you want to pick the one that is the most heavy to you or the one that seems the hardest to break through. Remember we are all here as one. Whichever brick you choose is relevant to you today. We all have bricks before us. I'm no different than you and you are no different than me." (Here you demonstrate and remind them of your sample brick.)

"You can use any of the art materials here today to help you create your personal brick. Whichever brick you chose, I'd like to encourage you to express yourself fully. You can use a word in graffiti or the word being fragmented or shattered. You can create an image of what it feels like or looks like to you. There are no rights or wrong in expressing yourself through art."

Once they are done, invite participants to share about their bricks.

Step 3: Beyond the brick wall (template 3)
"Now that you have worked on breaking through the first brick of your wall barrier, I invite you to look at your brick wall again looking at the words you have written on the bricks. If we/you were to remove those things one at a time you can start to dream again, and your vision would become clearer to you. So with that being true, now you can draw, color, or write about what's beyond the wall. What was the dream you always had that belongs to you? What does it look like? What would it look like? It can be a small dream or a big dream. What dream jumps out at you? Once you remove those bricks that where placed in front of you, by society, life circumstances etc. Go ahead and beautify through expression what's beyond the wall."
closing:
"We covered a lot today and I want to thank you for being here participating in the ways that you did. We talked about how our situations and circumstances can create a barrier that can block our view of our dreams and goals for our future. We were able to create a brick wall to show us visually what we are up against, and then began to start breaking it down one brick at a time to rediscover our future. I invite all of you to keep working towards removing those bricks, asking for help for those bricks that need extra support to be removed, working towards solutions to break through those bricks."

If time allows, create a circle and invite participants to openly share their experiences. You can offer this prompt to guide them.

"I invite you to use the following prompt to share with us today. You can hold up any of your templates to support you."
        Once I take a look at these bricks such as __________, then my vision is clear.
        What's beyond the wall is __________.

"I invite all of you to take your "Beyond the Wall" image and place it on your dorm's wall, cottage or sleeping place so you can always be reminded of “What’s Beyond the Wall" especially in times of discouragement or feelings of disillusion you have this tool to help inspire you and build the courage needed to continue on this phase of your life. Thank you for sharing such intimate and personal things with all of us. That’s courage. I feel privileged to walk with you."
introduction:
“I’d like to welcome you today and introduce myself (and my organization and/or why I do this work, etc). Before we begin, I want you to know that this is your Window of Time. It's a time for you to notice your thoughts, needs and feelings. During this time, there is no right or wrong way to participate — even observing is participating. You can follow along completely or you may want to do something different, it's completely up to you. During your Window of Time, you get to choose. I am here to support you in any way that I can, so please ask for what you need. Any questions before I begin?

"I want to invite you to participate in the “What’s Beyond the Brick Wall?” Project. (If there is a window nearby, point to it to help you symbolically and visually). Being behind these walls or with our daily routine, we can become discouraged or at times disillusioned. This can make us forget about our dreams and goals we once had. Also by "doing time" our dreams and goals can seem so far from reach. But today we have an opportunity to explore these bricks that make up this wall of incarceration, the bricks that we put for ourselves, maybe the ones that society has placed before us, or the ones that just seem very hard to break through. You might think of these bricks as barriers. Today you'll be invited to not only see these barriers, but to look beyond them to a future that you envision for yourself."

Note: Acknowledge each participant and invite them into the space by learning their first name (not the moniker given to them by the streets or last name commonly used by probation department to address them). This helps remind them of the name given to them by their loved ones. To help give participants a window to your sincerity and to help create a safe space, a personal story is always welcomed or those of participants that you worked with in the past that are signification to the space you are creating.
demonstration:
The demonstration will vary based on what materials you are allowed to bring into the workshop setting. Be mindful of showing all material possibilities to participants. If possible, make different samples that have used all material options.

"Today we are going to be working with different materials and three different templates. We will start off with a discussion about our bricks or barriers and we will use the full page of bricks. We will then move on to identifying one brick that we would focus on and possibly remove from our wall. The last template we will use is the wall template with the some bricks missing. This will give you an opportunity to visualize what's beyond the brick wall with those barriers removed. As a reminder, these materials and templates are here to guide you in your process, you don't have to use them. There is no right or wrong way to participate, even observing is participating."

Give the participants a few minutes to explore the materials and templates. Show some finished samples.

title: Childhood Memories
objective: This workshop aims to support participants in exploring the image of shoes hanging from a power line and addressing misconceptions by capturing positive childhood memories as a way to redefine its symbolism.
materials:
Shoes Template

  • Shoes template

  • Scratch sheet of papers for brainstorm or doodling

setup:
Possible Setup
     

If possible, we encourage you to have the materials and supplies set up prior to participants arriving in order to increase accessibility. We also invite you to create a simple sample for the participants in order to demonstrate how the final creation may look like and to invite the creativity of the participants.

To provide an image for the participants during the opening and warm-up, you are also welcome to print out images of shoes hanging from a power line. 

Note: If you are working with participants who are incarcerated, explain the importance of taking care of materials. You may provide clear directions; however, be mindful and gentle in delivery (e.g., “In effort to try to have the materials last us a long time, please make sure to take care of them and put them back when you are done using them.")
warm_up:
Journaling:

   
    Journaling Time!

"I would like to take this time to invite you to a quick journaling session, in order to get our creativity flowing." 

You are welcome to hold up the picture of shoes hanging from a power line. "Have you ever seen tennis shoes hanging from a power line? If so, what do you think this image symbolizes?

  • How does it make you feel? 

  • Where did you learn these messages?

You are free to journal about all these questions or just a few. Whatever feels best for you." Allow some time for participants to journal.

"Now I invite you to write about a memory that you recall that brought you joy as a child? For example: 

  • Is there a particular name given to you by a loved one? Such as Mi Flaco, or Chatito, Sinbad, Rocko, etc.

  • Who or what was significant to you in your childhood?

Again, allow some time for participants to journal. "Once you are ready, I invite you to create your tennis shoes with the thoughts of your childhood memories."
creation:
During this time, you may play calming music and offer assistance if needed. Time reminders may also be helpful in order for participants and the facilitator to be aware of time available.

 

 
Completed Tennis Shoes
closing:
Towards the end of the workshop, invite participants back into a circle (if the setting permits it) and welcome them to share their creation or anything that came up for them during the workshop. You may also ask some questions to encourage participants: What came up for you throughout this process? Did you recognize anything in particular when doing this workshop? Did it bring back any memories? What message is your creation trying to communicate?

"To end, I would like to invite everyone to lift their creation up by the string, as if they were hanging from a power line. Now look how you all were able to take such an image and re-define it. Just Amazing. Thank you for joining me and being in community with one another."

 

   
Completed Tennis Shoes

Durational Art Tip:

We encourage you to hang your shoes on a wall, or a place where you can always get a glimpse of them as a way for you to be reminded of your childhood memories. objective: This workshop aims to help empower participants by inviting them to listen to their hearts and discover what is inside without judgment.

Heart Template     Heart Template with Chambers

Optional Setup

If possible, we recommend having the materials and supplies within reach of the participants to increase accessibility. If space is limited, materials can be spread out visually on a separate table. We also encourage you to have a simple sample of a previous creation done by a participant who has been incarcerated or the facilitator.
 

Note: If you are working with participants who are incarcerated, explain the importance of taking care of materials. You may provide clear directions; however, be mindful and gentle in delivery (e.g., “In effort to try to have the materials last us a long time, please make sure to take care of them and put them back when you are done using them.")

Journaling prompt:

 
  Prepared Journal Paper

"For our warm-up today, you're invited to journal about the experiences that you have stored in your heart. These can be any type of expereinces, such as happy, sad, or calming. For instance, what are some things that have been said to you that have made your heart feel lighter or heavier? Remember there is no wrong or right way to participate. If you are feeling stuck, here are more questions that may help you out."

"As you look at your creation. Using one word, I welcome you to share what happened while creating these hearts? What did you think or feel?"

title: The Freedom Within
objective:
This workshop aims to provide participants with the opportunity to embrace their truth by discovering freedom from within.


Note from author

Originally designed for youth who are incarcerated, this workshop provides participants with an opportunity to be reminded as to what is real, even when behind institutional walls. Participants are invited to take a journey into their childhood memories that made them happy. By allowing participants to brainstorm on what it was like prior to their incarceration, this workshop will give them those memories that can bring them back to their “resiliency zone” as to stay grounded and focus on their truth.
materials:
Internal Freedom Template

  • Internal Freedom Template

  • Blank paper

  • Markers

  • Colored pencils

  • Writing utensils

  • Erasers
setup:
Possible Setup

You are invited to set up any materials and supplies prior to participants arriving in order to increase accessibility. It also may be helpful to create a simple sample of the finished creation as a reference for participants. Additionally, you are welcome to print the Internal Freedom Template for each participant and fold the templates in half with the fold going down the center of the person to represent gates opening.

Note: If you are working with participants who are incarcerated, explain the importance of taking care of materials. You may provide clear directions; however, be mindful and gentle in delivery (e.g., “In effort to try to have the materials last us a long time, please make sure to take care of them and put them back when you are done using them.")
warm_up:
Group Discussion:

     
      Completed Creation

To provide a visual for the participants, you're invited to take the closed template and place it on your chest and symbolically open the paper to imitate the image - opening the gates.

"To begin, I want to invite you all to look at this image on the template. What do you see? What is the person doing in this image?" Allow some time for participants to answer if they would like.

"Great! Sometimes we may keep things locked up inside us to protect us; however, it may also weigh heavy on our hearts. What are some things that may weigh heavy on us while incarcerated? For example, these can be feelings of shame, guilt, hurt, and more." Again, allow some time for participants to answer if they like.

"Now what are some things that are important to you that may bring a sense of comfort while in this institution? For example, this may be family, talents, and childhood memories." Pause on last time before closing the group discussion.

"Perfect. Thank you for sharing with us. Now, whenever you feel ready, you may go ahead and create the things that help bring you back to your 'resiliency zone' and provide comfort while feeling restricted."
creation:
The Freedom Within Creation

During this time, you may play some calming music and provide assistance if needed. Time reminders may also be helpful to participants in order to decrease their anxiety and the need to rush towards the end.
closing:
Completed Creation

Towards the end of the workshop, you can begin prepping participants to finish up what they are working on, and subtlety begin to set the stage as to invite those who are willing to share their work.

Please remind the group of the seriousness and sensitivity of the safe space that has been created, and to be respectful of everything being shared. Once someone shares, ask the group "How many of you can relate? And if so, can you find the freedom from within as, [NAME of participant] has? Who else would like to share?"

Acknowledge their courage and their strengths as a way to empower and bring comfort to their vulnerabilities in sharing openly. If time allows, you are invited to ask for feedback: How did they feel about this exercise? What did they like? What did they not like? Anything interesting? What did you learn? Did anything stand out to you? You may thank the participants for joining and being in community with one another.
tips:
Durational Art Tip:

"These pictures can now serve as a reminder that even when incarcerated/restricted, freedom is within regardless of our circumstances (behind these walls). You are invited to take these with you and place them on your wall, so that you can always take a look if times seem hard or you begin to feel discouraged. This can help you find and keep the freedom from within."
optional_materials:
Having some collage materials -in addition to drawing materials- will offer additional opportunities for participants to create and express their memories.

  • Magazine cut outs already prepped to be applied

  • Glue

  • Construction paper

  • Colorful patterned paper

You can follow along completely or you may want to do something different, it's completely up to you. During your Window of Time, you get to choose. I am here to support you in any way that I can, so please ask for what you need. Are there any questions before I begin?"
demonstration:
Participants are welcome to decorate the template with the things that bring them strength and calmness

You're encouraged to introduce the participants to the supplies they'll be working with and go over the basic creation process with them. If you've created a sample, you are welcome to share it during this time and remind participants that there is no right or wrong way to create or participate.

"Today you're invited to use the Internal Freedom Template, to visualize the things that center you and can make you feel calm, when things are challenging. For instance, this can include hobbies, loved ones, values, and more. Remember, you are free to decorate this template however you like. Are there any questions before we move on?"
opening_circle:
"Today's workshop is all about finding our truth to help us break free from being locked up internally. When we are in our resilient zone, we can bear the challenges of the day and respond to them in the best possible way. Therefore, when our body and mind feel calm and grounded, we are in the resilient zone. However, there are times when we can get bumped out of our resiliency zone, such as when we are really stressed or feel strong emotions, such as anger. With that being said, you will be invited to take a journey into thinking about what matters to you. You can use these truths to help bring you back to your 'resiliency zone' as a way to stay grounded and focused."

“We will start by going over the art materials and steps we can take to create our Freedom From Within images. Then, we’ll talk about some things that weigh heavy on us while being incarcerated (or restricted), and things that are important to us that bring comfort. Any questions before we begin?”

Note: Keep in mind this is not a competition. Art is art as long as it comes from the heart. All of you are artists. There is no right or wrong in art. (This may help bring comfort, and engage any self-conscious youth.)

title: The Homeboy or Homegirl in Me
objective:
This workshop aims to provide participants with the opportunity to explore their identities through the labels of "homeboy" and "homegirl" and identify what that means for them.

 

Note from the author

This workshop invites participants to explore their definition of what it means to be a “homegirl” or “homeboy” and to challenge societal connotations to what it means to adopt this label. Often associated with those who are impacted by gang activity, this workshop can serve as an opportunity to challenge the belief system that some have internalized through their upbringing as well as intergenerational trauma. A large part of this workshop is to acknowledge the phenomenon of masking ourselves to fit a certain role. Through art, we have the potential to remove these masks and instead manifest positivity through our own strength. Removing these masks is a constant practice. It can challenge us to confront our deepest triggers of anger, fear and resentment. We are imperfect, emotional beings and to be a “homegirl” or “homeboy” embodies everything in our psyche, good and bad.
materials:
Mask Template

  • Cardstock paper

  • Mask template

  • Pencils

  • Colored pencils

  • Markers

  • Blank paper
setup:
Optional Setup

Facilitators are welcome to put their art supplies in clear plastic containers to help organize the materials. Depending on the space, you may also set up stations for art supplies. For example, for larger groups, you may have 2 or 3 different stations with markers, pencils and paper. For a smaller group, you may have everything at the center of the table.

Note: If you are working with participants who are incarcerated, explain the importance of taking care of materials. You may provide clear directions; however, be mindful and gentle in delivery (e.g., “In effort to try to have the materials last us a long time, please make sure to take care of them and put them back when you are done using them.")
warm_up:
Journaling:

"For today's warmup, I invite you to join me in a small journaling session. I encourage you to take a few moments to think about the connotations that the label 'Homegirl' and 'Homeboy' carries. If you would like, on a piece of paper, you are welcome to think about these questions."

  • What are some projections that society puts on us?

  • What are some messages that have been internalized?

  • Have you ever felt ignored or shut out because of what others perceive you to be?

  • Who is that so-called Homeboy or Homegirl in you? What does it do to you?

"Remember journaling can look any way you'd like it to, just allow your thoughts to flow onto the paper no and try not to judge what comes out. Words and full sentences are welcomed!"

Allow some time for participants to think or write about their responses. Once participants have thought about what it means to carry the label of “homegirl" or "homeboy," they are invited to start creating an art piece that is inspired by it.
creation:
Completed Mask

While the participants are creating, you may play some calming music and offer assistance when needed. Time reminders may also be helpful to participants in order to decrease their anxiety and the need to rush towards the end.
closing:
Towards the end of the workshop, allow time for participants to share their creation, how the process was for them, or any feelings that came up. At the end of the shares, you may also invite participants to hold up their masks or put it in front of their faces. We also encourage you to thank the participants for coming and being in community with one another.   

“We went over a lot today and I want to thank you for participation. We talked about how the homeboy/girl label affects us and the masks that we wear. Everyone in this room has a mask that they carry through their lives. There is so much beauty in the colors and the uniqueness that each of you possess. It takes courage to create art that comes from the heart and each of you are a part of something special. What you shared today took strength, courage and vulnerability. I feel honored to have worked with you today. Thank you."
notes:
Durational Art Tip:

We encourage you to invite your participants to take their mask and place it where they can see it, as a reminder of the fact that they can create their own labels. Participants are also encouraged to look back on their creation over time and see how it has supported them or create new masks as they continue on their journey.
tips: Fabian created this workshop for those who are currently incarcerated, however, we invite you to use it in any setting you see fit. For specific adaptations, contact your Program Manager for support.

These labels can sometimes, consciously and unconsciously, bring up varying thoughts, feelings, and beliefs. However, they can also be a form of empowerment and become a part of who we are.
