title: Bridging the Divide
objective: This workshop utilizes meditation, art creation, writing, and self-reflection to cultivate a sense of cultural belonging, within the self and within the outer environment (geographically/culturally, etc.) by integrating our inner and outer selves.
materials:
• Paper to write on (few sheets, and two smaller pieces, like 3x5)
  • Pens/pencils to write with Blank paper for collage (at least 11x14 – ideally 14x17!) 
  • Glue sticks
  • Cutout magazine images
setup:
For meditation:

  • Provide cushions, if possible. If not, chairs are fine.

For creation:

  • Lay out a few pieces of paper for writing, two small pieces of paper and a pen/pencil for each participant. These can be placed in front of where they are sitting.
  • Lay out collage images in center of table, spread out.
  • Have a glue stick/scissors for each participant, or one for every two people. (Optional)
  • Have a whiteboard (or similar) to write prompts as you go.

We invite you to watch this panel discussion from our Facilitator Enrichment Training in 2018 that focused on adapting workshops for cultural responsiveness: https://youtu.be/NpyT284TUQs
warm_up:
Begin with a short meditation for grounding.

1. If you feel comfortable doing so, close your eyes. Find a comfortable seated position. Make an intention to remain still, simply observing feelings, sensations, etc.

2. [Body scan and relaxation] – Simply notice any sensations, varying temperatures, etc. from head to toe, relaxing as you go through body. (2 min)

3. Sit and observe the breath. You can inhale, exhale. Inhale, exhale. Count up to 10 and back down to 1. If you get distracted, let yourself start over from 1. (3 min)

4. [Continue for a minute or so.] When you feel ready, take a deep breath in, exhale. Slowly open your eyes.
creation:
1. Choose collage images

Keeping both words on the pieces of paper in mind, choose whatever images correspond. Make two piles.

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

2. Writing – Reflection on collage images

   a. One list - how one pile relates to how you identify yourself

   b. The other list - how the other pile relates to how you are perceived

   c. Reflection – a few sentences – could be anything!

      Ex. Are there similarities between the two piles? Differences?

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

3. Collage creation Create an (abstract) self-portrait using both images.

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

4. Writing - Story

   a. What are the past, present, and future of this image?
   b. What happened before, during, and after?

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

Final product
closing:
Each participant has the option to share his/her story, either read or paraphrased.

After each has shared, go around once more inviting each participant to state one word about how they feel in this moment.

A few deep breaths in and out, eyes closed.

“The point is not necessarily a happy ending, but self-awareness about where we come from, how we can connect to our deeper selves, beyond color or location, and how that translates our being able to connect to others, in a way where we all coexist equally.”
optional_materials:
You can also facilitate this workshop our printable worksheet. If you are utilizing this sheet in lieu of the regular workshop materials, be sure to send a digital copy or print them out beforehand for your participants if you are meeting in person.

  • Bridging the Divide Printable worksheet
introduction:
“Thank you for being here today. Before we begin, I want you to know that this is your Window of Time. It's a time for you to notice your thoughts, needs and feelings. During this time, there is no right or wrong way to participate or create. I'm going to share some instructions, but you get to choose how you want to participate. You can follow along completely, or you may want to do something different, it's completely up to you. During your Window of time, you get to choose. I am here to support you in any way that I can, so please ask for what you need. Any questions before I begin?

“I invite you to think about this: If there were one place or feeling that conjured up a sense of belonging for you, what would that place be? Have you felt it? Have you been there? Asian immigrants and even first-generation citizens have often touched on a sense of not feeling like they belong, of not feeling quite at home anywhere. There’s still a sense of shared discrimination, invisibility, irrelevance, loneliness. Those feelings arise from a fragmentation – disjointedness between who we are on the inside and who we are on the outside. Today I invite you to embrace, let go, and heal, or at least to ignite that process. To be open to writing and creating artwork in the hopes of Bridging the Divide between who we have been told to be, and who we truly are.”
demonstration:
“We will begin with an invitation to an opening circle where you will be invited to use the two smaller pieces of paper. After that we’ll have a brief meditation to allow our bodies and our minds to settle, then we will go over the rest of the steps.”

"In front of you are several pieces of paper for writing, two smaller pieces for our opening circle, and collage images for the art creation process. You’ll be invited to go through the collage images, picking ones that correspond with the words you wrote down, making two piles, one for each word. After, you will be invited to write a reflection list for each pile, as well as a few sentences, more or less, reflecting on any similarities or differences. After that, you’ll be invited to create the collage, creating a self-portrait of sorts. At the end, you will be invited to write a brief story about what you’ve created, followed by a sharing circle. Sharing is optional."
opening_circle: “I invite you to begin by stating one word describing how you feel right now in this moment. Take your two smaller pieces of paper. Write a word or two on one piece of paper – how you identify culturally/racially; and a word or two on the other piece of paper – how you feel you are perceived by others.”
extra_field:
Read workshop author Sharon Uy's blog that highlights the inspiration behind her workshop. 
Bridging the Divide

title: Let the Bad Feelings Fall Away
objective: This workshop gives children a chance to practice letting go of bad feelings, by creating leaves representing those negative feelings that have "fallen" off their tree.
materials:
• Construction paper (variety of colors)

  • Markers (variety of colors)

  • Scissors

  • Tree template

  • Leaves template
setup:
We invite you to watch this panel discussion from our Facilitator Enrichment Training in 2018 that focused on adapting workshops for cultural responsiveness: https://youtu.be/NpyT284TUQs

You have two options for the creation process. You can invite each participant to create a tree and feather individually, or you can print one tree for the group and invite each child to create the leaves and collectively glue the leaves onto the tree (see creation).


For individual creation:
You can print one tree template for each child on a colored card stock, and print as many leaves as you see fit for the children to choose from and decorate their trees with. For younger children, you may consider cutting the templates out in advance, so children wouldn't have to handle scissors. For individual creation, you also have the option for a more simplified creation where children don't have to cut. They can simply create on one template.


For group creation:
You can print one tree template for the whole group, and print enough leaves so that each child has two leaves to create. Again, you can precut the templates if you see fit.

As a facilitator, you have complete freedom to alter or adapt any portion or element of this workshop to cater to your specific group's needs.
 

Leaves with bad feelings written on them
warm_up:
You are welcome to use our suggested warm-up or your own.

“First, I'd like to invite you to join me in a brief warm-up exercise. You are welcome to follow along, or if you prefer, you can observe. Observing is participating."

"For those of you who want to follow along, I invite you all to pretend you are a tree. How do trees start out? Yes, very small; as seeds. Let’s see you be a seed. Good! And then what happens? Yes, you start to grow. Let’s see you growing, sending up a little sprout, and growing some leaves. And as you grow and grow, let’s see your branches grow. Beautiful. What color are you? Do you have lots of leaves? Or just a few? Let your fingers be the leaves. Can you feel them blowing in the wind? And see if they feel like falling down to the ground yet. When they are ready, let them fall down, dancing downward, all the way down to the ground (if possible, fall down gently until you lie on the ground). And as you rest on the ground, take a nice deep breath and feel how good it feels to let everything go.”
creation:
Bad feeling leaves fallen off tree

You can now invite those who wish to do so, to begin creating.

For individual creation, children can select any color leaves (or cut them out, if not precut) and as many as they like and on each, write a bad feeling they sometimes have and want to let go of. You can remind them that it can be any bad feeling. There is no judgment and anything they write will be perfect. Once they're done with the writing, they can then glue the leaves to the base of their tree, as if they are "fallen" leaves.

For group creation, you can invite the children to select 2 leaves (or as many as you see fit) and write one bad feeling on each. Note, that for group creation, there is limited space under the single community tree, so depending on the size of your group, you may consider limiting the number of leaves each child can create so that everyone's leaves can be glued at the base of the tree and remain visible. Once they are done creating their leaves, you can invite them to bring their leaves up to the community tree and glue them on during the closing.
closing:
For group creation, you can invite each child to bring their leaves and glue them onto the base of the community tree, and share their leaves, if they wish to do so.

For individual creation, you can invite each child to share their leaves, the bad feelings they shed today, or anything else they may wish to share. Of course, this is optional, so if no one feels comfortable sharing, that's perfectly okay.

You may wish to close out by reminding the children that they have the ability to let go of bad feelings, even outside of this workshop. You can encourage them to incorporate any technique you see fit. One suggested technique you can share with them is one that is often used with feeling of anger:
 

  • Stop

  • Take a deep breath in

  • Clench fists, and count to five

  • Let it out

  • Walk away
notes: This workshop has a complimentary workshop called "Show Me Your Tail Feathers," which is part of our fall workshop series.
optional_materials: • Tree with Leaves Template (for a simplified individual workshop that doesn't require cutting)
introduction:
"We’re going to start today with this tree (you can refer them to their individual trees or the community tree). What do you notice about it (it has no leaves)? Have you ever noticed a tree with no leaves? It’s something that happens to lots of trees at this time of the year. The trees let go of all their leaves. What happens to the leaves? Yes, they dance in the wind and fall onto the ground. It’s a beautiful thing when the trees let go of their leaves. They don’t need them for the winter, so they just let go. Then later, they grow new ones.”

“Today, we'll have a chance to notice how just as trees let go of their leaves when they need to, we can let go of things too. Sometimes there are bad feelings that we have that we need to let go of, or else they can get to us. This project is called ‘Let the Bad Feelings Fall Away.’ It’s a chance for each of us to notice any bad feelings we want to let go of."

"Before we begin, I want you to know that this is your window of time. This means that this can be a safe space to notice your thoughts, feelings, and needs. Since this space is your window of time, everything you say or do is voluntary. During this time, there is no right or wrong way to participate or create. I'm going to share some basic instructions, but you get to choose how you want to participate. You can follow along completely, or you may want to do something different, it's completely up to you. During your window of time, you have complete freedom to choose. However you choose to spend this time will be perfectly okay. I am here to support you in any way that I can, so please feel free to ask for what you need."

title: Gratitude Tins
objective: Participants will be invited to reflect on and practice gratitude by creating a tin box that holds their thoughts, reflections, and acknowledgements.
materials:
• Small tin boxes, Altoids tins or any small box (one per participant)
  • Mod Podge or matte medium
  • Collage cutouts or magazines
  • Gratitude worksheets (Choose one or all to offer)
  • Permanent markers
  • Pens
  • Pencils
  • Brushes (for matte medium)
  • Colored pencils
  • Tacky glue
  • Copy paper
  • Scissors
  • Embellishments
  • Relaxing music
  • Large paper or white/blackboard
setup: Fill out a couple of examples of the worksheets with words, shapes, and symbols to show a variety of responses. Brainstorm on a blank sheet of paper to show that option as well. Create a couple of tin box samples, one that is completely done and one that is halfway done that you will use to show creation steps. Write down a brief outline of the creation steps and other important information about the materials that participants may refer to throughout the workshop.
warm_up: Remind participants of their options for brainstorming. Show where you wrote down the creation steps so all participants can refer to them when needed. Give participants about 10-15 minutes to brainstorm.
creation:
When you notice that all participants have transitioned into their creations, give a gentle reminder of the creation steps and invite them to ask you for what they need. Remind them that this is their window of time and there is no right or wrong way.

As participants begin to move into creating things to put inside their boxes, give gentle time reminders like, “In about 15 minutes, we are going to transition over to our closing. Feel free to continue creating during the closing.” If you have the capacity to do so, invite them to take supplies with them to finish or consider doing
closing: “Thank you so much for being present today and for witnessing and participating in your own way. Today we had a chance to reflect on gratitude and create something that we can use as a special reminder. I’m going to invite volunteers to share about their experience today. You can share a word or brief sentence about how it was to think about gratitude, how it was to create your box, or you can even just take a moment to hold your creation up for everyone to see.”
optional_materials: • Article: Gratitude Physically Changes Your Brain (Can be shared with participants or used as a way to prepare yourself.)
introduction:
“Thank you for being here today. Before we begin, I want you to know that this is your Window of Time. It's a time for you to notice your thoughts, needs and feelings. During this time, there is no right or wrong way to participate or create. I'm going to share some instructions, but you get to choose how you want to participate. You can follow along completely, or you may want to do something different, it's completely up to you. During your Window of time, you get to choose. I am here to support you in any way that I can, so please ask for what you need.

“Today’s workshop is all about gratitude. I’ll start off by doing a materials and creation demonstration so you get to see all of the art materials and what you can do with them. Then, we’ll talk briefly about what we are grateful for, fill out a worksheet to guide us in creation, and then create our boxes.

“Since this is your Window of Time, you get to choose how to participate. Even observing is participating. Everything I share today is an invitation and you are in control of how you accept or don’t accept the invitation. My hope is that you’ll honor what’s best for you. Any questions before we begin?”
demonstration:
Step 1: Brainstorm Ideas
   
 
  Step 2: Decorate Your Box
   
 
  Step 3: Fill the Box
   
   

“The materials that we’ll be using are on the table. First, you have the tin. This tin box is yours to decorate, write on, and design however you like. During this demonstration, I’m going to show you a few ways you can use the art materials to add to it, but since this is your Window of Time, you can use any, all, or none of these these ideas - you get to choose.”

Creation Steps

Step 1: Brainstorm Ideas
Show a sample worksheet that has been filled out. Show blank pieces of paper with brainstorming ideas as well.

“With or without a worksheet, you’re invited to brainstorm ideas that will help you with your boxes. You can list names and/or things you are grateful for. We also have blank paper for you to use if you don’t want to use any of the worksheets.”

“Think about the words, shapes or symbols you can use represent what you are grateful for. What colors represent your gratitude?”

Step 2: Decorate Your Box
“Using your worksheet to guide you, decorate your box with any of the art materials. I’ll show you some different things you can do, but again, you get to choose how you decorate it.”

Show the different techniques participants can use to decorate their box. Answer any questions about materials that come up and remind participants that they get to choose how to create.

Important techniques to demonstrate:

  • Using matte medium (also called “Mod Podge”) or glue to adhere paper and other collage items to the box
  • Writing words, shapes, and symbols before matte medium is applied as a finish
  • Adding embellishments
  • Using matte medium to finish the box

Step 3: Fill the Box
“Your box can be a safe place to keep your thoughts, reflections, and acknowledgements about gratitude. Maybe you want to keep small strips of paper with the names of the people you are grateful for. You can write a letter of gratitude and place it in the box so you can read it when you need a reminder of what you’re thankful for. You can even fold up the worksheet you created and keep it in your box for safe keeping.”
opening_circle:
“I invite you to take three deep breaths together and get our bodies ready to reflect on gratitude…

“As we settle in, let’s take a moment to think about gratitude. When we take a look in the dictionary, it says that gratitude is “the quality of being thankful, readiness to show appreciation.” This is what I’m going to invite you to do with me today, be thankful and show appreciation. The great part of today is that we get to do this your way.”

“In a moment, we’ll begin our brainstorm, but before that, I’ll invite you to share one word or a brief sentence about what you are grateful for.”

Thank participants for sharing and witnessing. Invite them to move onto brainstorming. As you transition them over to brainstorming, let them know that they are welcome to move right into creating after they are done. Since some participants may finish brainstorming before others, you can ask participants who finish early to be mindful of the other participants who haven’t finished yet when gathering their art materials.”

title: Community Gratitude Tree
full_name: Rudy Hernandez special thanks to Theresa Black
objective: Participants will be invited to practice cultivating gratitude through paired sharing and contributing to a community tree.
materials:
• Craft paper roll or brown butcher paper
  • Leaf templates
  • White copy paper
  • Cardstock (white and/or multi-colored)
  • Pens
  • Pencils
  • Colored pencils
  • Markers
  • Painter’s tape
  • Masking tape
  • Hole punchers
  • Ribbon or string
  • Glue dots
  • Timer
  • Relaxing music
setup:
Prepare the tree on a vacant wall. You can use this tutorial to support you.

If you have the time, you can also make this tree with participants. Create a few leaf samples, with and without holes and ribbon/string. You can also draw an outline of a tree on a large piece of butcher paper or a white/chalkboard for a quick set up. If you are using leaf templates, print plenty for participants on heavy cardstock. You can cut each individual leaf out to save some time.
warm_up:
“I’m going to invite you to find a partner to participate in a paired sharing with.”

“Now that you’ve found your partner, I’m going to explain how paired sharing works. You’ll choose which one of you would like to speak first. I’ll put two minutes on the clock and you’ll talk about any one of these prompts, or you might want to share about gratitude in a different way.  I’ll set a timer for two minutes and the first person will begin. After I call time, the next person will begin their two minutes. As we are listening, try not to make this into a conversation. You are invited to be a witness to what your partner is sharing.”

Choose two or three prompts for paired sharing:

  • I am grateful for...
  • The relationships I value are...
  • Today I enjoyed...
  • I smile and laughed today when...
  • I am proud of...
  • I appreciate…

Survey the room to make sure everyone understands each prompt and that they are ready to being. Once they are ready, begin the timer for two minutes. Give a gentle time reminder before the first two-minute round is up. Repeat for the second round.

Once everyone is done, invite a few participants to share back what they shared NOT what they heard.

Transition to creation and remind participants to hold onto their leaves until the end of the workshop.
creation: Give time reminders well before time is up. Invite early-finishers to journal about their experience on a blank piece of paper or create additional leaves to take home.
closing:
“Thank you for being present today and participating in the ways that you did. As a closing, I’m going to invite volunteers to share about their experiences and/or about what they wrote on their leaves. If you feel comfortable enough to do so, you can come up and add your leaves to tree after you share, or you can wait to add them when everyone else goes up. You can even hold onto your leaves and keep them for yourselves. It’s up to you. During this tree ceremony, I’ll ask that we respect our speakers as we continue to listen and witness.”

When all participants are done sharing, invite the whole group to come up to add to the tree. Give participants time to step back and take a look at the finished tree. Invite them to give themselves a round of applause.
optional_materials:
• Article: Gratitude Physically Changes Your Brain (Can be shared with participants or used for your reference.)
  • Small sticky notes (can replace leaf templates, hole punchers, painter’s tape, and ribbon/string)
introduction:
“Thank you for being here today. Before we begin, I want you to know that this is your Window of Time. It's a time for you to notice your thoughts, needs and feelings. During this time, there is no right or wrong way to participate or create. I'm going to share some instructions, but you get to choose how you want to participate. You can follow along completely, or you may want to do something different, it's completely up to you. During your Window of time, you get to choose. I am here to support you in any way that I can, so please ask for what you need.

“During today’s workshop, we are going to explore gratitude and create a community tree that captures all of our thoughts, reflections, and acknowledgments in one place.

“I’ll begin by talking about the art materials and creation steps, invite to participate in a paired sharing exercise with a brief share back, and then into creating. At the end of the workshop, we’ll have a closing tree ceremony when we’ll add our leaves to the tree.”

“Since this is your Window of Time, you get to choose how to participate and observing is participating. Everything I share today is an invitation and you are in control of how you accept or don’t accept the invitation. My hope is that you’ll honor what’s best for you. Any questions before we begin?”
demonstration:
Step 1: Capture Ideas
     
   

    Step 2: Cutting, Hole Punching, Adding Ribbon/String
     
   

    Step 3: Adding to the Tree

“The materials that we’ll be using are on the table. During this demonstration, I’m going to show you a few ways you can use the art materials to add to it, but since this is your Window of Time, you can use any, all, or none of these these ideas - you get to choose.”

Demonstrate the following materials and creation steps:

  • Example of leaves with words, shapes, and symbols
  • Hole punching process (thinking about how it will hang)
  • Adding ribbon or string to the leaf
  • Cutting on/around the black lines of the leaf
  • Adding tape to the back of the leaf (if not using template)

Creation Steps
These steps follow the template procedure. Modify the steps if you will be using sticky notes.

Step 1: Capture Ideas
Show samples of completed leaves with words, shapes, and symbols. Make sure to include samples on punched and unpunched samples.

“On your leaf cutouts, using words, shapes, or symbols, you are invited to write down what you are grateful for. Ideas can be be anything from names of people, things, and even memories. There is no right or wrong way to add to your leaves.

“If you are punching a hole on your leaf, think about how you want it to hang. Punch your hole and add your ribbon or string.

“Hold onto your leaves. You’ll be invited to hang them onto the tree during the closing of the workshop.”

Step 2: Cutting, Hole Punching, Adding Ribbon/String
“Once you are done adding to your leaf, cut around the black line using scissors. Punch a hole where you would like it to hang from and add ribbon or string. If you are taping it on/near the tree, you can skip the hole punch and ribbon/string. Add tape to the back and apply to the tree or during the closing tree ceremony.”

Step 3: Adding to the Tree
“At the end of the workshop, we are going to add our leaves to the tree, together. You can use tape, glue dots, or string to hang your leaves. You may want to keep some leaves for yourself to keep with you as a reminder.”
opening_circle:
“Sometimes it can be nice to take the time to pause and notice the people and things we are grateful for. It can also be great to reflect with a partner, and celebrate as a group. Today you’ll be invited to create a community gratitude tree that captures all of our thoughts, reflections, and acknowledgements of gratitude.

“Studies have shown that the more we practice gratitude, the healthier our brains are. By noticing the things around us that we are grateful for, it makes it easier to notice them in the future.”

You can share as much of the article as you’d like.

“Today, we are going to get the chance to practice gratitude by sharing with a partner and then creating a community tree to help remind us of the things we’re grateful for.”

title: Self-Regulation Toolkits
objective: Participants will be invited to explore different tools to aid in self-regulation and create their own self-regulation toolkits.
materials:
• Pipe cleaners
  • Play-Doh or similar dough
  • Stress balls or other soft balls
  • Paper lunch bags or plastic zipper bags
  • Bubbles
  • Bottled water or cups of drinking water
  • Paper straws
  • Coloring books/pages (download mandala pages)
  • Crayons
  • Colored pencils
  • Markers
  • Display paper or white/chalkboard
setup:
Distribute materials on the table for easy accessibility. Make sure to have at least one item per person as they will be invited to pick and choose what to add to their bags. Write words, shapes, and symbols on a paper bag that can help with self regulation.

On display paper or a white/chalkboard, write down the different strategies for self-regulation.

  • Pause
  • Think
  • Visualize
  • Take Deep Breaths
  • Sip Water
  • Color/Doodle
  • Blow Bubbles
  • Keep Your Fingers Busy
warm_up:
“I’m going to invite you to find a participate in a paired sharing experience. If you would like to participate, I invite you to find a partner.

“Now that you’ve found your partner, I’m going to explain how paired sharing works. You’ll choose which one of you would like to speak first. I’ll put two minutes on the clock and you’ll talk about the prompt or any other thoughts you want to share with your partner.

“I’ll set a timer for two minutes and the first person will begin. After I call time, the next person will begin their two minutes. As a listener, try not to make this time a conversation but a time to witness and hear what your partner is saying.

“The prompt is: A time I felt dysregulated (not calm) was…”

Survey the room to make sure everyone understands the prompt and that they are ready to being. Once they are ready, begin the timer for two minutes. Give a gentle time reminder before the first two-minute round is up. Repeat for the second round.

Once everyone is done, invite a few participants to share back what they shared NOT what their partner shared.

“Thank you for those of you who shared and those of you who witnessed. "An important thing to remember about being dysregulated is that there are things we can do to get our brains back to a calmer state. I’d like to share some of them with you. As I’m sharing, I’m going to invite you to use any of the materials you see to follow along. You will also get time in a few minutes to create your own self-regulation kits that will have all of the things that can help you calm down."

Share the following techniques and give a few minutes after each technique for participants to practice.

  • Pause — This may be the easiest thing to do on the list. Taking a moment to pause and center yourself can be helpful. You can let people know that you are pausing by holding up your hand and saying, “I need a moment.”
  • Think — Bring to mind what you love about the child or a successful experience with the child. This releases positive neurotransmitters to balance out negative brain chemicals produced by frustration and stress.
  • Visualize — See the positive outcome in your mind. Practice visualization; it is a very powerful and effective tool not to be underestimated.
  • Take Deep Breaths — When we feel dysregulated, our body’s natural response might be to take short, quick breaths. Taking a moment to pause and take deep breaths can be helpful.
  • Sip Water — Sometime our bodies can be more sensitive when we are not hydrated. Taking the time to drink some and give your body what it needs. Even sipping from a straw can help calm you down! Sipping has been shown to help regulate the part of the brain that calms us down.
  • Coloring and Doodling — When practicing coloring and doodling, you can help your body reconnect to thinking and feeling. You can use coloring books and doodle to help regain those connections.
  • Blowing Bubbles — The deep breathing you need to blow bubbles helps relieve stress.
  • Keep Your Fingers Busy — Playing with soft objects like pipe cleaners, Play-Doh, and stress balls can help calm your nerves and improve focus and concentration.
creation: Now I’m going to give you some time to continue to explore all of these tools. Use your bag to keep any of your favorite tools in safe place. On your bag, you can write your name and any other words, shapes or symbols that remind you of self-regulation and feeling calm.
closing:
Welcome volunteers to share about their experience. Possible prompts:

  • I feel...
  • I learned...
  • How will you use your self-regulation toolkit?
  • If you could share one thing about what you learned today with someone who wasn’t here, what would you say?
optional_materials: • Gratitude worksheets
introduction:
“Thank you for being here today. Before we begin, I want you to know that this is your Window of Time. It's a time for you to notice your thoughts, needs and feelings. During this time, there is no right or wrong way to participate or create. I'm going to share some instructions, but you get to choose how you want to participate. You can follow along completely, or you may want to do something different, it's completely up to you. During your Window of Time, you get to choose. I am here to support you in any way that I can, so please ask for what you need.

“During today’s workshop, we’ll get a chance to talk about big, uncontrolled feelings and different ways we can notice these feelings, identify them, and come up with easy ways to calm down and control them, also known as self-regulating.”

“After I go over the materials, we’ll start with a brief discussion, paired sharing, and we’ll move on to practicing some self-regulation skills and make our very own bag full of tools that we can use in the future. Remember, everything is optional. Any questions before I begin?”
demonstration: Show the different materials that are available and show a completed bag. Explain that you will explain how to use each material in a few minutes.
opening_circle:
“Have you ever felt a feeling so big, it made you act in a different way? Maybe you were angry and did something you didn’t mean to do. Maybe you got frustrated and had an outburst. Or maybe you felt a big feeling of sadness and it made you cry, uncontrollably.

“All of these feelings and reactions are normal. When we are under a lot of emotional stress, our brains change and our big reactions are known as dysregulation.

“Our brains are always looking for a way to get back to a state of regulation or calm, and sometimes it can be really hard to find our way back. Today, we’re going to explore ways that can help get back to regulated or calm state by practicing self-regulation. Not everyone will need the same things to calm down and you might find today that you might need something different and that is OK. Today is about exploring and learning."

title: Riding the Grief Coaster
objective:
Participants will have the opportunity to learn about the five stages of grief and track their grief journeys by creating a roller coaster that can help them understand more about their feelings and who they can call on for support.

Inspired by The Five Stages of Grief developed by Elizabeth Kübler-Ross and David Kessler.
materials:
•  
    White copy paper or large white construction paper
  • Five Stages of Grief worksheet (one per participant)
  • Roller coaster car templates (one per participant)
  • Examples of roller coaster tracks for reference
  • Markers
  • Colored pencils
  • Regular pencils
  • Erasers
  • Rulers
  • Scissors
  • Transparent tape
  • Chalkboard or paper for displaying agenda and the five stages of grief
  • Background music
setup:
•  
      The Fives Stages of Grief worksheet.
       
     
      Car template
       
    Print the The Five Stages of Grief worksheet, car templates, and examples of roller coaster tracks.
  • Create a couple of simple samples of a completed worksheet, car, and track. Show the different stages of grief by labeling the track. You may want to create a sample of a long and short track.
  • Have several pieces of white paper of your choice for participants as they will be invited to tape pieces to create longer tracks as needed.
  • Display a brief agenda with creation steps as well as the five stages of grief for participants to refer to during the workshop.
     

The Five Stages of Grief

1. Denial: Not wanting to think that anything bad has happened. Can be used to protect us from feeling the pain of loss.

2. Anger: After denial goes away, reality can set in and we can become angry about many different things, even at people around us.

3. Bargaining: When we try make a deal with a higher power or someone to help make everything OK again.

4. Depression: After we have tried everything, the extreme sadness can set in when we begin to think about the person or thing we have lost.

5. Acceptance: We begin to be accept our loss and learn to live with it. This stage can help us move on.
warm_up:
"When we experience the loss of someone or something very special to us like a family member, friends, a pet, or even a home, we can go through what is called the five stages of grief. Not all grief journeys are the same, and we all experience these stages in different ways. We might spend more time on one stage than another or we may even skip a stage or experience them multiple times or never at all. Overall, these stages can be common when someone is grieving.

“Before we talk about the five stages, I’m going to invite you a moment to think about someone or something you have lost. If you can’t think of anything, that is OK, I’ll ask you to think of how it might feel to lose something or someone.

“As we talk about each of the stages, I’m going to pause to give you some time to think about a time you may have felt this way and fill in your worksheet. If you can’t think of anything to write, that’s OK, you might take some time to reflect on who/what you have lost. I will also welcome you to share other feelings other than the ones that are shared today. Your unique experiences are very important as we move throughout the workshop — I invite you to share anything you'd like. All feelings and experiences are welcome"

Note: Remind participants that not everyone goes through these stages and if they do, they may not experience them in this order or even at all. Be mindful to acknowledge and validate all feelings and experiences.

Refer to the different stages both on display and on The Five Stages of Grief worksheet.

The Five Stages of Grief

1. Denial: Not wanting to think that anything bad has happened. Can be used to protect us from feeling the pain of loss.

2. Anger: After denial goes away, reality can set in and we can become angry about many different things, even at people around us.

3. Bargaining: When we try make a deal with a higher power or someone to help make everything OK again.

4. Depression: After we have tried everything, the extreme sadness can set in when we begin to think about the person or thing we have lost.

5. Acceptance: We begin to be accept our loss and learn to live with it. This stage can help us move on.

As you go through each stage, invite participants to share their experiences. Give a few minutes after each section for participants to fill out their worksheet. Some questions you can ask are:

  • What other feelings or stages would you like to add or talk about?
  • How did you feel when you were going through any of these stages?
  • What did you do while you were feeling this or going through this stage?
  • What can you do in the future during these feelings or stages?
  • How did it feel to go from one feeling/stage to the another?
  • Did you reach out to anyone when you were going through these feelings?
  • What kind of advice can you offer others who may be going through this stage?
creation:
“Now that we’ve filled out our worksheets, it’s time to create our cars and coasters.”

Review the creation steps for participants and refer where you displayed them in the room. Invite participants to use the worksheets to help them with their cars and coasters.

Step 1: Design Your Car
"On your cars, I invite you to use words, shapes, and/or symbols to represent what you have lost. This might be a person’s name with their favorite colors on it, a drawing of a pet, or anything else that you have lost. Your car can be used as a tribute to who/what you have lost. Once you’re done with your design, you can cut the car out."

Step 2: "Track" Your Journey
“On a large sheet of paper, draw a track for your car to show the feelings you are experiencing or have experienced. Think about the five stages of grief as you show the changes in your track. Add your own feelings and experiences along the way. Labeling the reasons for each change can be helpful. You can also think about drawing people around your track that you can call on for support during this time. As you create, you may need more paper to make a longer track, feel free to use the tape and additional sheets of paper to make your track longer.”

Step 3: Ride and Share
“As you go through your grief journey, use your coaster to remind you of your thoughts and feelings as well as the people who can support you through these hard times.”
 

Step 1: Fill out worksheet during the discussion. Step 2: Design the car.
   
Step 3: "Track" your journey. Step 4: Ride and share.
closing:
“We covered a lot today and I want to thank you for being here. We talked about grief and the different stages we can go through and created cars and roller coaster tracks to represent our grief journeys. I’d like to invite anyone who would like to share to talk about their experience.”

Invite participants to openly share their experiences. You can assist by writing a few questions on the board to guide their thinking.

  • Who/what are you remembering today?
  • Would you like to honor someone/something you’ve lost by sharing a memory?
  • What did you learn about grief and your unique journey through it?
  • How will your roller coaster help you through your current experience or future ones?
  • Who are the people that can help you along your grief journey?
     

“Thank you so much for being present and participating in all the ways that you did. By being here, you have honored everyone and everything you have lost. What I ask is that you continue to honor not only who or what you’ve lost, but also the journey you take toward healing.”
optional_materials:
Since this can be a heavy topic and workshop, consider providing self-regulation tools such as pipe cleaners, Play-Doh, and stress balls. A good pre-workshop can be Self-Regulation Toolkits, found in our curriculum.

These books are good to have on hand for reference. You can also incorporate them into the workshop by reading aloud to the group.

  • On Grief and Grieving by Elizabeth Kübler-Ross and David Kessler
  • The Goodbye Book by Todd Parr
  • The Elephant in the Room: A Children’s Book for Grief and Loss by Amanda Edwards and Leslie Ponciano
  • One Wave at a Time: A Story About Grief and Healing by Holly Thompson
introduction:
“Thank you for being here today. Before we begin, I want you to know that this is your Window of Time. It's a time for you to notice your thoughts, needs and feelings. During this time, there is no right or wrong way to participate or create. I'm going to share some instructions, but you get to choose how you want to participate. You can follow along completely, or you may want to do something different, it's completely up to you. During your Window of time, you get to choose. I am here to support you in any way that I can, so please ask for what you need. Any questions before I begin?"

“Today’s workshop is all about the feelings we can go through when we lose someone or something very important to us. Sometimes in life, we experience the loss of a family member, a friend, a pet, or even a home. These feelings can feel like we are on a roller coaster. We’ll get a chance to talk about these feelings and create a roller coaster to track our feelings and help those around us understand what we are going through.

“To begin, I’m going to go over the art materials and steps we can take to create our roller coasters. Then, we’ll talk about the five stages of grief, gather our thoughts and ideas and begin creating our roller coasters. Any questions before we begin?”
demonstration:
“On the table we have markers, colored pencils, regular pencils, rulers, and tape. We are going to be using a worksheets to gather our thoughts and ideas for our roller coaster. Each of you has a car to design and white paper that you will use to create your track.”

Steps for Creation:

Step 1: Discussion and Worksheet

Show a sample worksheet. “We will be starting off by discussing the five stages of grief. As we are discussing, I’ll be pausing so you can take a few minutes to fill out each section of the worksheet. If you don’t get to finish each section, it’s OK, you can always go back and spend some more time on it. The ideas that you gather can help you learn more about your feelings and help prepare you for designing your track."

Step 2: Design the Car
“Each of you has one car to design. On your cars, you will be invited to use words, shapes, and/or symbols to represent what you have lost. This might be a person’s name with their favorite colors on it, a drawing of a pet, or anything else that you have lost. Your car can be used as a tribute to who/what you have lost. Once you’re done with your design, you can cut the car out."

Step 3: "Track" Your Journey
“Last, we will create a track that our cars will ride on show our unique grief journeys. For example, if I feel really angry during my grief journey my track might drop. If I spend a lot of time feeling disconnected or depressed, my track may not have a lot of ups and downs. As your track gets longer, you can tape pieces of paper together to make it longer. You will also be invited to draw people and things you can do to help you get through this process. I might draw a few friends around my track that I can call when I’m feeling angry so I can talk to them.”

Step 4: Ride and Share
"As you go through your grief journey, use your coaster to remind yourself and others of where you are on your journey and how you are feeling. It can be a conversation starter for those who are supporting you."
 

 
Step 1: Fill out worksheet during the discussion. Step 2: Design the car.  
     
 
Step 3: "Track" your journey. Step 4: Ride and share.
opening_circle:
“Have you ever experienced a time in your life when you were extremely sad because you had to say goodbye to someone or something? Maybe someone in your family passed away, you lost a pet, or you had to say goodbye to your friends and your home because you had to move away. If you have ever been through something like this, you were probably feeling the emotion of grief. Maybe you are going through some kind of loss right now and you're in the middle of your grieving process and maybe you've never felt anything like this before. Whatever is true for you, it is OK and welcomed in this space. Today, you will be invited to explore these feelings or think about how it might feel to go through something like this. This workshop is going to help us understand more about grief and all the things we can go through during this time.

"How many of you have been on a roller coaster? Grief can feel like riding a roller coaster. But unlike any roller coaster we have been on, grief doesn't ask permission, it just takes us for a ride. It can unexpectedly go up, down, on twists and turns, and we can feel completely out of control. Unlike any roller coaster you know, grief coasters aren’t the most exciting and fun. But, by learning more about what we can expect from grief, the feelings that we can feel, we prepare ourselves and create some skills to help us get through it and maybe even identify some people who can help us along the way. No matter what we learn about our grief journeys today, know that all of our feelings are OK and they are always welcomed. Grief is not easy and we are all here to support each other along the way."

title: Letters of Gratitude
objective: Participants will be invited to cultivate gratitude through journal and letter writing.
materials:
• Gratitude worksheets
  • Lined paper or journals
  • White and colored copy paper
  • Envelopes
  • Pencils
  • Pens
  • Colored Pencils
  • Fine-tipped markers
  • Relaxing music
setup: Distribute worksheets, paper, journals, and all other art materials for easy access for all participants.
warm_up:
Play relaxing music to accompany the meditation.

“The act of being grateful can be a practice that is as easy as taking a deep breath and letting all of your senses guide you. As we go through this mediation, you might find that closing your eyes to tune out the outside world makes it easier to bring your awareness inward."
"Let’s start off by grounding ourselves…

Notice the rhythm of your breath, in and out....

Feel your feet touching the floor...

Notice your bottom meeting your chair...

Feel the weight of your body as you move your attention to your back...

Take a moment to extend your back as we take a deep breath in together…

Take another deep breath and allow your shoulders to relax…

Bring your attention toward gratitude and allow yourself to take this journey....

Observe whether your mind is in another place or here in this moment…

Find someone or something to appreciate…

Allow yourself to see them/it...

As the vision comes to your mind, take a moment to explore…
What faces to you see?

What objects?

Notice the colors are present....

The shapes and textures...

Do you notice any movement?...

As we take a deep breath in, notice the scents…

What smells are you taking in?...

Maybe it's the smell of nature…

Or a place that’s very familiar to you…

Let those smells take you back to a special moment, a special place, or person...

Taking in a deep breath and feeling your chest rise and fall…

Allow yourself to tune into any sounds…

Are the sounds nearby or far away?..

Is it the sounds of a person’s voice?...

A favorite song?...

The sound of nature?...

Or maybe it’s laughter…

Sense the feeling of gratitude that is alive in your body…

Listen to the sound of your breath as you take a deep breath in…

Welcome your sense of touch…

Notice the textures…

Can you wrap your arms around someone or something?...

Maybe you are cuddling....

Wrapped around something…

Allow your sense of touch to embrace you…

One last deep breath in and out…

Take a step back and take in the big picture…

All of the sights…

Scents…

Sounds…

And feelings…

Feel your heart open up and fill with appreciation…

When you are ready, you can open your eyes and begin your letters of gratitude. You can use any of the worksheets to help you with your process."
creation: Give gentile time reminders throughout the creation process.
closing: Welcome participants to share about their experience or creation.
optional_materials: Article: Gratitude Physically Changes Your Brain (Can be shared with participants or used for your reference.)

title: Self-Regulation Toolkits
objective: Participants will be invited to explore different tools to aid in self-regulation and create their own self-regulation toolkits.
materials:
• Pipe cleaners
  • Play-Doh or similar dough
  • Stress balls or other soft balls
  • Paper lunch bags or plastic zipper bags
  • Bubbles
  • Bottled water or cups of drinking water
  • Paper straws
  • Coloring books/pages (download mandala pages)
  • Crayons
  • Colored pencils
  • Markers
  • Display paper or white/chalkboard
setup:
Distribute materials on the table for easy accessibility. Make sure to have at least one item per person as they will be invited to pick and choose what to add to their bags. Write words, shapes, and symbols on a paper bag that can help with self regulation.

On display paper or a white/chalkboard, write down the different strategies for self-regulation.

  • Pause
  • Think
  • Visualize
  • Take Deep Breaths
  • Sip Water
  • Color/Doodle
  • Blow Bubbles
  • Keep Your Fingers Busy
warm_up:
“I’m going to invite you to find a participate in a paired sharing experience. If you would like to participate, I invite you to find a partner.

“Now that you’ve found your partner, I’m going to explain how paired sharing works. You’ll choose which one of you would like to speak first. I’ll put two minutes on the clock and you’ll talk about the prompt or any other thoughts you want to share with your partner.

“I’ll set a timer for two minutes and the first person will begin. After I call time, the next person will begin their two minutes. As a listener, try not to make this time a conversation but a time to witness and hear what your partner is saying.

“The prompt is: A time I felt dysregulated (not calm) was…”

Survey the room to make sure everyone understands the prompt and that they are ready to being. Once they are ready, begin the timer for two minutes. Give a gentle time reminder before the first two-minute round is up. Repeat for the second round.

Once everyone is done, invite a few participants to share back what they shared NOT what their partner shared.

“Thank you for those of you who shared and those of you who witnessed. "An important thing to remember about being dysregulated is that there are things we can do to get our brains back to a calmer state. I’d like to share some of them with you. As I’m sharing, I’m going to invite you to use any of the materials you see to follow along. You will also get time in a few minutes to create your own self-regulation kits that will have all of the things that can help you calm down."

Share the following techniques and give a few minutes after each technique for participants to practice.

  • Pause — This may be the easiest thing to do on the list. Taking a moment to pause and center yourself can be helpful. You can let people know that you are pausing by holding up your hand and saying, “I need a moment.”
  • Think — Bring to mind what you love about the child or a successful experience with the child. This releases positive neurotransmitters to balance out negative brain chemicals produced by frustration and stress.
  • Visualize — See the positive outcome in your mind. Practice visualization; it is a very powerful and effective tool not to be underestimated.
  • Take Deep Breaths — When we feel dysregulated, our body’s natural response might be to take short, quick breaths. Taking a moment to pause and take deep breaths can be helpful.
  • Sip Water — Sometime our bodies can be more sensitive when we are not hydrated. Taking the time to drink some and give your body what it needs. Even sipping from a straw can help calm you down! Sipping has been shown to help regulate the part of the brain that calms us down.
  • Coloring and Doodling — When practicing coloring and doodling, you can help your body reconnect to thinking and feeling. You can use coloring books and doodle to help regain those connections.
  • Blowing Bubbles — The deep breathing you need to blow bubbles helps relieve stress.
  • Keep Your Fingers Busy — Playing with soft objects like pipe cleaners, Play-Doh, and stress balls can help calm your nerves and improve focus and concentration.
creation: Now I’m going to give you some time to continue to explore all of these tools. Use your bag to keep any of your favorite tools in safe place. On your bag, you can write your name and any other words, shapes or symbols that remind you of self-regulation and feeling calm.
closing:
Welcome volunteers to share about their experience. Possible prompts:

  • I feel...
  • I learned...
  • How will you use your self-regulation toolkit?
  • If you could share one thing about what you learned today with someone who wasn’t here, what would you say?

title: Community Gratitude Tree
full_name: Rudy Hernandez special thanks to Theresa Black
objective: Participants will be invited to practice cultivating gratitude through paired sharing and contributing to a community tree.
materials:
• Craft paper roll or brown butcher paper
  • Leaf templates
  • White copy paper
  • Cardstock (white and/or multi-colored)
  • Pens
  • Pencils
  • Colored pencils
  • Markers
  • Painter’s tape
  • Masking tape
  • Hole punchers
  • Ribbon or string
  • Glue dots
  • Timer
  • Relaxing music
setup:
Prepare the tree on a vacant wall. You can use this tutorial to support you.

If you have the time, you can also make this tree with participants. Create a few leaf samples, with and without holes and ribbon/string. You can also draw an outline of a tree on a large piece of butcher paper or a white/chalkboard for a quick set up. If you are using leaf templates, print plenty for participants on heavy cardstock. You can cut each individual leaf out to save some time.
