“I’m going to invite you to find a partner to participate in a paired sharing with.”

“Now that you’ve found your partner, I’m going to explain how paired sharing works. You’ll choose which one of you would like to speak first. I’ll put two minutes on the clock and you’ll talk about any one of these prompts, or you might want to share about gratitude in a different way.  I’ll set a timer for two minutes and the first person will begin. After I call time, the next person will begin their two minutes. As we are listening, try not to make this into a conversation. You are invited to be a witness to what your partner is sharing.”

Choose two or three prompts for paired sharing:

  • I am grateful for...
  • The relationships I value are...
  • Today I enjoyed...
  • I smile and laughed today when...
  • I am proud of...
  • I appreciate…

Survey the room to make sure everyone understands each prompt and that they are ready to being. Once they are ready, begin the timer for two minutes. Give a gentle time reminder before the first two-minute round is up. Repeat for the second round.

Once everyone is done, invite a few participants to share back what they shared NOT what they heard.

Transition to creation and remind participants to hold onto their leaves until the end of the workshop.
creation: Give time reminders well before time is up. Invite early-finishers to journal about their experience on a blank piece of paper or create additional leaves to take home.
closing:
“Thank you for being present today and participating in the ways that you did. As a closing, I’m going to invite volunteers to share about their experiences and/or about what they wrote on their leaves. If you feel comfortable enough to do so, you can come up and add your leaves to tree after you share, or you can wait to add them when everyone else goes up. You can even hold onto your leaves and keep them for yourselves. It’s up to you. During this tree ceremony, I’ll ask that we respect our speakers as we continue to listen and witness.”

When all participants are done sharing, invite the whole group to come up to add to the tree. Give participants time to step back and take a look at the finished tree. Invite them to give themselves a round of applause.
optional_materials:
• Article: Gratitude Physically Changes Your Brain (Can be shared with participants or used for your reference.)
  • Small sticky notes (can replace leaf templates, hole punchers, painter’s tape, and ribbon/string)
introduction:
“Thank you for being here today. Before we begin, I want you to know that this is your Window of Time. It's a time for you to notice your thoughts, needs and feelings. During this time, there is no right or wrong way to participate or create. I'm going to share some instructions, but you get to choose how you want to participate. You can follow along completely, or you may want to do something different, it's completely up to you. During your Window of time, you get to choose. I am here to support you in any way that I can, so please ask for what you need.

“During today’s workshop, we are going to explore gratitude and create a community tree that captures all of our thoughts, reflections, and acknowledgments in one place.

“I’ll begin by talking about the art materials and creation steps, invite to participate in a paired sharing exercise with a brief share back, and then into creating. At the end of the workshop, we’ll have a closing tree ceremony when we’ll add our leaves to the tree.”

“Since this is your Window of Time, you get to choose how to participate and observing is participating. Everything I share today is an invitation and you are in control of how you accept or don’t accept the invitation. My hope is that you’ll honor what’s best for you. Any questions before we begin?”
demonstration:
Step 1: Capture Ideas
     
   

    Step 2: Cutting, Hole Punching, Adding Ribbon/String
     
   

    Step 3: Adding to the Tree

“The materials that we’ll be using are on the table. During this demonstration, I’m going to show you a few ways you can use the art materials to add to it, but since this is your Window of Time, you can use any, all, or none of these these ideas - you get to choose.”

Demonstrate the following materials and creation steps:

  • Example of leaves with words, shapes, and symbols
  • Hole punching process (thinking about how it will hang)
  • Adding ribbon or string to the leaf
  • Cutting on/around the black lines of the leaf
  • Adding tape to the back of the leaf (if not using template)

Creation Steps
These steps follow the template procedure. Modify the steps if you will be using sticky notes.

Step 1: Capture Ideas
Show samples of completed leaves with words, shapes, and symbols. Make sure to include samples on punched and unpunched samples.

“On your leaf cutouts, using words, shapes, or symbols, you are invited to write down what you are grateful for. Ideas can be be anything from names of people, things, and even memories. There is no right or wrong way to add to your leaves.

“If you are punching a hole on your leaf, think about how you want it to hang. Punch your hole and add your ribbon or string.

“Hold onto your leaves. You’ll be invited to hang them onto the tree during the closing of the workshop.”

Step 2: Cutting, Hole Punching, Adding Ribbon/String
“Once you are done adding to your leaf, cut around the black line using scissors. Punch a hole where you would like it to hang from and add ribbon or string. If you are taping it on/near the tree, you can skip the hole punch and ribbon/string. Add tape to the back and apply to the tree or during the closing tree ceremony.”

Step 3: Adding to the Tree
“At the end of the workshop, we are going to add our leaves to the tree, together. You can use tape, glue dots, or string to hang your leaves. You may want to keep some leaves for yourself to keep with you as a reminder.”
opening_circle:
“Sometimes it can be nice to take the time to pause and notice the people and things we are grateful for. It can also be great to reflect with a partner, and celebrate as a group. Today you’ll be invited to create a community gratitude tree that captures all of our thoughts, reflections, and acknowledgements of gratitude.

“Studies have shown that the more we practice gratitude, the healthier our brains are. By noticing the things around us that we are grateful for, it makes it easier to notice them in the future.”

You can share as much of the article as you’d like.

“Today, we are going to get the chance to practice gratitude by sharing with a partner and then creating a community tree to help remind us of the things we’re grateful for.”

title: Gratitude Tins
objective: Participants will be invited to reflect on and practice gratitude by creating a tin box that holds their thoughts, reflections, and acknowledgements.
materials:
• Small tin boxes, Altoids tins or any small box (one per participant)
  • Mod Podge or matte medium
  • Collage cutouts or magazines
  • Gratitude worksheets (Choose one or all to offer)
  • Permanent markers
  • Pens
  • Pencils
  • Brushes (for matte medium)
  • Colored pencils
  • Tacky glue
  • Copy paper
  • Scissors
  • Embellishments
  • Relaxing music
  • Large paper or white/blackboard
setup: Fill out a couple of examples of the worksheets with words, shapes, and symbols to show a variety of responses. Brainstorm on a blank sheet of paper to show that option as well. Create a couple of tin box samples, one that is completely done and one that is halfway done that you will use to show creation steps. Write down a brief outline of the creation steps and other important information about the materials that participants may refer to throughout the workshop.
warm_up: Remind participants of their options for brainstorming. Show where you wrote down the creation steps so all participants can refer to them when needed. Give participants about 10-15 minutes to brainstorm.
creation:
When you notice that all participants have transitioned into their creations, give a gentle reminder of the creation steps and invite them to ask you for what they need. Remind them that this is their window of time and there is no right or wrong way.

As participants begin to move into creating things to put inside their boxes, give gentle time reminders like, “In about 15 minutes, we are going to transition over to our closing. Feel free to continue creating during the closing.” If you have the capacity to do so, invite them to take supplies with them to finish or consider doing
closing: “Thank you so much for being present today and for witnessing and participating in your own way. Today we had a chance to reflect on gratitude and create something that we can use as a special reminder. I’m going to invite volunteers to share about their experience today. You can share a word or brief sentence about how it was to think about gratitude, how it was to create your box, or you can even just take a moment to hold your creation up for everyone to see.”
optional_materials: • Article: Gratitude Physically Changes Your Brain (Can be shared with participants or used as a way to prepare yourself.) Test
introduction:
“Thank you for being here today. Before we begin, I want you to know that this is your Window of Time. It's a time for you to notice your thoughts, needs and feelings. During this time, there is no right or wrong way to participate or create. I'm going to share some instructions, but you get to choose how you want to participate. You can follow along completely, or you may want to do something different, it's completely up to you. During your Window of time, you get to choose. I am here to support you in any way that I can, so please ask for what you need.

“Today’s workshop is all about gratitude. I’ll start off by doing a materials and creation demonstration so you get to see all of the art materials and what you can do with them. Then, we’ll talk briefly about what we are grateful for, fill out a worksheet to guide us in creation, and then create our boxes.

“Since this is your Window of Time, you get to choose how to participate. Even observing is participating. Everything I share today is an invitation and you are in control of how you accept or don’t accept the invitation. My hope is that you’ll honor what’s best for you. Any questions before we begin?”
demonstration:
Step 1: Brainstorm Ideas
   
 
  Step 2: Decorate Your Box
   
 
  Step 3: Fill the Box
   
   

“The materials that we’ll be using are on the table. First, you have the tin. This tin box is yours to decorate, write on, and design however you like. During this demonstration, I’m going to show you a few ways you can use the art materials to add to it, but since this is your Window of Time, you can use any, all, or none of these these ideas - you get to choose.”

Creation Steps

Step 1: Brainstorm Ideas
Show a sample worksheet that has been filled out. Show blank pieces of paper with brainstorming ideas as well.

“With or without a worksheet, you’re invited to brainstorm ideas that will help you with your boxes. You can list names and/or things you are grateful for. We also have blank paper for you to use if you don’t want to use any of the worksheets.”

“Think about the words, shapes or symbols you can use represent what you are grateful for. What colors represent your gratitude?”

Step 2: Decorate Your Box
“Using your worksheet to guide you, decorate your box with any of the art materials. I’ll show you some different things you can do, but again, you get to choose how you decorate it.”

Show the different techniques participants can use to decorate their box. Answer any questions about materials that come up and remind participants that they get to choose how to create.

Important techniques to demonstrate:

  • Using matte medium (also called “Mod Podge”) or glue to adhere paper and other collage items to the box
  • Writing words, shapes, and symbols before matte medium is applied as a finish
  • Adding embellishments
  • Using matte medium to finish the box

Step 3: Fill the Box
“Your box can be a safe place to keep your thoughts, reflections, and acknowledgements about gratitude. Maybe you want to keep small strips of paper with the names of the people you are grateful for. You can write a letter of gratitude and place it in the box so you can read it when you need a reminder of what you’re thankful for. You can even fold up the worksheet you created and keep it in your box for safe keeping.”
opening_circle:
“I invite you to take three deep breaths together and get our bodies ready to reflect on gratitude…

“As we settle in, let’s take a moment to think about gratitude. When we take a look in the dictionary, it says that gratitude is “the quality of being thankful, readiness to show appreciation.” This is what I’m going to invite you to do with me today, be thankful and show appreciation. The great part of today is that we get to do this your way.”

“In a moment, we’ll begin our brainstorm, but before that, I’ll invite you to share one word or a brief sentence about what you are grateful for.”

Thank participants for sharing and witnessing. Invite them to move onto brainstorming. As you transition them over to brainstorming, let them know that they are welcome to move right into creating after they are done. Since some participants may finish brainstorming before others, you can ask participants who finish early to be mindful of the other participants who haven’t finished yet when gathering their art materials.”

title: The Trauma-Informed Lens
full_name: Rudy Hernandez special thanks to Tiombe Wallace
objective: Participants will be invited to explore Trauma-Informed Care, trauma-informed approaches to Windows workshops, and create flash cards than can support them with workshop preparation and facilitation.
materials:
• Pencils
  • Pens
  • Colored pencils
  • Markers
  • Scissors
  • White or light-colored copy paper or cardstock
  • Paperclips, binder rings, or ribbon (for binding flash cards)
  • Hole punches
  • Timers (or something that keeps time)
  • Large display paper or white/chalkboard
     

Handouts, Worksheet, and Template (click links to download)

  • Trauma-Informed Care and Art handout
  • Trauma-Informed Care in Context handout
  • The Trauma-Informed Lens worksheet
  • Trauma-Informed Flash Cards template
setup:
Trauma-Informed Care & Art handout

If you have time before the workshop, create a quick sample of the The Trauma-Informed Lens worksheet as well as the flash cards. This will help you during the demonstration. Print one handout per person. You can print the flash cards template on white or light-colored copy paper (or cardstock for durability). Place other art materials within easy reach of every participant. On large display paper, write The Six Key Trauma-Informed Principles (found in the Trauma-Informed Care and Art handout), the discussion and closing questions. On a computer, set up the Tiombe Wallace video to show participants 

For display paper or white/chalkboard:

  • The Six Key Trauma- Informed Principles
    1. Safety
    2. Trustworthiness & Transparency
    3. Peer Support
    4. Collaboration and Mutuality
    5. Empowerment, Voice, & Choice
    6. Cultural, Historical, & Gender Issues
  • Discussion Questions:
    • What trauma-informed principles are you looking forward to using?
    • What is going well that you would like to continue?
    • What is something you can add to your action plan today?
  • Closing Questions:
    • What are you taking away from this workshop?
    • What is something you would like to learn more about?
    • What compassion or support do you need from others?
warm_up:
Trauma-Informed Lens handout with words and drawings.
       
       

Invite participants to find a partner or small group. Reassure them that it's OK to work on this activity alone. Give them a few minutes to get settled.

"Now have found who we will be working with, I'm going to bring your attention to the The Trauma-Informed Lens worksheet. This worksheet can help you as you participate in the next activity which is very simple. With your partner/group, I invite you to answer the following questions:

  • What trauma-informed principles are you looking forward to using?
  • What is going well that you would like to continue?
  • What is something you can add to your action plan today?
     

"You can go through this activity however you'd like, you can each give each other a set time to answer the questions using the timers. I'll also be giving time reminders as we go along. As you discussion is taking place, you can use the worksheet to capture thoughts, ideas, and anything else that can help you when we move onto creating our flash cards. You can use words, shapes, and/or symbols to fill in the workshops — there is no right or wrong way. I'll be giving you 20 minutes for this activity. Any questions before we begin?"

To help keep participants on track and aware of their time, you can give time reminders throughout the activity and reassure them that they can continue filling in their worksheet during the next section of the workshop.

"I hope everyone was able to discuss and learn more about what's already taking place in your workshops and what things are planned for the future? I'd love to invite a few people to share about their experience. Please make sure only share what you contributed to the discussion and not what you heard. If you would like to share what you heard, please get permission from the person who contributed before sharing.

"Thank everyone for participating in all the ways that they did, including observing. Invite participants to settle back into their seats in case they moved during the activity."
creation:
Completed flash cards.

"Now that we've talked about Trauma-Informed Care and trauma-informed approaches, you are invited to begin creating your flash cards. You can use your worksheet to help you with the process or to gather more information before you add to your cards. Remember, there is no right or wrong way to create. If you need anything, please let me know."

You can give time reminders throughout the creation process. For participants who finish early, you can invite them to plan their next workshop and/or envision how their experience will change how they facilitate.
closing:
You can post the closing questions where all participants can easily refer to them.

"Thank you all for spending this time with me and taking this window of time to learn more about how we can approach our workshops with a trauma-informed lens. Before we close, I would like to invite anyone who would like to share about their experience, their creation, or the answers to any of the closing questions displayed.

  • What are you taking away from this workshop?
  • What is something you would like to learn more about?
  • What compassion or support do you need from others?
     

"Thank you to those who shared and those were able to hold the space and witness. As you continue on your journeys as facilitators, I hope that you will take what you've learned and use it in your own unique way. Trauma-informed Care is not only knowing about the six principles we talked about today, it is the action that we take to put them forward. Thank you for taking the time to put this into action — your workshop participants are very lucky to have you."
optional_materials:
You are invited to use the following resources to help prepare you for this workshop or to utilize throughout any part of the workshop.

  • Video presentation from our February 2019 Facilitator Enrichment Training facilitated by Tiombe Wallace, Feminist Therapist, Trainer and Consultant.
  • Tiombe's PowerPoint presentation, Integrating Trauma Informed Practice.
  • Annotated workshop (Creating a Safe Place) explaining Trauma-Informed Principles
introduction:
"I want to start today's workshop off with a heartfelt thank you. If you are here today, you are part of something very special. What you do is needed, appreciated, and valued. As a Windows Facilitator, you have been given the opportunity to support those you work with to tap into their resilience as they move through and beyond trauma – as this is in addition to everything else you do outside of the workshop setting! For this, I thank you. Thank you for going above and beyond to listen, empower, and support every one of your workshop participants.

"Today is all about adding to your tool belt through discussions, activity, and a helpful takeaway that can support you in facilitation. As with all Windows workshops, this is your window of time. You are invited to notice your thoughts, needs, feelings, and visions. I am here to support you every step of the way. I'll be inviting you to participate in discussions, activities, and creation, but you get to choose how to participate — even observing is participating!

"The name of this workshop is called The Trauma-Informed Lens. We will begin by talking about Trauma-informed Care and trauma-informed approaches to Windows workshops. You will then be invited to participate in an activity followed by the creation of flash cards and a brief closing."
demonstration:
Trauma-Informed handout completed during activity.
   
 
  Capture ideas.
   
 
  Cut out and punch a hole.
   
 
  Add binder clip or ribbon to keep together.

"Today's workshop will be separated into four different sections: Discussion, activity, creation, and closing. I will walk your through each section and all of the handouts and materials you have available to you."

1) Discussion
We will begin by going over a couple of handouts, Trauma-Informed Care and Art handout and the Trauma-Informed Care in Context handout. You will be invited to reference these two handouts during our first discussion.

2) Activity
After our discussion, you will be invited to use The Trauma-Informed Lens worksheet to work alone, with a partner, or in a small group. You're invited to add words, shapes, and symbols to capture some of the main ideas from the discussion. This can prepare you for the next step. You are welcome to use the colored pencils, markers, and/or pens to support you in this activity.

3) Creation
"The discussion and activity will lead up to creating flash cards that you can keep with you as a reference tool. Using the Trauma-Informed Flash Cards template you'll be invited collect helpful trauma-informed tips, guidelines, reminders, etc. to aid in your workshop facilitation.

  • Capture Ideas
    You can use words, shapes, and/or symbols using the available materials. You might want to capture ideas from the discussion and activity or you can begin planning out how you would like to structure your workshops. Each flash card is titled with a workshop section, from setup to closing. You're invited to follow the headers or flip the cards over and use the blank side.
  • Cut and Punch Hole
    When you're done capturing ideas, you can cut out each card and use the hole puncher to punch a hole in the same area for each card. The template has hole guides for you.
  • Bind
    Using a paperclip, binder clip or ribbon, you can bind the cards to keep them together.

4) Closing
"Last, we will close the workshop with a quick recap and reflection. Those who would like to share about their workshop experience and/or creation will be welcomed to do so. There will also be optional questions to answer as part of the closing as well. Any questions about the our time today?"
opening_circle: Open up the workshop going through the Trauma-Informed Care and Art handout and Trauma-Informed Care in Context handout. You can read through each question while pausing for questions/discussion, or you can invite participants to volunteer to read different sections. If you have time, you can also show key slides from Tiombe's presentation, Integrating Trauma Informed Practice.

title: I CAN WE CAN - Sexual Assault Awareness Month
objective:
Adapted from the workshop, I CAN WE CAN, participants will be invited to notice the possibility and power that lies within them and make a commitment of what they can do to help end sexual assault. Participants will have the opportunity to creatively explore their commitment on a paper hand and then add it to a collective art piece.

Note: Due to the subject matter, this workshop can be triggering. Please consider all participants and settings when facilitating this workshop.
materials:
• Pencils

  • Markers (Permanent markers show up best on darker colored paper)

  • Colored pencils

  • Cardstock/heavystock paper (different shades of blue for Denim Day and turquoise for Sexual Assault Awareness Month)

  • Pre-cut paper hands:

    • Hand template - Child

    • Hand template - Adult

  • Adhesive dots or tape

  • Large display board (foam core works great)

  • Easel or something hold large display board

 

Optional:

  • Metallic markers

  • White correction pens

  • Gel Pens

  • Stickers/other adhesives
setup:
•  
      Sample of a drop-in workshop set up.
       
       
    You can print the hand templates onto colored cardstock and/or heavy stock or use the templates as stencils and pre-cut the hands.
  • Prepare your table with supplies for participants to easily access them.
  • Write the prompt on a large piece of paper for display: What can you do to help end sexual assault?
  • Consider creating a couple of sample hands — one for the center of the mandala to use a starting point and one to use as an example of the creation process.
  • If you are outdoors, keep the weather in mind, specifically wind. Keeping supplies in baskets, weighed down with rocks or books can help keep things tidy.
warm_up:
Invite participants to get into pairs or groups.

"I invite you to think together with your partner/group about a question. For ten minutes, you can use the time to discuss the question however you'd like. If you find yourselves in silence, that is OK. You can take the time to write down your thoughts, doodle, explore the art supplies or just sit in silence.

"The question I invite you to think and share about is: What are some ways you can help prevent/end sexual assault?

"As you're thinking about this, allow this time to be a stream-of-consciousness exercise for you. There is no right or wrong answer and there is no idea too big or small."

"Are there any questions before we begin? I'll be giving you time reminders along the way so everyone is aware of how much time is left."

If you notice participants struggling with the prompt, offer a few examples:

  • I can speak out against rape jokes.
  • I can speak out against blaming victims of sexual assault for their assault.
  • I can support causes that help survivors.
  • I can use social media to speak out against sexual violence.
  • I can learn about toxic masculinity.
  • I can listen to and believe survivors.
  • I can learn more about what I don't know regarding sexual assault.
  • I can encourage others to educate themselves.
  • I can share hotline numbers.
  • I can ask for consent.

"Thank you all for participating in the ways that you did, including those who choose to observe. I'll invite anyone who would like to share anything they like from their discussion."
creation:
An example of the I CAN paper hand mandala,
created at a community event.

"As we move into creating our paper hands, I invite you to think about one 'I can' commitment you want to put forward today. Your commitment can be anything you like. When decorating the paper hand, you can use words, shapes, and/or symbols to represent your commitment."

Give time reminders throughout the creation process.

If you notice participants finishing early, invite them to create an additional I can hand for the group mandala art piece.

You can also encourage participants to write about their experience and/or offer a journaling prompt such as, "What is one thing you can put into action after today?"
closing:
A completed I CAN paper hand mandala
   

"Thank you for all the ways you chose to participate in the creation process. I welcome anyone who wants to, to share anything about their workshop experience today.  For example, you are invited to share about what you created, what came up for you, or anything else about your experience with the workshop today."

After each person shares, welcome them to add their creation to the mandala on the display board. "When attaching your hand to the display board, be sure to orient the hand so the wrist faces the center of the board to create a mandala. You're also welcome to keep your creation as a reminder of your commitment."  After everyone who wants to share has done so, welcome those who have not shared, if they like, you to add their paper hand to the mandala.

"I invite you to take a look at what we created today. I hope you can feel the power in our individual voices coming together to support change.

"Thank you for taking the time to identify your I can commitment today.  Keep in mind that each and everything we do to help create awareness about the issue of sexual assault helps us move towards future free of sexual violence.  Your voice, your commitment and your actions are important."
optional_materials:
You can provide additional writing utensils like white correction pens, paint pens, metallic markers and gel pens. Stickers and other fun adhesives that don't need time to dry can give participants different options to express themselves. If you are outdoors, keep the weather in mind, specifically wind. 

This workshop can be great for community workshops focused around Sexual Assault Awareness Month and Denim Day. If you decide to include information about and/or focus the workshop on Denim Day we encourage you to share about the history of Denim Day and pre-print the paper hands on blue cardstock as blue is the color that represents Denim Day.

If you are holding space at a community event, download our Exhibit/Community Engagement Planning Guide to help you organize your ideas. AWBW offers $300 Community Engagement Scholarships to support you. Visit the Scholarships section of the website or click here to learn more.

These handouts from The National Sexual Violence Resource Center can be great resources for your workshop or community event.

  • Sexual Assault Awareness Month Event Planning Guide
  • I Ask for Digital Consent - cards
  • I Ask for Digital Consent - handout
  • Power Dynamics - cards
  • Power Dynamics - handout
  • A Guide for Friends and Family of Sexual Assault Survivors
introduction:
The following write-up can be used for a contained workshop setting for a specific amount of time or it can be used for a drop-in (where participants do not start and end the workshop at the same time, but rather drop-in at different times to participate) art workshop. If you are holding a drop-in workshop you can use this write-up for speaking points as you engage with people.

"Thank you for being here today. As we move through the workshop, everything will be an invitation. This means that you get to decide how to participate. You can follow all of my instructions or participate by observing, there is no right or wrong way to participate. This is your window of time, a place for you to notice your thoughts, needs, feelings, and visions for the future. I am here to support you with anything you need along the way.

"April is Sexual Assault Awareness Month and it's a chance to increase awareness about sexual violence. This workshop is focused on giving you an opportunity to think about what you can do to help end sexual violence. When we think about the issue of sexual violence it can seem overwhelming as it is so prevalent in our society. We may think to ourselves, what can I possibly do to help end such a big problem? However if each of us thinks of one thing, no matter how big or small, about what we can do to help end sexual assault and commits to doing it, that will help create change. In the workshop you will have an opportunity to creatively explore what I can you want to embrace in regards to ending sexual violence through creating on a paper hand.

"First I will share about the art supplies we have available to create and we will have a short discussion about sexual assault. Next, I'll invite you to take part in a partner or small group activity. Then you will be invited to create on a paper hand that you can add to a mandala, a collective art piece that forms all of our paper hands in a circle as a unified voice.

"As a reminder, there is no right or wrong way to participate and everything will be an invitation. Are there any questions before I move forward?"
demonstration:
"In this workshop you are invited to write, words, shapes, colors or symbols to represent what you can do to help end sexual assault on a paper hand.

"Keep in mind no I can commitment is to big or too small. Your pledge can be, 'I can share what I have learned' or 'I will believe people who tell me they are a survivor of sexual assault.'

"Choose the hand that speaks to you. Turquoise is the color for Sexual Assault Awareness Month and blue for Denim Day.

"We have different writing utensils to create on your hand. After you are done creating, you'll will have an opportunity to add it to the group art piece. If you like, you can create two hands - one for the group piece and one to take home.

"Any questions about the process before we move forward?"
opening_circle:
"Thank you for being here today. As we begin our conversation, I acknowledge that this topic can be heavy one. I invite you to take care of yourself and do whatever you need to feel safe.

"April is Sexual Assault Awareness Month. We're going to begin by talking about what sexual assault is. I welcome anyone who would like to share their understanding of what sexual assault means."

Pause and give a chance for participants to respond.

"Thank you to those who shared and those who observed.

"According to the United States Department of Justice, sexual assault is 'any type of sexual contact or behavior that occurs without the explicit consent of the recipient.' The term sexual violence is also a term that is used interchangeably with sexual assault.

"Sexual assault can be defined as one person forcing another person to have sex, or perform sexual acts, through coercion, manipulation, threats, physical restraint, or physical violence. It also includes touching or grabbing intimate body parts for sexual gratification. In addition, unwanted sexually obscene behavior toward a person (in person or via phone calls, text, e-mail, social media, or other types of online formats).

"Sexual assault happens anytime a person does not give their consent to interactions of a sexual nature. Usually a sexual assault occurs when someone touches any part of another person's body in a sexual way, even through clothes, without that person's consent.

"According to the National Sexual Violence Resource Center:

  • One in five women and one in 71 men will be raped at some point in their lives
  • In the U.S., one in three women and one in six men experienced some form of contact sexual violence in their lifetime
  • 51.1% of female victims of rape reported being raped by an intimate partner and 40.8% by an acquaintance
  • 52.4% of male victims report being raped by an acquaintance and 15.1% by a stranger
  • Almost half (49.5%) of multiracial women and over 45% of American Indian/Alaska Native women were subjected to some form of contact sexual violence in their lifetime
  • 91% of victims of rape and sexual assault are female, and nine percent are male
  • In eight out of 10 cases of rape, the victim knew the perpetrator
  • Eight percent of rapes occur while the victim is at work

"Sexual Assault Awareness Month and Denim Day are both opportunities to help raise awareness and learn about preventing sexual violence not only in our own lives, but the lives of others as well. Taking action can be a very important part of this process.

"When you think about taking action, please know that it can be as simple as telling someone what you learned today. There not an action too big or too small.

"Today, you will be invited to think about ways that you can take action and create an I can hand to symbolize your commitment."

title: I CAN WE CAN - Sexual Assault Awareness Month
objective:
Adapted from the workshop, I CAN WE CAN, participants will be invited to notice the possibility and power that lies within them and make a commitment of what they can do to help end sexual assault. Participants will have the opportunity to creatively explore their commitment on a paper hand and then add it to a collective art piece.

Note: Due to the subject matter, this workshop can be triggering. Please consider all participants and settings when facilitating this workshop.
materials:
• Pencils
  • Markers (Permanent markers show up best on darker colored paper)
  • Colored pencils
  • Cardstock/heavystock paper (different shades of blue for Denim Day and turquoise for Sexual Assault Awareness Month)
  • Pre-cut paper hands:
    • Hand template - Child
    • Hand template - Adult
  • Adhesive dots or tape
  • Large display board (foam core works great)
  • Easel or something hold large display board

Optional:

  • Metallic markers
  • White correction pens
  • Gel Pens
  • Stickers/other adhesives
setup:
•  
      Sample of a drop-in workshop set up.
       
       
    You can print the hand templates onto colored cardstock and/or heavy stock or use the templates as stencils and pre-cut the hands.
  • Prepare your table with supplies for participants to easily access them.
  • Write the prompt on a large piece of paper for display: What can you do to help end sexual assault?
  • Consider creating a couple of sample hands — one for the center of the mandala to use a starting point and one to use as an example of the creation process.
  • If you are outdoors, keep the weather in mind, specifically wind. Keeping supplies in baskets, weighed down with rocks or books can help keep things tidy.
warm_up:
Invite participants to get into pairs or groups.

"I invite you to think together with your partner/group about a question. For ten minutes, you can use the time to discuss the question however you'd like. If you find yourselves in silence, that is OK. You can take the time to write down your thoughts, doodle, explore the art supplies or just sit in silence.

"The question I invite you to think and share about is: What are some ways you can help prevent/end sexual assault?

"As you're thinking about this, allow this time to be a stream-of-consciousness exercise for you. There is no right or wrong answer and there is no idea too big or small."

"Are there any questions before we begin? I'll be giving you time reminders along the way so everyone is aware of how much time is left."

If you notice participants struggling with the prompt, offer a few examples:

  • I can speak out against rape jokes.
  • I can speak out against blaming victims of sexual assault for their assault.
  • I can support causes that help survivors.
  • I can use social media to speak out against sexual violence.
  • I can learn about toxic masculinity.
  • I can listen to and believe survivors.
  • I can learn more about what I don't know regarding sexual assault.
  • I can encourage others to educate themselves.
  • I can share hotline numbers.
  • I can ask for consent.

"Thank you all for participating in the ways that you did, including those who choose to observe. I'll invite anyone who would like to share anything they like from their discussion."
creation:
An example of the I CAN paper hand mandala,
created at a community event.

"As we move into creating our paper hands, I invite you to think about one 'I can' commitment you want to put forward today. Your commitment can be anything you like. When decorating the paper hand, you can use words, shapes, and/or symbols to represent your commitment."

Give time reminders throughout the creation process.

If you notice participants finishing early, invite them to create an additional I can hand for the group mandala art piece.

You can also encourage participants to write about their experience and/or offer a journaling prompt such as, "What is one thing you can put into action after today?"
closing:
A completed I CAN paper hand mandala
   

"Thank you for all the ways you chose to participate in the creation process. I welcome anyone who wants to, to share anything about their workshop experience today.  For example, you are invited to share about what you created, what came up for you, or anything else about your experience with the workshop today."

After each person shares, welcome them to add their creation to the mandala on the display board. "When attaching your hand to the display board, be sure to orient the hand so the wrist faces the center of the board to create a mandala. You're also welcome to keep your creation as a reminder of your commitment."  After everyone who wants to share has done so, welcome those who have not shared, if they like, you to add their paper hand to the mandala.

"I invite you to take a look at what we created today. I hope you can feel the power in our individual voices coming together to support change.

"Thank you for taking the time to identify your I can commitment today.  Keep in mind that each and everything we do to help create awareness about the issue of sexual assault helps us move towards future free of sexual violence.  Your voice, your commitment and your actions are important."
optional_materials:
You can provide additional writing utensils like white correction pens, paint pens, metallic markers and gel pens. Stickers and other fun adhesives that don't need time to dry can give participants different options to express themselves. If you are outdoors, keep the weather in mind, specifically wind. 

This workshop can be great for community workshops focused around Sexual Assault Awareness Month and Denim Day. If you decide to include information about and/or focus the workshop on Denim Day we encourage you to share about the history of Denim Day and pre-print the paper hands on blue cardstock as blue is the color that represents Denim Day.

If you are holding space at a community event, download our Exhibit/Community Engagement Planning Guide to help you organize your ideas. AWBW offers $300 Community Engagement Scholarships to support you. Visit the Scholarships section of the website or click here to learn more.

These handouts from The National Sexual Violence Resource Center can be great resources for your workshop or community event.

  • Sexual Assault Awareness Month Event Planning Guide
  • I Ask for Digital Consent - cards
  • I Ask for Digital Consent - handout
  • Power Dynamics - cards
  • Power Dynamics - handout
  • A Guide for Friends and Family of Sexual Assault Survivors
introduction:
The following write-up can be used for a contained workshop setting for a specific amount of time or it can be used for a drop-in (where participants do not start and end the workshop at the same time, but rather drop-in at different times to participate) art workshop. If you are holding a drop-in workshop you can use this write-up for speaking points as you engage with people.

"Thank you for being here today. As we move through the workshop, everything will be an invitation. This means that you get to decide how to participate. You can follow all of my instructions or participate by observing, there is no right or wrong way to participate. This is your window of time, a place for you to notice your thoughts, needs, feelings, and visions for the future. I am here to support you with anything you need along the way.

"April is Sexual Assault Awareness Month and it's a chance to increase awareness about sexual violence. This workshop is focused on giving you an opportunity to think about what you can do to help end sexual violence. When we think about the issue of sexual violence it can seem overwhelming as it is so prevalent in our society. We may think to ourselves, what can I possibly do to help end such a big problem? However if each of us thinks of one thing, no matter how big or small, about what we can do to help end sexual assault and commits to doing it, that will help create change. In the workshop you will have an opportunity to creatively explore what I can you want to embrace in regards to ending sexual violence through creating on a paper hand.

title: Claiming Who I Am - Training Version
objective: This workshop aims to provide participants with an opportunity to dispose of any negative messages they have received and create an art piece that supports them in claiming and celebrating their unique identities.
materials:
• Card/Heavy Stock paper 

  • Collage material

  • Journaling paper

  • Writing utensil

  • Colored pencils

  • Markers

  • Scissors

  • Glue
setup:
Possible Setup
         

You may wish to prepare the art supplies on the table for easy transition during the workshop. Click here to listen to AWBW’s Spotify Playlist - it contains hours of background music with no lyrics that can be used during your art workshops. You may also consider creating a creation sample in advance to show participants what it can look like. If you choose to do so, we suggest creating a simple sample, so that participants aren't overwhelmed by any "artistic" challenges.
warm_up:
Journaling (5 minutes):  

       
        I Can't Journaling
         

“For our warm-up today, I would like to invite you to a journaling session. We’ll have the opportunity to get rid of our “I can’ts” by noticing them, speaking of them to release them, and shredding them. First we’ll take a few minutes to do some stream of consciousness writing then we’ll have an opportunity to share and shred them. Before I give you the final instruction, please remember that this is your window of time and during that window of time you always have a choice of how you participate. I will be offering you a writing prompt; however, please feel free to journal about whatever is coming up for you during this time.” 

“I'm setting a timer for 5 minutes and I’m going to ask you to choose a piece of copy paper to represent your “I can’ts.” If you can’t find the right color feel free to use any of the papers on the table. Once you pick a piece of paper using a writing utensil, write the words “I Can’t…” on the top of the paper. When I start the time – just write without censoring yourself or worrying about grammar or spelling. This is just a practice of getting it out. Are there any questions, before we begin?”

You can start a timer for 5 minutes and play some calming music during this time. 30 seconds or so into the journaling you can give participants a reminder that there is no wrong or right way to do this, just keep writing even if it’s just the phrase “I can't" over and over again. I’ll tell you when to stop.

 

Group Sharing, Shredding and Processing (10 minutes):

       
        Shredding your I Can'ts
         

“Anyone who would like to share their “I Can'ts” is invited to do so in the chat box or by unmuting themselves. You are also welcome to get rid of your “I Can’ts” by shredding or ripping your paper. Please know that this is a durational art, space, and window of time for you, so if you would like to continue your journaling please feel free to do so. I want to offer that this is a space, for those who would like to share out loud and/or us this time to process, to be witnessed, to rip up and shred those “I can’ts” or to share your journey or something you are releasing.”

Allow some time for individuals to share, if they would like to do so.

“Please know that you are witnessed at whatever point in the process you are releasing or even just starting to contemplate saying goodbye to some of those messages that are not yours or things that are no longer serving you. Maybe they served at a certain time or were a part of your survival. Maybe they have scaffolded survival and the incredible leaps and bounds that you are doing right now and so we honor that and want to respect that  your journey has been growing from that point and that those “I can’ts” don’t have to be centered any longer. So thank you all everyone for being willing to share that with us.”

“At this time, I want to let us hold this moment of gratitude for what folx have shared, for what we are releasing. Maybe we can feel our feet on the same earth, let the chair or whatever area you’re sitting hold us up and be aware that we are held up together in community. That there is strength in even check-in on what we may let go of and there is strength in releasing and moving towards, claiming who you are. So we thank those who shared with us, who held those intentions in your heart and mind. As well as everyone who observed and witnessed us in community.”

We will start off with 40 minutes to claim and to create our “I Am” portraits  using any materials and in any way that allows you to express yourself. I invite you to hold this window of time to honor your feelings, thoughts, expressions, dreams and needs. I’ll check back in with an update and will check-in with our timing and where we are.
creation:
Worksheet Examples
             

During this time you may play some calming music and provide time reminders to participants when you are halfway or 5 minutes away from transitioning into the closing. 

Example of time reminder/check-in: “Gentle check in to see what our best plan is. If we would like anywhere from 0 to 10 more minutes in creating your “I am” portraits. You can let me know by putting your hands up and indicating how much time you would like. If you feel like your creative time is finished, then you can think about this as a durational time for yourself and maybe check-in on what you would like to remember or carry forward about your “I Am” portrait.”
closing:
Breakout room sharing (Virtual):

         
        Creation Made by Matt from Buffalo NY  
           
           
           
           
           
           
           
         
        Claiming Who I Am Worksheets  
           
           
           
           

“Please feel free to continue creating, journaling, sitting with your “I am” portrait and sending yourself those messages of claiming who you are. In a moment you will have an opportunity to share about the process of moving from “I can’t to I can”, or talk about what you created in your “I am” portrait or what you would like to carry forward. In the breakout room you will have two minutes each to share and it’s okay to hold space and witness for each other, in whatever way feels right for each person.

 

Group Share:

“Welcome back to our larger community space. Thank you all for what you held in your breakout rooms and what you witnessed for each other. I want to give some space for those of you who would like to share with us what you would like to remember, the process of creating your “Claiming Who I Am” portrait or your journey from I can’t to I can.”

Allow a moment for participants to share if they would like.

“I see so much kindness pouring out into the chat for everyone who shared, for everyone who moved through this workshop together. For the ways that we are releasing and together starting to say goodbye and shredding those “I can’ts” and claiming and reclaiming “Who I Am.” 

 

Chat Fall (Virtual):

“Before moving into a sitting exhibit, I want to invite everyone to a “chat fall” and pick one of the things you would like to exclaim and put an “I AM” in the chat. Let's all breathe in all the beauty of claiming I am, so anything you would like to exclaim for yourself and put an “I am…” lets all put that in that chat, if you would like.

“Thank you all! Let us hold some space in this moment for being witnessed, for being just where we need to be, being enough, valid, for absolutely claiming who we are and claiming our joy, healing, and enoughness.”

 

Mini Sitting Exhibit:

       
        Claiming Who I Am made by Barbara
         

“I invite anyone who is willing and those who would like to just witness with us, let’s hold up our “claiming who I am” and do our mini-exhibit.”

Allow some time for participants to hold up their creations.

“I see all the portraits, you are seen, you are heard, you are valid, I see you. Thank you for what you have created and the community, and the space of healing that all of you have contributed to in this time together.” 

 

Noodling:

“Just as a way to transition, I’m going to offer for you to do some noodling. I invite you to visualize yourself as some hard pasta or ramen noodles. Tighten up a little or squeeze yourself. Maybe you imagine yourself straight like spaghetti or curvy like ramen, or thick like some udon. You decide the type of noodle you want to be.”

“Now visualize yourself going into this hot, wonderful, warm water and let yourself noodle. Feel it go down through our arms, limbs, legs, whatever way it feels best for you. Just noodling and letting that energy noddle its way out in whatever way you need to, while also listening and respecting your own body and mobility needs.”

“Thank you all so much.”
optional_materials:
Claiming Who I Am Worksheet
         

For this workshop you are welcome to use any art supplies that will help you tap into claiming who you are. You are also welcome to utilize the workshop worksheet or any other materials that work best for you. If you are utilizing the worksheet in lieu of the regular workshop materials, be sure to send the sheet or print copies out for your participants beforehand depending on the setting.
introduction:
This workshop is called “Claiming Who I Am.” We are going to start this workshop slightly differently than the others by showing you a wide variety of supplies. We are doing this because we really want you to know that you have the freedom to choose, to express, to play in creating your “I am.” As always, keep in mind that this Window of Time is yours and you get to choose how you use it. You can use this opportunity to explore who you are or claim it. It’s up to you!

In order to set the foundation of safety and trust with the group, you are welcome to share the Workshop Agenda. For example: “First I would like to invite you to participate in answering a Group Question on "I can’ts to I can"; then I will welcome those of you who wish to participate in a journaling session followed by a moment to shred our "I can’ts." Next, we will go into processing and "I Am" sharing then I’ll invite you to Create. We’ll then have some time for Sharing in breakout rooms and sharing back with the big group at the end. Please know that every aspect of this workshop is optional and observing is participating too, so you get to decide how you choose to participate or create today.”
demonstration:
“As we move into claiming who we are, I’m going to share a little bit of the options and invitations. You may utilize the worksheet or anything that you find will help affirm your “I am” portrait. Something that I have done before, is use the shreds of the journaling that I did and color them and put my “I Am” around it. I started to write my “I am” on the old shreds, like a collage. We have provided these templates for you to use in your art creation, feel free to use them to outline an image, trace and cut out a head shape or use the template itself in your creation. You can also use the paper to create images, symbols or even words.”

“These are just ways to help us expand and know that anyway you choose to create your “I am” portrait is absolutely up to you. It is as unique a creation as you are. You may use this time to claim what you need, which may be silence, a moment to be in community or to simply recognize that where you are on your path to claiming who you are is a brilliant part of your journey.”
opening_circle:
Group Question & Share:

“Take a moment to think - what is one thing you have overcome that you thought you couldn't or were told you couldn’t?” (Pause for a moment) “You have moved through challenges and obstacles and likely have come out stronger because of them. So take a moment to notice anything that comes to mind about something you overcame even though you thought or were told you couldn’t. If you’d like, in a sentence or two, you can share what that thing was.”

You may pause, to allow others to share or you can model it and ask a volunteer to start.

Example: “I overcame the fear of speaking in groups. Just the thought of it made me want to crawl in a hole and never come out. I’m glad I did so I can be here sharing this with all of you. So, we are going to try to keep it to about 1 to 3 sentences or about a minute per share. Any volunteers?”

“Thank you all so much for witnessing and being witnessed in this space. As humans we like to make meaning of every experience and sometimes to protect ourselves we see things from a place of fear. We are biologically wired to do so in order to stay safe and we do it even when we are not aware of it. For example, Have you ever made up a story in your head about what people think of you without ever asking? Have you told yourself you can’t do something without even trying? That’s okay…You aren’t alone, we all do it. Oftentimes we get help in creating those stories in our head or and create a reality of what we can and can’t do based on messages or negative thoughts that we get from society, authority figures, the media or even ourselves. This affects how we see ourselves and what we are capable of creating in our lives. Today we are going to take those “I can’t” thoughts and feelings and put them to rest or let them go so that they don’t have a hold on us.”

title: A Book About Me / Un Libre Sobre Mí
objective: This workshop gives participants an opportunity to tell their own story by creating a book that focuses on themselves.
materials:
• Book template
  • Dice template (Print one or two on heavy cardstock for warmup activity.)
  • Pencils
  • Pens
  • Colored pencils
  • Markers
  • Rulers
  • Hole punchers
  • Stapler (one or two)
  • Ribbon or string
setup:
•  
      Book template
       
     
      Dice template
    Print the pages from the book template that you will offer to participants.
  • The book template includes a page of directions, multiple prompts, mandala coloring pages, lined pages, and blank pages. Over 50 pages to choose from!
    • Multiple prompts add variety and choice for participants.
    • Mandala pages can be used for those who finish their books early or for those who need a break to think of what to do next.
    • Lined and blank pages can be offered for participants to come up with their own ideas.
  • Pre-cut the the templates pages so you can display them individually on the table for everyone to see. This can also help participants choose their page order when they are ready to bind.
  • Prepare table with book pages and art materials within easy reach of all participants.
  • Have a few pages available to show different ways to bind.
  • Create a finished sample for participants to see during the demonstration.
  • For the intro activity, print and construct one or two dice templates and add simple "get to know you" questions. See examples below. You can simplify or deepen the questions depending on the age of participants. This activity will also help them get ready for their books as these prompts show up on the different pages.
    • What is your favorite color?
    • What is one thing you would like people to know about you?
    • What is your favorite food?
    • If you could travel anywhere in the world, where would you go?
    • What is one thing that makes you special?
    • If you were a superhero, what would your super powers be?
    • What is one of your favorite memories?
    • What are you most proud of?
    • If you had three wishes, what would you wish for?
    • Tell your favorite joke.
    • Say one thing about yourself.
    • What makes you happy?
    • What is one thing you want people to know about you?
warm_up:
"To get us ready to create our books, I'm going to invite anyone who would like to participate to roll the dice to see what question comes up for them. You can choose to answer the question, roll again, or share one thing about yourself. Before you answer the question, I'll invite you to say your name. As a reminder, this activity is optional, if you would like to participate, raise your hand and the person who just finished sharing will hand you the dice. Who would like to be our first roller?"

If you have two dice, invite participants to choose one question to answer.
creation:
"Now that we learned a few things about each other, I'm going to invite you to begin creating your book. Here are few reminders:

  • There is no right or wrong way to create.
  • You get to choose what is in your book. [If books are pre-bound, you can simply invite participants to skip the page if they don't want to fill it out.]
  • You can use the blank pages to add your own ideas to your book.
  • If you finish early or need a break, you can work on a coloring page.

Give time reminders along the way. If possible, you can reassure participants that they can finish their book later or even take extra pages to work on.
closing:
"Thank you for participating in the ways that you did. I'm going to invite anyone who would like to share. You are invited to share one page from their book or anything that you want about your experience today."

Before you close, invite participants to continue to share their books with each other and with other people outside of the workshop. Remind them that this is optional and they get to decide what to do with their books, even if they just want to keep it to themselves and never share it. If you'd like, you can invite participants to take extra pages with them to work on.
description: This workshop assists children in exploring feelings about their stay in the shelter. This is especially important because all children who come to the shelter have had to deal with numerous losses as explained in the manual section, “What Happens to Children When They Go to Shelters?”

title: The Facilitator in Me
objective: Participants will have the opportunity to explore what it means to be a workshop facilitator and celebrate success, express challenges, name and validate feelings, and create an art piece that represents themselves as a facilitator.
materials:
• Markers
  • Colored pencils
  • Construction paper in multiple colors (9”x12” or 12”x18”)
  • Glue sticks
  • Scissors
  • Person stencils
  • Feeling Target Template
  • Paper plates (for Feelings Target)
  • Beanbag or something soft that can easily be tossed
setup: Set art materials on the table for all participants to easily access them. Print out Feelings Target templates, cut them out, and glue them to paper plates. Place the paper plates on the floor with enough room for all participants to gather around them in a circle. You can also do the activity on the table top as well.
warm_up:
Depending on which version of the Feeling Target you are playing, invite participants to gather around the paper plates or bring their attention to the feelings chart on the tables. If using the tabletop version, invite participants to get into small groups and invite them to toss their coins or wads of paper onto the targets. For the tabletop version, you can invite group members to toss more than once if time permits.

“To help get us ready to create, we are going to start off with an activity called Feelings Target. How this works is I’ll invite anyone who wants to participant to toss the bean bag toward the plates. The plates have different feelings on them. Whatever plate you land on or get close to, you’ll have the opportunity to share a couple of sentences about the last time you felt this feeling as a facilitator. For example, “The last time I felt proud was last week when a workshop participant came up to thank me after a workshop.”

Give participants an opportunity to share. If you’re running out of time, you can say things like “We have time for two more people to toss.”

Thank participants for sharing and witnessing. Invite them to go back to their seats and begin the meditation.

"If you feel comfortable enough to do so, I’m going to invite you to close your eyes or fix your gaze on something in the room.

"As you begin to get comfortable in your chair, I’m going to ask you to take one deep breath in and out. Feel your the weight of your body in your chair. If there are any places in your body that you feel tension or uneasiness, do what you need to make yourself comfortable.

"Take another breath in and out, I’m going to invite you to put your facilitator hat on and in your mind, prepare yourself to facilitate. Think about all the different ways you prepare yourself. Maybe you’re thinking about what your participants need and are looking through the workshops online. Maybe you’re creating a sample. Or maybe it’s something else. What did it take for your to get to this moment? Acknowledge all of the thought and planning it took to get here.

"As we take another deep breath in and out, you are now facilitating. As you scan the room to see the individual or group you’re working with, what do you notice? What things are going through your mind? What do you notice as participants begin to create? Are you creating with your participants?

"Now that the workshop is over, take another deep breath in prepare yourself for the closing. How do you end your time with your participants. What questions do you ask. What do you want them to leave with? How do you express to them that you are thankful for all the ways that they participated?

"Take one last deep breath in. Knowing that your workshop is over, what feelings are going through you? Were you able to offer the workshop in the way that you wanted. What would you do differently next time? What would you do the same?

"When you’re ready, open your eyes and begin creating the facilitator in you."
creation: Give gentile time reminders throughout the creation process. As you notice participants finishing their creations, invite them to journal or think about the following question. “What does the facilitator on the paper need?
closing:
“Thank you for taking the time to notice the facilitator in you. For our closing, I’m going to give you an opportunity to share about your experience with a partner. If you would like to participate, please find a partner. During this paired sharing, each person will have one minute to share about their creation, their experience, or anything else they want. After one minute, I’ll call time and then you can switch roles and the other person can share for one minute. Any questions before we begin?

“Thank you all for participating in the ways that you did. I’ll give anyone who would like to share, the opportunity to share a word or brief sentence about their experience here today.

“As you leave here today, my hope is that your use your creations as reminders of your special role as a facilitator. A suggested place to put them is in your work space where you prepare workshops or even in the room where you meet with participants. It can also be a topic of discussion with your participants into your life as a facilitator. As a final closing, I'll invite those who want to participate in a mini exhibit to hold up their creations where they are to show to the rest of the room. Thank you all for being here."
optional_materials:
Additionally, you may also like to facilitate this workshop using printable worksheets. If you are utilizing the worksheets in lieu of the regular workshop materials, be sure to send a digital copy or print them out for your participants if you are meeting in person.

  • The Facilitator in Me Workshop Worksheets

  • Tabletop version of Feelings Target (print one for every four or five participants)

  • Coins or small wads of paper to toss
