introduction:
“Thank you for being here today. Before we begin, I want you to know that this is your Window of Time. It's a time for you to notice your thoughts, needs and feelings. During this time, there is no right or wrong way to participate or create. I'm going to share some instructions, but you get to choose how you want to participate. You can follow along completely, or you may want to do something different, it's completely up to you. During your Window of time, you get to choose. I am here to support you in any way that I can, so please ask for what you need.

“Today’s workshop is all about you, the workshop facilitator. As you know, being a facilitator is something that takes dedication and a huge heart. Each one of you goes above and beyond to support your participants by creating special windows of time - time that they may not usually get in their lives outside of the workshop setting. This makes your job a very special. Just like every one of your workshop participants is different, so are you as facilitators - we all have different needs, feelings, challenges, and styles. And just like your participants, all of these things need to be acknowledged, validated, and celebrated. And today, you’re going to have a chance to do just that. This is your window of time you to notice and validate your thoughts, feelings, challenges and celebrate your success. You will have the opportunity to create an art piece that represents you. The name of this workshop is called, The Facilitator in Me.

“We will begin by going over the art materials that are available to you. Then, you will have the opportunity to participate in an activity and relaxation that can help prepare us to create an artistic representation of ourselves as facilitators. After you create, you will have the opportunity to share with a partner and the larger group about your experience. Any questions before I begin?”
demonstration: “On the table we have construction paper, colored pencils, markers, scissors, and glue. After opening activity and relaxation, you’ll be invited to create a representation of yourself as a facilitator. You also have these people stencils that you can use if you’d like. Your creation can be a collection of words, shapes, and/or symbols that act as a reminder of all of your great attributes, your challenges, things you want to remind yourself of, or even things you aspire to be as a facilitator. The most important thing to remember is that there is no right or wrong way to create — you get to decide what your creation looks like.”

title: Riding the Grief Coaster
objective:
Participants will have the opportunity to learn about the five stages of grief and track their grief journeys by creating a roller coaster that can help them understand more about their feelings and who they can call on for support.

Inspired by The Five Stages of Grief developed by Elizabeth Kübler-Ross and David Kessler.
materials:
•  
    White copy paper or large white construction paper
  • Five Stages of Grief worksheet (one per participant)
  • Roller coaster car templates (one per participant)
  • Examples of roller coaster tracks for reference
  • Markers
  • Colored pencils
  • Regular pencils
  • Erasers
  • Rulers
  • Scissors
  • Transparent tape
  • Chalkboard or paper for displaying agenda and the five stages of grief
  • Background music
setup:
•  
      The Fives Stages of Grief worksheet.
       
     
      Car template
    Print the The Five Stages of Grief worksheet, car templates, and examples of roller coaster tracks.
  • Create a couple of simple samples of a completed worksheet, car, and track. Show the different stages of grief by labeling the track. You may want to create a sample of a long and short track.
  • Have several pieces of white paper of your choice for participants as they will be invited to tape pieces to create longer tracks as needed.
  • Display a brief agenda with creation steps as well as the five stages of grief for participants to refer to during the workshop.


The Five Stages of Grief

1. Denial: Not wanting to think that anything bad has happened. Can be used to protect us from feeling the pain of loss.

2. Anger: After denial goes away, reality can set in and we can become angry about many different things, even at people around us.

3. Bargaining: When we try make a deal with a higher power or someone to help make everything OK again.

4. Depression: After we have tried everything, the extreme sadness can set in when we begin to think about the person or thing we have lost.

5. Acceptance: We begin to be accept our loss and learn to live with it. This stage can help us move on.
warm_up:
"When we experience the loss of someone or something very special to us like a family member, friends, a pet, or even a home, we can go through what is called the five stages of grief. Not all grief journeys are the same, and we all experience these stages in different ways. We might spend more time on one stage than another or we may even skip a stage or experience them multiple times or never at all. Overall, these stages can be common when someone is grieving.

“Before we talk about the five stages, I’m going to invite you a moment to think about someone or something you have lost. If you can’t think of anything, that is OK, I’ll ask you to think of how it might feel to lose something or someone.

“As we talk about each of the stages, I’m going to pause to give you some time to think about a time you may have felt this way and fill in your worksheet. If you can’t think of anything to write, that’s OK, you might take some time to reflect on who/what you have lost. I will also welcome you to share other feelings other than the ones that are shared today. Your unique experiences are very important as we move throughout the workshop — I invite you to share anything you'd like. All feelings and experiences are welcome"

Note: Remind participants that not everyone goes through these stages and if they do, they may not experience them in this order or even at all. Be mindful to acknowledge and validate all feelings and experiences.

Refer to the different stages both on display and on The Five Stages of Grief worksheet.

The Five Stages of Grief

1. Denial: Not wanting to think that anything bad has happened. Can be used to protect us from feeling the pain of loss.

2. Anger: After denial goes away, reality can set in and we can become angry about many different things, even at people around us.

3. Bargaining: When we try make a deal with a higher power or someone to help make everything OK again.

4. Depression: After we have tried everything, the extreme sadness can set in when we begin to think about the person or thing we have lost.

5. Acceptance: We begin to be accept our loss and learn to live with it. This stage can help us move on.

As you go through each stage, invite participants to share their experiences. Give a few minutes after each section for participants to fill out their worksheet. Some questions you can ask are:

  • What other feelings or stages would you like to add or talk about?
  • How did you feel when you were going through any of these stages?
  • What did you do while you were feeling this or going through this stage?
  • What can you do in the future during these feelings or stages?
  • How did it feel to go from one feeling/stage to the another?
  • Did you reach out to anyone when you were going through these feelings?
  • What kind of advice can you offer others who may be going through this stage?
creation:
“Now that we’ve filled out our worksheets, it’s time to create our cars and coasters.”

Review the creation steps for participants and refer where you displayed them in the room. Invite participants to use the worksheets to help them with their cars and coasters.

Step 1: Design Your Car
"On your cars, I invite you to use words, shapes, and/or symbols to represent what you have lost. This might be a person’s name with their favorite colors on it, a drawing of a pet, or anything else that you have lost. Your car can be used as a tribute to who/what you have lost. Once you’re done with your design, you can cut the car out."

Step 2: "Track" Your Journey
“On a large sheet of paper, draw a track for your car to show the feelings you are experiencing or have experienced. Think about the five stages of grief as you show the changes in your track. Add your own feelings and experiences along the way. Labeling the reasons for each change can be helpful. You can also think about drawing people around your track that you can call on for support during this time. As you create, you may need more paper to make a longer track, feel free to use the tape and additional sheets of paper to make your track longer.”

Step 3: Ride and Share
“As you go through your grief journey, use your coaster to remind you of your thoughts and feelings as well as the people who can support you through these hard times.”

 

Step 1: Fill out worksheet during the discussion. Step 2: Design the car.
   
Step 3: "Track" your journey. Step 4: Ride and share.
closing:
“We covered a lot today and I want to thank you for being here. We talked about grief and the different stages we can go through and created cars and roller coaster tracks to represent our grief journeys. I’d like to invite anyone who would like to share to talk about their experience.”

Invite participants to openly share their experiences. You can assist by writing a few questions on the board to guide their thinking.

  • Who/what are you remembering today?
  • Would you like to honor someone/something you’ve lost by sharing a memory?
  • What did you learn about grief and your unique journey through it?
  • How will your roller coaster help you through your current experience or future ones?
  • Who are the people that can help you along your grief journey?
     

“Thank you so much for being present and participating in all the ways that you did. By being here, you have honored everyone and everything you have lost. What I ask is that you continue to honor not only who or what you’ve lost, but also the journey you take toward healing.”
optional_materials:
Since this can be a heavy topic and workshop, consider providing self-regulation tools such as pipe cleaners, Play-Doh, and stress balls. A good pre-workshop can be Self-Regulation Toolkits, found in our curriculum.

These books are good to have on hand for reference. You can also incorporate them into the workshop by reading specific parts aloud to the group.

  • On Grief and Grieving by Elizabeth Kübler-Ross-Ross and David Kessler
  • One Wave at a Time: A Story About Grief and Healing by Holly Thompson
  • Grief Day by Day by Jan Warner
introduction:
“Thank you for being here today. Before we begin, I want you to know that this is your Window of Time. It's a time for you to notice your thoughts, needs and feelings. During this time, there is no right or wrong way to participate or create. I'm going to share some instructions, but you get to choose how you want to participate. You can follow along completely, or you may want to do something different, it's completely up to you. During your Window of time, you get to choose. I am here to support you in any way that I can, so please ask for what you need. Any questions before I begin?"

“Today’s workshop is all about the feelings we can go through when we lose someone or something very important to us. Sometimes in life, we experience the loss of a family member, a friend, a pet, or even a home. These feelings can feel like we are on a roller coaster. We’ll get a chance to talk about these feelings and create a roller coaster to track our feelings and help those around us understand what we are going through.

“To begin, I’m going to go over the art materials and steps we can take to create our roller coasters. Then, we’ll talk about the five stages of grief, gather our thoughts and ideas and begin creating our roller coasters. Any questions before we begin?”
demonstration:
“On the table we have markers, colored pencils, regular pencils, rulers, and tape. We are going to be using a worksheets to gather our thoughts and ideas for our roller coaster. Each of you has a car to design and white paper that you will use to create your track.”

Steps for Creation:

Step 1: Discussion and Worksheet

Show a sample worksheet. “We will be starting off by discussing the five stages of grief. As we are discussing, I’ll be pausing so you can take a few minutes to fill out each section of the worksheet. If you don’t get to finish each section, it’s OK, you can always go back and spend some more time on it. The ideas that you gather can help you learn more about your feelings and help prepare you for designing your track."

Step 2: Design the Car
“Each of you has one car to design. On your cars, you will be invited to use words, shapes, and/or symbols to represent what you have lost. This might be a person’s name with their favorite colors on it, a drawing of a pet, or anything else that you have lost. Your car can be used as a tribute to who/what you have lost. Once you’re done with your design, you can cut the car out."

Step 3: "Track" Your Journey
“Last, we will create a track that our cars will ride on show our unique grief journeys. For example, if I feel really angry during my grief journey my track might drop. If I spend a lot of time feeling disconnected or depressed, my track may not have a lot of ups and downs. As your track gets longer, you can tape pieces of paper together to make it longer. You will also be invited to draw people and things you can do to help you get through this process. I might draw a few friends around my track that I can call when I’m feeling angry so I can talk to them.”

Step 4: Ride and Share
"As you go through your grief journey, use your coaster to remind yourself and others of where you are on your journey and how you are feeling. It can be a conversation starter for those who are supporting you."
 

 
Step 1: Fill out worksheet during the discussion. Step 2: Design the car.  
     
 
Step 3: "Track" your journey. Step 4: Ride and share.
opening_circle:
“Have you ever experienced a time in your life when you were extremely sad because you had to say goodbye to someone or something? Maybe someone in your family passed away, you lost a pet, or you had to say goodbye to your friends and your home because you had to move away. If you have ever been through something like this, you were probably feeling the emotion of grief. Maybe you are going through some kind of loss right now and you're in the middle of your grieving process and maybe you've never felt anything like this before. Whatever is true for you, it is OK and welcomed in this space. Today, you will be invited to explore these feelings or think about how it might feel to go through something like this. This workshop is going to help us understand more about grief and all the things we can go through during this time.

"How many of you have been on a roller coaster? Grief can feel like riding a roller coaster. But unlike any roller coaster we have been on, grief doesn't ask permission, it just takes us for a ride. It can unexpectedly go up, down, on twists and turns, and we can feel completely out of control. Unlike any roller coaster you know, grief coasters aren’t the most exciting and fun. But, by learning more about what we can expect from grief, the feelings that we can feel, we prepare ourselves and create some skills to help us get through it and maybe even identify some people who can help us along the way. No matter what we learn about our grief journeys today, know that all of our feelings are OK and they are always welcomed. Grief is not easy and we are all here to support each other along the way."

  • Create a couple of simple samples of each template.

  • Write the creation steps and closing prompt on separate large papers to display during the workshop.
    Creation Steps:
    Step 1: Filling in the brick wall (using template 1)
    Step 2: Removing a brick (using template 2)
    Step 3: Beyond the brick wall (using template 3)

    Closing Prompt:
    Once I take a look at these bricks such as ________, then my vision is clear. What's beyond the wall is _______.
warm_up:
"Today we have an opportunity to explore the bricks that we, others, society, and circumstances place before us. I'll invite you to start thinking about the bricks that make up the wall in front of you right now. Could it be the educational system, your environment, or could it even be your household? What else comes to mind? Would anyone like to share about what comes up for them when they think about these bricks"

Give participants some time to think about these questions. You can also ask questions to get them thinking about placement of their barriers/bricks they will be adding to the brick wall template. Do you want to put the "heaviest" bricks on the bottom, in the center, staggered throughout or somewhere else completely?
creation:
"Now that we've talked about some of the things locking us up and keeping us from our goals and future, it's time to add them all to our brick wall." Throughout the creation process, continue to offer verbal reassurance and remind them that nothing is impossible. Refer to the steps written on the large paper.

Step 1: Filling in the brick wall (template 1)
"I invite you to start filling in your brick wall (using the brick wall template) with all of those 'bricks' you've identified for yourself. You can write words or draw symbols of all those things that make you feel trapped."

Step 2: Removing a brick (template 2)
"You are invited to choose one brick to focus on removing today from the wall barrier. Sometimes it helps to start with the easiest brick to remove. Which brick would be the most realistic for you to remove from the wall barrier? You don't have to pick the easiest brick. Maybe you want to pick the one that is the most heavy to you or the one that seems the hardest to break through. Remember we are all here as one. Whichever brick you choose is relevant to you today. We all have bricks before us. I'm no different than you and you are no different than me." (Here you demonstrate and remind them of your sample brick.)

"You can use any of the art materials here today to help you create your personal brick. Whichever brick you chose, I'd like to encourage you to express yourself fully. You can use a word in graffiti or the word being fragmented or shattered. You can create an image of what it feels like or looks like to you. There are no rights or wrong in expressing yourself through art."

Once they are done, invite participants to share about their bricks.

Step 3: Beyond the brick wall (template 3)
"Now that you have worked on breaking through the first brick of your wall barrier, I invite you to look at your brick wall again looking at the words you have written on the bricks. If we/you were to remove those things one at a time you can start to dream again, and your vision would become clearer to you. So with that being true, now you can draw, color, or write about what's beyond the wall. What was the dream you always had that belongs to you? What does it look like? What would it look like? It can be a small dream or a big dream. What dream jumps out at you? Once you remove those bricks that where placed in front of you, by society, life circumstances etc. Go ahead and beautify through expression what's beyond the wall."
closing:
"We covered a lot today and I want to thank you for being here participating in the ways that you did. We talked about how our situations and circumstances can create a barrier that can block our view of our dreams and goals for our future. We were able to create a brick wall to show us visually what we are up against, and then began to start breaking it down one brick at a time to rediscover our future. I invite all of you to keep working towards removing those bricks, asking for help for those bricks that need extra support to be removed, working towards solutions to break through those bricks."

If time allows, create a circle and invite participants to openly share their experiences. You can offer this prompt to guide them.

"I invite you to use the following prompt to share with us today. You can hold up any of your templates to support you."
        Once I take a look at these bricks such as __________, then my vision is clear.
        What's beyond the wall is __________.

"I invite all of you to take your "Beyond the Wall" image and place it on your dorm's wall, cottage or sleeping place so you can always be reminded of “What’s Beyond the Wall" especially in times of discouragement or feelings of disillusion you have this tool to help inspire you and build the courage needed to continue on this phase of your life. Thank you for sharing such intimate and personal things with all of us. That’s courage. I feel privileged to walk with you."
introduction:
“I’d like to welcome you today and introduce myself (and my organization and/or why I do this work, etc). Before we begin, I want you to know that this is your Window of Time. It's a time for you to notice your thoughts, needs and feelings. During this time, there is no right or wrong way to participate — even observing is participating. You can follow along completely or you may want to do something different, it's completely up to you. During your Window of Time, you get to choose. I am here to support you in any way that I can, so please ask for what you need. Any questions before I begin?

"I want to invite you to participate in the “What’s Beyond the Brick Wall?” Project. (If there is a window nearby, point to it to help you symbolically and visually). Being behind these walls or with our daily routine, we can become discouraged or at times disillusioned. This can make us forget about our dreams and goals we once had. Also by "doing time" our dreams and goals can seem so far from reach. But today we have an opportunity to explore these bricks that make up this wall of incarceration, the bricks that we put for ourselves, maybe the ones that society has placed before us, or the ones that just seem very hard to break through. You might think of these bricks as barriers. Today you'll be invited to not only see these barriers, but to look beyond them to a future that you envision for yourself."

Note: Acknowledge each participant and invite them into the space by learning their first name (not the moniker given to them by the streets or last name commonly used by probation department to address them). This helps remind them of the name given to them by their loved ones. To help give participants a window to your sincerity and to help create a safe space, a personal story is always welcomed or those of participants that you worked with in the past that are signification to the space you are creating.
demonstration:
The demonstration will vary based on what materials you are allowed to bring into the workshop setting. Be mindful of showing all material possibilities to participants. If possible, make different samples that have used all material options.

"Today we are going to be working with different materials and three different templates. We will start off with a discussion about our bricks or barriers and we will use the full page of bricks. We will then move on to identifying one brick that we would focus on and possibly remove from our wall. The last template we will use is the wall template with the some bricks missing. This will give you an opportunity to visualize what's beyond the brick wall with those barriers removed. As a reminder, these materials and templates are here to guide you in your process, you don't have to use them. There is no right or wrong way to participate, even observing is participating."

Give the participants a few minutes to explore the materials and templates. Show some finished samples.

title: A Window to Your Soul: Community Tile Wall Project
objective:
This workshop invites participants to reflect on someone/something they go to for inspiration, create art to represent it and add it to a community art piece.

Note from the author: This workshop will allow the participants to share a glimpse of who they are by reflecting on a person, a place or an object of importance. They can give the world a glimpse of something they are carrying that can weigh heavy on them, or a thing that they can turn to for inspiration and motivation. This workshop aims to help participants find commonalities in their stories and experiences. By the end of this workshop, a community tile wall can help portray the message of “There is no us, and them, only us." One in unity.
materials:
• Window to Your Soul worksheets (2 pages- landscape and portrait orientation)

  • 4" x 5" cardstock

  • Video of Fabian introducing A Window to Your Soul (begins at 1:15)

  • Color pencils

  • Markers

  • Pastels

  • Graphite pencils

  • Masking tape

  • Painter's tape

  • Empty wall space or large presentation board to display art.
setup:
• Print both pages of A Window to Your Soul worksheets for each participant. (They can choose which orientation the want.)
  • Create samples of a completed worksheet and final tile to share with participants.
  • Write down the agenda for the day:
    • Step 1: Worksheet
    • Step 2: Paired Sharing
    • Step 3: Create Your Tile
    • Step 4: Brining Our Art Together
  • Find a blank wall or presentation board to display participants' artwork.

If you’d like we you can have a sample of a previous work done by other (incarcerated) or participants. If you would like to make one yourself as to have for as a sample that would only help bring connection and openness for those participants.

Note: If working with participants who are institutionalized, all supplies should be counted thoroughly with an inventory list and ready to hand out as needed as to help keep track of what is being used. Materials should be spread out visually on a separate table if placing supplies on their table is not available due to space. Temptation for these incarcerated participants to gain an art tool is at hand, for they are limited in the institutions. Explain on the importance of this group and materials are ours and in order to continue having these groups we all need to care for our materials being returned and accounted for, be mindful in delivery not judgmental).
 

Worksheet with art space in portrait orientation.

Worksheet with art space in landscape orientation.
warm_up:
Worksheet:
Hand out the worksheets for each participant.

"To open up the space to our energy, I'm going to offer something for you to think about. When I give you the prompt, I'll invite you to sit for a moment to think about it and let it soak in. Something might automatically come to mind or it might take you a few minutes to think of something, however long it takes is fine. Your worksheets are here to guide your thoughts and the design of your final art piece.

"Today I invite you to think of a person, place, or thing that you go to for inspiration. You might also think about someone/something you would like to revisit to work on something that's been holding you back. I'll give you about 15 minutes to think and fill in your worksheet. I'll be giving you time reminders throughout this process."

Paired Sharing:
"I'm going to invite you to find a partner that you'd like to work on this next section with." Give participants a moment to find their partners.

"Now that you have your partner, decide who will speak first and who will listen. Each of you will have 2 minutes to be the speaker and 2 minutes to be the listener. I will give you time reminders and letting you know when to switch from listener to speaker. During your time as a speaker, you can share anything that came up for you when you thought about the prompt. You can even share about what you are planning to create for your final art piece. As a listener, try not to make this process a discussion, your role is to listen and witness what is being shared with you. Any questions before we begin?"

Bring the group back together and if time permits, ask for a few volunteers to share what they shared or what is coming up for them during this time. To honor confidentiality, ask participants not to share what anything their partner shared with them.
creation: Invite participants to begin creating on their cardstock. Give gentle time reminders.
closing:
Completed tile wall.

Putting Our Art Together:

Bring participants back to the group space. Invite them to sit with their art for a moment and think about what came up for them. Before participants share, ask them if it's OK for you to add their creation to the community display.

After all volunteers have shared, ask those who didn't share if they would like to add their art to the community piece. Once the collection is complete, invite participants to take it all in. You can ask them to notice similarities they noticed from what was shared or from what they are seeing on display.

As you close the workshop, point to the wall and let participants know that it represents that there is no us and them, only us. Thank all participants for showing up and participating in all of the ways they did. If you will be leaving the artwork on display, make sure it's OK with participants who contributed their art. Give them the option to leave it up or take it with them.
introduction:
Fabian demonstrating the window to your soul.

See Fabian introduce A Window to Your Soul in this video (begins at 1:15). You can use this for your reference and/or you can show it to participants.

“I’d like to welcome you today and introduce myself (and my organization and/or why I do this work, etc). Before we begin, I want you to know that this is your Window of Time. It's a time for you to notice your thoughts, needs and feelings. During this time, there is no right or wrong way to participate — even observing is participating. You can follow along completely or you may want to do something different, it's completely up to you. During your Window of Time, you get to choose. I am here to support you in any way that I can, so please ask for what you need. Any questions before I begin?

Point out the rough outline of the workshop for participants to refer to throughout the workshop:

  • Step 1: Worksheet
  • Step 2: Paired Sharing
  • Step 3: Create Your Tile
  • Step 4: Bringing Our Art Together (Closing)

Hold the cardstock up and ask participants what they see. Wait a few minutes to gather feedback. Place the cardstock on your chest and say that this is a window to their soul.

"Today's workshop is called, A Window to Your Soul. We will be starting off with a discussion where I will be inviting you to think about a something. I'll be giving you a worksheet to gather your thoughts and to practice by sketching what your final art piece will look like. You will have the opportunity to discuss your thoughts with a partner during a paired sharing exercise and prepare to make your tile."
demonstration:
Go over the different art materials that are available to the participants. Show them samples of the completed worksheet and final tile. Remind participants of the agenda for the day.

  • Step 1: Worksheet
    • The worksheet can be used to sketch out the final design. Invite participants to design their artwork in portrait or landscape orientation. See examples to the right.
  • Step 2: Paired Sharing
    • You will be invited to find a partner and discuss what you came up with and talk about your final design.
  • Step 3: Creating Your Tile
    • On the cardstock/canvas, you will create your final design
  • Step 4: Bringing Our Art Together (Closing)
    • We will bring the group back together and bring our art together on the wall.

title: Intersectionality Masks
objective: In this workshop, participants will have an opportunity to explore their identity through an intersectionality lens.  Specifically examining their social location within the dominant culture and how this affects “who” you are (as you see yourself) and “who” you are perceived to be by others.
materials:
Completed Intersectionality Mask
  • 3D Masks or Print outs of paper mask (print on card stock)

  • Collage items

  • Clear Tacky Glue or Mod Podge

  • Paint brushes

  • Water cups (2 per person)

  • Multicultural paint pallet

  • Paper towels

  • Strips of scrap paper to write words (Copy Paper works well for this)

  • Scissors

  • Black sharpies
warm_up:
Sample table set up  

You can facilitate option 1 or 2 or both.

Option 1: Inside/Outside Journaling

"Consider your experiences of privilege/status, power, race/ethnicity, class, gender, and sexuality/sexual orientation, ability status, religion, etc.

I invite you to take a piece of paper and divide it into two columns. On one side, write ‘Inside’ and on the other side, write ‘Outside.’
Fill the first side of the page with any words, shapes, colors or symbols that describe how you feel on the inside, and on the other side of the page write any words, shapes, colors or symbols that describe the ‘you’ that people see on the outside. Try not to think too much as you write. Allow the words to flow naturally.

If you get stuck in one column you can move on to the next and you can return to the first one later. After you are done, you can take a moment to observe the words that you wrote without any judgment."

Option 2: Exploring Social Identities Worksheet

Pass out the Exploring Social Identities Worksheet and invite participants to use the directions on the sheet to provide guidance when filling it out.

Time permitting: Offer participants an opportunity to share any discoveries, feedback, reflections, etc. about the warm-up activities(s).
creation:
Outside of completed mask Inside of completed mask  

"Now you have an opportunity to design a mask that reflects your intersectionality. You can be as creative as you’d like when making your mask.  You can follow the guidelines, go in a totally new direction, play with the art supplies, etc. Remember that observing is participating.

Here are some possibilities for what you can include on your mask:

  • The outer part of the mask can reflect how others perceive you. Think about colors, words, phrases, concrete objects, symbols and other representations that symbolize who others perceive you to be.  You’re invited to place these items on the outer side of your mask.

  • The inner part of the mask can reflect how you see yourself.  Once again, think about colors, words, phrases, concrete objects, symbols and other representations that symbolize who you are.  You’re invited to place these items on the inside of your mask.

  • We welcome you to reflect on the interactional experience and intersectionality of identity; that is, examine how others perceive you and its effects on your life experiences even if your own perceptions differ.

  • Be creative! It doesn’t have to make sense to anyone else.

  • You will have a chance to share about your experience, what you created, etc. at the end of the workshop."
closing:
Thank folks for honoring the way they chose to participate.  Provide participants an opportunity to share anything about:

  • What they created

  • Meaning ascribed to the mask

  • Feelings during and after creating the mask
notes: If participants use paint brushes to apply Mod Podge or Clear Tacky Glue make sure to wash them right after the workshop ends as if the glue dries it can ruin the paint brush.
optional_materials:
Strips of paper, embellishments, etc. for the masks

Embellishments (stickers, gems, etc.)
Glitter Glue
introduction:
Precut collage items from magazines  

"Before we begin, I want you to know that this is your Window of Time. During this time, there is no right or wrong way to participate or create. I'm going to share some instructions, but you get to choose how you want to participate.  During your Window of time, you get to choose.

In this workshop, you will have an opportunity to explore your identity through an intersectionality lens.  Specifically examining your social location within the dominant culture and how this affects “who” you are (as you see yourself) and “who” you are perceived to be by others."
demonstration:
"Before we move into the warm-up I wanted to give you some information about the art supplies available.  You can use the paint pallet, water cups and paint brushes to paint your mask.  We provided you with a white mask and a multicultural paint pallet so you can create the color the best represents your skin.

If you don’t paint the mask:

  • You can write directly on the mask using markers, colored pencils, sharpies, etc.

If you do paint the mask:

  • Do not write directly on the mask with markers as it will not work well and will ruin the markers

  • You can write on strips of paper using permanent markers and then use Mod Podge or Clear Tacky Glue to adhere words, images, etc. to your mask.

  • Can also use the Mod Podge or Clear Tacky Glue to attach other collage items, different types of paper, embellishments, etc.

    • Mod Podge and Clear Tacky Glue can be used as an adhesive and as a top coat

    • You can apply Mod Podge and Clear Tacky Glue using paint brushes, foam brushes or your fingers

Remember that all the art supplies are optional, you get to use whatever you like to create."

title: Virtual Art Workshop Facilitation
objective: Tips and resources on how to facilitate virtual art workshops.
extra_field:
Rose Curtis holds up her Inside/Outside
creation for her participants to see.
   
 
  Facilitating from home, Stacia Kato holds
up her Personal Needs Flower.
   

Virtual Art Workshop Facilitation

Depending on different circumstances, it can be challenging to physically meet with your workshops participants. Virtual art workshop facilitation is a great solution to this. Even though in-person workshops are ideal, meeting with your participants can be equally beneficial. We have compiled a list of resources, tips, and best practices to prepare you to facilitate virtually while maintaining safety, confidentiality, and fun! As you read watch videos and read through the information, make sure to share your experience back with us.

Video Resources:

  • Exploring Virtual Art Workshop Facilitation

  • Sample Virtual Art Workshop Facilitation

Other Resources:

  • Virtual Workshops 101

A Learning Journey

Given that this may be new for you and for your participants, proceed with gentleness. Learning new technology can feel stressful and even trigger a trauma response. Practicing your grounding tools and making room for lots of imperfections helps. We hope these tips can make learning a little more stress-free and even fun!

What Technology?

There’s a whole spectrum of tools. What’s best depends on you and your group. For example:

  • Conference Call — Could be your best tool if you are facilitating an outreach group, for example. Your participants can join wherever they are, even while walking.

  • Facebook Live — An incredible way to broadcast and record your facilitation so it’s accessible long term for folks to view when they have a safe space and time to do so.

  • Zoom — Most similar to in-person workshops, those who have RSVP’d can enter the “room,” capability to see and hear each other, chat, raise hands, and break into pairs for sharing.

  • Other free virtual meeting options

  • Creating Inclusive Virtual Spaces

  • Information about technology safety for online groups and services for survivors

What Supplies?

Flexibility and variety is the name of the game here. You might:

  • Encourage folks to gather whatever supplies they have on hand

  • Reassure them that any supplies are OK - pencil or pen and paper are great, or even just their body and breath! 

As you facilitate, it will be important to seek language that is inclusive of the many materials folks may have. If you are facilitating via conference call as participants walk, you might offer finding a pebble or scrap, taking a photo along the way, moving one's body, or sharing a word as options for creative expression. Bottom line, the most important “supply” we all bring is simply our presence, our body, our heart, our breath.

The Window of Time

Whatever supplies we have or don’t have, pausing to hold a window of time together can be transformative. 

  • As with in-person workshops, each aspect of the virtual workshop should be an invite or an offering.

  • This space of listening deeply to ourselves, following our inner guidance can be very special. We have the opportunity to connect deeply within ourselves and with each other.

  • Whatever emerges from this space, be it a sketch, a word scribbled on a paper, a hand gesture, a thought, a twig adopted from the ground, may it be a resource to access our own strength and vision.

   
  Body scans are a great way to prepare participants to create. Sharon Uy joins her participants as she facilitates.  
     
       
  Karen Gonzalez guides her participants through a meditation.  
     
   
 

Eunice Vargas shares her personal experience with the art to deepen her connection with her participants.

  
     
    
  AWBW Founder, Cathy Salser takes deep breaths with her workshop participants.  
     

The 3 P’s

Prepare Yourself

  • Try It Out: Pick a workshop and do it yourself so you can speak to any issues that arise.  

  • Agenda: Map your agenda flow (e.g., Intro, Demo, Relaxation/Warm-up, Creation, Closing) How much time do you want to allow for each? How would you like to facilitate each section virtually? How would you like to encourage voice and choice virtually?  

  • Tech: Reduce stress by allowing time to explore your tech in advance. Practice with family and friends to get comfortable with features you plan to use (chat, screen share, breakouts). Greet imperfections! You’ll learn each time you facilitate! If possible, secure a co-facilitator who can be available to help with any tech issues as they arise.

  • Slides: If you’re prepping slides, keep it simple. Many folks access virtual workshops from their phones, so just a few words per slide is plenty.

  • Eye Contact: You may want to practice the strange-at-first art of talking into the camera. It is your window to “see” and connect, and believe it or not, can become comfortable once you get a feel for it. 

  • Self-Care: Stop and self-regulate as needed, especially if you encounter stress along the way! You’ve got this!

Prepare Your Supplies

  • Supplies: What supplies do you need? How could it work with a range of supplies? Are there samples you want to have on hand to share?

  • Background and Lighting: Play with it. What do you want behind you? How do you want to be lit? Perhaps grab a lamp to have next to you?

  • Music: Do you want to play music for participants during the “create” window? If so, have it ready.

  • Timer: You might want to have a timer to track the sections of your agenda easily.

  • Tripod: If you’re using your phone to film, it’s great to be able to set it down. You can create your own “tripod” by taping a small box on top of a large one. 

  • Water/Tea: You might be encouraging your participants to get comfortable with snacks, water, a cup of tea. Likewise, be sure to think of what you need, so this is a nurturing space for you too!

Prepare Your Participants

  • Links: Just as with an in person workshop, you’ll need to provide details so they can access the virtual workshop. This could be a link, a call-in number, etc. 

  • Supplies: Share any handouts, templates, supplies to have on hand, but remember participants may not have access to a printer. A plain piece of paper can often be just as effective as using a template. Reassure them that whatever supplies they have or do not have is fine and there is no right or wrong way to participate. Observing is participating.

  • Arrivals: Plan for “arrival” time, just like in person so folks can get “in the room,” figure out how to navigate their choices with microphone, camera, chat window, etc. You (and/or your co-facilitator) can offer tech support as you greet, encourage folks to get grounded, and invite check-in thoughts in the chat window. It can be good to have a prompt for folks during this arrival window (e.g., “I invite you to share three words for how you’re feeling right now, as we arrive and get in the room”).

  • Reminder Emails: If you have capacity, reminder emails can be extra helpful. In our busy lives it can be hard to find the info, so re-sending the link and details the day before the workshop can greatly reduce stress. It can even be lovely to send a quick welcome message an hour or so before going live. For example, “I’m getting my tea and settling in, so excited to “see” you at 4:00!”  

Bottom Line — Be You!

As you invite participants to truly be themselves, don’t forget to invite yourself to do the same. Feel free to share how you’re really feeling (e.g., nervous about this new technology, wishing for connection, sharing, courage). By modeling your own vulnerability and openness, you can invite courage for each participant to share where they are really at and their wishes too.

title: Standing Up for Justice
objective: Around the United States and the world, people are holding demonstrations against the racial injustice and inequality that has been ingrained in our society for centuries. You can support this movement for change by creating messages of solidarity to put in your window, your yard, or even to hold while protesting. Using words, shapes, images, and symbols, explore what messages feel right for you on the signs below. You can then use your ideas here to make larger signs, adding your voice to this collective call to action.

title: Up Brother
objective: To clarify some of the emotions brought on by injustice and promote healing through catharsis for men of color.
materials:
• Watercolor paper

  • Writing utensils: pencils, colored pencils or markers

  • Oil pastels

  • Watercolors

  • Cups of water

  • Paper towel/napkins

  • Head with hair template

  • Head without hair template

  • Head with hat template

  • Song: What’s Going On by Marvin Gaye (can played on any mobile device with Internet access and speakers)

  • What's Going On Lyrics

  • Problems, Thoughts, Solutions Worksheet
Head with hair template Head without hair template Head with hat template Worksheet
setup: Have watercolor paper already at place setting, with pencils, markers, oil pastels, and watercolors and brushes. It is good to have cups of water (for paints) as well as paper towel or napkins for clean-up or spills.
warm_up:
Relaxation: "Sit comfortably and if you like you can close your eyes or look at one area in the room. Take a few moments to "simply be". Notice whatever is being experienced in the moment -- sounds, physical sensations, thoughts, feelings -- without trying to do anything about it. Continue like this a little while, allowing yourself to settle down.

Now bring the attention to the breath. Simply notice the breath as it moves in and out as the body inhales and exhales. Notice how the breath moves in and out automatically, effortlessly. Don't try to manipulate it in any way. Notice all the details of the experience of breathing -- the feeling of the air moving in and out of the nose, the way the body moves as it breathes, etc.

The mind will wander away from the breath -- that's fine, it doesn't matter. That's a part of the meditation! When you notice that you are no longer observing the breath, easily bring your attention back to it.

Let all of your experiences -- thoughts, emotions, bodily sensations -- come and go in the background of your awareness of the breath. Notice how all of your experiences -- thoughts, emotions, bodily sensations, awareness of sounds and smells -- come automatically and effortlessly like the breath.

In time, you can become aware of the tendencies of your mind. You will see how it resists certain experiences and tries to hold onto others. The natural settling down of the mind allows you to notice these underlying tendencies and creates the possibility to let them go. If you experience a resistance to what is occurring, an attempt to change what is happening, a tendency to hold on to some experience -- let it go."
creation:
Step 1: Describe the materials available. Have participants choose their templates or they may decide to draw their own, (suggest color resist and give a demonstration of using oil pastels then painting over it with watercolors,) Have examples to show the outcome.

Step 2: At this time, they may want to use the words from their worksheet on the head area for “problems and reactions”, to show their thoughts and then use the body for “solutions” to show the heart of the matter, if they'd like, they can then paint the background of their art with watercolor, this creation process is totally up to the participants.

There is no right or wrong way to do this workshop. The hope is that this workshop art helps you uncover what is in your thoughts, and find a way to best utilize them to be the change that you want to see in the world.
closing: Invite participants to share their artwork and/or any outcomes that arose from participating in this workshop. Let participants know that you see them, you support them and that you are here for change.
optional_materials: • Ribbon (for border)
introduction:
"Thank you for being here today. Before we begin, I want you to know that this is your Window of Time. It's a time for you to notice your thoughts, needs and feelings. During this time, there is no right or wrong way to participate or create. I'm going to share some instructions, but you get to choose how you want to participate. You can follow along completely, or you may want to do something different, it's completely up to you. During your Window of Time, you get to choose. I am here to support you in any way that I can, so please ask for what you need. Any questions before I begin?"

"This difference has affected our personal lives, emotions and health, also the impact we have on our world. Today we will use art to address some of the problems, reactions and solutions in order to empower ourselves and those in our circle of influence."

title: Window of Time Workshop Series
objective: To address some of the thoughts and feelings surrounding COVID-19.
extra_field:
We are here to support you in the face of COVID-19 and its impact on our lives and communities. We invite you, along with your families, friends, and co-workers, to participate in these self-led art workshops as a way to explore your experiences, feelings, and needs. Your creations can also be useful in communicating and connecting with others, both directly and virtually.

You can download and print the worksheets or follow the prompt and create your art on a blank sheet of paper or other material. Use whatever supplies you have available for your creation. There is no right or wrong way to create or participate!

We hope your “Window of Time” promotes wellness and resilience for you and your loved ones as we work through these unusual circumstances together.

You can download each worksheet individually or you can download all of them here.

 

Safe Home

Being out of our routines and dealing with the constant stream of information about this ever evolving pandemic can disrupt our sense of safety and control.

What makes you feel safe at home? It is different for each of us. This workshop is designed for individuals and families to creatively explore what their safe home looks, feels, sounds, and smells like. Your safe home creation can serve as a reminder of the various things you can do to help yourself feel safe while home.

Also, sharing your creation with people you live with is a great way to spark a conversation around any conflicting needs between people in the home, giving you a way to work together to find balance while meeting everyone’s unique needs.

Download the worksheet: English  |  Spanish
Resource: Creating a Safe and Open Home Environment

Community Agreements

With the current state of affairs, it is even more important that we care for ourselves and others. We are all dealing with this situation differently. Taking time to identify and share what you, and those you interact with, need to feel safe can help us be kind and patient with ourselves and one another.

Creating community agreements can be beneficial in setting up clear communication, boundaries, and expectations to create a safer environment for yourself and those you are in direct and virtual contact with. The agreements can be used to address any conflict and miscommunication that may arise in a gentle and productive manner. If an agreement is not followed, take the time to discuss and make adjustments as necessary.

Download the worksheet: English  |  Spanish
Resource: Developing Community Agreements

 

Personal Needs Flower

During this stressful time, we can be so good at taking care of other people that we forget someone who is very important — ourselves!

This workshop gives you an opportunity to creatively explore your core needs, and perhaps even discover new ones! Your flower can serve as a reminder of all your unique needs and the various ways you can meet those needs. It can also be used as a tool to communicate your needs with others so you can support one another in ensuring that they are tended to.

Download the worksheet: English  |  Spanish
Resource: Self-Care is Important: Why Is It So Hard to Practice?

 

Take a Break, Self-Regulate!

Even in normal circumstances, it can be difficult to stay grounded and present in our bodies. Being regulated refers to the central nervous system being in balance, calm, and alert. There are many ways to self-regulate, and taking breaks is a great way to move toward feeling calm and grounded.

How do you like to take breaks? We all enjoy doing different things. This workshop provides an opportunity to identify various activities you like to do when taking a break. Make spinners to remind you of the ways you can calm your mind and nervous system in order to feel more in control.

Download the worksheet: English  |  Spanish
Resources: AWBW 50 Ways to Take a Break Handout

 

Gratitude Journal

As we move through this time, things are happening that might make us feel worried, uncertain, scared, and a lot of other emotions. Keeping a journal that gives us time and space to focus on what we are grateful for can help put things in perspective and provide a much-needed sense of calm.

Being grateful takes practice, and this workshop provides you with a place to capture and remind you of the various things you are thankful for. Research has shown that directing our attention towards the things we are grateful for, both big and small, has a domino effect by helping our brain to move away from fear and anxiety and towards well-being. Sharing your journal with loved ones (virtually or in person) is a great way to spread positivity and foster connection and inspiration.

Download the worksheet: English  |  Spanish
Resources: Gratitude Physically Changes Your Brain

Treasure Boxes

With everything the world is going through, it is easy to feel overwhelmed and get stuck in negative thoughts. To counteract this we can focus on the people, places, memories, things, and anything else in our lives that we deeply value.

What do you treasure? What is important or meaningful to you that you want to keep safe and protected? This workshop provides an opportunity to identify and connect with what is close to your heart. Fill your own treasure box to serve as a tangible reminder you can use to keep you grounded in what is truly important to you. If you’d like, share your treasure box with others as a way to stay connected to what you value and help others do the same!

Download the worksheet: English  |  Spanish
Resources: 10 Proactive Ways to Figure Out What’s Most Important to You

Inside/Outside

Many of us are having to hide the stress and anxiety we are feeling as a result of this world health crisis. It is not always easy to do this, and hiding emotions and other aspects of yourself can drain our energy.

In this workshop, you are invited to explore the “you” that you know on the inside and the “you” that people see on the outside. As you explore these different sides of yourself you might learn something new and connect with any thoughts or feelings you have kept hidden, particularly about COVID-19. After completing your creation, you can share the “you” on the inside with a supportive person so you don’t have to keep hiding.

Download the worksheet: English  |  Spanish
Resources: The Tension Between the Inner and Outer Self

Coat of Arms

Having loved ones to lean on can be especially important for staying grounded as this pandemic unfolds. Who are the people in your life you can turn to for support? Who do you consider family?

A coat of arms symbolizes the strength and pride of a family. This workshop gives you the opportunity to represent the uniqueness of your own family, whoever it may be. You can create your coat of arms as a group or individually. Either way, it can serve as a tangible reminder of how you are getting through these challenging times together.

Download the worksheet: English  |  Spanish
Resources: Some Definitions of Family  |  Meaning of Family

Heart Stories

Even in normal circumstances, it is easy to pay more attention to what we think than what is in our hearts. With everything going on, your head may be especially full of thoughts. Listening to our hearts can help us stay connected to who we are.

If your heart could talk about what is happening right now what would it say? What story would it tell? This workshop invites you to think about all of the different ways your heart is currently feeling and bring them out onto paper. By listening to your heart you can better understand what it needs and also talk to others who can help you meet those needs.

Download the worksheet: English  |  Spanish
Resources: How To Really Listen To Your Heart

My Time

There is so much we cannot control right now, but we can control how we spend our time. Balancing what we have to do with what we want to do is especially important to our well-being.

This workshop gives you a chance to envision how you will fill your extra time through the creation of a special clock. What are some new things you can do while staying home? Talking to others about what you created on your clock will allow them to support and encourage you to spend your time doing things that bring you joy.

Download the worksheet: English  |  Spanish
Resources: 100 Things To Do While Stuck Inside Due to a Pandemic

The Lotus Flower

Rooted firmly in the mud, the lotus flower grows in murky water. Because of this, it can be a representation of growth during difficult times — like the one we are in now.

You too can grow out of the mud! This workshop provides an opportunity to create a lotus flower to represent challenges you’ve been through and how you overcame them and blossomed. Use your finished flower to remind you of your resilience and ability to successfully navigate through this challenging time.

Download the worksheet: English  |  Spanish
Resources: Being Resilient During the Coronavirus

Positive Piggies

It can be hard to stay positive with everything that is happening, including thinking positively about ourselves. Positive self-talk is something you can do to build your self-esteem, support you when you are feeling down, or to battle negative thoughts.

In this workshop you have the chance to create positive and uplifting messages for yourself, more valuable than money, to fill your very own piggy bank. When you’re feeling down, or just need a little boost, you can look at your piggy and take a moment to remind yourself of how special you are. Spread your positivity to others by sharing your creation.

Download the worksheet: English  |  Spanish
Resources: Five Reasons Why You Should Think Positively

Story Tree

The world has gone through a lot of change recently, which has caused us to look at life a little differently. Through it all, we are still constantly growing — just like a tree.

With their strong trunks and long, expansive branches, trees can help us tell the story of what we have been through and remind us of our strength as we continue to move forward. How have you changed in response to current events? In this workshop you have opportunity to explore your growth, using the tree as a symbol of life and courage. Use your tree to share your journey with others.

Download the worksheet: English  |  Spanish
Resources: Psychological Growth During the COVID-19 Crisis

Flying Tall

During unpredictable times like these, feeling strong can be very hard to do. However, if you take a closer look inside, you can begin to notice the many strengths you have.

There are many ways to be strong and we all have our own definition of what it means to us. What strengths do you have? How have they helped you in the past? How are they helping you now? This workshop invites you to create a flag symbolizing all the different strengths you can depend on in the face of challenges. Keep your flag to remind you of your resilience when you are struggling to feel strong.

Download the worksheet: English  |  Spanish
Resources: How to Find Emotional Strength & Resilience During COVID-19

Life is Sweet

Right now, we are faced with not getting to do a lot of the things we want to. This doesn’t mean we can’t remember the good times we’ve had and dream of what brings us joy.

What are some of your positive memories? What memories do you hope to create in the future? In this workshop you can reflect on experiences that make you happy. Add as many scoops to your ice cream cone as you wish, each representing a memory from the past or an idea for the future. Keep your creation nearby to remind you of the sweeter side of life!

Download the worksheet: English  |  Spanish
Resources: The Power of Positive Memories

Messages of Hope

Hope is exactly what we need to boost our well-being during these difficult times!

Creating and reading positive messages is a great way to build hope and happiness. In this workshop you are invited to create your own messages to inspire yourself and others. If you like, you can make larger signs to put inside or outside your home for everyone to read and enjoy.

Wishing you all the best as we move forward together!

Download the worksheet: English  |  Spanish
Resources: Words Can Change Your Brain

Bonus: We Rise Touchstones

AWBW Founder Cathy Salser facilitated this interactive art workshop as a part of WE RISE 2020: Virtual May. In collaboration with Los Angeles Department of Mental Health, We Rise is a month-long spotlight on wellbeing and healing through art, music and creative expression, and we are so honored to be a part of it.

What are you rising from and toward? In the face of stress & trauma, it can be hard to remember our inner strength, especially when we need it most. We invite you to create “WE RISE Touchstones” as a resource to bring clarity into moments of challenge.

Download the worksheet: English  |  Spanish

Facebook Live Sessions

Windows Facilitators hosted a Weekly “Window of Time” on Facebook Live. Each session included a meditation and the host shared about their experience with the workshops.

• Safe Home & Community Agreements: AWBW Founder & Windows Facilitator Cathy Salser

• Story Tree & Flying Tall: Windows Facilitator Karalee Hayes, LMFT

• Life is Sweet & Messages of Hope: Windows Facilitator Susan Lee, PhD

title: When I First Understood My Race
objective: This workshop aims to give participants a safe space to process the moment when they realized they were not part of the dominant race and create an artistic representation of how it made them feel.
materials:
Optional printable self-led worksheet
     
     

  • Pencils

  • Watercolors

  • Brushes

  • Watercolor paper or thick cardstock

  • Water

  • Cups for water (two cups per person, one for dirty water, one for clean water)

  • Markers

  • Colored pencils

  • Erasers

  • Paper towels

You can also facilitate this workshop using this printable self-led worksheet. If you are utilizing this sheet in lieu of the regular workshop materials, be sure to send a digital copy or print them out beforehand for your participants depending on the setting.

Optional materials for self-led worksheet:

  • Self-led worksheet

  • Pencils

  • Pens

  • Colored pencils

  • Markers

  • Erasers
setup:
Before the workshop, consider going through the workshop on your own and create a sample of a finished art piece to show during the demonstration portion of the workshop.

Prepare the materials for your workspace and allow for easy access to all art materials for all participants. If you are using the optional self-led worksheets, print them out and place in front of each seat.

On a whiteboard, chalkboard, or large piece of paper, write the prompt for the writing exercise, "How did you feel when you first realized people would treat you poorly because of your race?"

warm_up:
"We’re going to take a few minutes to relax. During this time, I'm going to invite you to get in a comfortable position in a chair, on the floor, or wherever feels right for you. We invite you to close your eyes or you can keep them open with a soft focus on something in front of you."

Close your eyes, sit back in your chair or wherever you're sitting, feet flat on the floor or in a comfortable position in front of you and your hands resting in your lap."

Take a deep breath to the count of three: Inhale, one… two… three…
Now exhale, one… two… three… Inhale again, one… two… three…
And exhale, one… two… three. One more time, inhale, one… two…three and exhale, one… two… three."

Now sit quietly for a moment and check your body for any tense areas.
When you find one, take a deep breath and sigh as you exhale releasing that tension.
Check your face and jaw… your neck and shoulders… your chest and back… your arms and stomach… check your thighs and legs… now check your feet.

Take one last deep breath and open your eyes.

"We’re now going to move into our writing exercise. However you would like to participate in the writing exercise is OK. The prompt I'm going to invite you to think and write about is, "How did you feel when you first realized people would treat you poorly because of your race?" Take about 15 minutes to write or participate in any other way."

Give time reminders as participants write. When they're done, invite anyone who would like to share to talk about what they wrote down. They can read what they wrote down or share a few words or sentences to summarize their thoughts.

Thank everyone for participating in all they ways they did, even if they participated.
creation:
"Now you have an opportunity to utilize art materials to create words, colors, and/or symbols to represent how you felt, or make a drawing of yourself in that situation, or do something completely different, whatever feels right to you."

Give time reminders throughout the creation process.

Note: If participants are able to continue creating after the workshop is over or even at home, you can let them know this when giving time reminders. This can help alleviate anxiety around time.
closing:
Welcome participants back to the group. Invite them to find a partner and take turns sharing their experience with one another. You can give each partner a set time to share and notify them when it's time to switch from speaker to listener. After paired sharing, you can invite a few participants to share with the group about their experience.

Thank participants for participating in all the ways that they did, even if they observed.

Share the following quote with participants as a final parting message:
"It is necessary while in darkness to know that there is a light somewhere, to know that, in oneself waiting to be found, there is a light. May you find the light that is within you and may it comfort you and bring you strength and peace."
— James Baldwin

Thank everyone for honoring all of the ways they chose to participate, including those who solely observed. Invite them to be gentle with themselves and enagge in some self-care after they leave.
introduction:
"Thank you for being here today. Before we begin, I want you to know that this is your Window of Time. It's a time for you to notice your thoughts, needs and feelings. During this time, there is no right or wrong way to participate or create. I'm going to share some instructions, but you get to choose how you want to participate. You can follow along completely, or you may want to do something different, it's completely up to you. During your Window of time, you get to choose. I am here to support you in any way that I can, so please ask for what you need. Any questions before I begin?"

"For many people of color, there comes a moment when they realize what it means to not be part of the dominant culture which is white and steeped in racism. The moment can happen as the result of a talk with their parents, an experience at school or on the street, or even from being bullied by their own people. Did your moment come as the result of such an experience? If so, what was it? Think about it and then think of how it made you feel. If you were to draw that experience, what would it look like? How would you show the world how it made you feel?"
demonstration:
"Before we dive into our creation, I'll invite you to start off with a brief relaxation and a writing exercise. These activities can be done any way that feels comfortable to you. I'll be offering some directions, but you get to choose how you would like to go through them. Then I'll show you the different art materials that are available to you and check to see if you have any questions about them of any of the other activities."

Show a brief overview of all the materials that participants have available to them along with a finished sample. Invite participants to ask questions about the materials or any other aspect of the workshop before moving into the relaxation.
extra_field:
Message from the Author:
I'm an African American woman who has lived with racism for almost seventy years. I created this workshop as a way of opening the door on feelings about racism that most of us have shut away. In my journey to heal myself, I learned that hiding the truth means that trauma never gets healed and keeps re-traumatizing. I hope this workshop is helpful to opening that door for you.

— Fran Sutton-Williams

title: Growing Resilience
objective: This workshop aims to guide participants to identify the trauma that has been present throughout their lives and to honor their resilience.

setup:

warm_up:
"To help prepare us to create, we're going to take about 10 minutes to journal. I invite you to choose any kind of paper that you would like to use. I'm going to offer you a prompt and you can choose if and/or how you would like to follow along. This can be a stream of consciousness journal activity where you let anything that comes to mind out on the paper. It can be words, sentences, symbols, or even colors that come to mind. When I offer you the prompt, you can begin to write down whatever comes to mind. I'm going to give you about 10 minutes and I'll give you a time warning when time is almost up.

"The prompt I'll offer you is this: How have you navigated the obstacles that you have been challenged with throughout your life? What are these obstacles and what did you do to overcome them? When you're thinking about this, I'll offer to especially think about any racial and historical trauma that you have experienced."

You can play relaxing background music and offer a one minute time reminder to give participants a chance to get their final thoughts down.

Welcome participants back to the space and invite a few participants to share one or two words about what they wrote down and/or about their experience.

closing: Invite participants back to the group and welcome anyone who would like to share about their creation and/or their experience. When everyone is done, thank everyone for participating in all the ways that they did, even if they only observed.
introduction:
“Thank you for being here today. Before we begin, I want you to know that this is your Window of Time. It's a time for you to notice your thoughts, needs and feelings. During this time, there is no right or wrong way to participate or create. I'm going to share some instructions, but you get to choose how you want to participate. You can follow along completely, or you may want to do something different, it's completely up to you. During your Window of Time, you get to choose. I am here to support you in any way that I can, so please ask for what you need.

“Today is all about our resilience and honoring the strength it has taken for us to be here in this moment. Throughout our lives, we have been met with many different kinds of obstacles that provided challenges for us. As we begin take a look into our past, we'll begin to name those challenges and even notice if any are still present today.

“After I go over the art materials, you'll be invited to participate in a warmup journal activity, and then we will move onto creating. At the end of the workshop, you will have the chance to share your story with the group. Any questions before I begin?"
demonstration: Show the two different worksheet options and invite participants to choose which one they would like to create on. You can offer that one can be used to practice on and the other for the final creation or you can invite them to create two creations, whatever works best for them. These invitations are meant for the participants to have options when creating, not to limit them to specific things.

title: Container of Overwhelming Feelings
objective: This workshop aims to support participants in identifying and managing overwhelming feelings using art to foster a sense of harmony and wellbeing inside.
materials:
• Mason jar or repurposed sauce jar

  • Construction paper, Index cards or paper cut into small strips

  • Popsicle sticks (can be used instead of paper)

  • Journal or scratch paper

  • Pencils

  • Pens

  • Colored pencils

  • Markers

  • Crayons

  • Journal or scratch paper
setup:
Before the workshop, consider going through the workshop on your own and create a sample of a finished art piece to show during the demonstration. You can show different examples of jars that participants can use like mason jars or repurposed sauce jars. If you are using the worksheets, you can create a simplistic sample to show.

If meeting in person, prepare the materials for your workspace and allow for easy access to all art materials for all participants. If you are using the optional worksheets, send them to your participants beforehand or print them out and place in front of each seat if you are meeting in person.
warm_up: "Today you will be invited to notice the feelings inside. You may notice what feels pleasant, neutral or unpleasant. I want to invite you to first identify a resource that can serve as a support to you on this journey inside. A resource is a person place or things that generates joy or a sense of well-being. I invite you to identify one resource at this time. I invite you to write your resource  on a sheet of paper and name at least three pleasant or neutral qualities about your resource. You may notice what you feel inside as you describe your resource. Does it feel pleasant? If yes, I invite you to bring your attention to that pleasant feeling for as long as needed. As we shift into the workshop you will be invited to name any overwhelming feelings that would be helpful to contain until you have capacity to experience them and the support that you may need. As explore this window of time you may return to your resource at any time to best support you."
creation: "Journal any feelings that you are holding and notice the feelings that may be overwhelming. Please write your top three overwhelming feelings or concerns on a separate sheet of paper and add any color or images to it to flag it. You can then place it in the jar to contain it and hold it for you to return to later or you may decide that you would like to hold it outside of the container and seek immediate support for it. You may place all of the feelings in your jar at the same time or one before the other. You may also create notes of gratitude or positive words to add to the jar to balance that space. You may create notes that identify what you need. This jar is your container  and can hold what feels best for you in this  moment. You may return to your jar when you are ready and as often as needed to add or remove the feeling or concern. You are invited to journal about your experience as well."
closing:
"What insights are you taking away from this window of time? What do you need? What is supporting you right now? Is there anything more you want to add to the container or not at this time? Where will you store your container? Why? Is there a name you want to give to your container?  If yes what will you name it?" 

Closing self-compassion exercise: I invite you to will this for yourself. “May I be calm. May I have peace. May I be whole. May I have all that I need.”

You can also facilitate this workshop using printable worksheets. If you are utilizing this sheet in lieu of the regular workshop materials, be sure to send a digital copy or print them out beforehand for your participants if you are meeting in person.
