introduction:
"Before we begin, I want you to know that this is your Window of Time. It's a time for you to notice your thoughts, needs and feelings. During this time, there is no right or wrong way to participate or create. I'm going to share some instructions, but you get to choose how you want to participate. You can follow along completely, or you may want to do something different, it's completely up to you. During your Window of Time, you get to choose. I am here to support you in any way that I can, so please ask for what you need."

"Today I invite you to notice what you are holding in your mind, body and spirit that feels overwhelming so that you may contain it as a way to manage any distress that is attached to your feelings. You will have an opportunity to slow down and decide how you would like to proceed in addressing your feelings. Using the three step D.I.P process:

  • Decide to notice the feeling
  • Inquire how is it impacting you now and does it feel overwhelming in the present moment? If yes,
  • Put the overwhelming feeling away as needed.
     

"You may name and write the feeling on a piece of paper and place it in the container to hold it. You may also give the feeling a color or design and place that on the piece of paper. You may give yourself permission to return to your container to address it when you feel ready or have the internal capacity to process the overwhelming feeling. When you return to the container you can draw out the feeling at your own pace and you may journal ideas for what you need to turn the volume down on the feeling."

Alternate intro if using the worksheets:

"During this window of time you may choose to add resources to your handout as well as name the overwhelming feelings or things that are coming up for you. Remember that a resource gives you life and brings forth feelings or sensations of calm, joy, pleasant energy or something else that is uplifting or affirming. You may choose to add a note or image or color to represent your resource to your jar so that there is a sense of balance present. This is your window of time and you get to decide. If you are using the worksheet you may choose add the resources outside of the jar image or inside, you get to decide. 

It may also be helpful to date your sheets of paper or the images on your handout. You can track or journal your journey and the things that you are moving through, over time. 

During this window of time you may also choose to notice what your losses during a challenging time. Feel welcome to add that to your container or you may draw it wherever it feels best.
demonstration:
"The art supplies consists of a container like a mason jar that has a lid. Please have colored paper, construction paper or blank white paper available to write your feelings on. You can use markers, crayons, colored pencils and collage to decorate your sheets of paper with the feelings written on it. You can place the overwhelming feelings in the container as you wish or hold on to the feelings that appear to be manageable for as long as you need to. You may journal about how you plan to process or address the feeling, what you need to address the feeling or something else. You may want to only observe it without judgement and that is enough. You may also create words or express practices that can help you and you may add those words and ideas to the jar to bring balance into that space. At the close of the workshop you can contain all that you choose and hold on to what feels manageable."

   
Words inside jar Completed worksheet with instructions    
       
   
Popsicle sticks inside jar Completed worksheet without instructions
opening_circle:
"Today’s workshop will serve as a safer space to identify and contain your overwhelming feelings. You are invited to journal, color, write or something else during this window of time. This is your window of time and being present is enough, already. Over the past several months our sense of safety and predictability has been significantly challenged. There has been too much shift, too fast and for too long. Many have also experience a major decrease in physical connection with other people for too long and the experiences have resulted in feeling overwhelmed. How do you hold space inside for all that is happening, even the things that bring us joy? We are invited into this window of time to slow down, observe the feelings and contain the feelings that are overwhelming at a given time so that you can mindfully address the feelings when you are ready to do so. 

To begin, I’m going to go over the art materials and steps we can take to create our container for overwhelming feelings. Then, we’ll talk about how overwhelming feelings can cause us to feel flooded. The Container for Overwhelming Feelings workshop will offer tools to bring the volume or waters of emotions down. Are there any questions before we begin?
extra_field: Windows Facilitator and workshop author, La Shonda Coleman, LCSW, RYT 200 is a licensed clinical social worker and wellness practitioner specializing in trauma healing and resilience. She has integrated art, movement and mindfulness onto her clinical work to support individuals, groups and communities heal and live life wholeheartedly. La Shonda created the Container of Overwhelming Feelings Workshop to help people manage distressing feelings during the pandemic and time of overwhelming attention to social injustices. La Shonda hopes that this workshop serves a window of time to engender wellness by created greater capacity to rest (mind, body, soul) and to manage overwhelming feelings during challenging times.

title: Cup of Gratitude
objective: This workshop aims to promote positive or neutral thoughts, feelings and sensations by engaging in expressions of gratitude. Practicing gratitude daily can boost one's mood, improve sleep, and uplift one's overall well-being.
materials:
• Coffee cup or mug
  • Sheets of paper 
  • Scissors
  • Writing utensils: Pencils/colored pencils/markers/crayons
setup: You may display an empty coffee cup/mug, the Cup of Gratitude worksheets, and any other art supplies you like.
warm_up: "Today, you are invited to hold gratitude for people, time, places, things, beliefs, understandings, space or anything else. You get to decide what you want to fill your cup with as we pour into our Cup of Gratitude. I invite you to notice all the places where your body is making contact with a surface and, without judgement, notice where you feel more connected, sturdy, or neutral. You are invited to be here now, in this moment, this is your window of time to be. You can decide if you would like create today. There is no right or wrong in this space. You are enough, and being here today is enough. I invite you to notice at least three colors around you that bring you a sense of joy or calm. I welcome you to take all the time you need to prepare for your workshop experience."
creation:
"The Cup of Gratitude worksheet with the lines inside can serve a space to journal. You are invited to journal any thoughts that may arise as you settle into the workshop. You can add to your journal as needed to help capture your expressions." 

Here are some questions you can journal about:

  • What are your initial thoughts about gratitude?
  • What are you grateful for in this moment?
  • Does it unlock the door or open a window to more or not? 
  • The saucer or plate can also be used to identify resources and support in your life.  A resource is a person, place, song, color, scent, or something else that brings you a sense of joy and wellbeing. What or who helps hold your cup?

"After 3-5 minutes of journaling, you can begin to use words, shapes, symbols, images or anything else you like to create your expressions of gratitude for your cup. I invite you to pour your items into your cup at your own pace. You can also create representations of your resources and what supports you to add to the plate or saucer that holds your cup."

"This cup can serve as a practical space to add thoughts and feelings of gratitude daily. You can drink (so to speak) from your cup each morning or like a warm cup of tea, you can drink from your cup before bed to help you feel warm or calm inside. You are welcome to return to your cup as often as needed to add or remove the contents."

"Now, if you would like, you can journal about your experience for 3-5 minutes after you fill and drink from your cup of gratitude. To drink from your cup can mean to pause and, with intention, notice what you are grateful for. Practicing gratitude regularly may help to improve physical, mental and spiritual well-being."  

Here are some things you might consider as you journal:

  • While savoring your awareness for that which you are grateful for, what do you notice inside or externally?
  • Where would you like to practice this more often (home, work, with your friend group or somewhere else)? 
  • What time of day would you like to fill your gratitude cup? 
  • How often would you like to refill your cup?"
closing:
Welcome anyone who would like to share their Cup of Gratitude or workshop experience. Here are some examples of questions for the closing:

  • What insights are you taking away from this window of time?
  • What do you need?
  • What is supporting you right now?
  • Is there anything more you want to add to your cup?
  • Where will you store your cup? Why?
  • What time works best for you to experience your cup of gratitude?
  • Is there a name you want to give your cup or mug? If yes, what will you name it?"
  • You can hold gratitude for as much time as you choose.  Is there anything that you would like to take with you as you go?  If yes, what are you holding gratitude for a bit longer?

Once the participants who wanted to share are finished speaking, thank everyone for being present and for filling their cups by honoring the way they chose to participate.

You may also share some quotes to close the workshop:

  • "Enough is a feast.” --Buddhist Proverb
  • "Acknowledging the good that you already have in your life is the foundation for all abundance.” --Eckhart Tolle
  • "Gratitude turns what we have into enough, and more.  It turns denial into acceptance, chaos into order, confusion into clarity… it makes sense of our past, brings peace for today, and creates a vision for tomorrow.” --Melody Beattie

introduction:
"Thank you for being here today. According to Dr. Lillian Nejad in '4 Ways to Practice Gratitude and Build Resilience' by Dawn Teh, grateful people are more likely to seek support, utilize resources available to them, and approach problems directly and with a positive outlook. Practicing gratitude can help to alleviate pain and suffering, boost mood, improve sleep and elevate one’s mental and physical health and wellbeing. We can practice gratitude daily in a variety of ways that may include journaling, sharing verbal expressions of appreciation, or pausing to notice all that we are grateful for in any given moment."

"Today, I will offer you a way to connect to what you are grateful for. The Cup of Gratitude workshop invites you to literally fill a coffee cup or mug with expressions of gratitude. You are welcome to return to your cup for a boost or to help awaken your senses to all that you have at that moment in time. Like a cup of coffee or tea, your Cup of Gratitude can provide energy, comfort, calm or warmth to enhance your wellbeing."
demonstration: "The art supplies include a coffee/tea cup/mug or you are welcome to use the Cup of Gratitude worksheets. The Cup of Gratitude worksheet with the lines inside of the cup can be used for journaling as you'll have an opportunity to spend time savoring your awareness for that which you are grateful for and journal about what you notice inside or externally as you do so.  You can use any writing utensils you like on any type of paper, or rocks, or popsicle sticks to write your expressions of gratitude and then attach them to the worksheet or fill the actual cup or mug. You may also want to glue collage items to represent your gratitude."
opening_circle:
"This can be ‘A Window of Time’ for you to practice respecting your feelings, your thoughts, your needs and your visions. During this time there is no right or wrong way.  Observing is participating. Whatever supports you in expressing, connecting and attending to your needs and feelings is the number one priority."

"Today's workshop provides a space to identify and express gratitude as a way to enhance well-being. You are invited to journal, color, write or whatever you would like during this window of time. This is your window of time and being here is already enough. You are invited into this window of time to slow down and notice all that you are grateful for. This mindful moment is a time to fill your cup (mind, body and spirit). You may fill your cup with appreciation for people, places traveled recently or in the past, victories, insights, pets, pictures, sounds, and more. You are welcome to fill your cup with anything that you hold gratitude for. Each day you can empty your cup and refill it as needed."

"To begin, I will go over the art materials and steps we can take to create our Cup of Gratitude. Then, I will invite you to use your worksheet or a piece of paper to capture your thoughts. You can then begin creating expressions of gratitude on paper, your worksheet or any other material you like. This is your window of time and can be used in any way that is meaningful for you. Are there any questions before we begin?"
extra_field:
Windows Facilitator and workshop author, La Shonda Coleman, LCSW, RYT 200 is a licensed clinical social worker and wellness practitioner specializing in trauma healing and resilience. She has integrated art, movement and mindfulness onto her clinical work to support individuals, groups and communities heal and live life wholeheartedly.

This workshop was created when La Shonda worked with a group of first responders that were mentally and emotionally fatigued due to the overwhelming impact of COVID-19.  During their meeting she noticed that most of the participants were sipping from cups of coffee to help them stay awake and alert, some drank for comfort and others loved the aroma.  In all, she noticed that the cup held and offered a boost, it offered a sense of goodness.  She then invited the first responders to share at least one thing they were grateful for and to do this regularly by identifying words, images, expressions and adding them to paper or an item that could be placed in a coffee cup to help them as they started their day or as needed to give them a boost (sense of goodness) in the middle of their challenging days.  

La Shonda discovered that by providing participants with practical tools to practice gratitude, their lives can be enriched.  Participants have reported a reduction on stress and sensations of anxiety following this workshop.  This practice of adding gratitude to one’s cup helps to shift their mindset to a more positive or neutral place.  This workshop has also supported participants in feeling more connected with others on online platforms.

title: My Internal Dashboard
objective: This workshop aims to support participants in becoming self-aware of their internal emotional states in order to feel empowered to make changes based on their own indicators.
materials:
•    
        Road Symbols
         

    Road symbols

  • Construction paper

  • Writing utensil

  • Markers

  • Colored pencils

  • Glue

  • Scissors
setup:
Possible Workshop Setup
         

We encourage you to have all the materials set out for the participants prior to them attending the workshop. You can also have the materials set up on a different table for participants to grab during the workshop. What’s important is that each person has easy access to all the supplies. You can also play some ambient music, like Reiki or Deuter, up until the time we start engaging in the group process.
warm_up:
Journaling:

To get us started on bringing our awareness to the present moment and to how we are currently feeling, mentally, emotionally, physically and spiritually, I would like to invite you all to a journaling session. Please feel free to take a minute or less to write down your initial thoughts for each question or feel free to focus on just one or a few. I will give us a quick time reminder when we have 5 minutes left and then again when we have a minute left. Are there any questions before we begin?” 

 

Note: You are welcome to play some music and write down the question on paper or a white board, if available.  

 

Tire

  1. How much or how little pressure have you felt yourself under recently?

  2. Imagine each tire represents your mental, emotional, physical, and spiritual health. Which tire do you feel is full or needs to be filled?   

Road Sign: 

  1. There are many road signs that warn us that there's construction ahead, that one lane is closing, where the next rest stops are, or perhaps warnings about rockslides and slippery road conditions. What signs are your mind and body telling you now?

  2. When you notice these signs, what do you typically do? (e.g., seek support, become more isolated)

Fuel:

  1. Think about the last two weeks and ask yourself, how much fuel do you have left or what fuels are you getting filled with (e.g., family, passions, goals)? 

  2. What quality of fuel are you putting into your mind and body?

Car: 

  1. What is your destination?

  2. Have you been moving at a healthy, sustainable speed or are you speeding to this destination?
creation: During this time, we invite you to play some calming music and provide time reminders when participants are halfway and when they have a minute left to create. Doing so can help participants transition from the creation portion of the workshop to the closing.
closing:
Group Sharing: 

“We have about a couple minutes left before we have to end our workshop for today. However, before we do that I would like to take a few minutes to invite anyone who would like to share their creation or anything that stood out for them.” For additional questions, you are welcome to ask the group:

  • Is there anything new that you learned about yourself?

  • Are there any area(s) in your life that need more nurturing or care?

  • How do you plan to use your creation beyond this space?

 

Mini Art Exhibit:

“Before we say goodbye, I would like to invite you all to a mini sitting exhibit. During this time, you are welcome to hold up your creation, while also viewing the creation of others in the group. If you would like to join, I welcome you to hold up your creations.” Allow some time for participants to share their creations, while also viewing others. 

“Thank you all for joining me today and being present in whatever way felt right for you.”

 

           
        My Internal Dashboard Creations
tips:
Durational Art Tip:

As you take a look at your internal dashboard, you’re encouraged to check-in with yourself at the end of each week to see your progress. Questions to ask yourself are: How are you feeling? What is filling you? What is required to make it to your destination? Through this process we hope you feel empowered to take control of your journey at any point in time.

You can also facilitate this workshop using a printable worksheet. If you are utilizing the worksheet in lieu of the regular workshop materials, be sure to send a digital copy or print them out for your participants if you are meeting in person.

introduction:
“Thank you for being here today. Before we get started, I first wanted to share that this space is a window of time for you; unique, curious, passionate, creative you! During this time, you are welcome to focus on whatever you need. For our agenda today, I’ll first provide you with some creation instructions, but please feel free to follow along completely or do whatever feels best for you. After these instructions, I’ll be inviting you to a journaling warm-up followed by an opportunity to create for about 30 minutes. Then we will close with a group share. Are there any questions on the agenda before we begin?”  

 

Pause for a moment to allow participants to ask questions if they like.
demonstration:
“Before we begin creating, I invite you to look at the materials around you. At your station, you should have a road symbol page, construction paper, a writing utensil, markers, colored pencils, glue, and scissors.”

 

  1. Using the road symbol page, you will find four tires, four signs, a fuel pump, and a car. For each symbol you will be invited to fill it in using  words, colors, phrases and much more.  

    1. Tire: For each tire, I invite you to think about your mental, physical, emotional, and spiritual needs. Are they being filled? What are they being filled with? This can include hobbies, traditions, exercise, and more.

 

  1. Road Signs: Similar to road signs, our mind, body, and soul present different signs to us when we are feeling happy, sad, anxious, and much more. What signs is your body indicating to you, that you need rest, food, or that you are taking on too much stress? Maybe your body temperature goes high or maybe you feel depleted.

 

  1. Fuel: The fuel represents the things that keep you going. Are you feeling full or feeling empty? What is fueling you and what type of fuel are you inputting into your vehicle? Maybe you’re eating three meals a day or connecting with loved ones. What do you need to feel good about yourself? 

 

  1. Car: What or where is your destination? Where are you at now? What is your journey looking like?  Are you speeding down the roads or are you cruising? How can you make this journey enjoyable?

 

  1. After filling out your symbols you can cut out the tires, signs, fuel pump and car. 

  2. Next, you can pick whichever color construction paper you like and create a road unique to your journey. Feel free to share the Road Template during this time as an example. 

  3. Once you are done, you can assemble and glue your symbols onto your road.

 

     
  Step 1: Fill out your road symbols     Step 1 (continued): Color
         
     
  Step 2: Cut out     Step 3: Create your road
         
       
  Step 4: Assemble and glue your symbols onto your road
opening_circle:
“To get us started on today’s art workshop, I would like to invite you to a quick check-in. Using a single word, I welcome you to describe how you are feeling or how your day is going. We can go in a circle, starting on the left hand side and if you would like to skip, say SKIP and we will move on to the next person.” 

Once everyone who would like to check-in has, you can thank the participants for sharing and move into the workshop details. 

“For our workshop, you will have the opportunity to check-in with yourselves and assess where you are physically, mentally, and emotionally in order for you to continue on your journey. Sometimes, in our busy everyday lives, it can be easy to drift away or forget about our personal needs. Things like our own healing, health, or goals get sidelined in order to fulfill the demands and responsibilities that are required of us. Through this process we end up 'disconnecting,' or neglecting the things that mean the most to us. The signs can be subtle and playing out right in front of our own eyes, but we rarely even notice it! This has become so much more common that we sometimes can no longer even recognize it happening! The process of disconnection can lead us away from our personal and collective power and can disconnect us from our own authenticity.”

title: Coping Skills Bingo
objective: This workshop aims to teach coping skills to participants in a fun, creative way.
materials:
• Coping Skills Bingo cards

  • Small paper squares, pennies, or any small objects participants can put on the bingo squares

  • Writing utensils (colored pencils, crayons, markers, etc.)

    • You may invite participants to mark off their bingo square by drawing something on the square with a writing utensil as well

  • Paper

  • 99 Coping Skills handout

  • Prize for bingo winner(s)

    • This website has ideas for small bingo prizes for all ages
setup: Print out the bingo cards and 99 Coping Skills handout, prepare the paper squares/small objects/writing utensils for marking off the squares, gather pieces of blank paper and writing utensils. You can either use the blank bingo card to add all of your own coping skills or add a few to the partially filled out bingo card. Make a list of all of the coping skills on the bingo cards you're using so you can call those out during the bingo game. The coping skills on the partially filled out card are: ask for a hug, talk to a friend, drink water, play a game, take 3 deep breaths, sing a song, eat a healthy snack, spend time outdoors, listen to music, play with a pet, laugh, draw or doodle, stretch, journal, slowly count to ten, read a book, blow bubbles, make a gratitude list, and talk about your feelings.
creation:
Bingo:

Pass out materials to each participant who wishes to participate and remind them to say "bingo" out loud if they got five in a row. Invite participants to cover up their free space in the middle of the card. Then, call out each coping skill on the cards at random until a participant gets a bingo. After the first bingo, you can decide how many rounds you want to do depending on time limitations. Give out the prizes to the winner(s).

Drawing/Writing Coping Skills:

After bingo, pass out the 99 Coping Skills handout as the participants are ready to start drawing or writing their coping skills on a piece of paper. However they prefer to express themselves on the cards is perfect. You may encourage a minimum of 3 coping skills on the paper if you would like. Participants may choose coping skills from the bingo cards, ones they already use, or find new ones on the 99 Coping Skills sheet. They are welcome to draw, color, or write the coping skills. During creation is a great time to talk more about coping skills, home life, struggles, and strengths if they feel comfortable. You can invite participants to tape their creation onto their wall, fold it and keep it in their pocket, or leave it in a special place to remember their coping skills.
closing: When everyone is finished or it's close to ending time, invite participants to share any part of their creation as well as their thoughts about the activity if they want to. Remind them that it is okay not to share and that you will be ready to listen and learn more about them at their pace. Once everyone who wanted to share does so, thank everyone for coming and for participating in any way that they did, whether it's sharing, creating, or observing.
optional_materials:
You can also facilitate this workshop using a printable worksheet. If you are utilizing the worksheet in lieu of the regular workshop materials, be sure to send the sheet or print copies out for your participants beforehand depending on the setting.

  • Coping Skills Bingo (English and Spanish)

 

       
Coping Skills Bingo- English         Coping Skills Bingo- Spanish
introduction: As participants come in, try to greet each individual as much as possible. Finding a personal way to connect with the participants will help them feel recognized, remembered, and thought of. Introduce yourself and then invite the group to introduce themselves by stating their name and answering the focus question: "What is a coping skill and do you have any that you use?" After everyone who wanted to share does so, thank everyone for participating, even if they only observed.
opening_circle:
"Now, I invite you to think to yourself about what coping skills are, what coping skills you utilize, if they work, who taught you them, and anything else that comes up along the way. For those of you that are unfamiliar with coping skills, don’t worry. Today we are going to talk about them-- what they are, when to use them, and all the different ones you may try. After you have had a moment to think about coping skills and your experiences with them, I will explain what we are going to be doing today for our creation."

"Today, I welcome you all to play Coping Skills Bingo. I have a small prize for the winner(s). After bingo, I will invite everyone to use writing utensils to write or draw coping skills you currently use and/or would like to use on a piece of paper. However you choose to finish your creation is perfect because it's the way you chose to do it. Remember, there is no wrong way to make art. This is your window of time."

title: I Can: Requiem for I Can't
objective: This workshop is about confronting the things we feel we cannot do in our lives, allowing us recognize and embrace that we can do anything!
materials:
•
    Paper for I Can't journaling
  • Colored paper for I Can statements
  • Shrinky Dink paper
  • Shrinky Dink templates
  • Colored pencils
  • Permanent markers, like Sharpies
  • Hole puncher
  • Scissors
  • Toaster oven
  • Ribbon
  • Beads
  • Timer
creation:
Writing I Cant's:
Pass out pieces of paper to each participant who wishes to participate in the journaling activity.

"I welcome you to identify and release your I Cant's during ten minutes of journaling. You may take this ten minutes to write all the I Cant's that come up in your mind. You are welcome to use a colored pen to write your I Cant's... are your I Cant's yellow, red, green, or blue? They can be whatever color you'd like."

"Keep in mind that there is no right or wrong way to do this writing exercise. You may write sentences, words, lists or draw symbols, shapes-- whatever you would like. Throughout this exercise, I welcome you to try not to censor yourself and keep writing through the whole ten minutes. You can let go of spelling or grammar, just allow your thoughts to flow onto your paper without judgment. What you write is just for you and does not have to make sense to anyone but you!"

"You may begin by writing the words "I Can't" on the top of your paper. As you write, trust whatever comes to mind. It doesn't have to make sense. It's okay if you repeat one I can't over and over again. Now, we are going to begin the ten minutes to write all the I Cant's that come up." You may play music now.

Note: If you have a participant who has difficulty identifying an I Can't you can say: "If you feel powerful today and have no I Cant's to speak of, think of a time when you did have I Cant's and just keep writing."

In the last minute, remind them to keep trusting what comes to their mind. "We have about one more minute. As you finish up, read over your thoughts and notice what stands out..." You may pause the music now.
───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Sharing & Shredding:

  

"Now, you all are invited to come up one at a time and share your I Cant's with the group. Then, you may destroy them by either shredding or tearing them. Remember, this is voluntary, and you don't have to share anything you don't want to. Even if you don't want to share what you wrote, you are welcome to come up and shred your I Cant's. This is your opportunity to let go of your I Cant's. Would anyone like to come up here with me and share your I Cant's and then shred them?" 

Standing at the front of the room, next to the shredder (they can also tear it up by hand), invite others to come shred. As each person comes up, tell them it's okay to take their time and notice how brave they are. Continue until each participant who wants to participate has had an opportunity to share their I Cant's and shred/tear them.

Note: If this is a bilingual group, do not translate simultaneously while the participant shares as it may be disruptive. We ask that you wait until after the participant has shared and shredded.
───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
I Can Circle:
"Now that those who wanted to have let go of their I Cant's, we are going to take this opportunity to notice and celebrate our strength. I welcome everyone to stand up, gather in a circle, and hold hands. You may share something significant in your life that you thought you couldn't do, but you did and it made you stronger. There is no right or wrong way to share, and you don't have to share anything if you don't want to."

Note: If a participant is having a hard time thinking of something you can say: "One thing that you did was come to this group. By coming to group you are saying: 'I can take care of myself.'" After each person who wanted to has shared, have the participants sit back down and begin the I Can statement writing portion of the workshop. 

───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

I Can Statements:

 
   
  

Pass out pieces of colored paper to each participant who wishes to participate in this activity.

"Now that we have let go of our I Cant's and noticed our strength, we are ready to focus on our I Can's. You may think about all of the things that you can do, and choose one that really stands out. I invite you to pick a color to represent your I Can. Is your I Can purple, green, pink? It can be whatever color you'd like. Then, you can write your I Can statement on the paper provided by us."

If they choose, the participants can make more than one colorful I Can statement. You may play music during this activity.

───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
I Can Shrinky Dink:

  

"Next, I welcome all of you to create an I Can Shrinky Dink to remind you of the I Can's you chose to embrace today! Don't worry if your I Can seems impossible. Be bold! Never underestimate the power of putting our I Can's out into the world!" You can now play music.

  • Step 1: "Keeping in mind all of the things you can do, you can use colored pencils and/or permanent markers, write words, colors, shapes, or scribbles on the Shrinky Dink to help you remember your I Can's. You can color with permanent markers on both sides of the Shrinky Dink, but can only use colored pencils on the rough side. If you'd like to use a template, choose the one that best represents your I Can (remind participants that using a template is optional). Then, you may trace the template or draw on the Shrinky Dink and add color to fill in your design."
  • Step 2: "When you are finished coloring, if you would like, cut out your I Can Shrinky Dink with scissors. Make sure to punch a hole in the Shrinky Dink so it can be hung up. Make sure your don't punch your hole too close to the edge of the Shrinky paper as it may break after cooking."
  • Step 3: Now the I Can Shrinky Dinks are ready for baking. Bake the Shrinky Dink with the shiny side facing up. This will prevent it from folding while baking. Place the Shrinky Dink on either a small piece of a brown paper bag, parchment paper, or aluminum foil. Then place the paper, parchment paper, or foil with the Shrinky Dink on top on a metal tray. Put the metal tray in the toaster oven.
  • Step 4: Cook the Shrinky Dinks at 300 degrees for 1-3 minutes. After the Shrinky Dink lies flat, allow an additional 15 seconds of baking time to complete the process. If you pull the Shrinky Dink out prematurely, it is okay to put them back in the oven. 
  • Step 5: Remove paper, tray, or foil and let Shrinky Dinks cool. "If you like, you can add ribbon so you can hang your I Can Shrinky Dink. You can also add beads if you choose."
closing:
Invite each participant share anything they want about their experience writing their I Cant's, and the I Can's they represented on their I Can statement and Shrinky Dink. 

Thank the participants and suggest they use their I Can Shrinky Dink as a reminder that they can do anything!
optional_materials:
• Pens/Multi-colored pens
  • Paper shredder machine
  • Music
introduction:
If you want to view the exhibit of this workshop, click here.

"This workshop is about inspiring us to have the courage to release all of the things we think we cannot do. Confronting the things we feel we cannot do in our lives is the first step towards recognizing that we can do more than what we think. In today's workshop, I invite you all to come together and collectively let go of our I Cant's while embracing our I Cans."

"First, I will welcome you all to write and then shred your I Cant's, which are all the things we think we cannot do. Next, you may focus on all of the things you can do by writing an I Can statement. Finally, you can create an I Can Shrinky Dink to serve as a reminder that anything is possible and we can do anything we put our minds to!"

"This workshop is an opportunity for you to practice noticing your feelings and respecting what needs to come out. Every part of this is voluntary and you are welcome to participate in any way you'd like, including observing. Please know that everyone in the room supports you, and notice you are safe and among friends."
opening_circle: Invite the participants to share their name and how they're feeling right now. It is okay if participants do not choose to share.

title: Touchstone Journey Workshop Series
objective:
Welcome Journeyers!

From the very beginning, AWBW has been a circle of innovation with each participant and facilitator creating this journey. So now, at our 30th Anniversary, there is no way I’d rather move into this moment than by journeying creatively together.

Touchstone Journey invites a circle of innovation and practice of art transforming trauma, with Touchstones as a way to connect deeply to ourselves and each other. There are many layers to trauma and healing. From individual to relational, family, community and systemic layers, legacies of trauma ripple generations back. Actions of healing can ripple generations forward. This project welcomes a "learning lab" investigating Touchstones as an anchor for change, from the cellular to the systemic.

The following workshops were derived from co-journeyers that have been using Touchstones within their communities. Learn more about the Touchstone Journey Circle and join our Learning Labs here.

You can check out our AWBW Durational Art Supplies page to find tips on using touchstones, inspiration, AWBW offerings, and recommended links to all the supplies! You're also welcome to watch a full facilitation video of the art workshop Touchstone Journey here. 

Cathy Salser
AWBW Founder and Co-Journeyer
 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 



 

 
  Cathy Salser
   

 

Grounding

What transformations are you navigating or wishing for right now? Touchstone Journey offers space to listen deeply and plant seeds of change, dialog and vision to carry as a resource. Your touchstone may simply begin as a question, to be answered as lived as a journey day by day.

As we move forward on your journey, continue experimenting with what grounds you. Is it taking a cleansing breath? Is it noticing your feet touching the floor? Is it noticing your five senses? Is it practicing self-care in some way?

The more you consciously practice grounding (even something seemingly silly, like noticing your feet on the ground), the more you'll notice it's automatically there for you in moments of stress. What works for you?

  • Touchstone Journey worksheet
     

 

 

 

 

 

 

 


 

 

Your Journey Seed Kit:

  • Dream: This Touchstone Journey worksheet welcomes you to pause, breathe and invite an anchor for your journey. What vision, wish or seed of transformation is at the edge of your impossible?

  • Nest: For this workshop you may want to use the glass touchstone supplies. Glass Stone kits available here. See bulk links at bottom of the page to create your own kits. It’s also great to use the paper template, or any supplies you wish.

  • Connect: You are welcome to use the private FB Touchstone group as a space to stay connected as you journey. (For those on Facebook, search “Touchstone Journey”, request to join, and make yourself at home). And another opportunity: Journey buddies. We welcome you to find a buddy and support each other. Here’s a Journey Buddy Worksheet to vision and explore. At each Zoom gathering, there will be an opportunity for anyone seeking a Journey Buddy to pair up.

Additional Resources:

  • Glass Stones resource list
  • Video: Paper Touchstone TikTok
  • Video: Pencil Touchstone TikTok
  • Video: Colored Pencil & Sharpie TikTok
     
   
    Teresa Smith
     
   

Minimum Daily Stones by Teresa Smith

This Touchstone Journey offering is shared by Windows Facilitator, Teresa Smith from Being the Best Me. Teresa shares, “I was experiencing depression for some years. I was managing well until I made some life changes that caused me to relapse. I created what I call my Minimum Daily Function Stones to assist me in getting back on track. I’m excited to share this with you and invite you to name them whatever you like. My daily stones are: 1) Vitamins; 2) Exercise; 3) Self-care/get dressed; 4) 10 minutes of cleaning my surroundings; 5) Connect with my 5 senses. Each morning I put all five stones in my pocket. As I complete them, I put each into a basket. By the end of the day, my goal is to have all 5 in there.”

  • Video: Learning Lab | Grounding Practices - Minimum Daily Stones
  • Minimum Daily Stones worksheet
     

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 



 

   
    Susan Lee
     
   

Relationship Reset Stones by Susan Lee

Relationships affect every aspect of our lives and can be critical to our personal growth and development. Relationship Reset Stones, developed by Dr. Susan Lee from United American Indian Involvement in Los Angeles, CA, can be used to invite a shift where there are challenges. This can be used individually for self-care and personal growth or with another person, inviting dialogue and co-creation. Either way, it is meant to open a creative seed of change. If you’re considering including the other person, you might check in to see if they have the heart and mind space to join you. Please remember to always be safe in your journey.

  • Video: Learning Lab | Relationship Reset Stones
  • Relationship Reset Stones worksheet
     

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

   
    La Shonda Coleman
     
   

Relational Resilience from the Inside Out by La Shonda Coleman

This workshop, developed by La Shonda Coleman, founder of Trauma and Healing in Colour, offers a window of time for you to explore your relationships and notice points of activation that can make it difficult to engage with those that you do life with: loved ones, friends, co-workers or someone else. This workshop also offers an opportunity to move through these points and be resilient.

Our autonomic nervous system experiences activation when we are faced with a real or perceived threat (we may feel scared, anxious, disconnected, tense, sad or something else). In these moments, our nervous system response may be in survival mode (fight/flight/freeze). It is hard to be relational in this mode. It can be helpful to identify the points of activation and attend to it by identifying a resource that can help you feel safer. With this activity, you are invited to build relational resilience from the inside out.

Defeating My Giant by Karen Gonzalez

This workshop was created by Windows Facilitator, Karen Gonzalez, founder of Helping Hands Resource Center in Los Angeles, California. Karen uses art as a resource for survivors of domestic violence and trauma in a faith-based setting. She shares the story of David and Goliath and invites us to create our own “Defeating My Giant” Touchstones. This story represents David having his faith and trust in God. Regardless of how big the giant looked, he leaned on God and used a single stone to defeat the giant. We invite you to adapt this to any faith-based setting or spiritual practices you wish.

  • Video: Learning Lab | Defeating My Giant
  • Defeating My Giant worksheet
     

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 


 

   
    Starla Faye
     
   

Loving Kindness Stones by Starla Faye

This Touchstone Journey offering is brought to us by Windows Facilitator, Starla Faye from Southern California, who is engaged in a two year mindfulness leadership program with Jack Kornfield and Tara Brach. Starla invites us to create Touchstones to practice Metta, a Pali word that is most often translated as “loving kindness.” Metta is the quality of the heart that allows us to show up with care for others. Through this practice we can come to respond with less reactivity and more gentleness toward our own thoughts, emotions, and experiences. We invite you to explore what works for you and search online for mindfulness resources.

  • Video: Learning Lab | Loving Kindness Stones
  • Loving Kindness Stones Worksheet
     



 

 
  Aaron Mason
   
 

Mission Statement Mementos by Aaron Mason

This Touchstone Journey offering is shared by Windows Facilitator Aaron Mason from REACH LA in Los Angeles, CA. “The inspiration for this came from a young father that was participating in an intimate partner violence class that I used to facilitate. The man pulled a small baby sock out of his pocket and shared with the group that it belonged to his daughter. He went on to share that whenever he found himself challenged by habitual unhelpful ways of responding to the world, he would reach into his pocket and touch the sock as a reminder of his mission to complete his classes and utilize the tools gained to be a better version of himself.  I immediately thought ‘Wouldn’t it be wonderful for all of the participants to have a tangible reminder of their personal missions as fathers’.” I invite you to create your own touchstone to ground yourself in your personal mission. This workshop can serve as a wonderful way to set intentions for your healing journey.

  • Video: Learning Lab | Mission Statement Mementos
  • Mission Statement Mementos Worksheet

 


 

 
  Jamie Escoto and Lorenzo
   
 

Justice Journey Jars by Jamie Escoto

Last year, Touchstone Journeyer Jamie Escoto struggled with how to respond to her five-year-old son Lorenzo’s questions on the murder of George Floyd, race and racism. They created Justice Journey Jars to guide their discussions and reflect on readings. She shares: “Touchstones have been a powerful tool to anchor our learnings and ongoing conversations—from Black Lives Matter to Stop Asian Hate to celebrating Pride—creating tangible pieces that hold and support our journey. I invite you to use Justice Journey Jars as a way to birth your own journey or journeys with loved ones.”

  • Video: Learning Lab | Justice Journey Jars
  • Justice Journey Jars Worksheet

 

 

 
  Natalia Muñoz
   
 

Power of Ten by Natalia Muñoz and AWBW founder, Cathy Salser

This Touchstone offering was born during the 2020 US Presidential election cycle focused on voter mobilization. Created by Brooklyn-based artist and Touchstone Journeyer, Natalia Muñoz and AWBW founder, Cathy Salser, it is an invitation to use art to imagine ad anchor 10 actions to challenge oppressive systems and dominant narratives. Through Touchstones, we can set intentions as a collective and not in isolation, create a tangible resource to sustain transformative action, and center self-care at the heart of our liberation.

  • Video: Learning Lab 10 | Power of Ten
  • Power of Ten Worksheet
     

 

 

Windows of Gratitude

This Touchstone invitation welcomes you to explore gratitude as a “window” of change. Practiced mindfully, gratitude can allow us to become present to what is, aware and open to important gifts even when faced with deep challenges. More than a candy-coated concept—is it a dynamic tool that can be used, moment by moment, as an anchor in our lives. 

  • Windows of Gratitude worksheet
     

 

 
   
   

Vision Seeds

You are invited to create Vision Seeds as a way to reflect on this moment, notice seeds of change you hold, and carry them forward. What transformations are you wishing for — in your own body and heart, relationships, community and world? Personally? Professionally? May this become a tool to support your journey.

title: My Cup of Tea
objective: To offer an opportunity of letting go of negative messages we tell ourselves and hold onto words of encouragement and compliments we tell others... holding onto them for ourselves,drinking them in on a daily basis!
materials:
•  

    Pencil

  • Pens

  • Watercolors

  • Cups of water for watercolors

  • Colored pencils

  • Scratch paper

  • Scissors

  • Glue

  • Foam squares

  • Paper towels

  • 8” by 4” tag

  • 4x4 piece of white cardstock

  • Tag and cup template
setup:
If you are facilitating this live... make it into a Tea Party with hot tea and pretty tea cup set would be awesome even if they didn’t all match! Have enough supplies on the table for everyone to either have their own or share with one other person

Tip: If virtually leading the workshop, encourage all the participants to have a cup of their favorite hot tea with them to drink and savor during the workshop, and to gather the supplies they need ahead of time so they can create un interrupted.
warm_up:
Before we start with the creation process,sometimes it is helpful to relax our body and our mind so we can go within our mind and heart so we can truly focus on ourselves. Relaxation may feel uncomfortable at first but please give it a chance, you may find you end up loving it!

Relaxation: Speak slowly with soft music playing in the backgroundIf it feels safe for you, gently close your eyes andjust imagine yourself sitting on acomfy couch with your feet up and a snuggly blanketaround you...You have pouredyourself your favorite cup of tea ... and you beginto feel its warmth, you see the heatwaves rising above it and you begin to smell the delicateflavor scents of your favoritetea. As you sit there you begin to relax by wigglingyour toes, then moving yourawareness to the calves of your legs and your thighs,you begin to feel safe and cozyunder your fluffy, comfy blanket... take a deep breathand let any tension you areholding out...whosh... and just breathe in relaxation..Move your awareness to your shoulders and gently shrugthem around... keepbreathing deeply and you notice you are intuitivelyfeeling the relaxation move overyour entire bodytake another deep breath in and let it out slowlytake another deep breath breathing in the warmth andscent of your favorite tea andbreathing out any tension.And as you totally relax, begin to visualize yourcup of tea, actually visualize the teacup... what kind of cup is it?
