title: My Treasure Chest: The Power of Me - Staying Regulated & Connected to Your Values When Talking About Race
extra_field:
Tracie Stafford

This workshop was part of a Facilitator Enrichment Training titled My Treasure Chest: The Power of Me - Staying Regulated & Connected to Your Values When Talking About Race hosted by Tracie Stafford. Tracie is the CEO of Stafford Consulting Group and a cultural responsiveness facilitator, social sustainability scientist, and advocate. She has traveled the country delivering anti-bias and behavioral leverage trainings for corporations, political organizations and activists.

During the workshop, Tracie guides participants through the following topics:

  • Examining the physiological impacts on conversations about race.

  • Uncovering what hijacks us and the soothing mechanisms we currently use.

  • Identifying new tools to stay regulated and connected with our values in difficult situations.

Download Tracie's slides from this presentation here.

Download all the worksheets here.
 

 

Physiology: Fight, Flight, Freeze

Understanding your physiology in times of stress or discomfort is critical to your ability to give and receive information effectively. Being consistently in survival brain (fight, flight or freeze/hijacked) can also negatively impact your long-term health and happiness. What hijacks you and how do you feel in those moments?

       

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 


 

Automatic Soothing Mechanisms

How you react when hijacked (fight, flight or freeze/survival brain) is often a natural response developed during infancy, childhood, and young adulthood. During times of stress, did you suck your thumb, need to be held, go to sleep, cry, shut down or scream in anger? When in survival brain, the body does not know right from wrong, good from bad, healthy from unhealthy it is merely attempting to right itself. Do your automatic/natural soothing mechanisms serve you or work against you?

       

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 


 

Adaptive Soothing Mechanisms

Now that you have identified some natural or automatic soothing mechanisms, how have they changed over your lifetime? Has sucking your fingers become overeating, shutting down become self-harm, the need for hugs become sexual behavior or has anger become abuse?

       

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

Our Treasure Chest

What tools do you have, including new ones you discovered that you can add to your treasure chest? What are these tools and how will you use them?

The fight or flight response is a beautiful thing. Soothing mechanisms are beautiful things!! But most importantly, You Dear Heart, are a beautiful, powerful and beloved being. Be courageous, be vulnerable and be kind to yourself. This is YOUR summary to reference as you continue your ever evolving journey.

title: Anti-Racism Curriculum Series
objective: This workshop series invites participants to engage in learning opportunities, discussions, and cultivate tools to support ongoing action against marginalization, racism, and oppression.
materials:
• Guiding Questions Worksheets

  • Creation Worksheets

  • Pens

  • Pencils

  • Rulers

  • Erasers

  • Colored pencils

  • Markers
setup:
We recommend that you share the following resources with participants before you begin any of the workshops in the series.

  • Community Agreements

  • Definition of racism: Prejudice, discrimination, or antagonism directed against a person or people on the basis of their membership in a particular racial or ethnic group, typically one that is a minority or marginalized. The belief that different races possess distinct characteristics, abilities, or qualities, especially so as to distinguish them as inferior or superior to one another. The short version is that racism is prejudice plus power.

  • Definition of trauma: Trauma is the response to a deeply distressing or disturbing event that overwhelms an individual’s ability to cope, causes feelings of helplessness, diminishes their sense of self and their ability to feel a full range of emotions and experiences.

  • Healing Your Thousand-Year-Old Trauma

  • 'Movement and Space': Civil Rights Center Community Guide to Help Fight Racism in America

  • The Invention of Whiteness: The Long History of a Dangerous Idea

  • White Supremacy Culture - Still Here

Videos:

  • Feudalism in Medieval Europe

  • Ghost in Your Genes

  • What is the Doctrine of Discovery? | NDN POV | TVO Today

  • The Truth About the Confederacy of the United States
creation:
The Roots & Symptoms of Racial Trauma
Download the Grounding Worksheet
Download the Creation Worksheet

We recommend sharing the following with participants days before the workshop to help ground and prepare them.

  • Grieving the White Void

Deeply embedded into the soil of ourselves, our families, and our society is unresolved trauma. Trauma has a direct connection to the history of racism and how it manifests in our minds, bodies, and the world. By mapping the root of trauma in our life and our family’s lives, we can begin to see how our responses and those of others have contributed to the perpetuation of racism. Using this worksheet, you are invited to map the origins of trauma in your life, including historical and intergenerational trauma. In and around the roots and stem use words, drawings, and colors to represent the traumatic events and experiences that you and your family/ancestors experienced. Next, create in and around the leaves to represent the responses and symptoms that sprouted from these experiences. There is no right or wrong way to create. When you’re done, you can refer back to your creation to ground yourself in the understanding of the root causes of racial trauma as we work to weed it out of ourselves, our families, and society as a whole.

 

 
   

The Man Box
Download the Grounding Worksheet
Download the Creation worksheet

We recommend sharing the following with participants days before the workshop to help ground and prepare them.

  • Breaking Out of the "Man Box": The Next Generation of Manhood

  • Brené Brené Brown’s interview with Oprah Winfrey and Dr. Bruce D. Perry on Trauma, Resilience, and Healing

  • Grieving the White Void

  • Helping Men Breat Out of the Man Box

  • Video: Tony Porter's TED Talk

  • Video NFL player's abuse video puts the spotlight on domestic violence. *Trigger warning as this video shows an incident of domestic violence

Tony Porter, along with the Oakland Men’s Project, created The Man Box. The Man Box focuses on male gender socialization — the traditionally constructed rules on what it means to be a man, rules that are grounded in the marginalization of women and people who are queer, genderqueer, and transgender. These rules create norms in society that include: 

  • Viewing women and girls as objects, the property of men, who have less value than men

  • Boys and men should not cry or openly express emotion, except for anger

  • Boys and men should not show fear or weakness

  • Boys and men should “be a man,” “man up,” and not “act like a girl”

  • Boys and men should be decisive and not ask for, offer, or accept help

  • Aggression equals dominance

Using the space worksheet, you are invited to use words, shapes, colors, and symbols to explore how the The Man Box has impacted you. Toxic masculinity, sexism and patriarchy play a large role in creating and perpetuating racism and racial trauma. As we explore and share our experiences, we can better understand and address the root causes of racial trauma as we work to weed it out of ourselves, our families, and society as a whole. While creating, we invite you to explore the following questions:

  • If you identify as male, what has been your experience with The Man Box? How did it feel to be taught this? How did it feel to practice this?

  • If you do not identify as male, how has The Man Box impacted your life? 

  • How does The Man Box tie into race and culture? How does it play a role in the racism experienced in this country and the world?

  • How can you break out of the Man Box? What can help you? How can you help others do the same?

 

 
   

Anti-Racism Toolbox
Download the Grounding Worksheet
Download the Creation Worksheet

We recommend sharing the following with participants days before the workshop to help ground and prepare them.

  • California Towns Where Blacks Feared Sundown Towns
  • Video: ABC Tried to Buy This James Baldwin Interview
  • Video: Get Comfortable with Being Uncomfortable - Luvvie Ajayi Jones
  • Video: Beah Thus A Black Woman Speaks

Anti-racism work is a process that involves ongoing learning, unlearning, dialogue, information exchange, leadership, courage  and action. Over the past few months, we’ve had the opportunity to engage in brave and honest discussions to open up, share, listen, and grow. As we prepare ourselves for the work ahead, it’s important to check-in. The work we do together and individually allows us to create a toolbox of collective resources we can utilize to dismantle racism. You are invited to use words, shapes, symbols, and colors to creatively explore the questions below. Your creation can serve as a point of reference and resource to ground you in your ongoing commitment to take action against racism.

  • What have you learned? What are some of your takeaways from the past few months? What actions have you taken/supported others in taking?

  • What has shifted? How has your perspective on racism and how you can work against it evolved? Have you used what you’ve learned with family, friends, coworkers? If so, how?

What do you need? Is there any additional information, tools, or support you need as we continue learning and growing together? What would you like more or less of?

 

 
   
   
   

Examining & Addressing Implicit Bias
Download the Grounding Worksheet
Download the Creation Worksheet

We recommend sharing the following with participants days before the workshop to help ground and prepare them.

  • The Four Types of Fear - Foundation for Conscious Living

An implicit bias is an unconscious association, belief, or attitude toward a social group. They show up when we attribute certain qualities or characteristics to specific groups of people. In addition to explicit bias, intentional and conscious beliefs and attitudes, implicit biases play a huge role in racism. They are influenced by personal experiences, including cultural conditioning, media exposure, upbringing, and so much more. By diving deeper into these biases, we can notice how the show up in our thoughts and actions. You are invited to use the worksheet to explore your implicit biases and map how they may show up for you and how you might derail and dismantle them. You can use words, shapes, and/or drawings to represent your thoughts and feelings. There is no right or wrong way to create. When you’re done, use this page as a reminder of the ongoing action we all must take to uproot and end racism.
 

 
   

Heart-Centered Action Planning
Download the Grounding Worksheet
Download the Creation Worksheet

It may be true that hurt people, hurt people, but it’s also true that healed people heal people. Our individual and collective work toward ending racism begins with, and is sustained by, listening to our hearts. Creating an action plan that can support you with engaging in difficult conversations, sharing your knowledge, and taking care of yourself along the way is very important.

Using the worksheet, use words, shapes, colors, and drawings to represent your thoughts and feelings. In the center circle, capture the healing you have experienced while doing this work and what you would like to pass along to others. Outside of the circle and inside of the heart, show what reminders, affirmations, and other things you need to keep you moving forward. In the space around the heart and hands, show some of the things you’re still dealing with that you might need more support with.

At the bottom of the page, use your creation as a resource to come up with an action plan with easy steps, a timeline, and measurable goals. Maybe you’d like to begin conversations with family, friends, or coworkers. Maybe you’re planning to engage art workshop participants in this work. Or maybe you want to carve out more time to dive deeper into personal work. There is no right or wrong way to create, just trust whatever is in your heart. Together we change the dynamic and heal.

 

 

Taking Time to P.A.U.S.E for Empathy
Download the Grounding Worksheet
Download the Creation Worksheet

One of the main roots of structural racism is nourished by the notion of othering — the manufactured act of distancing oneself from a group of people who are outside of one’s own group. Othering became the foundation in which many systems and laws were put into place in the United States and abroad, many of which are alive and well today. As lifelong learners and activists living within these systems, learning P.A.U.S.E (People Are Uniform with Sincere Empathy) can be helpful in our ongoing efforts against marginalization and oppression. Before the external journey, we must start with the internal journey and examine the personal experiences that influenced us. Through this work, we aim to open our heart to increased empathy for everyone.

Using the chart, you are invited to examine the influences in your life, including your environment, the media, politics, family, friends, etc. and chart out what actions you’d like to take. There is no right or wrong way to create, just trust whatever comes out. When you’re done, consider sharing with a safe person.

 

 
 

Flower Power: Examining Our Social Identities
Download the Grounding Worksheet
Download the Creation Worksheet

Social identities are how we identify ourselves and understand who we are. As we construct these social identities internally for ourselves, there are simultaneous identities put onto us by the outside world. Through these identities, dominance and non-dominance has been established and woven into the fabric of American culture, society, and laws, upholding many systems of oppression, including racism. Examining our social identities can help us understand our past and look at our role moving forward. We can better identify injustices and stand up for ourselves and others.

Consider each petal a part of your identity. You are invited to use words, shapes, and images to describe how you see yourself as a part of that group. You can choose to create one color to symbolize areas where you are seen as dominant/socially powerful/privileged and another color for petals where you are viewed as subordinate/not socially powerful/not privileged.

How does membership in these groups impact your interactions with people not in this group? What are the consequences in the workplace?

 

 

Recognizing Power: Becoming Color Conscious
Download the Grounding Worksheet
Download the Creation Worksheet

Colorblind racial ideology is a harmful way of viewing the world. By ignoring race and not engaging in conversations around the disadvantages that people of color face in this world allows implicit and racial biases to thrive. This workshop invites us to lean into color consciousness by first recognizing the beauty we possess. As we step into this acknowledgment, we step into our power, leading by example and opening ourselves to deeper conversations around opression and racism.

You are invited to make a self-portrait focusing on the beauty of your color – your skin, your eyes, your hair textures, your nose or any other body parts you would like to show some positive attention towards. You are invited to consider the messages you would like to give to your younger self about color. Feel free to use words, images and colors to demonstrate your embodiment of power, beauty, and healing.
introduction:
Fran Sutton-Williams
   
 
  Melodie Lopez

As we started 2021, we were faced with images of our nation's Capitol being attacked by violent, fascist mobs in a misguided attempt to overrun our country's democratic process. This wasn't only an attack on our democracy, it was one of many displays of how white supremacy manifests in our society every day.

The events of 2020 brought increased awareness around how rampant racial injustices are in this country. In response, we've been working on creating a space to come together for much-needed conversations around the history of racism, our experiences with it, and our commitment to taking action against racism in our professional and personal lives.

Our Anti-Racism Group began in April 2021 and invites Windows Facilitators to engage in learning opportunities, small group discussions, and cultivate tools to support ongoing action.

2021 Anti-Racism Group Facilitator: Fran Sutton-Williams

Windows Facilitator, author, trainer, and activist, Fran Sutton-Williams speaks from her lived experience as a Black woman and guide our monthly sessions, sharing her knowledge and wisdom along the way.

2022 Anti-Racism Group Facilitator: Melodie Lopez

Melodie is a longtime Windows Facilitator, Co-founder of Native Education Alliance and Founding Matriarch, HONOR Collective in Arizona. She will bring her unique lens and voice to the Anti-Racism Group through her lived experience as an indigenous woman working with indigenous communities.

title: The Ripples of Self-Care
objective: This workshop centers on self-care for the service provider. It uses the metaphor of skipping stones on water to invite thinking about how performing small acts of self-care can have a ripple effect on our bodies, lives, life’s work, and beyond.
materials:
• Watercolor paper

  • Watercolor paint sets

  • Paintbrushes

  • Cups of water

  • Napkins or paper towels

  • I Can Pause Handout by Big Life Journal
setup:
If you are using the watercolor paint sets, you can set up each participant’s space at the table with an individual paint set, two pieces of paper, two cups of water (one for wetting brushes and one for changing colors), and a napkin or paper towel to dry their brushes.

Depending on the availability of supplies, paintbrushes, liquid watercolors, and watercolor pencils can placed in the center of the table to be shared between two or three people.

If you are facilitating virtually, you can share the printable Ripples of Self-Care Worksheet and invite participants to print or create on a separate piece of paper with a pencil or pen, or with any art supplies that they happen to have on hand.

You may want to consider writing the different steps to the creation process somewhere your participants can easily see them. If you are facilitating virtually, you can also type the creation steps into the chat.

         
     
Setup with watercolors       Setup with worksheet
warm_up:
I Can Pause Handout

For this section, you have the option of guiding participants through a brief brainstorming session. We recommend writing the self-care ideas participants share somewhere they can see and refer back to them during the creation portion. You can use the questions below to help guide your discussion, or come up with your own:

  • When you think about self-care, what's the first thing that comes to mind?

  • What is something you already do for self-care?

  • What is something you'd like to do for self-care?

  • Is there anything on the handout you would like to try?

  • When you step outside of yourself, what can you see that you need? What self-care act could meet that need?

  • What is the smallest act of self-care you could perform on a regular basis?

  • What is the greatest gift you could give yourself when it comes to self-care?

You can start with this opening script, or however you'd like to begin:

"Before we move into creating, I’d like to invite you to join me in brainstorming some of the ways we can practice self-care. Using the metaphor of skipping stones, these would be the stones themselves. Let's start with what you already do and build on that. We can also use the I Can Pause Handout to help us generate some ideas around relaxing, being mindful, getting outside, connecting, and creating."
creation:
You may wish to remind participants about the steps for creation. If you've written the creation steps somewhere they can see, you can remind participants where to find them. Or, if you are facilitating virtually, you can type the creation steps into the chat for them to read.

 
  Creation on worksheet

Step 1 Participants can practice using the watercolors on the extra piece of paper before starting on their Ripples of Self-Care art.

Step 2 When they are ready to get started, they can paint the stones to represent the acts of self-care they want to practice.

Step 3 Then they can paint the ripples created by the stones. The ripples can represent the need the self-care arises from, how the self-care will positively impact their lives, life situations in which it might be helpful to perform the self-care, or something else.

Step 4 They have the option of writing or painting any words, shapes, or symbols they want on their paper before painting over them with the watercolors, or writing any words on top once the paint dries.

Step 5 Finally participants can include any other details like images of nature, people, or anything else to complete their art.
closing:
"At this time I’d like to invite whomever wishes to share to do so. You can share your art, about your process, or anything else that may have come up for you during the workshop today, including:

  • How it felt to think about self-care today

  • The acts of self-care you want to practice

  • The ripple effect you imagine will be created by your self-care

  • What your art tells you about what self-care means to you

  • How we can support you with your self-care, or anything else you may need from the group

"Now that everyone who wanted to share has had a chance to do so, I want to thank you all for taking this Window of Time to create ripples of self-care through your presence here and honoring how you chose to participate today, whether that was creating, sharing, observing, or another way.

"It’s powerful to think about the ripples of change and self-compassion that go out from each one of us today as we carry what we have discovered within ourselves forward into the world and the work that we are doing every day."
optional_materials:
• Cardstock paper or any heavy stock paper is a great alternative to watercolor paper.

  • Liquid watercolors are a nice alternative to watercolor paint sets because they remove the need for cups of water and can be distributed into dauber bottles or dropper bottles to create different effects.

  • Watercolor pencils are another great option because they allow for greater control and can be used for writing and shading. Can be used on their own or in combination with watercolor paints.

  • Oil-based mediums like crayons and Cray-Pas can also be used for writing as the oil in these mediums will resist the water in the watercolors. (We don't recommend markers for writing as they smear when they get wet.)

  • If facilitating virtually, the printable Ripples of Self-Care Worksheet can be used in lieu of the other supplies and participants invited to print or create on a separate piece of paper with a pencil or pen, or with any art supplies that they happen to have on hand.

 

You may wish to share these articles on self-care with your participants:

  • Self Care 101

  • What Is Self-Care and Why Is It Important?

  • Why Self-Care Is Vital for Social Service Professionals

  • 25 Stay-At-Home Self-Care Ideas During COVID-19
introduction:
"The workshop I’ll share with you today is called The Ripples of Self-Care. Every time we perform an act of self-care it is like skipping a stone on water, it has a ripple effect on our bodies, lives, life’s work, and beyond. In this workshop I’ll invite you to identify the stones you can skip or acts of self-care you can practice, as well as to imagine the ripples created by these acts and meaning they hold for you personally.

“Before we begin, I’d like to invite you to let this workshop be a Window of Time for you– a safe/brave space to notice your thoughts, feelings, and needs. During our Window of Time, everything is voluntary. I’ll offer a suggested workshop idea, share about the materials we have available, and invite you to create, but there’s no right or wrong way. What matters is just taking this time to truly listen within and honor your own thoughts, feelings and needs. Are there any questions before we begin?”
demonstration:
Creation with watercolors

"Today I'll be inviting you to create using watercolors. I’m going to begin by demonstrating how the watercolors can be used to create your art today. You have two cups of water, one for wetting your brushes and one for cleaning your brushes when you want to change colors. After you get your brush wet you can use it to water down one of the colors. The more water you use, the lighter and more diluted the color will be. The less water, the bolder and more concentrated the color. (You can demonstrate this effect for your participants.) You have an extra piece of paper to practice on, or you can just dive right in!

"When you are ready to get started, you can begin by painting the stones to represent the acts of self-care you want to practice. Then you can paint the ripples created by the stones when they are skipped on the water. The ripples around each stone can represent the need that act of self-care arises from, for example, taking a break to drink a glass of water might arise from the need to survive, satisfy thirst, or perform a life-giving act of service for one’s body. Or the ripples could represent the positive effects you anticipate experiencing from performing that caring act for yourself, like having your thirst quenched, centering in gratitude for yourself for this small act of kindness, or connecting with the sensation of being alive. The ripples could also represent situations in your life in which you think it might be helpful to take a break for self-care as this can help you to remember your tools (stones) when you are feeling activated or dysregulated. For example, when I am feeling burned out at work and need a break, I can drink a nice glass of ice water out of a clean glass, being mindful of the sensations I experience as I perform this loving, life-giving act for myself.

"You have the option of writing or painting any words, shapes, or symbols you want on your paper before painting over them with the watercolors, or you can write any words on top once the paint dries. Finally you can complete your art by adding any other details like images of nature, people, or anything else.

"Please know that it’s perfectly okay if the metaphor of skipping stones doesn’t resonate with you as you are more than welcome to express this idea in a new way or express something else entirely! For example, instead of 'The Ripples of Self-Care' you could explore 'The Winds of Change' or 'The Rays of Service' or 'The Waves of Compassion,' just to name a few."
opening_circle:
"Today’s workshop is all about self-care for the service provider. As service providers our bodies, minds, and hearts are the very tools with which we work. We use our minds to help people solve problems and navigate oppressive systems, our hearts to care and have compassion for their experiences, our hands and feet to help them in very practical ways, maybe even a deeper part of ourselves to find a higher meaning and sense of fulfillment in what we do. Because our bodies, minds, and hearts are our means for doing this work in the world, it can benefit us to serve them in the same way that we provide service to others.

"It can be helpful to go even a step further and picture ourselves as someone else. Just as you step outside of yourself to imagine what someone else might need, I invite you to step out now and see what you might need. (You can pause here and give participants a moment to reflect.)

"Self-care can look like performing very basic, life-giving activities for ourselves like drinking water and breathing deeply. It can look like giving ourselves a gift, creating a new daily ritual, or doing something spontaneous. Or it can look like setting something down that’s no longer serving us, giving up a harmful habit, or ending a toxic relationship. It can even look like giving ourselves credit for what we are already doing, or doing those things with greater intentionality and awareness. These can be things like calling old friends, cooking good meals, watering our plants, petting our dogs, and many of the other things we do daily to care for ourselves and through mindful care of others.

"When we practice self-care we can start to feel the effects on our bodies and see the effects in our lives. We might feel more positive, less anxious, and better regulated. These effects extend outwards, positively impacting the people closest to us and wider circles to which we belong. Thus, the self-care has a ripple effect on our relationships, communities, and even our world.

"As service providers, making self-care a part of our everyday practice can support the work we are doing for longer and model care and compassion for ourselves to the people we serve. By showing up for ourselves in a very loving and intentional way we show others how to do the same, while also being better able to show up for them in service, support, and solidarity. This, too, has a ripple effect.

"In today’s workshop, I’ll invite you to identify some of the stones you can skip or acts of self-care you can practice, as well as to imagine the ripples created by those acts and meaning they hold for you personally."

title: Poems from the Heart
objective: To write poems about our hearts as a way of showing or sharing about our experiences. To use poetic metaphor to make connections between our hearts and the world around us.
materials:
• Loose leaf paper

  • Journals

  • Pens and pencils

  • Pencil sharpeners

  • Erasers

  • Scissors

  • Glue sticks

  • Magazines for collage

  • Copies of example poems

  • Poems from the Heart Worksheet
setup:
You can offer participants a choice between loose leaf paper or a journal they can keep. You can invite participants to use their favorite writing utensil or choose from the different pens and pencils you have available for them.

You may want to have other art materials like scissors, glue sticks, and magazines for collage available for participants who express themselves better visually or who want to add visual elements to their finished poems.

You can choose from the example poems above which ones will work best for your participants, or use your own examples. It's best to offer a variety of poems written by people writing from different subject positions, in different styles (long and short poems, song-like and story-like, rhyming and not), and about self-love as well as romantic love.

If you are facilitating virtually, the Poems from the Heart Worksheet can be shared with participants electronically. Participants can print it out or use a separate piece of paper and pencil or pen to do their writing.
warm_up:
Reading example poems

"Before we get started on our Poems from the Heart, I’d like to share some of my personal favorite “poems from the heart” with you. For those of you who wish to participate, I’ll invite you to first read the poems to yourself and then if anyone would like to opt into reading one of them aloud to the group they can.

"Reading the poems, what did you notice about the way the poets talk about the experiences of their hearts and the metaphors they use for their hearts? Did you have a favorite poem? Did you have a favorite metaphor or part?"
creation:
Adding visual elements

Step 1 Participants can use the Poems from the Heart Worksheet to make a list of metaphors for their heart, then they can pick their favorite metaphor or metaphors to use in their poem. They can start their poem with their favorite metaphor or use it as the title.

Step 2 Participants can write their Poems from the Heart. If they get stuck, they can go back to their list of metaphors or make a new list of words they associate with their chosen metaphor, then try to work these words into the poem.

Step 3 Participants can add any visual elements to their finished poems like magazine clippings or decorative collage.
closing:
"At this time I’d like to invite anyone who wishes to share to do so. You can read your poem or ask a volunteer in the group to read it for you. Then you can share anything else about the poem, your process, or anything that came up for you during the workshop.

"Thank you so much for taking this window of time to honor how you chose to participate today, whether that was writing a Poem from the Heart or being present with your heart in another way. It’s wonderful to think about how connected our hearts are to the world around us and how special they are to remind us of so many beautiful things."

introduction:
"The workshop I’ll share with you today is called Poems from the Heart. In a way, all poems are from the heart, but our poems will be special because they’ll be all about our hearts and the different things our hearts have experienced. Using a poetic tool called metaphor, you’ll be able to share about your experience by showing it with your words.

"This is your Window of Time, separate from the rest of the day, to practice respecting your thoughts, your needs, and your feelings. A space that can carry us from where we are now and towards where we want to go – a space for change. When we take a Window of Time to listen to our heart, it creates change and we are not the same afterwards and that, in and of itself, is art.

"To begin, I’m going to go over the materials we have available to us and steps we can take to create our Poems from the Heart. Then you’ll have the chance to read some poems that use metaphors for the heart and make a list of metaphors for your own heart. Are there any questions before we begin?"
demonstration:
Making a list of metaphors

"For your writing today you can use your favorite writing utensil or choose from the pens and pencils we have available. You also have a choice between doing your writing on loose leaf paper or in a journal you can keep.

"Before we get started on our poems, I'll invite you to make a list of metaphors for your heart. Metaphor is a tool in poetry that links two things together using "like" or "is." For example, "My heart is like a treasure chest" and "My heart is a precious gem" are two metaphors for the heart. In the first example, "heart" and "treasure chest" are linked together using the word "like." In the second example, "heart" and "gem" are linked using "is."

"You can use the Poems from the Heart Worksheet to help you get started. On the left you will see that there are sentences with blanks you can fill in to create different metaphors for your heart. Once you have your metaphors you can pick your favorites to use in your poem. You can start your poem with your favorite metaphor or even use it as the title of the poem."
opening_circle:
"In today's workshop, you'll be invited to use metaphor to write about what your heart reminds you of or is like. What comes to mind when you think about your heart? A valentine, a locket, a treasure chest? What sounds do you hear in your heartbeat? A horse’s hooves, the beat of a drum? What makes your heart special? Is it precious like a gemstone, is it unique like a snowflake? Is it gentle or wild like an animal? These are some of the questions you can explore in your poem.

"In writing your Poem from the Heart you can ask yourself questions like, “Why or in what ways does my heart remind me of this thing?”, “What are some of the qualities I associate with this thing?”, and “What does this thing tell me about my heart?” If you get stuck you can go back to your list of metaphors or make a new list of words you associate with your favorite metaphors. For example, if one of your metaphors for your heart is that your heart is like a horse, you can make a list of words you associate with horses like "hooves," "saddle," "stallion," and "freedom." Then you can try to work those words into the poem.

"It’s okay if you’ve never written a poem or worked with metaphor before because there is no right or wrong way to write from your heart. Your poem doesn’t have to make sense to you or anyone else. It doesn’t have to rhyme unless you want it to. It can be long or short, happy or sad, song-like or story-like. This is your window of time so you get to decide, you can write a Poem from the Heart, a song or story from the heart, or even make a collage from the heart! It’s up to you how you choose to use this window of time to honor your heart today."

 

Note: Some folks may feel activated by the invitation to express themselves in writing because of negative or traumatic past experiences or perceived skill or ability. You can be sensitive to this by making every aspect of the workshop optional, allowing folks to opt in to any reading you do, and offering alternatives to the writing like collage. You can assure participants that spelling and grammar don’t count when writing from the heart.

title: Windows of Gratitude: A Durational Art Experience
objective:
Welcome to your year of gratitude!

Gratitude allows us to be present to what is, aware and open to important gifts even when faced with deep challenges. It is more than a candy-coated and rose-colored concept — it is a dynamic tool to be used as an anchor in our hectic lives.

I invite you to notice what happens when you invite gratitude in. Does something shift in your body or heart? What enters? What drains away? This journal was created as a way for you to connect with your own embodied lens of gratitude and have a tangible reminder to invite it into your being daily.

As you begin your durational gratitude journey, remember: the art is not just what you create in your journal, it is the process of contemplating, of expressing, and it is the moments you reference your creation, especially in moments of challenge, to return to your own place of serenity and connection.

Cathy Salser

Artist & AWBW Founder

How to use this journal:

Using this journal as your guide, we invite you to embark on a year-long journey of gratitude. We have provided 12 prompts to ground you in your monthly practice, or to use at whatever pace you’d like to move through them. Follow the suggested steps below to stay connected to all that you are grateful for.

  • Print each journal and creation page as you go or print them all at once.

  • Gather whatever art supplies you’d like to use for your expression of gratitude.

  • Before you create, begin by grounding yourself in the present in any way that feels right for you.

  • Read the prompt and take a few moments to write down your thoughts on the lines provided.

  • On the “My expression of gratitude” page, use shapes, colors, images, and words to create art as an extension of your journaling.

  • Cut down the center of each page and bind them together using staples or holes and string.

  • To be reminded of your gratitude, keep this journal nearby.

title: Exploring Your Unique Textures
objective: This workshops aims to support us in finding acceptance and compassion for all parts of ourselves and our lives.
materials:
•  

       
       

    Paper (4 pieces per person)

  • Markers

  • Colored pencils

  • Regular pencils

  • Pens

  • Erasers

  • Hard, rough, soft, and smooth objects (like rocks, sandpaper, silk, ribbon, cotton balls, etc.) to see and feel. At least one rough and one smooth object per person.
warm_up:
Timed Writing Exercise

If participants are using their own paper instead of the worksheets, invite them to fold a piece of paper in half and label one side “Soft/Smooth” and the other side “Hard/Rough.”

“We’re now going to move into our timed writing exercise where we’ll be getting our first thoughts and feelings onto the paper. There are two sides to your paper, one labeled “Soft/Smooth” and the other “Hard/Rough.” First, you can choose one hard/rough item from the center of the table and one soft/smooth item, taking a moment to feel both items in your hand and think about what you see and feel.

"You’ll have 5 minutes to focus on one side of your paper at a time. When I start the clock, you can jot down the first thoughts that come to mind when you think about the soft/smooth parts of yourself and your life. You can use words, sentences, drawings, and shapes to describe what comes to mind. 

"As you’re writing, you can think about these questions: 

  • What parts of your life feel soft/smooth? 

  • What feelings come up for you when you think about the soft/smooth parts of your life?

"When the time is up, you can move over to the hard/rough side of your paper:

  • What about your life feels hard/rough?

  • What feelings come up for you when you think about the hard/rough parts of your life?"

       
      Inhale and squeeze   Exhale and release
           

Body Movement

“Before we get into our creation, I’ll invite you to use your body for this next activity. It can help us get into the mindset of moving through the soft and hard places we just wrote about. As you’re going through this activity, keep in mind the words, shapes, drawings you put down.

“I invite you to get in a comfortable position, either sitting or standing. If you feel comfortable enough to do so, you can close your eyes or fix your gaze on something in the room. We’re going to lengthen our inhales and exhales as we tune into our bodies. If lengthening your breath is not comfortable for you, you can simply pay attention to your inhales and exhales and count slowly to 10. You can also do anything else that works best for you and your body. Let’s begin….

"During our first inhale together, you’ll tense every muscle in your body as tightly as you can, letting go as you exhale. You’ll squeeze your hands into fists, squeeze your eyes shut, tense your legs, arms, and stomach muscles. Let’s practice together once…. Squeeze your muscles as you inhale and release your muscles as you exhale.

"Now that we’ve practiced, let’s try it again all together.... Inhale, squeeze your muscles…exhale and release."

Repeat this process two more times, then invite participants to begin their creation.
creation:
Based on your time frame and whether you are doing this workshop in one session or over multiple days, you can give anywhere from 10 to 20 or more minutes for each of the three creations.

  1. On your first piece of paper you can use your writing from the timed writing exercise to create art that represents the soft/smooth places in your life. You might want to use the words and images from your writing and add colors, lines, shapes, and other things to represent them.

  2. On your second piece of paper you can follow the same process for the hard/rough places in your life.

  3. Before moving on to the final step, you may wish to take a moment to observe what was created on each piece of paper, noticing what emotions or bodily sensations arise as you look at each one.

  4. On a third piece of paper you can let the soft and hard mingle on the same page, noticing what it feels like to allow hard and soft to coexist and interact.
closing:
"Now that we've had a chance to explore a little more about ourselves and our lives, I invite you to share about your experience with the group. As we explore, listen, create, and share together in community, we are engaging in the art process. Sharing and listening to stories can create safe spaces where we can all heal."

While participants are sharing, you can invite them to hold up their creations if they feel comfortable doing so. Consider asking these questions before inviting sharing. You can write the questions where participants can easily refer to them throughout the sharing portion. You can also periodically repeat them as a reminder.

  • What feelings came up for you during this process?

  • Did you notice any sensations in your body as you explored these different topics?

  • What’s different about the soft and hard creations? What’s similar?

  • What was it like to allow both hard and soft to exist on the same page?

  • What did you learn from your art and how can you use it moving forward?

"Thank you for all the different ways you chose to participate during this Window of Time. Moving forward, I invite you to use your creation as a reminder to embrace and validate all the different textures in you and your life. If you feel comfortable enough to do so, share your art and experience with a safe person and consider inviting them to look inside themselves and learn a little more about their own unique textures."
optional_materials:
You can also facilitate this workshop using printable worksheets. If you are utilizing the worksheets in lieu of the regular workshop materials, be sure to send a digital copy or print them out for your participants if you are meeting in person.

 

Optional Materials:

  • Timed writing exercise worksheet

  • Creation worksheets (soft/smooth, hard/rough, and combined)

introduction: “Thank you for being here today. Before we begin, I want you to know that this is your Window of Time. It's a time for you to notice your thoughts, needs and feelings. During this time, there is no right or wrong way to participate or create. I'm going to share some instructions, but you get to choose how you want to participate. You can follow along completely, or you may want to do something different, it's completely up to you. During your Window of time, you get to choose. I am here to support you in any way that I can, so please ask for what you need."
demonstration:
Take a few minutes to go over the supplies and the creation steps with participants. Steps 1-3 can be done with one piece of paper, working on both sides, or with two pieces of paper side by side. The goal is to be able to review what was created on each piece of paper before combining them into a final creation in Step 4.

  1. On your first piece of paper you can use your writing from the timed writing exercise to create art that represents the soft/smooth places in your life. You might want to use the words and images from your writing and add colors, lines, shapes, and other things to represent them.

  2. On your second piece of paper you can follow the same process for the hard/rough places in your life.

  3. Before moving on to the final step, you may wish to take a moment to observe what was created on each piece of paper, noticing what emotions or bodily sensations arise as you look at each one.

  4. On a third piece of paper you can let the soft and hard mingle on the same page, noticing what it feels like to allow hard and soft to coexist and interact.

   
Creation with soft/smooth textures   Creation with hard/rough textures   A mixture of soft/smooth and hard/rough textures
opening_circle:
“Our workshop today will focus on the different textures that we’re made of. We’ll get a chance to notice the things that feel soft and smooth and look into the things that feel rough and hard. When we take the time to notice all parts of our lives, especially the things that feel hard or difficult, it can help us increase our self-awareness and acceptance and move toward compassion and resilience. This self-awareness can help us unpack the feelings that we carry, leading us toward more self-acceptance and compassion for ourselves and others. Before we create, we’ll explore these ideas with a writing exercise and some body movement. 

“Even though we are all together on Earth, we walk different paths. Paths that are made up of our unique feelings and experiences. One day, everything is going your way. You feel calm, cool, and collected. Then something happens that changes that. The experience can change how you feel inside and how you show up to the outside world. Sometimes the change in you lasts for a short amount of time, sometimes a lot longer.

"As we begin to explore the different parts of our lives, we’ll focus on the different textures. The soft and smooth parts of your life might be the things that feel easy, joyful, or happy. We’ll also take a look at the things that are rough and hard, those difficult and challenging things. By taking a look at these different textures, we’ll get a chance to understand our feelings and actions, learn how to embrace and accept them, and, in turn, begin to notice and embrace them in others."
extra_field: Note: Since this workshop has many components to it, you are invited modify the time frame to fit the needs of your participants. If your schedule permits, consider breaking this workshop into multiple days. For example having day 1 be for the timed writing and soft/smooth creation, day 2 for the body movement and rough/hard creation, and day 3 for the conclusion of the workshop with the focus being on the final combined creation.

title: Incoming Call
objective: This workshop aims to heal our inner child by allowing participants time to reflect on the messages they wish they received growing up and to share their experiences as adults to their younger self.
materials:
• Incoming Call Template printed on construction or cardstock paper

  • Colored pencils 

  • Markers

  • Scissors

  • Glue

  • Yarn or string

 
Incoming Call Template
setup:
Possible Setup for the workshop

We invite you to create a simple sample for the participants in order to demonstrate how the final creation may look like. If possible, we invite you to have the materials and supplies set up prior to participants arriving for easy accessibility.
warm_up:
Guided Meditation:

“For today’s warm-up, I invite you to join me in a guided meditation. If you would like to join, I encourage you to get comfortable in your chairs and allow your feet to rest on the floor. If you feel comfortable, you may also close your eyes.”

“To start I would like us to take a deep breath in to unite us as a group, however, if you prefer to roll your shoulders or neck instead that is completely okay. For those who would like to take a deep breath, I encourage you to breathe in through your nose and out through your mouth."

“Now I invite you to imagine your younger self."

  • How old are they?

  • What do they look like? 

  • What color is their hair? 

  • How tall are they? 

  • Are they smiling, frowning, angry? 

“Once you can visualize your younger self, I now invite you to imagine yourself, as the person you are today standing right in front of them."

  • How would your younger self be looking at you? 

  • What facial expression would they have? 

  • What questions would they have for you? 

  • What would you want to say to them? 

  • Would you want to give them a big embrace? 

“I invite you to tell them something that you are proud of in your life.”

 

Note: Allow some time in between questions in order to allow participants time to visualize what is being asked. 

 

“Now I invite you to wave at your younger self and tell them “I’ll talk to you soon”. When you feel ready, I invite you to take a deep breath in again. In through your nose and out through your mouth. And when you feel ready you may open your eyes and create.”
creation:
While the participants are creating, you may play some calming music and offer assistance when needed. Time reminders may also be helpful to participants in order to decrease their anxiety and the need to rush towards the end.

     
Completed Creation
closing: At the end of the workshop, provide some time for participants to share something they spoke about to their younger self, if they would like. Participants are also welcome to share any thoughts, feelings, or emotions they experienced during the workshop. Once everyone who would like to share has done so, thank the participants for being present with you in this safe/brave space.
tips:
Durational Art Tip

If possible, we encourage you to place your creation somewhere visible such as a desk or on your night stand just in case you ever need to hear a message from your younger self.
optional_materials:
You can also facilitate this workshop using printable worksheets. If you are utilizing the worksheets in lieu of the regular workshop materials, be sure to send a digital copy or print them out for your participants if you are meeting in person.

title: Waves of Resistance
objective: This workshop invites participants to reflect on their hardships, both past and present, while highlighting the inner and outer strengths they possess that have helped them get through such challenges.
materials:
• Surfboard Template (printed on regular paper)

  • Wave Template (printed on cardstock paper)

  • Marker

  • Colored Pencils

  • Glue

  • Scissors

  • Paper (for journaling)

  • Writing Utensil

     
Surfboard Template     Wave Template
setup:
Possible Setup

If possible, we encourage you to have the materials and supplies set up prior to the participants arriving. We also invite you to create your own “Wave of Resistance” in order to provide a visual for the participants. However, try to make it a simple sample in order not to overwhelm participants.
warm_up:
Journal:

“If you would like to join the journaling prompt, I welcome you to think about any current or past hardships that you have faced that felt out of your control. 

  • What was going on? 

  • How did the situation make you feel? 

  • How did you react?

Note: Allow some time for the participants to write down their thoughts, if they like.

“Now I invite you to write about the things that were in your control or things that allowed you to survive the hardship.”

  • What or who helped you out?

  • Did you learn or try anything new?

  • Did anything change?

 

Once participants are finished, you are welcome to invite participants to share if they like.
 

Grounding Technique:

“I invite you all to join me in a grounding technique that will focus on 4 things that are in your control. However, before we begin I want to take some time to highlight that this is an invitation for you to honor your body and to do whatever feels right for you.”    

  • First, I can control my breathing. If you feel comfortable, you may take a deep breath in (through your nose) and a deep breath out (though your mouth). Perfect!

  • I can control my body. If you would like, you can wrap your arms around yourself and give yourself a big hug. 

  • Third, I can control the words I tell myself. If you’d like, give yourself a compliment out loud or in your mind. Great!

  • Last, I can control my facial expressions. If you feel comfortable, you may make any facial expression you like. It can be a happy, angry, sad, and/or a silly face.

“Thank you for joining me in this grounding technique and when you feel ready, you may begin to create.”
creation: During the creation process, you may play some music and offer assistance if needed. Time reminders may also be helpful to participants in order for them to be aware of their progress.
closing:
As the workshop comes to an end, invite participants to share one thing that has been their surf-board against their waves of resistance. Participants are also welcome to share any feelings or thoughts they had throughout the workshop. You may also remind participants that if they are ever experiencing times of stress or hardship, they can always look at their surfboard as a reminder of their inner and outer strengths.

If time is running out, we suggest doing a “sitting exhibit” in which all the participants can hold up their creation, while sitting down.

title: Absorb and Release
objective: This workshop aims to invite participants to explore the things they have absorbed in their minds, bodies, and hearts, especially throughout the pandemic, and to help release anything that may be causing ongoing harm.
materials:
• Sponge

  • Tie-dye paint

  • Squeeze bottles

  • Cardstock Paper

  • Markers

  • Color Pencils

  • Paper

  • Writing Utensils

  • Blower Dryer
setup: In order to increase accessibility, we invite you to set up the materials and supplies prior to the participants arriving. If you are utilizing paint for the creation portion of this workshop, we encourage you to have cups filled with water for the participants to use. We also invite you to create your own example in order to demonstrate to the participants what the final creation can look like. However, it’s important to make a simple sample in order to not overwhelm participants.
warm_up:
Fold paper in half
       
     
      On one side write 'Absorb' and on the other 'Release'

Journaling:

“Before we begin the creation process, you are invited to join me in a journaling warm-up. For those who would like to join, I invite you to think and write about the things you have absorbed in the last few years due to Covid. These can be new things that you have gained based on how you experienced the pandemic, such as new thoughts, habits, insights, and feelings. Even though we are all going through the same pandemic, we all could have done so differently depending on a multitude of factors. For instance, those who continue(d) to work during the pandemic, or for those who lived with family members with underlying health conditions. All these factors and more could have altered the ways you experienced the pandemic, and the things you absorbed.”

“If you would like to engage in this journaling warm-up, I invite you to fold your paper in half and at the top of one side write ‘Absorb’ and on the other you may write ‘Release’. On the side that says ‘Absorb’ I encourage you to write about the things you have soaked up during the pandemic. These can be both negative and positive experiences, thoughts, feelings, and more. For instance: Are you more cautious or anxious when you are around crowds? Do you prefer to spend more time with loved ones than before? Or maybe like to spend more time alone? If you are feeling suck, here are a couple other questions you may consider:” 

  • What memories stick out to you from the last few years?

  • What are the new habits that you have developed because of Covid? How are they supporting you? 

  • Are these habits you want to keep or something you should let go of? 

  • Did you learn a new skill such as being computer- savvy? Or having more patience and kindness?

  • Are there new thoughts that you have regarding friendships, family, or society? If so, what are they?

Take some time to allow for participants to write and if you would like you may also set a time for participants to switch over from the ‘Absorb’ side to the ‘Release’ side. 

“When you are done writing what you have absorbed, I encourage you to go to the ‘Release’ side of your paper. In this column, I invite you to think about the things you would like to let go of. Based on the things you have absorbed, is there anything you would like to release? These can be thoughts, feelings, habits and more. For example, some people may want to release some anxiety or anger they have. Remember, everything that you have absorbed, may have helped you get to where you are today, therefore you have the power to choose what you release and hold on to.”

Once participants are done writing, you are encouraged to offer an opportunity for participants to look at the thing they absorbed and highlight the strength and resilience they have to be present today.
creation:
During this time, you may play some calming music and offer assistance to the participants if asked. Time reminders may also be helpful in order to help participants be aware of the time they have to create.

 

 
Completed Creation   Completed Worksheet
closing:
As the workshop comes to an end, invite participants to engage in a body movement that will welcome them to release the things their mind, body and heart has absorbed due to Covid-19. First, invite participants to cross their arms in front of their chest, as tight as they can and on a count of three, participants are invited to stretch their arms out, representing the release.

If time is running out, invite the group to share one thing they would like to release and invite the group to join in a sitting exhibit, in which participants hold up their creation to share with others.
notes: This workshop may elicit big feelings for some participants. If you find yourself having questions or need guidance regarding navigating big feelings, please see the attached resource here.
tips:
Durational Art Tip:

Unfortunately, Covid-19 is still a big part of our lives. Therefore, whenever you are feeling overwhelmed and want to release some of those feelings, we encourage you to keep adding to your artwork and draw on the resilience you already possess and will continue to develop as you overcome obstacles in the future.

“For our warm-up today, I invite you all to a small breathing exercise. If you prefer, you are also welcome to just count, notice your breath, or do whatever works best for your body. Breathing is the process of moving air into and out the lungs and to feel this, I welcome you to place your hand on your stomach and if you feel comfortable you can have your eyes closed. Take a deep breath in with your nose and feel your stomach expand. Now release that breath, through your mouth and feel your stomach deflate. I welcome you to take three deep breaths and when you feel ready you may open your eyes if you have them closed.”

 

Journaling Questions: 

“Before we begin creating, I invite you to take inventory of your core values. These questions may help guide you to a better understanding of what your values are and begin to see how you present yourself in these spaces:”

  • At work?

  • At home?

       
       

Values Inventory

  • Within my relationships?

  • Within my community?

Invite the participants to share their journal entries if they like. Remember, everything is voluntary and participants are encouraged to share as much or as little as they like.

  • Did you explore anything new about your values that you might have forgotten or would like to exemplify more of in your life?

closing:

demonstration:
You may wish to familiarize the participants with the materials they will be using and share the basic creation steps with them. If you've made a sample, you can show it to them, and remind them there is no right or wrong way to create.

Step 1: “For the creation steps, you are first welcome to draw a heart and key on the Shrinky Dink paper. If it’s easier, you may also use the Lock and Key Template to trace on the Shrinky dink paper.” 

Step 2: Once you finish drawing your heart you are welcome to use the markers and colored pencils to decorate/fill your heart with the things that you have difficulty forgiving. Note: You may remind the participants that colored pencils only work on the rough side of the paper, while permanent markers can work on either side.

Step 3: “Once you have decorated your heart with the things that are difficult to forgive, I invite you to decorate your key however you like. This key can represent forgiveness and only you have the power to unlock that.”

Step 4: “After you finish decorating your heart and key, you are welcome to cut it out. If you like you may also cut out the lock in the center of the heart, this will allow you to insert your key once it has shrunk.”

Step 5: “Now that the Shrinky Dink heart and key is cut, you can punch a hole on your heart and key before shrinking it. This will allow for participants to put a string in it later. Once you finish with that you can, place your Shrinky Dink paper into the oven! If you are hesitant to put the Shrinky Dink paper in the oven, I [facilitator] can always do it for you.”

Step 6: “Once your Shrinky Dink paper is shrunk you may take it out and let it cool down or you can flatten it out by placing a hard-cover book on top of it. After it cools down, you may loop any colored string onto the heart and key.”

  • Are these goals in alignment with your values?

  • Are these goals in alignment with your personal vision statement?

  • After assessing your goals alongside your values and personal vision statement, do you need to revise your current goals?

  • What are the new goals written with your personal vision in mind?

 

Group Discussion: 

You may invite the participants to share anything they wrote/thought about during the journaling warm-up. Remember, everything is voluntary and participants are encouraged to share as much or as little as they like.

Some questions that can be asked to encourage participants to share include:

  • What goals did you think/write about?

  • Have you ever attempted to achieve your goal before? If so, how did it go?

  • Were your goals in alignment with your values or your personal vision statement?

“Thank you for joining me in this group discussion. Now that you have explored the goal(s) you have, I invite you to begin creating your plan to achieve it!”
creation:
Completed Creation

You are welcome to play some relaxing music while the participants are creating, and help out when asked. Participants may also benefit from time reminders in order to lessen their worry and urge to rush towards the end.
closing:

  • What is your financial goal?

  • What mini goal do you think will be the hardest and/or easiest to achieve?

  • What did you learn today regarding your financial goals and the steps needed to achieve them?

title: Loving Your Inner Child
objective: This workshop provides an opportunity for participants to go back in time to comfort, love, and protect their inner child.
materials:
Loving Your Inner Child Journaling Handout

  

  • Tag

  • Loving Your Inner Child journaling handout

  • Photos 

  • Magazines (or pre-cut images, symbols, words etc.)

  • Glue

  • Scissors

  • Markers

  • Colored pencils

  • Blank paper for journaling
setup:
Possible Setup

We encourage you to have the supplies set up on placemats for each participant, prior to them arriving in order to increase accessibility. We also invite you to create your own example to demonstrate to the participants what the final creation can look like. However, it’s important to make a simple sample to not overwhelm participants.
warm_up:
Journaling:

       
       

Loving Your Inner Child Creations
         

"For today's warm-up, I welcome you to a journaling session that can help remind you of some good memories about your childhood. Remember throughout this workshop, do what you need to feel safe and to care for yourself. If something feels too painful or hard you can always skip it and/or go back to it later. This journaling session can also be the beginning of re-parenting yourself. The goal is to nurture you, to really love and re-parent that inner child that belongs only to YOU."

"You are welcome to write down some things you really enjoyed doing as a child. Feel free to focus on one age, or your whole childhood. Additionally, you can look at the ‘Loving your Inner Child Journaling Handout’ for questions to answer; however, feel free to answer all the questions, just a few, or none at all. This is your time and you choose how you would like to use it.”

  • What were your favorite colors as a child?

  • What was your favorite article of clothing?

  • What was your favorite snack?

  • What did you watch on TV?

  • What type of music did you like?

  • Recall a childhood friend. What was your favorite memory together?

  • What is something you are proud of about yourself as a child? (e.g., personality wise and accomplishments)

  • What is something you would want yourself to hear if you could go back in time right now?

    • What is that one thing you would want YOU to know?

Allow some time for the participants to journal or even just think about the questions presented. You are also welcome to play some calming music during this time.

 

Guided Meditation:

       
       

Completed Creation
         

"Now that we have finished journaling, I welcome you to a guided meditation. During this exercise, you’ll be invited to take a few deep breaths; however, if this doesn’t work for you feel free to count, or notice your breath, or just do what works best for your body. For those who would like to join, I invite you to make yourself comfortable. This can include having your eyes closed, sitting with your back straight, your feet flat on the floor and your hands lying loosely in your lap. Now I invite you to take a deep breath in and out. This is a special time just for you to breathe in love and breathe out any tension."

“You can take another deep breath in and exhale softly. Now I invite you to move your awareness down to your feet and gently wiggle your toes. Feel the relaxation moving up your calves. Breathe in slowly and exhale slowly. Feel all your stomach muscles gently relax. I welcome you to breathe in love and breathe out any tension, especially around your shoulders. If there's any tension left in your body, just imagine it sliding down and off your body. Breathing in love and breathing out tension. Feel yourself relaxing more and more deeply. Imagine your entire body is now totally relaxed."

"Now, I invite you to begin thinking about a time your inner child needed something from you. Visualize yourself in that moment. Think about what the room looked like, the sounds you hear and perhaps the scents you smell. Know that right now you are totally safe, you are older now and you are going to protect and love your inner child. See yourself now walking up to your inner child. Notice what they are wearing? How are they feeling? What are they saying? I invite you to ask your inner child what they need most from you at this moment. Tell them what you want them to know. Picture yourself there, strong, loving and kind. See yourself taking care of your inner child, offering them a hug, a place of safety, or words of encouragement. Tell them you are there for them and you are going to protect them. Let those words sink in and see their face when you say those words. 'I will protect you. I love you.'

“In your mind see yourself supporting your inner child during a difficult time. Imagine taking them by the hand and leading them away or even picking them up and holding them close. You are older now and can give your inner child the comfort they needed back then. Once you feel safe and your inner child feels safe, I encourage you to take a big deep breath in and let it out slowly. When you feel ready, you may bring yourself back to the room and begin to write or draw whatever your inner child needs to hear or have."
creation:
During this time, you may put on some soothing music and assist the participants as needed. Additionally, you can remind participants that they are older now and they can give their inner child and themselves the comfort they needed back then. Remind them to be gentle with themselves. Congratulate them for being brave and courageous. Finally, in order to reduce the need to rush towards the end, it may also be useful to offer participants with time reminders, one or two times, before moving into the closing.

 

       

Loving Your Inner Child Completed Creations
closing:
Towards the end of the workshop, you are welcome to invite participants to share how it felt to comfort their inner child. If nobody wants to share you may add: "If you would like, the ocean is also open for anyone to jump right in and share anything regarding their creation or how they felt throughout the whole process of the workshop."

You can also invite participants to a group discussion. Some possible questions include:  

  • How did it feel to be the adult that comforted your inner child? 

  • What are some words that you will tell yourself and your inner child when you need comfort? 

  • How can you support your inner child and yourself in the present moment and in the future?

As a reminder, allow space for participants to cry, to be angry about what happened, give them permission to take back their childhood and to make it their own, if they wish. Once everyone who would like to share has, thank the participants for being present and in community with you.
notes: To read more about how you can love your inner child, check out this Blog Post by Rose Curtis.
tips:
Durational Art Tip:

This can be a breakthrough workshop or some participants may just tread lightly, therefore we encourage you to invite participants to continue to add to their creation or to place their artwork somewhere visible, so they can comfort their inner-child whenever they like. It may also be a reminder that they are in charge, and that they have the right to love their inner child and to comfort them.

Tag Template

You can also facilitate this workshop using a printable tag template. If you do not have a physical tag, you are welcome to utilize the tag template as a substitute; however, be sure to send a digital copy or print them out for your participants if you are meeting in person. For durability purposes, it may be beneficial to print the template on cardstock paper and once the creation is completed you can attach your tag to a metal ring, which can be used throughout the workshop series.

This workshop is all about letting out what you need to, finding out what you need to find out, and answering questions that you may need answers to! "For today's creation, I invite you to challenge yourself and draw with your non-dominant hand! Remember, the outcome is not important, as long as you're having fun and enjoying the process that is all that matters!"

Step 1: "I invite you to write a note of forgiveness to yourself. This note can include your thoughts on perfectionism and how it has benefited you, but also how it may have harmed you. You are welcome to write your note on both sides of your tag or on just one side.

Step 2: "After you have finished writing your note, you are welcome to tear strips of the tissue/dictionary paper and glue them down over your note, then add a layer of white paint/gesso. To speed up the drying process, you may dry it with a blow dryer."

Step 3: "Once your tag is dry, I encourage you with your non-dominant hand to sketch out anything you like, such as flowers, leaves, swirls, and more. Remember, the process is more important than the completed creation so I invite you to let go, play with the supplies and be willing to see what happens!"

Optional: "You may repeat the process on both sides of the tag and once you are done you may add the affirmation “I embrace imperfection.” You may also write it on a piece of paper and glue it to your tag."
