title: A Journey With Purpose
objective: The objective of this workshop is to aid participants in visually creating a path to reach their personal/professional goals by breaking it down into smaller steps to make the journey feel empowering, motivating, and obtainable.
materials:
Mile Marker- circle signs  
           
       
Mile marker- square signs
 

  • Paper Charcuterie Box (you can use the lid or box) and/or a shallow plastic box

  • 5 Glass Dome Cabochons (approx. 1 1/4") per participant (Stones of various sizes are available at craft stores, garden stores and online)

  • Card stock in various colors cut into circles in the same dimension as the stones (Circle hole punchers in various sizes are available at most craft stores)

  • Clear tacky glue bottles with a tip

  • Mile markers template

  • Scissors

  • Toothpicks

  • Colored pencils

  • Permanent Markers

  • Clear Packing Tape

  • Soil

  • Grass/moss

  • Real or fake plants

You can check out our AWBW Durational Art Supplies page to find tips on using touchstones, inspiration, AWBW offerings, and recommended links to all the supplies!
setup:
Possible setup

We encourage you to have all the materials for the workshop placed on a table in front of the participants before the workshop begins. We invite you to create a simple sample to demonstrate to participants what the final creation can look like.
warm_up:
Guided Meditation:

“For our warm-up, I invite you to guided meditation. During this time you'll be invited to take some deep breaths; however, if this doesn't work for you, please feel free to count, notice your breath, or just do whatever works best for your body. I invite you to close your eyes and sit or lay down wherever you feel most comfortable. Let your whole body relax, from the top of your head all the way down to your feet..." (Pause for 10 seconds).

"I welcome you to take a slow deep breath in, inhale through your nose…hold for a moment… then breathe slowly out through your mouth. Again, breath in through your nose… hold… then breathe out through your mouth." (Pause) I invite you to take a few minutes before we get started to envision what your life would be like if you could do or be anything? (Pause) How would that feel? (Pause) What contributions would you be making to yourself or to the world? (Pause) I invite you to picture it."

"Now imagine taking a small step towards this goal. What would that look like for you? I invite you to envision what it would be like to take another step, then the next, until you reach your goal (Pause for 10 seconds)."

"I invite you to take one more slow deep breath in through your nose… hold for a moment… And slowly exhale out through your mouth. When you feel ready, you can open your eyes and begin paving the way to your goal.”

 

Journaling:

“Thank you for joining me in that guided meditation. Now to help us start thinking about our goals, I would like to invite you to a quick 3 minute journaling session. During this time, please do not focus on your grammar, punctuation, or anything of that sort. These three minutes are for you to express yourself and to explore your initial thoughts regarding your goals. I will be providing some questions, but please feel free to just answer a few or none at all. The questions are as followed: 

  1. What is my ultimate purpose or goal that I want to achieve? 

  2. Are there any steps I need to take to make it into a reality? 

  3. In order to push forward, what obstacles can I anticipate having to overcome?

  4.  What support do I already have in place that can support and motivate me along the way (example: emotional support from family and friends)?
creation:
Final creation example
           

You're invited to give participants a few minutes to brainstorm a goal that they want to work on and the steps it would take to get there. For the next 30 minutes the group can work on their creation, however it feels right for them. During this time, we invite you to play some calming music and provide time reminders halfway and when there is just a minute left to create. Doing so can help participants transition from a creation to closing.
closing:
Final creation in a basket

The last  few minutes will be allotted to giving the participants time to share (one at a time) if they desire.

"For the remaining few minutes of our group, I would like to take some time to invite you to a group share. I invite anyone to share a goal that came up for them and what you need to reach them. If you like, you’re also welcome to share what you learned throughout this experience, or anything else that came to mind for you during this process."

Once those who would like to share have, you are welcome to end the group share.

"First of all, I want to thank all of you for embarking on this journey. It takes courage and determination to allow yourselves to be vulnerable with others and know that we are all here to support, to lift up, and to aid you in your journey whenever you need it. You are part of a community who lifts you up, supports you, and will be here for you whenever you need it. Thank you all for being here."
tips:
Durational Art Tip:

"As you continue on this journey, you’re invited to create more touchstones to represent any new goal(s) and the smaller steps you need to reach it. You can then place them along your path and read/create new mile markers to help you keep going! Wendi made her mile markers with motivational quotes to keep her going and believing that she can accomplish her goals. This brought her journey to life in a creative fashion that she can care for and look at daily.”
optional_materials:
A Journey With Purpose Workshop Worksheet

This workshop can be done in various ways. For instance, you can invite participants to create with just markers and paper or you can facilitate this workshop using a printable worksheet. If you are utilizing the worksheets in lieu of the regular workshop materials, be sure to send a digital copy or print them out for your participants if you are meeting in person.  

  • A Journey With Purpose Workshop Worksheet

 

You can also create your “path” in different ways. Get creative with the process!

  • Garden Signs

  • Laminator / Lamination paper

  • Crayons

  • Sand (substitute for soil)

  • Crinkle Cut Paper Shred Filler (substitute for soil)

  • Shells
introduction: "Before we begin, I want you to know that this workshop is a window of time for you. This means that this is a safe/brave space to notice your thoughts, feelings, and needs. Since this space is your window of time, everything you say or do is voluntary. I’ll offer a suggested workshop idea, share about the materials we have available, and invite you to create, but there’s no wrong way to do this. It doesn't matter what it looks like. What matters is taking this time to truly honor your thoughts and feelings, however they come out. Please ask for what you need, and know that I’m here in support of you. If you can’t think of anything or draw a blank on what to create or write, feel free to just play with the materials."
demonstration:
Facilitators are encouraged to demonstrate a completed path and give examples of small steps someone can take toward their goals.

Step 1: “To get us started, I invite you to create some touchstones. The first touchstone I invite you to create can describe your main goal, you can do this by grabbing a cardstock circle and writing, drawing, or coloring in the goal you would like to achieve. This goal can be whatever you like, professionally or personally. Some questions to consider while you think about your main goal are: If you could do or be anything you like, what would it be? What brings you the most meaning? What do you feel you need most in your life right now (e.g. more quality time with loved ones or more time for yourself)? What is something you hope to accomplish within the next week, month, or year? What contributions would you like to make to yourself or to the world? Remember, there is no goal too big or too small. The rest of the stones can be used as smaller steps to reach your main goal. For example, maybe your main goal is to incorporate self-care into your everyday life. A small step can be to set a timer everyday as a reminder to take a break.”

Step 2: “Once you have created your touchstones, you're welcome to add a small amount of clear tacky glue to the cardstock paper and place a clear stone on top of it. You can press down for a few seconds or until you feel like the paper is set in place.” Tip: For guidance on how to create touchstones, you're welcome to check out this handout.

Step 3: “After, you are welcome to start assembling your path. Using one paper box, you can fill it up with soil, add plants (real or fake), and grass/moss. Then you can create a path using the touchstones you created.” 

Step 4: “When you're done assembling your path, you’re welcome to use the mile maker template and fill it up with words, drawings, and symbols of encouragement. These mile markers can be filled with encouragement that can help you keep going.” Optional: You are also welcome to laminate your mile makers or protect them by covering them with clear packing tape. This can help avoid smearing the words/drawing once you place the markers into the soil.

Step 5: “Once you’re done creating your mile markers, you are welcome to cut them out with scissors, and tape a toothpick to the back in order to stick them into your path.”

 

   
Step 1: Express the needs and goals you have!     Step 1 (Optional): Laminate with tape
       
   
Step 2: Place tacky glue on your cardstock circle and then place a stone on top
       
   
Step 3: Assemble everything into the container     Step 4: Create your mile markers
       
   
Step 4 (Continued): Cut them out     Step 4 (Optional): Laminate the mile markers with tape
       
   
Step 5: Tape the toothpick to the back of the mile markers and arrange them into your container
opening_circle:
Wendi's path forward
             

"Our goals, dreams, and sense of purpose sometimes emerges when we discover who we are, who we want to be, and pursue the things that bring us the most meaning. During this time, you’ll be invited to think about all your goals and choose one you would like to prioritize. Sometimes a goal may appear out of reach or unobtainable until you’re able to break it down into smaller steps. You’ll be invited to think about the things you may need to reach your goals, such as emotional or physical support, resources, and much more. You can also explore any barriers you may have to reaching your goals. This journey may become exhausting at times, so while you're on this path, you’re encouraged to tap into your strengths and words of encouragement, to motivate you to keep going."

"Are there any questions or thoughts before we move into the warm-up?”
extra_field: A message from the author:

title: Creating a Safer/Braver Place - Training Version
objective: This workshop aims to help participants feel a sense of their own power through exploring and creating a safer/braver place within themselves.
materials:
• Rough & Ready shrinky dink paper

  • Permanent markers

  • Colored pencils

  • A hole punch (Single or three-hole punch is fine)

  • Thin ribbon or wire (1/8 in or thinner)

  • Oven to cook shrinky paper (you may want to buy a toaster oven, not toaster, to cook the shrinky paper)
setup:
Possible Setup
           

You may wish to prepare the art supplies on the table for easy transition during the workshop. Click here to listen to AWBW’s Spotify Playlist - it contains hours of background music with no lyrics that can be used during your art workshops. 

An open space for the Opening and/or Guided Imagery can be helpful but is not necessary. If an open space is not available, the activities can be done at the table.

You may also consider creating a sample Safe Place in advance to show participants what it can look like. If you choose to do so, we suggest creating a simple sample, so that participants aren't overwhelmed by any "artistic" challenges.
warm_up:
Group Discussion: What Makes You Feel Safer/Braver?

“We all have different thoughts and feelings about what makes us feel safe or brave. What makes YOU feel safe? At this time I’ll invite you to take about a minute to think about what makes you feel safe or brave, jotting down any words or images that come to mind when you think about what makes you feel safe or brave. I’ll let you know when it’s been a minute and invite whomever wishes to share to do so. (Wait 1 min.)

Would anyone like to share? To share you can type into the chat or raise your hand and we will invite you to unmute yourself and share. Take some time to allow participants to share if they would like. 

“Thank you so much to everyone who shared and who witnessed the sharing by observing.”

 

Guided Meditation: What Is Your Safer/Braver Place?

“I am now going to invite you to use your imagination to picture your safe or brave place in your mind. After that you’ll get the chance to create your safer or braver place using the Safer/Braver Place worksheet and any of the art materials or supplies that you happen to have on hand. There is no right or wrong way to imagine or create your safe or brave place!”

“As this guided imagery includes an invitation to participate in some deep breathing, I want to acknowledge that there are people with respiratory issues, asthma, or just a plain old cold who may not find it relaxing when the breathing aggravates the symptoms. So as an alternative I invite you to try counting, tapping, or imagining soothing imagery instead, anything that helps you to be present in your body.”

“Before we begin, I'm going to invite you to find the place where you feel the most comfortable. This can look like you sitting in a chair, sitting or lying on the floor, standing, or anything in between. Once you get to your comfortable place, you can close your eyes or gently affix your gaze on a point somewhere in the room.”

“And now I invite you to rest your mind on your breath. Breathing in through your nose and out through your mouth if you are able. And if it feels good for you, to start to lengthen your inhale and exhale. One way to look at it is to breathe in like you are smelling a flower and breathe out like you are blowing out a candle. Noticing the rise and fall of your chest or stomach with each breath.”

“And now bring your attention to your body and your awareness to your connection to the earth. You can do this by feeling the weight of your body on your chair or whatever you’re sitting or laying on. And now you can begin to notice your feet, give them a squeeze, and let go. Notice your knees, give them a shake, and pause. Notice your shoulders, moving them up and down several times. Notice your arms and wiggle them around and pause. Now your hands. Squeeze your hands tightly and let go, and repeat.

“And taking a deep breath in (Pause) and out (Pause), make any adjustments you need to feel comfortable in your space. And now taking another deep breath, begin to imagine your safe or brave place…”

  • What does your safe or brave place look like?

  • What colors do you see?

  • What does your place feel like?

  • What does your place sound like?

  • Is it quiet in your place?

  • What do you hear?

  • Are you alone in your place?

  • If you're not alone, who's with you?

  • What are you doing in your place?

  • Did you bring something with you to your place?

  • What did you leave behind?

  • Is your place somewhere you've been before or a place you've made up?

  • How does your safe or brave place make you feel?

“When you’re ready, I invite you to slowly bring yourself back to the virtual room, open your eyes if they were closed, and using words, images, shapes, or colors, begin to create your safe or brave place. We will take about 25 minutes to create, and I’ll keep track of the time and give you reminders so you don’t have to worry about that. 'll check in with you in about 15 minutes to see where we're at, but please let us know if you need anything as we are here to support you as you create your safe or brave place.”
creation:
During this time, you may play some calming music and provide time reminders for participants when there are 5 minutes left into the creation. 

Time reminder Example: “So we are about 15 minutes in. Feel free to continue creating long past the time we are sharing. This is all about the process, we have about 5 more minutes left to create and then we will go into breakout rooms. Feel free if you are at a stopping point to look at what you created or think about ways you would like to share about your safe/brave space. See you back here in about 5 minutes.”
closing:
Breakout Room Sharing

     
      Final Creation using Shrinky Dink Paper
       

“I welcome folks to come back into this space and again you can continue creating as we go into the sharing. In the breakout rooms, you can share  what you created, what it means to you, and how you want to use it. It's a way for you to not only be listened to, but also to be a listener, while also being in community with one another. As you're in your breakout rooms, maybe think about expanding those parentheses around you. Maybe if you're a little bit more shy, maybe sharing first, or if you want to just share a little bit more than you usually anticipated,  we invite you to use that space as a safe place for you as well. We also anticipate that it may not be a safe space for you, so you do whatever works best for you as well.” 

“We'll have 3 to 4 people per room and there will be a message that pops up to invite the next person to share. As we go along, we invite you to use the first 30 seconds to introduce yourself, say hello, and if you'd like, we'd love for you to be the first person to share in your group. As a reminder, we are upholding those community agreements in the breakout rooms as well.  Are there any questions before we begin? 

“All right. Enjoy your breakout rooms.”

 

Group Sharing

       
        Final creation using the worksheet
         
         
         

“Welcome back everyone. We're going to wait for some folks to trickle back in from their breakout rooms. I invite you just to sit with your safe

space, your creation, and think about maybe 1 or 2 words that you like to throw into the chat, maybe even raise your hand and share what you want about your creation or about your experience.” 

Allow some time for participants to share back to the larger group if they would like. 

“Thank you so much for being present here and honoring the way you chose to participate today! Sometimes we find ourselves in life in places where even though we are physically in a safe place, we may feel unsafe. Maybe we see, smell, or hear something that causes us to feel unsafe. If that occurs, I encourage you to remember the safe or brave place you created today. Even if we can’t physically be in that safe or brave place we’ve created, imagining it can help calm us and keep us centered so we can move forward in safety and bravery.”

 

Mini Exhibit

         
          Worksheets
           

Before we say goodbye, I invite you to click on Gallery View and hold up your art so we can see and celebrate all the different creations there were made today.
optional_materials:
Creating A Safer/Braver Place Worksheet
         

For this workshop you are welcome to use any art supplies that will help you tap into creating a safer/braver space for you. You are also welcome to utilize the workshop worksheet or any other materials that work best for you. If you are utilizing the worksheet in lieu of the regular workshop materials, be sure to send the sheet or print copies out for your participants beforehand depending on the setting.
introduction:
“Before we begin I want you to know that this workshop can be A Window of Time for you. A time out, separate from the rest of your day, to look inside, listen to your heart, and honor whatever comes up for you or comes out in the art. This is not like an art class, so it doesn’t matter what the art looks like. It’s really all about the process and taking this time to honor your thoughts and feelings. During your Window of Time there is no right or wrong way to participate or create, and however you choose to do so will be honored and respected. I invite you to use this time in the way that works best for you and best serves your needs today. Please type in the chat box if you have any questions or needs during this time and we will be happy to assist as we are here to support you.”

To set the foundation of safety and trust you're encouraged to share the workshop agenda with participants.

“First I would like to share about the art supplies you can use. Then I will invite you to participate in a Group Discussion on what makes us feel safe; then I will guide those of you who wish to participate through some Guided Imagery to help us generate some images for our art; I’ll invite you to Create; and then we’ll have some time for Sharing in breakout rooms and sharing back with the big group at the end. Please know that every aspect of this workshop is optional and observing is participating too, so you get to decide how you choose to participate or create today.”
demonstration:
To create your safer/braver space, you are welcome to use any supplies you like including the worksheet.

If you so choose, you can create on shrinky dink paper. 

  1. You can create freehand or can trace images to use as a template you have printed and/or on your phone.

  2. If you decide to use an image as a template, start by tracing your creation on shrinky dink paper and then coloring it in. A few reminders include: 

    1. Permanent markers can be used on both sides. 

    2. You can also combine both for more depth. 

    3. You may want to make the color darker by retracing certain areas you created with markers

    4. Tend to look darker and denser

  3. If you like, you can cut out your creation with scissors

  4. When you are finished cutting out, decide whether you want to add wire or ribbon to your creation.

    1. Use the hole punch to punch one or more holes (Don’t punch too close to the edge!)

  5. Last, the shrinky dinks will be ready for baking. Be sure to put your oven to bake. You’ll know they are done when they lay back down flat. Take a look at this video to see how to bake your shrinky dinks! 

  6. Decorate as you wish with ribbon or wire!

 

     
Step 1: Freehand or trace your image on Shrinky Dink Paper      Step 2: Color and Decorate your Creation  
         
     
Step 3 (Optional): Cut out your Shrinky Dink     Step 4: Decide if you would like to add ribon & hole punch  
         
     
Step 5: Bake your Shrinky Dink     Step 6: Decorate as you wish!
opening_circle: “The workshop I will share with you today used to be called Creating a Safe Place but we are now calling it Creating a Safer/Braver Place or Creating a Brave Place as it is more inclusive. Maybe the idea of creating a safe place feels inaccessible- we acknowledge and honor wherever you may be and invite you to create whatever you need for yourself today.”

title: In This Moment
objective: This workshop aims to support participants in exploring storytelling through physical expression.
materials:
• Storyboard Workshop Worksheet (with instructions and without instructions)

  • Magazines

  • Scissors

  • Glue

  • Markers

  • Pencils

  • Colored pencils

 

     
Worksheet with instructions       Worksheet without instructions
setup:
Possible Setup
             

To help with accessibility, we invite you to have the materials available and within easy reach of all the participants. To save some time during the creation, you’re also welcome to cut out some pictures from the magazines, especially for younger participants.
warm_up:
Physical Warm-up: 

“To get us started on I would like you to invite you to a full body warm-up. Throughout this process, we will be connecting with our bodies; however, know that if this does not work for you, please feel free to listen, imagine yourself moving your limbs or simply do whatever feels best for you.”

“To get us started, I welcome you to move your eyebrows. You can move them up and down." (Pause)

"Great, now let's move down to our nose, we can scrunch up and wiggle our nose." (Pause)

"Next, tighten your lip and open your mouth." (Pause)

"Now we will move to our neck. Slowly roll it from side to side to relax and decompress." (Pause)"

"Perfect, now we can move to our shoulders, moving them up and down." (Pause)

"We can do our hands, opening and closing, or making a tight fist and expanding as wide as we can." (Pause)

"Next, to our arms, you can open them wide then tighten them by giving yourself a hug." (Pause)

"For our bellies, take a deep breath in and expand as much as you can and then exhale, contracting your belly." (Pause)

"For your legs, shake your left leg for a few seconds then switch to your right leg." (Pause)

"Now our toes, wiggle your toes as much as possible." (Pause)

"Great, now finally, I invite you to do a full body shake." (Pause)

"Thank you so much for joining me, in getting our bodies warm and ready.”

 

One Word Storytelling:

“I would like to invite you to a one word storytelling exercise. For this warm-up each person adds one word and we go around the room creating a story with that single word. For instance, someone can start the story by saying “today” and the next person says “I” and the next “went” and another “to” and another “the” and another “mall” until a story is created. We will have a timer set for three minutes and within that we will try to create a story. Remember there is no wrong or right way to tell this story and it can be of any length. Are there any questions before we begin?”

You’re welcome to set a timer for three minutes or however long you have available. To see an example of how to do this activity, check out this video.
creation:
“During your creation time you may also choose to create physically instead of on the worksheet. Feel free to use your body and voice and the space around you while also being mindful of other people’s process and space. We will have around 30 minutes to create and I will be providing a time reminder when we are halfway through and then again when we have a minute left. If you happen to finish your creation early, I invite you to try your movement and notice what feelings come up. Alright, are there any lingering thoughts or questions before we get started?” Pause for a movement to allow the participants to share if they like.

“Great, I’ll check back in soon!”

During the creation portion, you are welcome to play some calming music. For a selection of calming tunes check out the AWBW spotify playlist here.
closing:
Final Creation with instructions
         
         
         

Group Share:

“We will now take some time to give those who would like to share the opportunity to do so. You can share about any aspect of your creation such as the creation itself, why this scenario and/or anything else that came up for you during the workshop.”

 

Movement Share Back:

“To close us out, I would like to invite you to a movement share back. For this portion, you’re welcome to share about the person, setting, prop, and feeling and movement in your story. I also welcome you to physically do the movement if you’d like to. I’ll go first as an example: My person is myself, in the future, and I am at school with my laptop. I’m feeling excited and nervous, especially since I will be going back to school after a break and my movement is very rapid, clacking on the computer. Would anyone like to go next?”

Allow some time for participants to share if they like.

“Thank you all so much for participating in whatever way you chose and for creating and sharing your stories.”
notes: If you are facilitating this workshop with just one participant, you are encouraged to do all the warm-up exercises and closing shares (e.g., movement share back) with the participant. Doing so can help reduce the fear of doing the activities by oneself.
tips:
Durational Art Tip

As you create your story and continue along your journey, you’re welcome to storyboard different moments/experiences. Doing so can help bring awareness to your feelings and how they show up in your physical movements. For example, on your first day of school you may find yourself nervously tearing up pieces of paper at your desk. Storyboarding your experience can help you notice how your feelings affect your actions. Bringing this awareness to your experiences can empower you to make choices that may better align with your desires and intentions.
optional_materials:
• This workshop can be facilitated using the workshop worksheet; however, if you don’t have access to a printer, a piece of paper works as well.

  • Other collage material: stickers, construction paper, flowers, glitter
introduction:
“Before we get started, I would like to mention that this is a Window of Time for you to explore in whatever way feels comfortable for you. A time to give yourself permission to play and to be curious. There will be moments, where physical movement will be encouraged or mentioned and it is entirely up to you if you choose to participate in that way. If you do not feel comfortable with that you can choose to use only the art materials in your exploration. There is no right or wrong way to use this time.”

“In just a bit, I will be sharing some instructions for today’s creation; however, feel free to follow along completely or take your story in a different direction. Remember all forms of storytelling are welcome! Are there any questions before we begin?”
demonstration:
“Around your area, you should see the workshop worksheet, magazines, scissors, glue, markers, pencils, and colored pencils. Using the materials of your choosing, you’re invited to collage a moment or scenario that you would like to explore. Some questions to consider, before you get started are who, what, where and why? Each section of the worksheet will help you build your story. I will describe each section to give you some ideas, but again these are just suggestions.”

Step 1: In the ‘Person’ box you’re invited to collage about a person, which could be yourself. As you create, think about if this person is you in the past, present, or future. How do they look? What facial expressions are they making?

Step 2: In the ‘setting,’ where is your person at this moment? Are they at school, work, indoors, outdoors? What is this person seeing around them? 

Step 3: For the prop, what is the person holding, carrying, playing with? It could be a computer, an ice cream cone, or a pen. What item is relevant to the story, your person or this moment. 

Step 4: What is your person feeling? Are they filled with joy, excitement, nervousness, anxiety? How do they feel about where they are or what they are doing?

Step 5: What movement is your person doing? Is there a physical action related to this moment? How does this feeling show up in something they are doing physically? Are they vigorously typing at their computer or nervously chewing their pen at an interview?

“Are there any questions regarding your storyboard that you would like to ask before we move into the warm-up?”  

 

     
Step 1: Fill in person section       Step 2: Fill in the setting section
         
     
Step 3: Fill in the prop section       Step 4: Fill in the feeling section
         
       
Step 5: Fill in your movement section
opening_circle: “A movie is made up of hundreds of different moments that have been pieced together to tell a story, also known as a storyboard. Sometimes a very small moment can tell us a great deal about a person or a circumstance. Similarly, our lives are made of many different moments, interactions, experiences, feelings and more, yet we do not always get the chance to explore them or delve into the details. For today’s workshop, I invite you to explore a moment within a story that you want to tell. This is an opportunity to bring your attention to any behaviors, gestures, movements, or actions you may not notice otherwise. You can choose to take a look at a moment that has passed or one that hasn't happened yet. You decide how you would like to share your story.”
extra_field: Kat Mardo holds a BFA in Theatre Performance from New World School For the Arts and considers herself a lifelong student and enthusiast of the ‘art of being human’. Her performance training and art studies sparked a specific interest in the useful and unique role that art plays in the development of emotional intelligence. Kat is particularly interested in the exploration of physical and verbal communication, language and storytelling as methods of creating tools that aid in navigating the landscape of emotional health and expression within the context of trauma. She is also the Outreach Coordinator at A Window Between Words and enjoys connecting with everyone she meets.

title: Transforming Grief
objective: This workshop aims to assist participants in their healing journey by providing them an opportunity to process and share their stories of grief and love.
materials:
• Round embroidery hoop

  • Hole Puncher

  • Yarn (26 inches)

  • Cardstock paper

  • Colored pencils

  • Markers

  • Pencils 

  • Scissors

  • Paper - for journaling
setup:
Possible Setup
         

We invite you to prepare all the art supplies in advance so participants can view their options. You’re encouraged to prepare a sample creation in advance to illustrate to participants as you explain the process. You are also welcome to play some calming music during the warm-up and creation portion of this workshop.
warm_up:
Guided Meditation (5 minutes):

“I would like to invite you all to a guided meditation. During this time, I will invite you to take a few deep breaths; however, I encourage you to do whatever works best for your body. If counting, thinking about your breath or simply just being present is helpful, I encourage you to please do that. Alright, are you ready to begin? I invite you to relax in your chair, lay on the floor, or wherever it feels most comfortable for you. Close your eyes if you feel safe or you can simply lower your gaze. I invite you to take a deep breath in through your nose, exhale through your mouth.”  (Repeat 2x). 

“Now I welcome you to bring to mind your loved ones or an event that changed your life. Take a moment to connect with your body, with your feelings, with your thoughts about your loved ones or events. (Pause for a moment) Consider what you miss, what changed for you or what you want to take with you. (Pause for a moment).”

“What do you want to carry in your heart? Might it be humor, intelligence, or balance. I welcome you to take a couple more breaths in your nose and out your mouth. Then when you feel ready, you can slowly open your eyes.”

 

Journaling (10 minutes): 

“To help us get started and to think about our grief and the strengths we hold through this process, I invite you to a 10 minute journaling session. I will have some questions that you can answer or just simply think about. During this time, I invite you to not focus on your spelling, grammar or have any judgment for what comes up for you. Just let it all out onto the page. I will be giving us a time reminder when we have 1 minute left of journaling. Are there any questions or thoughts before we begin?” 

Pause for any questions and if there are none you can begin saying the journaling prompts or you can also write them down somewhere for the participants to see.  

  1. What does your grief look and feel like? Where does it live in your body? 

  2. How is this grief affecting your relationships or your thought processes? 

  3. What did you appreciate about the person you love? What parts of this person do you want to carry forward? 

  4. What do you want to carry in your heart about the person you love? What parts of yourself do you want to revive? 

“Thank you all for participating in whatever way felt best for you. Now I welcome you to create the way in which you transform your grief.”
creation:
“Using the materials provided, you are invited to draw, write, or create symbols that represent the love you have for the person and/or the parts of yourself that you want to bring forward. We will take about 45 minutes to create and I’ll be providing time reminders when we are halfway through and then again when we have a few minutes left. Afterwards, you will have the opportunity to share your creation with others in the group. Are there any questions before we begin?”

During this time, you're welcome to play some calming music and provide time reminders along the way.
closing:
Paired Sharing (5 minutes):

“Before we close out, I would like to invite you all to a paired share before we share with the larger group. If you wish, I welcome you to turn to whomever is sitting next or close to you and share your creation, what you discovered about your journey, or anything else that came up for you during your Window of Time. You each will have about 2 minutes or more to share, before we come back for the larger group share.”

 

Larger Group Share (10 minutes):

“Alright, I would like to take time to open the ocean to anyone who would like to share with the larger group their creation, what you discovered about your journey, or anything else that came up in your paired sharing.” Allow some time for participants to share if they like. 

“Thank you all for sharing and participating in whatever way felt right for you! As you continue on your healing journey remember to honor where you are at, in this moment and the strength it takes to be here. Now that we had a chance to connect, each person in this room is on the path to transforming their grief. Remember healing takes time and you are right where you need to be.”

 

     
Front of final creation       Back of final creation
notes:
Tip during sharing: 

In the event that someone is sharing their grief, invite participants to listen and offer positive support, such as, “I appreciate that you must have great love for that person,” or “Thank you for honoring us to share your grief,” or “I hear you.” We do not need to fix grief, we need only witness it. Do not ask questions about how the person died or anything about the trauma event. The focus is to allow space for the expressions of their grief.
tips:
Durational Art Tip: 

Grief and loss is a part of life, and this is a journey that doesn’t end here. As you continue on your path, I encourage you to create art or anything else to process other losses in your life. Remember healing is fluid and not linear and there is a lot of strength in where you are at!

introduction: “During this time, I would like to invite you to participate in this transformative session. You will have the opportunity to identify your unique grief experience and healing journey through art expression. This space is a Window of time for you, to process and focus on yourself or whatever feels best for you. Everyone’s healing journey is unique and I hope this moment, your creation, and experience can be something you can tap into or create for yourself at any time throughout your healing journey.”
demonstration:
“Before we get started I would like to share with you the workshop materials and steps. At your table, you will find a round embroidery hoop, hole puncher, yarn, cardstock paper, colored pencils, markers, scissors, pencils and some journaling paper.” 

Step 1: First, I invite you to grab a writing utensil and trace two circles with the embroidery hoop onto the cardstock paper. 

Step 2: On one circle, you’re welcome to draw, color, and write what your grief looks like, how it travels through your heart, and how it has changed throughout your journey. 

Step 3: Using colors, words, symbols and more you can fill the second circle with all your strengths and what you are carrying forward from this journey. This can include symbols that represent the love you have for the person and/or parts of yourself,  words of wisdom, things you have learned from your grief and much more. 

Step 4: Once you have finished creating, you are welcome to cut out the two circles and punch 6 holes around the circles. It may be helpful to do it simultaneously with the two circles placed on top of each other.  

Step 5: Finally, you can choose a yarn color that you like and start looping it through the holes on the circle and the embroidery hoop. Continue until you have looped it all around and tie both ends together.

opening_circle:
“Grief is an individual journey and transforming grief can be an ongoing process. Whether you are at the start of the healing process or continuing your journey, this  workshop can help you connect and honor the grief and loss, while also acknowledging the strength and love you hold. Grief can occur from a variety of losses. Some of those losses can include someone close to us, a trauma event that changes our lives, or from historical events. There are some important things to know about grief. People experiencing grief are not broken and do not need to be fixed. They need to be heard and witnessed.” 

“Connection to grief is a mind, body, and spirit approach. Some types of grief include, death of a loved one. Some are disenfranchised in our society, such as miscarriage or death of a pet. Others include trauma. All trauma includes grief but not all grief includes trauma. There are secondary losses that involve additional losses, such as when a partner dies, other couples may no longer invite you to events or activities. There is also complicated grief or mixed emotions in grief. This can happen when an abusive parent or partner dies. The grief can be about the love that is lost but mixed with the abuse that happened in the relationship. Throughout our time together, you will have the opportunity to process and share your stories of grief and love. However, know that no matter where you are along this journey, remember that transforming grief takes time, patience, and kindness.”

title: Joy Menu
objective: The aim of this workshop is to help participants explore and celebrate the things that bring them joy.
materials:
• Joy Menu worksheet

  • Scratch paper - journaling

  • Markers

  • Colored pencils

 

   
Joy Menu Workshop Worksheet
setup:
Possible Workshop Setup
       

We invite you to have all the materials set up prior to participants arriving. Doing so can help participants realize what is available to them. At different points in the workshop, you are welcome to play some calming music; we encourage instrumental music without any lyrics. For recommendations check out our AWBW spotify playlist.
warm_up:
Journaling:

“For our warm-up, I invite you to journal about a time in your life that you felt joyful. It can be a memory of you laughing so hard it made you cry, an activity or experience that took your breath away, or anything that felt absolutely magical. We will take about 10 minutes to journal and I’ll provide a reminder when we have 1 minute left.  Are there any questions before we begin?”

Allow some time for participants to ask questions and if they don’t you can start a timer and play some calming music.
creation:
“Once you feel ready to begin creating your joy menus, you’re welcome to do so. We’ll have about 30 minutes to create and I’ll provide a time reminder when we are halfway through our time and then again when we have five minutes left.”

During the creation portion of the workshop, you are welcome to continue playing some music and provide support when needed. Remind participants when they are halfway through the allotted time and then again when they have 5 minutes left. Doing so can help transition participants from the creation process to closing. You are also welcome to offer participants to continue their creation as you move into the closing of the workshop.
closing:
Completed Joy Menu
       

“As our time together comes to an end, I would like to take this opportunity to invite anyone who would like to share what they created, what the process of tapping into your joy felt like, or anything else you would like.” 

Other questions to consider to increase engagement include: 

  • What is one joy you described on your plate? 

  • What about this person, place, or activity brings you joy?

  • How might you make more time for the people, places, and activities that bring you fulfillment?
tips:
Durational Art Tip:

Learning to tap into your joy can be a great way to ground ourselves and navigate life's challenges. As you continue on your journey, consider how you can continue to incorporate these sources of joy into your daily life.

introduction:
“Welcome to today’s workshop called Joy Menu. Before we get started, I would like to invite us to take three grounding breaths together to settle us in. If deep breathing doesn’t work for you, please feel free to count, notice your breath or just do whatever works best for your body.” 

“The first breath I invite you to take will be to join us together as a group.  You can take a deep breath in, in from your nose and out from your mouth. Perfect. The next breath will be to ground us in the present moment. Again, take a deep breath in and then out. Great. Our last breath will be to inhale joy and exhale any unwanted feelings or thoughts that do not serve us.”  

“Thank you for joining me in those grounding breaths. During our time together, I want to preface that this is a Window of Time for you. You get to decide how you will participate today. I will go into providing a few creation steps for our joy menus. However,  while suggestions are provided to spark your creativity, remember that the best menus are the ones you personalize. Take or leave anything as needed - because you are the head chef!”
demonstration:
“Around you, you should see the workshop worksheet, markers, and some colored pencils.”

  1. Design your menu: Using the menu, you can jot down your ideas of what brings you joy. It can serve as a canvas for elaborating on details or even as a journaling space, assisting you in creating your unique menu.

  2. Fill your plate: Use your menu to inspire the words, colors, and shapes and fill your plate with joy.

  3. Reflect: Take a moment to pause to reflect on your creation. Ponder the items you've selected and the emotions they evoke.

opening_circle: “Joy has the ability to reduce stress and uplift our spirits. It can also play an important role in our healing and well-being. Today, you're invited to embark on a journey of self-discovery by crafting a menu that celebrates the things that bring you joy. A menu that can serve as a reminder of the goodness in your life, ready to be revisited whenever you need a lift.”

warm_up:
Three Breaths Warm-up:

Click here for the warm up script and video of the Three Breaths in action with AWBW Founder Cathy Salser

"As we come together right now, I invite us to begin by creating a “window between worlds” with our breath. To prepare for this, I’ll invite you to get comfortable in your seat and make any adjustments you need."

"As we move into this activity I want to acknowledge that breath work has played an important role in many faith and healing traditions and cultures and we honor and offer gratitude to those who created and carried breath work practices forward."
 

"I acknowledge that deep breathing may not work for you and/or your body. I invite you to count slowly, notice the natural cadence of your breath, or anything else that helps you ground in this moment." There are people with respiratory issues, asthma, etc. who may not find it relaxing when the breathing aggravates the symptoms....so offer an alternative there, like counting, imagery, etc.

  • Welcome to get present in their bodies, perhaps motion

  • Tapping 

"My instructions will be focused on breathing, but please know I honor and validate any and all ways you choose to ground yourself in this moment. I’ll be inviting us to take 3 breaths together: one for the past, one for the present, and one for the future."
 

"I’ll say a couple of words before each breath and guide us through each breath inviting you to just lengthen your inhales and exhales in and out and feeling and listening to the air entering and leaving your lungs." 

  • "So first, let’s invite a breath for the past. We can notice anything in our bodies that we want to let go of. It could be the past from 10 minutes ago. Is there anything you would like to release at this moment in your journey? I invite us to take a breath together to release it. Breathing in…." (breathe in deeply and hold for a moment) "... And Letting go" (breathe out).

  • "And now I invite us to take a breath for the present. Maybe notice your feet touching the floor right now, touching down into the earth. And notice we are together, all touching this same earth. Simply being present — together — is a powerful thing. So for the power of this present moment, I invite us to take a breath together.  Breathing in…" (breathe in deeply and hold for a moment). "And Letting go" (breathe out).

  • "And now I invite us to take one more breath together - this one for the future. I welcome you to notice any wishes you have, that you would like to move toward at this moment in your journey. How would you like your body to feel? Or maybe a word of wishes comes to mind? Notice whatever comes to you, or maybe just blank space. It’s fine not to know. With this breath I welcome us to just breathe in space for the future we are creating. So one more breath together. Breathing in…" (breathe in and hold for a moment) "... And Letting go" (breathe out). "Thank you!"

 

"With these deep breaths, notice that you’ve just created your own window between worlds. This is a resource you can return to any time along your path. At any moment when you’re stuck in a hard spot, you can practice your three breaths – seeing if you can let go of even a little bit of tension… get a little bit grounded in the present… and gain even a little bit of clarity for the future." 

 

"As you notice your “From” and your “Toward”, I invite you to imagine any shapes or colors that come to mind as touchstones for your journey. We will have 20 minutes of creation time to explore the art supplies, and create your Journey Touchstones. You can keep your eyes closed as long as you like, noticing whatever shapes and colors come to mind, and whenever you’re ready you can open your eyes and begin to let it out with wherever art supplies you wish." 

 

Journaling Warm-up: (alternative)

"Before we create with the art supplies, I welcome us to just take a window of time to listen to our hearts and notice anything we are wishing to move from or toward at this moment of our journeys. I welcome us to do “free-flow-writing” where we honor first thoughts with no judgment and just keep writing the whole time. We will start with 2 minutes of “free-flow” sharing anything that comes to mind for what you are wishing to move “from” in your journey right now."

"And now I invite you to transition to taking 2 minutes of “free-flow” to express whatever you are wishing to move toward. Notice whatever comes to mind with no judgment."

"As we close this 2 minutes, I invite you to take a moment to read what you’ve written and circle anything that seems important to you, that you would like to bring into your creative Touchstone Journey. When you are ready, I welcome you to dive in and create your Touchstones — a resource for your path."
creation:
As you begin the creation time, it can be helpful to let folks know how much time they will have for creating, and provide relaxing music if you wish. When there is about 5 minutes of Creation time remaining, it can be helpful to give a gentle heads up:

“We have about 5 more minutes left of creation time, and then we’ll be holding some space for sharing. If you’re already finished making your Touchstones, I welcome you to journal about what you have created, what it means to you, and any wishes about how you want to use it to support your journey.”
closing:
"As we bring our creative time to a close, I welcome you to reflect on any Touchstones you have created and the intentions and wishes they hold. Sometimes sharing aloud in a circle of support can be a way to water the seeds of change we are planting. Our voices and our listening to one another is part of the art supplies we can use to create healing and strength."

 

Sharing Options:

(As facilitator, feel free to mix and match any/all of these options to suit the needs of your group)

"As we return to the larger group, I invite you to supercharge your touchstone with the support of the group. I’ll offer some options and you can participate in whatever ways you like."  

  1.  
      Pendant Creation 
       
     
      Love Pendant

    Paired Sharing: "I welcome you to turn to the person next to you (or if in Zoom, use break-out rooms). We will take 5 minutes to each share with one another. I’ll let you know when we’re halfway through the time, so you can make sure you both get to share."

  2. Group “Exhibit”: "As we come back to the larger group, I invite us all to have a mini-exhibit by just holding up what we each created and looking around. (pause and welcome folks to all hold up their creations and look around the circle, taking it all in). As we look around I invite us to notice we are a circle of support for one another."

  3. Giving Voice: "Now I welcome you to notice if there’s something you want to voice, to support your journey. If you could put your Touchstone intention into just a few words, what would they be?" (Invite those who wish to share or if the group is small enough you might be able to have a circle of sharing)

  4. Collective Breath: "Finally, I invite us to give strength to the journey forward with a few collective breaths. If breathing deep isn’t comfortable for your body, I invite you to enjoy whatever motions and/or type of breath works for you."  

  • "First, I invite a breath of appreciation for everything that has been expressed and created here today.  Breathing in… and letting it go…" 

  • "And second, I invite a breath for what YOU have created here, holding it in your mind and heart for the journey forward.  Breathing in…. And letting go…"  

  • "And finally, for our third collective breath, I invite you to imagine carrying the support of this group forward, as you live into your Touchstone Journey. With a deep breath in… And letting go…"

title: Intention Journey Wheel
objective: This workshop gives participants the opportunity to identify an intention that they would like to set and to create a piece of art that will help them explore that intention over time.
materials:
• Thick paper (i.e. cardstock or other heavy weight paper) 

  • Scratch paper (to journal, draw, etc.)

  • Colored pencils

  • Ultra Fine Tip Sharpies/markers

  • Pens

  • Pencils
setup: If you choose, you may place one set of materials (a piece of thick paper, a piece of scratch paper, and a variety of drawing/writing materials) at each participant’s station.
warm_up:
Guided Somatic Exploration 

     
       
       

"To help us warm-up before the creation time I invite you to participate in a guided somatic exploration - that is, an exploration of the sensations within your body. If you prefer a different warm-up activity you could instead take slow calming breaths, meditate on a word or thought, journal, stretch, or simply observe."

[The following activity should be done calmly and slowly, giving lots of time for participants to explore.]

"For those who would like to participate, I invite you to ground yourself by noticing that you are here in this time and place. You might begin by noticing your surroundings (pause). I invite you to take a look around the room (pause), find the walls, the corners, and the boundaries of the room (pause), and notice what is around you (pause). Notice what your eyes are drawn to (pause)." 

"Now, I invite you to notice the chair you are sitting in (pause). Notice where it comes into contact with your body (pause). Notice how it holds and supports you (pause). Allow the weight of your body to be fully supported by the chair (pause)." 

"I invite you to notice your feet (pause). Notice how they come into contact with the ground (pause). Notice how the ground supports your feet (pause). Allow the ground to hold the whole weight of your feet (pause)."

"Now I invite you to take a moment to arrive here in the present and be fully in your body (pause). So often, we feel rushed to go from one task to the next (pause). It can be difficult to be fully “here” (pause). So, I welcome you to take the next few moments to bring your presence into the here and now (long pause)." 

"Try to notice your body without any judgment (pause). You may discover sensations that are pleasant, unpleasant, or neutral (pause). Allow yourself to notice without trying to change anything (pause), just being present with whatever you discover (long pause)."

"As you continue to  scan your body - take a moment to seek out any sensations that are pleasant (long pause). Look for any sensation at all that feels even the slightest bit enjoyable or comforting (pause). Perhaps you notice a solid and secure comforting spot where your feet meet the ground, or an expansive openness as your breathing naturally slows and deepens to its own rhythm, or an effervescent and radiating warmth inside your chest, or perhaps noticing your earlobes brings a smile to your face and fills you with a sense of lightness (long pause). If you are struggling to find a pleasant sensation within, you can bring to mind a favorite person, place, pet or memory that you associate with feelings of love or joy (pause). Once you find a pleasant sensation, take your time soaking it in & exploring its qualities (pause). Notice if it has a shape and size (pause). Does it have a center? Where are its edges? (pause). If it could be a color, what color might it be (long pause). Notice if it moves (pause). If so, how does it move (pause)? Is it pulsing, radiating, flowing (pause)? And does it have a direction (pause)? Continue to enjoy it and soak it in (long pause).

"Now that you are grounded and present in your body, take a moment to reflect on the following prompts and notice what comes up in your body or in your mind."

  • What am I experiencing in life right now? (long pause)

  • Considering what I’m experiencing, what do I want or need? (long pause)

  • What do I hope to move toward over time (long pause)? 

  • What intention might help me on my journey (long pause)?

"In a moment I will be opening up the space for creation time. As we wrap up this warm-up, you are welcome to take as long as you need to either stay with your body sensations and reflections or transition into creating. Whenever you are ready you can choose to journal, draw, or move into creating your Intention Journey Wheel."
creation:
"I’ve set aside X minutes for creation to participate or observe in whatever way will best serve you."

[Set a countdown timer participants can see or provide reminders regarding how much time is left as you near the end of the creation portion. You may also choose to play some relaxing music.]
closing:
"Now there is an opportunity to share in small groups. During this time you have the opportunity to share in whatever way you choose. For example, you can share about your intention, your artwork, what the experience was like, or just be witnessed." 

 

Closing Tips and Suggestions:

  •      
           

    If desired/helpful, remind participants of the Community Guidelines “Create Space for Everyone: Share the Air / Move Up and Move Back” as well as “Focus on Yourself: Use “I” statements Practice boundaries and consent]

  • Manage creation of groups - i.e. creating breakout rooms or letting people know how many people to the group. 

  • Notify participants of how much time they will have for sharing and approximately how many minutes per person. Provide time reminders or cues as needed.

  • Optional for large groups: Let people know before going into small groups that there will be an opportunity for sharing in the larger group. When small groups return, facilitate sharing within the larger group. Manage time and notify participants ahead of time when there is time for 1 final share.

  • Share the Durational Art Tips

  • Or facilitator to choose their own closing ritual: "To close out our time together I’ll invite you in a moment to take three breaths as a group. Or if three breaths doesn’t work for you you could join in a silent intention setting or whatever works best for you. The first breath honors the ancestors - that could include ancestors of the land, your personal ancestors, and even the ancestors who were part of the field of work that you are in or the social movements you are part of. The second breath honors this special group that has come together today, celebrating this unique time and the witnessing that has been given and received. The third breath honors yourself - acknowledging what you are moving from and towards." [Lead three breaths]

  • Take care of any closing logistics (e.g. group photo, evaluations, next workshop date, etc.)

 

"Thank you for coming!"
tips:
Durational Art Tips: 

     
       
       

"The art you are creating today, can then be used after this workshop and into the future for your ongoing exploration of your intention. So for example, you can journal or draw, using up one space between the spokes for each journal entry. You might choose to journal about how you are feeling in the present, how you are connecting to that intention, or just to honor what your experience is."

"You can also decide whether to explore this journey on your own, or pair up with one or more other participants. If you choose a practice partner you can decide how frequently to reach out and share how your journey is going. introduction:
"Thank you for being here today. During this workshop you will have the opportunity to identify an intention that you would like to set for yourself and to create a piece of art that will help you explore that intention over time."

"Let me begin by sharing an overview of what you can expect in this workshop. First, I’ll anchor us by setting an intention for our time together called the “Window of Time”. Then, I’ll do a brief demonstration so you can get a sense of the materials provided and begin to imagine how you might use them. Afterwards, we’ll have an opportunity to explore the practice of Intentions in more depth. Next, I’ll offer a somatic warm-up activity followed by the opportunity to create your piece of art. Finally, at the end we’ll have opportunities to share and connect with others before we close out. What questions do you have before we get started?"

"To open our time together, I welcome you to close your eyes or soften your gaze as I invoke what we call the “Window of Time”. (Allow participants a moment to close their eyes). This is your Window of Time. That means, it's a time for you to notice your thoughts, needs and feelings. During this time, there is no right or wrong way to participate or create. I'm going to share some instructions, but you get to choose how you want to participate. You can follow along completely, or you may want to do something different, it's completely up to you. During your Window of time, you get to choose. I am here to support you in any way that I can, so please ask for what you need (pause). Whenever you are ready, you can open your eyes."
demonstration:
"Let’s review the activity as well as the materials available for your use. These are all suggestions and you could do something completely different if you like. These are the materials available for your use today" (share what materials are available). 

Step 1: "Identify an intention or a belief that you would like to explore over time. Before we begin creating, you’ll have the opportunity to use the guided somatic exploration from the warm-up to help you determine your belief, intention or goal or  you can just pick one." (Demonstrate by providing 2-3 examples such as “I’m enough” or “Connecting with Loved Ones”.)

Step 2: "Choose an image that goes with that intention and draw it in the center of the page. Some examples are: a butterfly, heart, handprint, or something else entirely. You could also just choose a shape like a circle." (Demonstrate drawing an image as the example in the center of the page). [Note: If using the worksheet, this step may need to be modified or deleted to reflect that one of the worksheet options already contains a circle in the middle.]

Step 3: "Explore this intention by journaling or drawing. Use whatever colors, words, shapes, or symbols represent this intention." (Demonstrate adding images, words, colors or shapes to the central image). 

Step 4: "Create spaces for your ongoing journey around the central image." (Demonstrate adding spokes coming out from the central image and how they could be straight, wavy, or something else). [Note: If using the worksheet, this step may need to be modified to reflect that one of the worksheets already contains spokes].

"The blank area between each set of spokes serves as space to journal or draw about that intention in the future. You’re invited to journal daily or whenever you feel moved, inspired, or troubled."

"The number of spokes and space between them depends on how you want to use your artwork as well as how much space you want for each exploration. So for example, if you want to revisit this intention daily for a month, you could draw enough spokes to make 30 spaces for journaling on a daily basis." 

"Some participants like to add a special space to journal or draw at the beginning and end of their series. This serves as a way to honor where they started and where they end up. If you choose to do this you could journal or draw your starting entry today as well." 

Step 5: "If you have extra time you might choose to decorate your intention journey wheel, journal freely, meditate, or spend time noticing and soaking up the sensations in your body when you embrace your intention fully." 

 

Examples and Variations:

  • "Here are some examples of what some finished journey wheels look like." [If available - show some examples of what finished journals might look like, including  variations mentioned below.]

  • You can date the entries or not. 

  • Some participants create small swirls as a meditative moment - with each circle indicating a calming breath

 

"Throughout the creation time I want to encourage you not to judge yourself or your artwork. Remember, there is no wrong or right way to create and each breath, insight, and moment of the journey IS the art. What questions do you have about the materials or the art activity?"

opening_circle:
"Now that we know the basics of the art activity, let’s discuss the value and purpose of setting intentions. As we move through life there are times when we feel the need or desire to make a change -  whether it’s achieving a goal, shifting a perspective, or calling in a different state of being. There can be a discrepancy between where we are right now and where we want to be."

"This is where setting an intention can be helpful. An intention, simply put, is the act of deciding in your mind upon some action or result. Since all action - whether internal or external - starts with a thought in our head, setting an intention can be a key step in moving towards that change."  

"In order to set intentions effectively it can be helpful to start by grounding in the present, acknowledging and honoring where you are coming “from”. Then, you can reflect and set your intention on what you want to move “toward.” Setting an intention is almost like training an arrow on a bullseye - it helps to direct our mind and body towards what we are intending and move things in that direction."

"I invite you to take a moment now to identify something you would like to move “from” and something you would like to move  “toward”. Some examples include: from scarcity toward abundance, or from self-judgment toward self-acceptance."   

[Invite folx to share with the group verbally or in chat (if online). It’s okay if not everyone shares. And, if no one wants to share, you can give some additional examples. Examples: from fear toward peace, from others first toward self-care first]

[Alternate embodied activity: Invite participants to show their “from” and “toward” nonverbally by making still images - like statues - with their bodies. To help put nerves at ease let them know this is just a fun activity to express themselves in a different way. It also can help if the facilitator demonstrates with their own example first.]

"One of the challenges with setting an intention, is that it can be hard to sustain this focus over time. Life can get busy and we can feel pulled in many directions. The art activity in this workshop is designed to help with that very challenge. It acts as an anchor, providing an opportunity to come back to your intention over and over again through periodic journaling or art-making. Revisiting your intention regularly can help keep it at the forefront of your mind even when life pulls you in other directions."

title: Wellness in the Workplace Toolkit

extra_field:
Wellness in the Workplace: Addressing Secondary Traumatic Stress & Burnout Through Art

 
   
   
   
   

Crafted by six esteemed Windows Facilitators and consultants, each an expert in their respective fields of practice, this toolkit offers innovative approaches to address the challenges of stress and burnout in professional settings. Drawing from a comprehensive range of holistic approaches, including trauma-informed care and wellness practices, this toolkit empowers individuals and organizations to foster well-being and resilience by inviting a creative journey of exploration, skill-building, empowerment, and sustained personal and professional growth.

We culminated our work with our first-ever Wellness in the Workplace Virtual Conference. This is just the beginning, and we are committed to continuing the conversation and supporting the well-being of professionals everywhere.

Wellness in the Workplace Virtual Conference

On Friday, October 4, 2024, AWBW hosted a virtual conference focused on addressing workplace stress and burnout, a major contributor to employee dissatisfaction and turnover.

The conference brought together direct service providers, nonprofit leadership and executives, HR professionals, and others to explore innovative strategies for fostering resilience and navigating workplace challenges.

Attendees had the opportunity to:

  • Learn about the root causes of workplace stress and burnout.

  • Discover creative approaches to manage stress and enhance well-being.

  • Participate in collaborative discussions to develop practical strategies for individual and organizational change.

By attending this conference, participants gained valuable insights and tools to create healthier, more productive, and supportive work environments.

Wellness in the Workplace Toolkit

The workshops in the toolkit were created to encourage introspection, providing insight, and sparking new ideas. Through this process, we might find ourselves inspired to establish boundaries, identify resources, and act on our insights in ways that help us truly thrive.

Every workshop in the toolkit follows the AWBW Arc of Healing, which was intentional to set the foundation of trust and safety. Each workshop thereafter continues to build on this foundation to include grounding, expression, awareness, empowerment, and integration. Each workshop includes an overview of the art workshop, suggestions for creation, grounding exercises, a creation worksheet, and an opportunity to journal. The Wellness in the Workplace Toolkit can be your next resource for building lasting wellness practices.
 

Theme 1: Arriving — Connecting to Your Surroundings & Grounding
Workshop: Rooted in Purpose by Elizabeth Eastlund, MSW

In today’s fast-paced work environment, constant changes from one day to the next have become the norm. It is essential, amidst this whirlwind, to ground ourselves and prioritize our mental, emotional, and physical well-being. By dedicating time to being present and fully aware of our surroundings, we can alleviate feelings of anxiety and stress while fostering a stronger sense of belonging, connection, and focus. Engaging meaningfully with our environment equips us to navigate life’s ups and downs with clarity and resilience. Incorporating grounding techniques into our daily routine can profoundly impact our lives for the better.

It can be beneficial to identify our current position and embrace it with openness. This approach enables us to set meaningful goals and take proactive steps towards positive change.

It enables us to regulate our emotions more efficiently, reducing stress and anxiety, and cultivating a greater sense of inner peace. However, achieving this state of mind may require us to step outside of our comfort zones and tap into our inner strength and bravery to obtain what we need. Creating a more nurturing environment for ourselves allows us to live in alignment with our values and deepen our self-understanding. However, it can be easy to get caught up in the hustle and bustle of work and neglect both our physical and emotional needs. To avoid burnout, it’s important to prioritize self-care. This means taking breaks throughout the day, practicing mindfulness techniques like meditation or deep breathing, and setting boundaries within our schedules. It’s important to remember that taking care of yourself isn’t selfish; it’s a necessary process that supports you, your family, coworkers, and anyone else you interact with daily.
