title: Getting Back in the Zone
objective: This workshop aims to support participants in mapping their personal "Resiliency Zone"—a state of emotional and physiological well-being—and identify/represent self-regulation tools to facilitate their return to this balanced state when experiencing dysregulation.
materials:
Getting back in the Zone Worksheet

  • Getting Back in the Zone Worksheet

  • Blank paper for journaling

  • Writing utensil

  • Colored pencils

  • Markers
setup:
Possible Setup

To foster a welcoming environment, prepare the art supplies ahead of time for each participant, ensuring everything is easily visible and accessible upon their arrival. For in-person workshops where you are using the worksheet, be sure to print out copies for your participants. If you're meeting virtually, send a digital copy to your participants beforehand, giving them plenty of time to print.

To effectively guide participants' creativity, take some time before the workshop to create a simple sample for the demonstration. This tangible example will help participants understand and imagine their own versions. Additionally, writing the creation steps on a whiteboard or chart paper will serve as a clear and supportive reference, allowing participants to work at their own pace throughout the workshop. Consider also providing self-regulation tools to help participants ground themselves, such as pipe cleaners, bubbles, stress balls, mandalas for coloring, and other similar options.
warm_up:
Journaling:
"To support us in reconnecting with our resiliency, I’d like to invite you to a journaling warm-up. If it feels right for you, you can reflect on a moment when you navigated a difficult experience. As you think about that time, you might find it helpful to respond to these questions to guide your writing:

  • What emotions or physical sensations did you notice during the challenge? (e.g., frustration, sadness, tension in your body)

  • What helped you navigate through that moment? (e.g., reaching out to others, focusing on your breath, self-regulation tools)

  • What did you learn from that experience about your strengths, boundaries, or what supports you in moving forward?"

You’re welcome to play some calming music during this time and provide assistance when needed. Once participants finish writing, you’re welcome to invite them to a group discussion.   

Group Discussion: 
“Before we move into the creation portion, I’d like to invite anyone who feels comfortable to share what came up for them during the journaling session. You’re welcome to share as much or as little as feels right for you."  

Allow participants to share if they like and if nobody is jumping in to start, you’re welcome to share what you wrote to model what the discussion can look like. 

Once everyone who would like to share has, you are welcome to transition into the creation.

"Now that you've spent some time exploring what shifts you out of your Resiliency Zone and what helps you find your way back, let your eyes gently wander over your journal page. If taking a deep breath isn't accessible or comfortable for you right now, that's perfectly alright. Simply allow yourself a moment to pause and notice what's on your page. For those who would like to, take a slow, deep breath in, and as you exhale, allow that breath to softly guide you into the space of creation."
creation: During this time, you’re welcome to play calming music and offer support as needed. Remind participants about the creation steps and let them know how much time they will have to create. Gentle time reminders (e.g., halfway, 5 minutes left) can also help participants pace themselves and avoid feeling rushed toward the end.
closing:
Completed Creation
     

"As we come to the end of our time together, I want to take a moment to acknowledge the resilience you’ve all demonstrated throughout your creative journey. As you reflect on our time together, I invite you to consider these questions:

  1. What's one key takeaway from our shared experience that you can carry with you as a reminder of your resilience?

  2. How did the process of creating your resiliency zone affect your ability to feel grounded or calm today?

  3. How might you incorporate self-regulation tools into your daily life to support staying in your resiliency zone?"

Once everyone who wants to share has had the opportunity, thank the group for their presence and connection. Remind them that their visual representation of their resilience zone can serve as a practical tool. When they notice themselves feeling off-balance, this visual can help them remember what brings them back to that centered and resilient space.
tips:
Durational Art Tip:

Consider letting your visual representation of your Resilient Zone become a living anchor in the weeks and months ahead. Throughout your day, cultivate mindful awareness of your internal state, noticing and naming when you feel "bumped out." When this occurs, consciously engage with your visual anchor – whether by looking at it, recalling it, or touching a symbolic object. Use the tools learned in our workshop to actively guide yourself back towards your Resilient Zone through breath, movement, or sensory engagement.

As you consistently practice returning to regulation, observe the subtle shifts in your interactions, noticing any increased calm or connection, and recognize the profound impact of your regulated presence on those around you, fostering moments of co-regulation. This ongoing exploration is an invitation to deepen your awareness, build resilience, and embody the powerful connection between your nervous system health and your ability to positively influence your environment.

introduction:
“As we continue, I want to emphasize that this is A Window of Time for you. That means that you get to decide how to participate and create. I invite you to take a moment to tune into how you're feeling in your body, mind, and soul. Your comfort matters, so feel free to make any adjustments that help you feel more at ease and present.” 

If you’d like, now is also a good time to share an agenda or anything that might help everyone feel safe/brave and grounded. For example, reviewing community agreements can help create a sense of safety/bravery and trust.
demonstration:
"However you've chosen to create today, whether with the worksheet, a piece of paper, or other supplies, I'd like to offer a few optional creation steps. Consider keeping a pen or pencil handy to capture any thoughts or ideas that come to mind during the process. Remember, these are just suggestions. You have complete freedom in how you create."

 

Step 1: Outside the Zone
"In the areas outside of the Resiliency Zone (represented by the straight lines above and below the center), you're invited to use colors, shapes, and symbols to capture the unique thoughts, feelings, and physical sensations you experience when you're out of your zone. This could include thoughts like self-criticism or worry, feelings of anger, sadness, or fear, or physical sensations like a knot in your stomach, shallow breathing, or feeling restless."

          

 

 

 

 

Step 2: Getting Back in the Zone
Explore what personally helps you self-regulate and find your way back into your zone. Within the Resiliency Zone (the space between the two lines), use shapes, words, or symbols to depict the actions, tools, or practices that bring you back to balance. If you're still discovering what helps you return to your zone, take this time to consider possibilities. What activities, sensations, or practices might offer you a sense of calm or balance? Some examples include:

  • Moving your body, such as taking a walk

  • Pausing to focus on your breath

  • Sipping a comforting beverage

  • Engaging your senses by noticing something beautiful or meaningful around you

 

        

 

 

 

 

Step 3: Carrying it Forward
Consider how you can gently use this experience and your creation to become more aware of when you might be moving outside your Resiliency Zone. Notice any early signals, without judgment. Reflect on the strategies you've identified that can help you return to your zone. It's understandable that it can be challenging to remember self-regulation skills when feeling dysregulated. Regularly practicing these techniques, even in small ways, can help strengthen your body's and mind's ability to access them and support you in finding your footing when big feelings arise.
opening_circle:
In and out of the Resiliency Zone
   

Exploring Your Resiliency Zone
"Think of your Resiliency Zone like your personal "feel good" space for your mind and body. It's a state where you generally feel balanced, capable, and able to handle life's ups and downs without feeling completely overwhelmed or disconnected."

Understanding Your Resiliency Zone
"Your Resiliency Zone is a state of overall well-being where your mind feels clear and focused, your body feels grounded and at ease, and your spirit feels balanced and connected. It's when you feel most like yourself and have the capacity to navigate challenges."

Inside Your Zone:
"When you're in your Resiliency Zone, you generally feel capable and like your best self. You can experience both good and bad times without feeling completely overwhelmed by your emotions. You can handle stress without going to intense emotional highs or lows."

Outside Your Zone:
"When you experience strong or overwhelming emotions, you've likely moved outside your Resiliency Zone. Think of it like this:

  • The "High Zone": This is when you might feel overly activated, experiencing emotions like intense anger, irritability, or frustration.
  • The "Low Zone": This is when you might feel under-activated, experiencing emotions like sadness, disconnection, or exhaustion."


Returning to Your Zone:
"It's completely normal to get bumped out of your Resiliency Zone, especially during stressful times. The good news is there are ways to help yourself return. Research shows that using sensory tools can be really helpful for calming your nervous system and helping you feel more in control. Things like pipe cleaners, bubbles, stress balls, and coloring pages can offer a gentle way to ground yourself."

"Becoming aware of your own internal signals – what you feel in your body and your emotions – and practicing simple self-regulation techniques can help you find your way back to your Resiliency Zone. Over time, with practice, you might even find that your Resiliency Zone becomes a little wider."

title: Here & Now Grounding Exercise
objective: This warm-up aims to help participants reconnect with the present moment using this adaptable, sensory-based grounding exercise designed to reduce stress and support mindfulness.
materials: • Here & Now Handout
warm_up:
"Let’s begin by gently bringing awareness to our surroundings."

  1. First, I invite you to take a look around. Notice where you are in this very moment, in your current environment. What do you see? Take in the objects around you—what colors, shapes, or textures do you notice? Are you in a room, an office, or somewhere else? Just observe without judgment, simply acknowledging your surroundings.

  2. Next, shift your awareness to the temperature. Is it cool or warm where you are? Do you feel a breeze or still air? Notice if the air feels dry or humid against your skin. Simply observe how the temperature feels in your environment.

  3. Now, bring your attention to any scents or smells around you. Is there a fragrance in the air? Perhaps the scent of coffee, food, or a candle?Maybe you notice the smell of fresh air, or a fragrance someone is wearing. Allow yourself to tune into any aromas, no matter how subtle.

  4. Then, shift your awareness to sound. What do you hear? Maybe the hum of an air conditioner or heater, the sound of typing, or distant voices. Perhaps there are cars outside or other noises around you. Simply listen, taking in each sound as it comes to your awareness.

  5. Finally, bring your attention to what you can feel. Notice the points of contact between your body and the surfaces around you. Can you feel the chair beneath you? The desk or table your hands might be resting on? What about the fabric of your clothing against your skin or your feet making contact with the ground? Allow yourself to notice these sensations fully.

"Take a few moments to hold all of this awareness—the sights, the sounds, the smells, the temperature, the sensations—and just be present in your space. If taking a deep breath feels good for you, I invite you to do so."
closing: "As we move forward together, know that you can return to this grounded state at any time. Whenever you feel stuck or disconnected, take a moment to pause, bring your attention to something in your environment, engage your senses and bring yourself back to the Here & Now."
optional_materials: You're welcome to experience the Here & Now in action with AWBW staff Kat Mardo.
introduction: "As we come together right now, I invite us to take a moment to ground ourselves in the present. Take a moment to get comfortable in your space. Feel free to make any adjustments you need— whether that’s shifting in your seat, softening your posture, or just allowing yourself to settle in."

title: Foster Care Workshop Series
full_name: AWBW Staff & Foster Care Advisory Board
extra_field:
About AWBW in Foster Care

Young people in foster care, whether minors or young adults transitioning into independence (ages 18–26), often move through many placements, face constant uncertainty and carry the impact of separation, loss or instability at home and in school. These experiences can affect trust, relationships, and self-esteem, yet they also reveal incredible strength and creativity.

This workshop series is designed for facilitators and partners who want to support youth and families involved in foster care. It includes art-based activities that encourage self-expression, healing and connection. Through art, participants can explore feelings safely, build confidence, develop resilience and strengthen relationships with themselves and others. 

 

 

       
        2025 Foster Care Advisory Board
         

About the Workshop Series

Developed in collaboration with AWBW's Foster Care Advisory Board (pictured right), this series is intended to help you identify the best workshops from the AWBW library for supporting individuals and families impacted by foster care. The workshops below are organized by service population and emotional theme, but since all of the workshops can be modified for different ages and settings we encourage you to check them all out to see if they'd be a good fit for participants. If you are facilitating a series of workshops, we recommend choosing 1 or 2 workshops from each theme for a series of 4-6 total workshops.

 

Creating Safety: Workshops for Foster Youth

Most young people enter foster care after experiencing trauma, neglect, abuse or instability at home. Even if the home was unsafe, it’s still their home, and leaving it can feel like a profound loss. Once in care, youth face a new environment, new caregivers and sometimes new schools or communities. These constant changes can make it hard to trust others or feel secure. Young people might also feel caught between two worlds—missing their family while being told to adjust to a new one. Yet, with consistent care and understanding, youth can build strength, confidence and a sense of belonging. Art can pave the way to that healing by helping them express feelings that may be difficult to put into words and reconnect with their inner resilience. Through art, they can begin to see themselves as capable, grounded and worthy of care.

Accessing Strength: Workshops for Biological Parents

Biological parents of children placed in care often experience profound emotional turmoil. The separation can bring grief, guilt, shame and a deep sense of loss, even if the removal was meant to protect the child. Many parents feel powerless and judged, struggling with feelings of failure and fear that they may never reunite with their children. The process of navigating child welfare systems can be overwhelming and confusing, often compounding feelings of frustration and hopelessness. Yet alongside the pain, many parents also hold love, hope and determination—wanting to heal, regain stability and rebuild their relationship with their children. With the right support and compassion, parents can find pathways toward growth, accountability and eventual reunification. Art can support this process by providing tools to help parents regulate, process and cope.

Promoting Bonding: Workshops for Biological Parents and Their Children

Monitored visitations, while important for eventual reunification, can be extremely demanding for both biological parents and their children. The limited time can make it hard to build trust, have meaningful conversations or engage in spontaneous play, particularly when the visit takes place in an environment without the comfort and familiarity of home. During visits between parents and children or siblings in separate placements, art activities provide a structured, positive way for family members to connect, reduce stress and encourage meaningful communication in limited time.

Celebrating New Beginnings: Workshops for Resource and Kinship Families

Resource parents or kinship caregivers and the children in their care experience a unique and often intense emotional landscape. There can be joy, connection and love as bonds form, alongside stress, uncertainty and tension as everyone adjusts to new routines, behaviors and expectations. These families may also carry layers of grief, loss and fear. Children can feel voiceless, unsure if it’s safe to speak up or trust the adults around them. The constant changes and conflicting loyalties between families can leave their minds overloaded with stress and confusion. Caregivers, too, may struggle with the uncertainty of temporary placements and the emotional weight of transition. At the same time, families can experience growth, resilience and deepened empathy, learning to communicate, support one another and celebrate small victories together. As they navigate this terrain, art can be a helpful guide to creating their new community by encouraging connection among family members and helping them adjust to change. Each workshop offers space to strengthen trust, honor each person’s story and nurture a sense of belonging in their shared home.

Honoring Journeys: Workshops for Transition Age Youth and Former Foster Youth

Transition age youth (ages 18–26) and former foster youth face a unique set of challenges as they move toward independence. Many experience anxiety, uncertainty and fear about navigating adulthood without the consistent support systems other young people have. They may carry residual trauma from past instability and separation from family. Feelings of self-doubt and pressure to succeed can be intense, especially when juggling housing, education, work and relationships. In spite of these challenges, many youth develop resilience, resourcefulness and a strong sense of self-reliance, drawing on their experiences to advocate for themselves and pursue their goals. Art workshops that give young people the chance to honor where they have been and imagine where they want to go can have an immediate and lasting impact as they carry what they created with them as a tangible reminder of their journey they can lean into for support over time.

Prioritizing Wellness: Workshops for Foster Care Service Providers

Foster care service providers—social workers, therapists, case managers and others—often carry a heavy emotional load. They frequently experience stress, burnout and secondary trauma from witnessing children’s pain, family struggles and systemic challenges. Feelings of frustration, helplessness or guilt can arise when resources are limited, progress is slow or children face repeated instability. At the same time, providers can feel deep satisfaction, purpose and hope when they help children heal, support families or make positive changes in the system. Emotionally, their work requires resilience, empathy and self-care, balancing compassion for others with attention to their own wellbeing. More than just a helpful tool for staff's self-care, creative art workshops give organizations a way to foster greater community care and improved workplace wellness overall.
